In the Ethiopic church, a small building attached to a churchedifice, in which the bread for the eucharist is made. Audsley.
To reduce to thralldom; to inthrall. [Obs.] Spenser.
To handle; to wear or soil by handling; as books. Poe.
To beat or thump soundly. Shak.
To happen to; to befall; to come to ; as, woe betide thewanderer.What will betide the few Milton.
To furnish with a title or titles; to entitle. [Obs.] Carlyle.
The French name for concrete; hence, concrete made after theFrench fashion.
To attack with the tongue; to abuse; to insult.
A plant of the genus Betonica (Linn.).
To put in violent motion; to agitate; to disturb; to toss. "Mybetossed soul." Shak.
The act or the result of betraying.
One who, or that which, betrays.
To set in order; to adorn; to deck, to embellish; to trim.Shak.

The act of betrothing, or the fact of being betrothed; a mutualpromise, engagement, or contract for a future marriage between thepersons betrothed; betrothment; affiance. "The feast of betrothal."Longfellow.
The act of betrothing, or the state of being betrothed;betrothal.
The act of intrusting, or the thing intrusted. [Obs.] Chipman.
To become better; to improve. Carlyle.
An improvement of an estate which renders it better than mererepairing would do; -- generally used in the plural. [U. S.] Bouvier.
A small, leaping Australian marsupial of the genus Bettongia;the jerboa kangaroo.
One who bets; a better. Addison.
A short bar used by thieves to wrench doors open. [Written alsobettee.]The powerful betty, or the artful picklock. Arbuthnot.
A substance of a resinous nature, obtained from the outer barkof the common European birch (Betula alba), or from the tar preparedtherefrom; -- called also birch camphor. Watts.
To throw into disorder; to tumble. [R.]From her betumbled couch she starteth. Shak.
Intermediate time or space; interval. [Poetic & R.] Shak.
A beurré (or buttery) pear, one with the meas, Beurré d'Anjou;Beurré Clairgeau.
To cut to a bevel angle; to slope the edge or surface of.

A kind of gear in which the two wheels working together lie indifferent planes, and have their teeth cut at right angles to thesurfaces of two cones whose apices coincide with the point where theaxes of the wheels would meet.
The replacement of an edge by two similar planes, equallyinclined to the including faces or adjacent planes.
A light repast between meals; a lunch. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.
A chief broken or opening like a carpenter's bevel. Encyc.Brit.
To express deep sorrow for, as by wailing; to lament; to wailover.Hath widowed and unchilded many a one, Which to this hour bewail theinjury. Shak.
Such as may, or ought to, be bewailed; lamentable.
To keep watch over; to keep awake. [Obs.] Gower.
To avoid; to take care of; to have a care for. [Obs.] "Priest,beware your beard." Shak.To wish them beware the son. Milton.
To drench or souse with water. "Let the maids bewash the men."Herrick.
To weep over; to deplore; to bedew with tears. "His timelessdeath beweeping." Drayton.
To cover (the head) with a wig. Hawthorne.
To lead into perplexity or confusion, as for want of a plainpath; to perplex with mazes; or in general, to perplex or confusegreatly.Lost and bewildered in the fruitless search. Addison.
Greatly perplexed; as, a bewildered mind.
The state of being bewildered; bewilderment. [R.]
Causing bewilderment or great perplexity; as, bewilderingdifficulties.-- Be*wil"der*ing*ly, adv.
A double slip of leather by which bells are fastened to ahawk's legs.
The state of being bewitched. Gauden.
The power of bewitching or fascinating; bewitchment; charm;fascination.There is a certain bewitchery or fascination in words. South.
Having power to bewitch or fascinate; enchanting; captivating;charming.-- Be*witch"ing*ly, adv.-- Be*witch"ing*ness, n.
To wrap up; to cover. Fairfax.
One who, or that which, bewrays; a revealer. [Obs. or Archaic]Addison.
To wreak; to avenge. [Obs.] Ld. Berners.
A governor of a province or district in the Turkish dominions;also, in some places, a prince or nobleman; a beg; as, the bey ofTunis.
The territory ruled by a bey.
Further away; at a distance; yonder.Lo, where beyond he lyeth languishing. Spenser.
The second branch of a stag's horn.
A circle in or, i. e., gold, representing the gold coin calledbezant. Burke.
The rim which encompasses and fastens a jewel or other object,as the crystal of a watch, in the cavity in which it is set.
A game at cards in which various combinations of cards in thehand, when declared, score points.

A calculous concretion found in the intestines of certainruminant animals (as the wild goat, the gazelle, and the Peruvianllama) formerly regarded as an unfailing antidote for poison, and acertain remedy for eruptive, pestilential, or putrid diseases. Hence:Any antidote or panacea.
Pertaining to, or compounded with, bezoar.-- n.
A low fellow or scoundrel; a beggar.Great men oft die by vile bezonians. Shak.
To plunder; to waste in riot. [Obs.]
An astringent and narcotic drug made from the dried leaves andseed capsules of wild hemp (Cannabis Indica), and chewed or smoked inthe East as a means of intoxication. See Hasheesh.
An Indian monkey (Macacus Rhesus), protected by the Hindoos assacred. See Rhesus.
Having two hydrogen atoms which can be replaced by negativeatoms or radicals to form salts; -- said of bases. See Diacid.
Occurring twice a year; half-yearly; semiannual.
Having, or consisting of, tow joints.
In a slanting manner; crosswise; obliquely; diagonally; as, tocut cloth bias.
Having two auricles, as the heart of mammals, birds, andreptiles.
An arctic fish (Gadus luscus), allied to the cod; -- calledalso pout and whiting pout.
The practice or habit of drinking too much; tippling. Blount.
Having to hydrogen atoms which can be replaced by positive orbasic atoms or radicals to form salts; -- said of acids. See Dibasic.
One given to drinking alcoholic beverages too freely; atippler; -- chiefly used in composition; as, winebibber.
Pieces of timber bolted to certain parts of a mast tp supportthe trestletrees.
A cock or faucet having a bent down nozzle. Knight.
A small decorative object without practical utility.
Of or pertaining to drinking or tippling.

A book with an authoritative exposition of some topic,respected by many experts on the field. Bible Society, an associationfor securing the multiplication and wide distribution of the Bible.-- Douay Bible. See Douay Bible.-- Geneva Bible. See under Geneva.
A great drinker; a tippler. [Written also bibbler andbibbeler.]
Pertaining to, or derived from, the Bible; as, biblicallearning; biblical authority.
The quality of being biblical; a biblical subject. [R.]
Learning or literature relating to the Bible. [R.]
One skilled in the knowledge of the Bible; a demonstrator ofreligious truth by the Scriptures.
One who writes, or is versed in, bibliography.
A history or description of books and manuscripts, with noticesof the different editions, the times when they were printed, etc.
Book worship, esp. of the Bible; -- applied by Roman Catholicdivine Coleridge. F. W. Newman.
A kind of divination, performed by selecting passages ofScripture at hazard, and drawing from them indications concerningfuture events.
One who has a mania for books.-- a.
Pertaining to a passion for books; relating to a bibliomaniac.
Relating to the binding of books. [R.]
Pertaining to the art of binding books. [R.] Dibdin.
The trade or business of selling books.
Of or pertaining to bibliopolism. Dibdin.
Furnished with, or having, two bracts.
In a bibulous manner; with profuse imbibition or absorption. DeQuincey.
Having two spurs, as the wing or leg of a bird.
Consisting of, or including, two chambers, or legislativebranches. Bentham.
Having two capsules; as, a bicapsular pericarp.

A carbonate in which but half the hydrogen of the acid isreplaced by a positive element or radical, thus making the proportionof the acid to the positive or basic portion twice what it is in thenormal carbonates; an acid carbonate; -- sometimes calledsupercarbonate.
Having two keel-like projections, as the upper palea ofgrasses.
Having, or terminating in, two tails.
Pecked; pitted; notched. [Obs.] Chaucer. Bicched bones, pecked,or notched, bones; dice.
Of or pertaining to two hundred, esp. to two hundred years; as,a bicentenary celebration.-- n.
The two hundredth year or anniversary, or its celebration.
A muscle having two heads or origins; -- applied particularlyto a flexor in the arm, and to another in the thigh.
A remarkable ganoid fish (Polypterus bichir) found in the Nileand other African rivers. See Brachioganoidei.
A compound consisting of two atoms of chlorine with one or moreatoms of another element; -- called also dichloride. Bichloride ofmercury, mercuric chloride; -- sometimes called corrosive sublimate.
A salt containing two parts of chromic acid to one of the otheringredients; as, potassium bichromate; -- called also dichromate.
To combine or treat with a bichromate, esp. with bichromate ofpotassium; as, bichromatized gelatine.
Dividing into two parts at one extremity; having two heads ortwo supports; as, a bicipital tree.
Having two heads; bicipital. "Bicipitous serpents." Sir T.Browne.
A small wooden vessel made of staves and hoops, like a tub.[Prov. Eng.]
An anvil ending in a beak or point (orig. in two beaks); also,the beak or horn itself.
Having the anterior toes connected by a basal web.
Concave on both sides; as, biconcave vertebræ.
Twice paired, as when a petiole forks twice. Gray.
Convex on both sides; as, a biconvex lens.
Double-bodied, as a lion having one head and two bodies.
Having two principal ribs running longitudinally, as a leaf.
Twice crenated, as in the case of leaves whose crenatures arethemselves crenate.
Having the form of a double crescent.
One of the two double-pointed teeth which intervene between thecanines (cuspids) and the molars, on each side of each jaw. SeeTooth, n.
A light vehicle having two wheels one behind the other. It hasa saddle seat and is propelled by the rider's feet acting on cranksor levers.
The use of a bicycle; the act or practice of riding a bicycle.
The art of riding a bicycle.
An invitation of friends to drink ale at some poor man's house,and there to contribute in charity for his relief. [Prov. Eng.]
One who bids or offers a price. Burke.
A kind of metallic ware made in India. The material is acomposition of zinc, tin, and lead, in which ornaments of gold andsilver are inlaid or damascened. [Spelt also bidry, bidree, bedery,beder.]
The prayer for the souls of benefactors, said before thesermon.
A name used in calling a hen or chicken. Shak.
An instrument or weapon with two prongs.
Having two teeth or two toothlike processes; two-toothed.
Having two fingers or fingerlike projections.
Continuing for two years, and then perishing, as plants whichform roots and leaves the first year, and produce fruit the second.
A count of forty threads in the warp or chain of woolen cloth.Knight.
A church road (e. g., a path across fields) for funerals.[Obs.] Homilies.
Pointing two ways, as leaves that grow only on opposite sidesof a branch; in two vertical rows.
Cleft to the middle or slightly beyond the middle; opening witha cleft; divided by a linear sinus, with straight margins.

Two-threaded; involving the use of two threads; as, bifilarsuspension; a bifilar balance. Bifilar micrometer (often called abifilar), an instrument form measuring minute distances or angles bymeans of two very minute threads (usually spider lines), one ofwhich, at least, is movable; -- more commonly called a filarmicrometer.
Having two long, narrow, whiplike appendages.
Having two foci, as some spectacle lenses.
Twofold; double; of two kinds, degrees, etc. Shak.
Having two leaflets, as some compound leaves.
An oval sac or cell, found in the leaves of certain plants ofthe order Araceæ. It has an opening at each end through whichraphides, generated inside, are discharged.
Having two forms, bodies, or shapes. Croxall.
A forking, or division into two branches.
Barley, especially the hardy four-rowed kind."Bear interchanges in local use, now with barley, now with bigg." NewEnglish Dict.
Having a great belly; as, a big-bellied man or flagon; advancedin pregnancy.
One who is guilty of bigamy. Ayliffe.
Guilty of bigamy; involving bigamy; as, a bigamous marriage.
The offense of marrying one person when already legally marriedto another. Wharton.
Having a forked petiole, and a pair of leaflets at the end ofeach division; biconjugate; twice paired; -- said of a decompoundleaf.
Including two tribes or races of men.
A fish of the genus Priacanthus, remarkable for the large sizeof the eye.
To make or become big; to enlarge. [Obs. or Dial.] Steele.
A child's cap; a hood, or something worn on the head.An old woman's biggin for a nightcap. Massinger.
A measure of land in India, varying from a third of an acre toan acre.
The Rocky Mountain sheep (Ovis or Caprovis montana).
A bend in a coast forming an open bay; as, the Bight of Benin.
Having two glands, as a plant.
In a tumid, swelling, blustering manner; haughtily; violently.He brawleth bigly. Robynson (More's Utopia. )
The state or quality of being big; largeness; size; bulk.

A large genus of American, mostly tropical, climbing shrubs,having compound leaves and showy somewhat tubular flowers. B.capreolata is the cross vine of the Southern United States. Thetrumpet creeper was formerly considered to be of this genus.
Of pertaining to, or resembling, the family of plants of whichthe trumpet flower is an example.
Bigoted. [Obs.]In a country more bigot than ours. Dryden.
Obstinately and blindly attached to some creed, opinionpractice, or ritual; unreasonably devoted to a system or party, andilliberal toward the opinions of others. "Bigoted to strife." Byron.
In the manner of a bigot.
A person of consequence; as, the bigwigs of society. [Jocose]In our youth we have heard him spoken of by the bigwigs with extremecondescension. Dickens.
A compound of two atoms of hydrogen with some other substance.[Obs.]
A trinket; a jewel; -- a word applied to anything small and ofelegant workmanship.
Small articles of virtu, as jewelry, trinkets, etc.
Having two pairs, as of leaflets.
A nest of wild bees, wasps, or ants; a swarm. [Scot.] Sir W.Scott.
The East Indian name of a virulent poison extracted fromAconitum ferox or other species of aconite: also, the plant itself.
Having two lips, as the corols of certain flowers.
A two-masted passenger boat or small vessel, used in the bay ofManila.
A small two-masted merchant vessel, fitted only for coasting,or for use in canals, as in Holland.Why choose we, then, like bilanders to creep Along the coast, andland in view to keep Dryden.
Of or pertaining to the two sides of a central area or organ,or of a central axis; as, bilateral symmetry in animals, where thereis a similarity of parts on the right and left sides of the body.
The European whortleberry (Vaccinium myrtillus); also, itsedible bluish black fruit.There pinch the maids as blue as bilberry. Shak.

A long bar or bolt of iron with sliding shackles, and a lock atthe end, to confine the feet of prisoners or offenders, esp. on boardof ships.Methought I lay Worse than the mutines in the bilboes. Shak.
The toy called cup and ball.

A yellow, or greenish, viscid fluid, usually alkaline inreaction, secreted by the liver. It passes into the intestines, whereit aids in the digestive process. Its characteristic constituents arethe bile salts, and coloring matters.
That portion of a group of moldings which projects beyond thegeneral surface of a panel; a bolection.
A gallstone, or biliary calculus. See Biliary. E. Darwin.
That part of a ship's hull or bottom which is broadest and mostnearly flat, and on which she would rest if aground.
Having the smell of bilge water.
Relating or belonging to bile; conveying bile; as, biliaryacids; biliary ducts. Biliary calculus (Med.), a gallstone, or aconcretion formed in the gall bladder or its duct.
The production and excretion of bile.
A brownish green pigment found in human gallstones and in oldbile. It is a derivative of bilirubin.
A name applied to the amorphous or crystalline mass obtainedfrom bile by the action of alcohol and ether. It is composed of amixture of the sodium salts of the bile acids.
Of, pertaining to, or included by, two lines; as, bilinearcoördinates.
Containing, or consisting of, two languages; expressed in twolanguages; as, a bilingual inscription; a bilingual dictionary.-- Bi*lin"gual*ly, adv.
Quality of being bilingual.The bilingualism of King's English. Earle.
Having two tongues, or speaking two languages. [Obs.]
A dark green pigment found in small quantity in humangallstones.
A reddish yellow pigment present in human bile, and in thatfrom carnivorous and herbivorous animals; the normal biliary pigment.
Consisting of two letters; as, a biliteral root of a Sanskritverb. Sir W. Jones.-- n.
The property or state of being biliteral.
A green pigment present in the bile, formed from bilirubin byoxidation.
To frustrate or disappoint; to deceive or defraud, bynonfulfillment of engagement; to leave in the lurch; to give the slipto; as, to bilk a creditor. Thackeray.
A beak, as of a bird, or sometimes of a turtle or other animal.Milton.
A book in which a person keeps an account of his notes, bills,bills of exchange, etc., thus showing all that he issues andreceives.
One who negotiates the discount of bills.

In Australia, a blind channel leading out from a river; --sometimes called an anabranch. This is the sense of the word as usedin the Public Works Department; but the term has also been locallyapplied to mere back-waters forming stagnant pools and to certainwater channels arising from a source.
and v. t. & i. Same as Bilge.
An English fish, allied to the cod; the coalfish. [Written alsobillet and billit.]
A piece of thick plank, armed with iron plates, and fixed onthe bow or fore channels of a vessel, for the bill or fluke of theanchor to rest on. Totten.
Furnished with, or having, a bill, as a bird; -- used incomposition; as, broad-billed.
To direct, by a ticket or note, where to lodge. Hence: Toquarter, or place in lodgings, as soldiers in private houses.Billeted in so antiquated a mansion. W. Irving.
A love letter or note.A lover chanting out a billet-doux. Spectator.
A round piece of timber at the bow or stern of a whaleboat,around which the harpoon lone is run out when the whale darts off.

A name applied to several distinct fishes: (a) The garfish(Tylosurus, or Belone, longirostris) and allied species. (b) Thesaury, a slender fish of the Atlantic coast (Scomberesox saurus). (c)The Tetrapturus albidus, a large oceanic species related to theswordfish; the spearfish. (d) The American fresh-water garpike(Lepidosteus osseus).
A printed form, used by merchants in making out bills orrendering accounts.
A thick, heavy knife with a hooked point, used in pruninghedges, etc. When it has a short handle, it is sometimes called ahand bill; when the handle is long, a hedge bill or scimiter.
Of or pertaining to the game of billiards. "Smooth as is abilliard ball." B. Jonson.

A game played with ivory balls o a cloth-covered, rectangulartable, bounded by elastic cushions. The player seeks to impel hisball with his cue so that it shall either strike (carom upon) twoother balls, or drive another ball into one of the pockets with whichthe table sometimes is furnished.
According to the French and American method of numeration, athousand millions, or 1,000,000,000; according to the English method,a million millions, or 1,000,000,000,000. See Numeration.
One who uses, or is armed with, a bill or hooked ax. "A billmanof the guard." Savile.
An alloy of gold and silver with a large proportion of copperor other base metal, used in coinage.
Bullion in the bar or mass.
To surge; to rise and roll in waves or surges; to undulate."The billowing snow." Prior.
Of or pertaining to billows; swelling or swollen into largewaves; full of billows or surges; resembling billows.And whitening down the many-tinctured stream, Descends the billowyfoam. Thomson.
A flat-bottomed river barge or coasting vessel. [Eng.]
Divided into two lobes or segments.
Double location; the state or power of being in two places atthe same instant; -- a miraculous power attributed to some of thesaints. Tylor.
Divided into two cells or compartments; as, a bilocularpericarp. Gray.
Lean meat cut into strips and sun-dried. H. R. Haggard.
Having, or marked with, two spots.
Animals having two hands; -- a term applied by Cuvier to man asa special order of Mammalia.
Having a double margin, as certain shells.
The condition of having two mammæ or teats.
Applied to a line which is the sum of two lines commensurableonly in power (as the side and diagonal of a square).
Having two members; as, a bimembral sentence. J. W. Gibbs.
Of or relating to, or using, a double metallic standard (asgold and silver) for a system of coins or currency.
The legalized use of two metals (as gold and silver) in thecurrency of a country, at a fixed relative value; -- in opposition tomonometallism.
Pertaining to, or formed from, two molecules; as, a bimolecularreaction (a reaction between two molecules).
Occurring, done, or coming, once in two months; as, bimonthlyvisits; bimonthly publications.-- n.
Having two adductor muscles, as a bivalve mollusk.
A box, frame, crib, or inclosed place, used as a receptacle forany commodity; as, a corn bin; a wine bin; a coal bin.
Twofold; double. [R.] "Binal revenge, all this." Ford.
A salt having two equivalents of arsenic acid to one of thebase. Graham.

Compounded or consisting of two things or parts; characterizedby two (things). Binary arithmetic, that in which numbers areexpressed according to the binary scale, or in which two figuresonly, 0 and 1, are used, in lieu of ten; the cipher multiplyingeverything by two, as in common arithmetic by ten. Thus, 1 is one; 10is two; 11 is three; 100 is four, etc. Davies & Peck.-- Binary compound (Chem.), a compound of two elements, or of anelement and a compound performing the function of an element, or oftwo compounds performing the function of elements.-- Binary logarithms, a system of logarithms devised by Euler forfacilitating musical calculations, in which 1 is logarithm of 2,instead of 10, as in the common logarithms, and the modulus 1.442695instead of .43429448.-- Binary measure (Mus.), measure divisible by two or four; commontime.-- Binary nomenclature (Nat. Hist.), nomenclature in which the namesdesignate both genus and species.-- Binary scale (Arith.), a uniform scale of notation whose ratio istwo.-- Binary star (Astron.), a double star whose members have arevolution round their common center of gravity.-- Binary theory (Chem.), the theory that all chemical compoundsconsist of two constituents of opposite and unlike qualities.
Double; growing in pairs or couples. Gray.
Of or pertaining to, or used by, both ears.
A major in the Turkish army.
Indurated clay, when much mixed with the oxide of iron. Kirwan.
A place where books, or other articles, are bound; abookbinder's establishment.
An amorphous antimonate of lead, produced from the alterationof other ores, as from jamesonite.
That binds; obligatory. Binding beam (Arch.), the main timberin double flooring.-- Binding joist (Arch.), the secondary timber in double-framedflooring.
A metallic post attached to electrical apparatus forconvenience in making connections.
A set screw used to bind parts together, esp. one for making aconnection in an electrical circuit.
The condition or property of being binding; obligatory quality.Coleridge.

A plant of the genus Convolvulus; as, greater bindweed (C.Sepium); lesser bindweed (C. arvensis); the white, the blue, theSyrian, bindweed. The black bryony, or Tamus, is called blackbindweed, and the Smilax aspera, rough bindweed.The fragile bindweed bells and bryony rings. Tennyson.
The winding or twining stem of a hop vine or other climbingplant.
Two-nerved; -- applied to leaves which have two longitudinalribs or nerves.
A heap or pile; as, a bing of wood. "Potato bings." Burns. "Abing of corn." Surrey. [Obs. or Dial. Eng. & Scot.]
A case or box placed near the helmsman, containing the compassof a ship, and a light to show it at night. Totten.
A large species of barbel (Barbus bynni), found in the Nile,and much esteemed for food.
A dioptric telescope, fitted with two tubes joining, so as toenable a person to view an object with both eyes at once; a double-barreled field glass or an opera glass.
A binocular glass, whether opera glass, telescope, ormicroscope.
An expression consisting of two terms connected by the signplus (+) or minus (-); as, a+b, or 7-3.
Of or pertaining to two names; binomial.
Consisting of two notes; as, a binotonous cry.
A salt having two equivalents of oxalic acid to one of thebase; an acid oxalate.
A small Asiatic civet of the genus Arctilis.
Having two ocelli (eyelike spots); -- said of a wing, etc.
The chemistry of living organisms; the chemistry of theprocesses incidental to, and characteristic of, life.
The doctrine of vital forces or energy.
A believer in the theory of biogenesis.

The branch of biology which deals with the geographicaldistribution of animals and plants. It includes both zoögeography andphytogeography. -- Bi`o*ge`o*graph"ic (#), a. --Bi`o*ge`o*graph"ic*al*ly (#), adv.
An animated picture machine for screen projection; acinematograph.
One who writes an account or history of the life of aparticular person; a writer of lives, as Plutarch.
To write a history of the life of. Southey.
Of or relating to biology.-- Bi`o*log"ic*al*ly, adv.
A student of biology; one versed in the science of biology.

The science of life; that branch of knowledge which treats ofliving matter as distinct from matter which is not living; the studyof living tissue. It has to do with the origin, structure,development, function, and distribution of animals and plants.
Relating to the destruction of life.
Measurement of life; calculation of the probable duration ofhuman life.
The physiological individual, characterized by definiteness andindependence of function, in distinction from the morphologicalindividual or morphon.
An instrument combining a cinematograph and a phonograph sothat the moving figures on the screen are accompanied by theappropriate sounds.

A name suggested by Dr. Beale for the germinal matter supposedto be essential to the functions of all living beings; the materialthrough which every form of life manifests itself; unalteredprotoplasm.
Pertaining to, or consisting of, bioplasm.
A tiny mass of bioplasm, in itself a living unit and havingformative power, as a living white blood corpuscle; bioblast.
A physiological organ; a living organ; an organ endowed withfunction; -- distinguished from idorgan.
A view of life; that which gives such a view.
The physical phenomena of organized bodies, in opposition totheir organic or vital phenomena.
The classification of living organisms according to theirstructural character; taxonomy.
Relating to life; as, the biotic principle.
Mica containing iron and magnesia, generally of a black or darkgreen color; -- a common constituent of crystalline rocks. See Mica.
Palmately branched, with the branches again palmated.
Of or pertaining to the diameter of the cranium, from oneparietal fossa to the other.
Bringing forth two at a birth.
Capable of being divided into two parts.
The act of dividing into two parts, or of making twocorrespondent parts, or the state of being so divided.
Having a shell or covering like a double shield.
An ax with an edge or blade on each side of the handle.
The larva of certain starfishes as developed in the free-swimming stage.
An aëroplane with two main supporting surfaces one above theother.
The state of being twice folded; reduplication. [R.] Bailey.
Doubly polar; having two poles; as, a bipolar cell orcorpuscle.
A prism whose refracting angle is very nearly 180 degrees.
Having an eyelike spot on the wing, with two dots within it ofa different color, as in some butterflies.
Consisting of two pyramids placed base to base; having apyramid at each of the extremities of a prism, as in quartz crystals.
The fourth power, or the square of the square. Thus 4x4=16, thesquare of 4, and 16x16=256, the biquadrate of 4.

Of or pertaining to the biquadrate, or fourth power.Biquadratic equation (Alg.), an equation of the fourth degree, or anequation in some term of which the unknown quantity is raised to thefourth power.-- Biquadratic root of a number, the square root of the square rootof that number. Thus the square root of 81 is 9, and the square rootof 9 is 3, which is the biquadratic root of 81. Hutton.
An aspect of the planets when they are distant from each otherby twice the fifth part of a great circle -- that is, twice 72degrees.
Having, or consisting of, two branches.
Of or pertaining to the birch; birchen.
Of or relating to birch.He passed where Newark's stately tower Looks out from Yarrow'sbirchen bower. Sir W. Scott.
A warm-blooded, feathered vertebrate provided with wings. SeeAves.
A shrub (Prunus Padus ) found in Northern and Central Europe.It bears small black cherries.

The name of several very beautiful birds of the genus Paradiseaand allied genera, inhabiting New Guinea and the adjacent islands.The males have brilliant colors, elegant plumes, and often remarkabletail feathers.
A species of capsicum (Capsicum baccatum), whose small,conical, coral-red fruit is among the most piquant of all redpeppers.
Quick-sighted; catching a glance as one goes.
Flighty; passing rapidly from one subject to another; nothaving the faculty of attention. Bacon.
A short blunt arrow for killing birds without piercing them.Hence: Anything which smites without penetrating. Shak.
One whose employment it is to catch birds; a fowler.
The art, act, or occupation or catching birds or wild fowls.
A pretty or dear little bird; -- a pet name. Tennyson.
Birdcatching or fowling. Shak. Birding piece, a fowling piece.Shak.

An extremely adhesive viscid substance, usually made of themiddle bark of the holly, by boiling, fermenting, and cleansing it.When a twig is smeared with this substance it will hold small birdswhich may light upon it. Hence: Anything which insnares.Not birdlime or Idean pitch produce A more tenacious mass of clammyjuice. Dryden.
Canary seed, hemp, millet or other small seeds used for feedingcaged birds.
Containing or having two right angles; as, a birectangularspherical triangle.
An ancient galley or vessel with two banks or tiers of oars.
A birch tree. [Prov. Eng.] "The silver birk." Tennyson.
To whip with a birch or rod. [Obs.]
A lively or mettlesome fellow. [Jocular, Scot.] Burns.
To revolve or cause to revolve; to spin. [Scot.] Sir W. Scott.
A law made by husbandmen respecting rural affairs; a rustic orlocal law or by-law. [Written also byrlaw, birlie, birley.]
To make, or move with, a whirring noise, as of wheels inmotion.
A coarse kind of thick woolen cloth, worn by the poor in theMiddle Ages; also, a woolen cap or hood worn over the shoulders orover the head.
A fish of the turbot kind; the brill. [Written also burt, bret,or brut.] [Prov. Eng.]
Of or pertaining to the day of birth, or its anniversary; as,birthday gifts or festivities.
The land of one's birth; one's inheritance. [R.] Shak.
Anything added to raise the sides of a ship. Bailey.
Of mean extraction. [R.] Sir W. Scott.
Some peculiar mark or blemish on the body at birth.Most part of this noble lineage carried upon their body for a naturalbirthmark, . . . a snake. Sir T. North.
The night in which a person is born; the anniversary of thatnight in succeeding years.The angelic song in Bethlehem field, On thy birthnight, that sungthee Savior born. Milton.
The town, city, or country, where a person is born; place oforigin or birth, in its more general sense. "The birthplace ofvalor." Burns.

Any right, privilege, or possession to which a person isentitled by birth, such as an estate descendible by law to an heir,or civil liberty under a free constitution; esp. the rights orinheritance of the first born.Lest there be any . . . profane person, as Esau, who for one morselof meat sold his birthright. Heb. xii. 16.
An herbaceous plant (Trillium erectum), and its astringentrootstock, which is said to have medicinal properties.
A genus of herbs and shrubs (Aristolochia), reputed to havemedicinal properties.
Twice; -- a word showing that something is, or is to be,repeated; as a passage of music, or an item in accounts.
Having two little bags, sacs, or pouches.
Of or pertaining to Biscay in Spain.-- n.
A confection made of flour, sugar, marmalade, and eggs; a sweetbiscuit.

A species of white, unglazed porcelain, in which vases,figures, and groups are formed in miniature. Meat biscuit, analimentary preparation consisting of matters extracted from meat byboiling, or of meat ground fine and combined with flour, so as toform biscuits.
Resembling two bucklers placed side by side.
A cold north wind which prevails on the northern coasts of theMediterranean and in Switzerland, etc.; -- nearly the same as themistral.
To divide into two equal parts.
Division into two parts, esp. two equal parts.
One who, or that which, bisects; esp. (Geom.) a straight linewhich bisects an angle.
The line bisecting the angle between the optic axes of abiaxial crystal.
One of tow equal parts of a line, or other magnitude.
With two partitions or septa. Gray.
Doubly serrate, or having the serratures serrate, as in someleaves.
Of both sexes; hermaphrodite; as a flower with stamens andpistil, or an animal having ovaries and testes.
of Besee. [Obs.] Chaucer. Evil biseye, ill looking. [Obs.]
To admit into the church by confirmation; to confirm; hence, toreceive formally to favor.
A wide sleeve, once worn by women.
Jurisdiction of a bishop; episcopate. "Divine right ofbishopdom." Milton.
Resembling a bishop; belonging to a bishop. Fulke.
A plant of the genus Mitella; miterwort. Longfellow.
A salt of metasilicic acid; -- so called because the ratio ofthe oxygen of the silica to the oxygen of the base is as two to one.The bisilicates include many of the most common and importantminerals.
Soup or broth made by boiling several sorts of flesh together.King.
An adjuration or exclamation common among the Mohammedans.[Written also Bizmillah.]

One of the elements; a metal of a reddish white color,crystallizing in rhombohedrons. It is somewhat harder than lead, andrather brittle; masses show broad cleavage surfaces when brokenacross. It melts at 507º Fahr., being easily fused in the flame of acandle. It is found in a native state, and as a constituent of someminerals. Specific gravity 9.8. Atomic weight 207.5. Symbol Bi.
Of or pertaining to bismuth; containing bismuth, when thiselement has its higher valence; as, bismuthic oxide.
Of, or containing, bismuth, when this element has its lowervalence.
Hydrous carbonate of bismuth, an earthy mineral of a dull whiteor yellowish color. [Written also bismuthite.]
A truck for railroad rolling stock, consisting of two ordinaryaxle boxes sliding in guides attached to a triangular frame; --called also pony truck.

Leap year; every fourth year, in which a day is added to themonth of February on account of the excess of the tropical year (365d. 5 h. 48 m. 46 s.) above 365 days. But one day added every fouryears is equivalent to six hours each year, which is 11 m. 14 s. morethan the excess of the real year. Hence, it is necessary to suppressthe bissextile day at the end of every century which is not divisibleby 400, while it is retained at the end of those which are divisibleby 400.
An herbaceous plant of the genus Polygonum, section Bistorta;snakeweed; adderwort. Its root is used in medicine as an astringent.
A surgical instrument consisting of a slender knife, eitherstraight or curved, generally used by introducing it beneath the partto be divided, and cutting towards the surface.
Cloven; said of a foot or hoof.

A sulphate in which but half the hydrogen of the acid isreplaced by a positive element or radical, thus making the proportionof the acid to the positive or basic portion twice what it is in thenormal sulphates; an acid sulphate.
A sulphide having two atoms of sulphur in the molecule; adisulphide, as in iron pyrites, FeS2; -- less frequently calledbisulphuret.
A salt of sulphurous acid in which the base replaces but halfthe hydrogen of the acid; an acid sulphite.
To put a bridle upon; to put the bit in the mouth of.
Possessing the property of touching at two points.-- n.
A salt of tartaric acid in which the base replaces but half theacid hydrogen; an acid tartrate, as cream of tartar.
A blank on the edge or corner of a page, owing to a portion ofthe frisket, or something else, intervening between the type andpaper.
Doubly ternate, as when a petiole has three ternate leaflets.-- Bi*ter"nate*ly, adv. Gray.
Belief in the existence of two gods; dualism.
That bites; sharp; cutting; sarcastic; caustic. "A bitingaffliction." "A biting jest." Shak.
The process of corroding or eating into metallic plates, bymeans of an acid. See Etch. G. Francis.
Not having a bit or bridle.
A stock or handle for holding and rotating a bit; a brace.
AA turn of the cable which is round the bitts. Bitter end, thatpart of a cable which is abaft the bitts, and so within board, whenthe ship rides at anchor.
A common name of dolomite; -- so called because it containsmagnesia, the soluble salts of which are bitter. See Dolomite.
A bitter compound used in adulterating beer; bittern.
A wading bird of the genus Botaurus, allied to the herons, ofvarious species.
The swamp hickory (Carya amara). Its thin-shelled nuts arebitter.

A plant (Lewisia rediviva) allied to the purslane, but withfleshy, farinaceous roots, growing in the mountains of Idaho,Montana, etc. It gives the name to the Bitter Root mountains andriver. The Indians call both the plant and the river Spæt'lum.
A liquor, generally spirituous in which a bitter herb, leaf, orroot is steeped.
Sweet and then bitter or bitter and then sweet; esp. sweet witha bitter after taste; hence (Fig.), pleasant but painful.
A species of Ambrosia (A. artemisiæfolia); Roman worm wood.Gray.
A West Indian tree (Picræna excelsa) from the wood of which thebitter drug Jamaica quassia is obtained.
The yellow gentian (Gentiana lutea), which has a very bittertaste.
A small bit of anything, of indefinite size or quantity; ashort distance. [Scot.] Sir W. Scott.

A frame of two strong timbers fixed perpendicularly in the forepart of a ship, on which to fasten the cables as the ship rides atanchor, or in warping. Other bitts are used for belaying (belayingbitts), for sustaining the windlass (carrick bitts, winch bitts, orwindlass bitts), to hold the pawls of the windlass (pawl bitts) etc.
Smeared with bitumen. [R.] "The hatches caulked and bitumed."Shak.
Any process in which  advantage is taken of the fact thatprepared bitumen is rendered insoluble by exposure to light, as inphotolithography.
To treat or impregnate with bitumen; to cement with bitumen."Bituminated walls of Babylon." Feltham.
To prepare, treat, impregnate, or coat with bitumen.

Having the qualities of bitumen; compounded with bitumen;containing bitumen.Near that bituminous lake where Sodom flamed. Milton.Bituminous coal, a kind of coal which yields, when heated, aconsiderable amount of volatile bituminous matter. It burns with ayellow smoky flame.-- Bituminous limestone, a mineral of a brown or black color,emitting an unpleasant smell when rubbed. That of Dalmatia is socharged with bitumen that it may be cut like soap.-- Bituminous shale, an argillaceous shale impregnated with bitumen,often accompanying coal.
A white, crystalline, nitrogenous substance, C2O2N3H5, formedby heating urea. It is intermediate between urea and cyanuric acid.
Equivalent in combining or displacing power to two atoms ofhydrogen; dyad.

A mollusk having a shell consisting of two lateral plates orvalves joined together by an elastic ligament at the hinge, which isusually strengthened by prominences called teeth. The shell is closedby the contraction of two transverse muscles attached to the innersurface, as in the clam, -- or by one, as in the oyster. SeeMollusca.
Having two valves, as the oyster and some seed pods; bivalve.
A term made up of the two parts
(Anat.) Having two bellies or protuberances; as, a biventral,or digastric, muscle, or the biventral lobe of the cerebellum.
Of or relating to the bivium.
Having, or leading, two ways.Bivious theorems and Janus-faced doctrines. Sir T. Browne.
One side of an echinoderm, including a pair of ambulacra, indistinction from the opposite side (trivium), which includes threeambulacra.
Occurring or appearing once every two weeks; fortnightly.-- n.
Odd in manner or appearance; fantastic; whimsical; extravagant;grotesque. C. Kingsley.
The upper faceted portion of a brilliant-cut diamond, whichprojects from the setting and occupies the zone between the girdleand the table. See Brilliant, n.
To utter or tell unnecessarily, or in a thoughtless manner; topublish (secrets or trifles) without reserve or discretion. Udall.And yonder a vile physician blabbing The case of his patient.Tennyson.
Sullenly; threateningly; maliciously; so as to produceblackness.
The art practiced by conjurers and witches; necromancy;conjuration; magic.
A pestilence which ravaged Europe and Asia in the fourteenthcentury.

An organization composed originally of Chinese rebels that hadbeen driven into Tonkin by the suppression of the Taiping rebellion,but later increased by bands of pirates and adventurers. It took aprominent part in fighting the French during their hostilities withAnam, 1873-85.
A friar of the Dominican order; -- called also predicant andpreaching friar; in France, Jacobin. Also, sometimes, a Benedictine.

Any Friday on which a public disaster has occurred, as: InEngland, December 6, 1745, when the news of the landing of thePretender reached London, or May 11, 1866,  when a financial paniccommenced. In the United States, September 24, 1869, and September18, 1873, on which financial panics began.
A sweet and juicy variety of European grape, of a dark purplishblack color, much grown under glass in northern latitudes.
A Spanish anarchistic society, many of the members of whichwere imprisoned in 1883.

A dungeon or dark cell in a prison; a military lock-up orguardroom; -- now commonly with allusion to the cell (the Black Hole)in a fort at Calcutta, into which 146 English prisoners were thrustby the nabob Suraja Dowla on the night of June 20, 17656, and inwhich 123 of the prisoners died before morning from lack of air.A discipline of unlimited autocracy, upheld by rods, and ferules, andthe black hole. H. Spencer.
Plumbago; graphite.It leaves a blackish mark somewhat likelead. See Graphite.
The old English or Gothic letter, in which the Early Englishmanuscripts were written, and the first English books were printed.It was conspicuous for its blackness. See Type.
A kind of sausage made of blood, suet, etc., thickened withmeal.And fat black puddings, -- proper food, For warriors that delight inblood. Hudibras.
One of an old and well-known Mediterranean breed of domesticfowls with glossy black plumage, blue legs and feet, bright red comband wattles, and white face. They are remarkable as egg layers.
A copious vomiting of dark-colored matter; or the substance sodischarged; -- one of the most fatal symptoms in yellow fever.
Having black eyebrows. Hence: Gloomy; dismal; threatening;forbidding. Shak. Dryden.
Having a black, dark, or gloomy face or aspect.
Having a wicked, malignant disposition; morally bad.
A name given by English miners to sphalerite, or zinc blende; -- called also false galena. See Blende.
Using foul or scurrilous language; slanderous.
An earthy carbonate of iron containing considerablecarbonaceous matter; -- valuable as an iron ore.

The fruit of several species of bramble (Rubus); also, theplant itself. Rubus fruticosus is the blackberry of England; R.villosus and R. Canadensis are the high blackberry and low blackberryof the United States. There are also other kinds.

In England, a species of thrush (Turdus merula), a singing birdwith a fin note; the merle. In America the name is given to severalbirds, as the Quiscalus versicolor, or crow blackbird; the Agelæusphoeniceus, or red-winged blackbird; the cowbird; the rusty grackle,etc. See Redwing.
A slave ship; a slaver. [Colloq.]  F. T. Bullen.
A broad board painted black, or any black surface on whichwriting, drawing, or the working of mathematical problems can be donewith chalk or crayons. It is much used in schools.
A beautiful warbler of the United States (DendroicaBlackburniæ). The male is strongly marked with orange, yellow, andblack on the head and neck, and has an orange-yellow breast.
An apple roasted till black, to be served in a dish of boiledcustard.
A clergyman; -- familiarly so called, as a soldier is sometimescalled a redcoat or a bluecoat.
The male of the European black grouse (Tetrao tetrix, Linn.); -- so called by sportsmen. The female is called gray hen. See Heathgrouse.
A tribe of North American Indians formerly inhabiting thecountry from the upper Missouri River to the Saskatchewan, but nowmuch reduced in numbers.
A small kind of whale, of the genus Globicephalus, of severalspecies. The most common is G. melas. Also sometimes applied to otherwhales of larger size.
Of or pertaining to the Blackfeet; as, a Blackfoot Indian.-- n.
To revile or abuse in scurrilous language. Southey.
The conduct or language of a blackguard; rufflanism.
In the manner of or resembling a blackguard; abusive;scurrilous; ruffianly.
A heart-shaped cherry with a very dark-colored skin.
To coat or to polish with black lead.

To put in a black list as deserving of suspicion, censure, orpunishment; esp. to put in a list of persons stigmatized as insolventor untrustworthy, -- as tradesmen and employers do for mutualprotection; as, to blacklist a workman who has been discharged. SeeBlack list, under Black, a.If you blacklist us, we will boycott you. John Swinton.
In a black manner; darkly, in color; gloomily; threateningly;atrociously. "Deeds so blackly grim and horrid." Feltham.
Black rent, or rent paid in corn, flesh, or the lowest coin, aopposed to "white rent", which paid in silver. To levy blackmail, toextort money by threats, as of injury to one's reputation.
One who extorts, or endeavors to extort, money, by blackmailing.
The act or practice of extorting money by exciting fears ofinjury other than bodily harm, as injury to reputation.
The quality or state of being black; black color; atrociousnessor enormity in wickedness.They're darker now than blackness. Donne.
A warbler of the United States (Dendroica striata).
One who,makes crude potash, or black salts.
A fish of the Pacific coast (Chromis, or Heliastes,punctipinnis), of a blackish color.
A fish; the ruff or pope.
Nebraska; -- a nickname alluding to the dark color of the waterof its rivers, due to the presence of a black vegetable mold in thesoil.
A name given to several dark-colored timbers. The East Indianblack wood is from the tree Dalbergia latifolia. Balfour.
Work wrought by blacksmiths; -- so called in distinction fromthat wrought by whitesmiths. Knight.

A bag or sac in animals, which serves as the receptacle of somefluid; as, the urinary bladder; the gall bladder; -- appliedespecially to the urinary bladder, either within the animal, or whentaken out and inflated with air.
A genus (Utricularia) of aquatic or marshy plants, whichusually bear numerous vesicles in the divisions of the leaves. Theseserve as traps for minute animals. See Ascidium.
Having bladders; also, resembling a bladder.
The principal rafters of a roof. Weale.
Composed of long and narrow plates, shaped like the blade of aknife.
A long, thin, marine fish of Europe (Trichiurus lepturus); theribbon fish.
Dark blue or bluish gray; lead-colored. [Scot.]
A bladder growing on the root of the tongue of a horse, againstthe windpipe, and stopping the breath.
Deserving of censure; faulty; culpable; reprehensible;censurable; blameworthy.-- Blam"a*ble*ness, n.-- Blam"a*bly (, adv.

Free from blame; without fault; innocent; guiltless; --sometimes followed by of.A bishop then must be blameless. 1 Tim. iii. 2.Blameless still of arts that polish to deprave. Mallet.We will be blameless of this thine oath. Josh. ii. 17.
The quality or state of being blameless; innocence.
Deserving blame; culpable; reprehensible.-- Blame"wor`thi*ness, n.
A kind of linen cloth made in Normandy, the thread of which ispartly blanches before it is woven.
To bleach by excluding the light, as the stalks or leaves ofplants, by earthing them up or tying them together.
A mode of tenure by the payment of a small duty in white rent(silver) or otherwise.

A kind of wood-turning lathe for making noncircular andirregular forms, as felloes, gun stocks, lasts, spokes, etc., after agiven pattern. The pattern and work rotate on parallel spindles inthe same direction with the same speed, and the work is shaped by arapidly rotating cutter whose position is varied by the patternacting as a cam upon a follower wheel traversing slowly along thepattern.
One who, or that which, blanches or whitens; esp., one whoanneals and cleanses money; also, a chemical preparation for thispurpose.
An instrument for measuring the bleaching power of chloride oflime and potash; a chlorometer. Ure.
A preparation for desserts, etc., made from isinglass, seamoss, cornstarch, or other gelatinous or starchy substance, withmild, usually sweetened and flavored, and shaped in a mold.
A sort of fricassee with white sauce, variously made of capon,fish, etc. [Obs.] Chaucer.

The act of blandishing; a word or act expressive of affectionor kindness, and tending to win the heart; soft words and artfulcaresses; cajolery; allurement.Cowering low with blandishment. Milton.Attacked by royal smiles, by female blandishments. Macaulay.
In a bland manner; mildly; suavely.
The state or quality of being bland.
A piece of metal prepared to be made into something by afurther operation, as a coin, screw, nuts.
A piece of rubber, felt, or woolen cloth, used in the tympan tomake it soft and elastic.
A clause, as in a blanket mortgage or policy, that includes agroup or class of things, rather than a number mentioned individuallyand having the burden, loss, or the like, apportioned among them.
A buttonhole stitch worked wide apart on the edge of material,as blankets, too thick to hem.

One that covers a group or class of things or propertiesinstead of one or more things mentioned individually, as where amortgage secures various debts as a group, or subjects a group orclass of different pieces of property to one general lien.
A large fish of Florida and the W. Indies (Caulolatiluschrysops). It is red, marked with yellow.
To sound loudly and somewhat harshly. "The trumpet blared."Tennyson.
Smooth, wheedling talk; flattery. [Colloq.] Blarney stone, astone in Blarney castle, Ireland, said to make those who kiss itproficient in the use of blarney.
Having the sensibilities deadened by excess or frequency ofenjoyment; sated or surfeited with pleasure; used up.
To utter blasphemy.He that shall blaspheme against the Holy Ghost hath neverforgiveness. Mark iii. 29.
One who blasphemes.And each blasphemer quite escape the rod, Because the insult's not onman, but God Pope.

Speaking or writing blasphemy; uttering or exhibiting anythingimpiously irreverent; profane; as, a blasphemous person; containingblasphemy; as, a blasphemous book; a blasphemous caricature."Blasphemous publications." Porteus.Nor from the Holy One of Heaven Refrained his tongue blasphemous.Milton.
A lamp provided with some arrangement for intensifyingcombustion by means of a blast.
The exhaust pipe of a steam engine, or any pipe deliveringsteam or air, when so constructed as to cause a blast.
The structureless, protoplasmic tissue of the embryo; theprimitive basis of an organ yet unformed, from which it grows.
Connected with, or proceeding from, the blastema; blastemal.
One who, or that which, blasts or destroys.
A small, clear space in the segments of the ovum, the precursorof the nucleus.
A sudden stroke or injury produced by some destructive cause.[Obs.] Shak.
Germinating inside the pericarp, as the mangrove. Brande & C.
The cavity of the blastosphere, or segmentation cavity.
The germinal membrane in an ovum, from which the embryo isdeveloped.
Multiplication or increase by gemmation or budding.
One of the divisions of Crinoidea found fossil in paleozoicrocks; pentremites. They are so named on account of their budlikeform.
One of the segments first formed by the division of the ovum.Balfour.
That portion of the spermatospore which is not converted intospermatoblasts, but carries them.
The pore or opening leading into the cavity of invagination, orarchenteron.
The hollow globe or sphere formed by the arrangement of theblastomeres on the periphery of an impregnated ovum.
In certain hydroids, an imperfect zooid, whose special functionis to produce medusoid buds. See Hydroidea, and Athecata.
That stage in the development of the ovum in which the outercells of the morula become more defined and form the blastoderm.
To cry, as a calf or sheep; to bleat; to make a senselessnoise; to talk inconsiderately. [Low]

Bellowing, as a calf; bawling; brawling; clamoring;disagreeably clamorous; sounding loudly and harshly. "Harsh andblatant tone." R. H. Dana.A monster, which the blatant beast men call. Spenser.Glory, that blatant word, which haunts some military minds like thebray of the trumpet. W. Irving.
To talk foolishly, or nonsensically.  G. Eliot.
A blustering, talkative fellow. [Local slang, U. S.] Barllett.

To prate; to babble; to rail; to make a senseless noise; topatter. [Archaic] "The rain blattered." Jeffrey.They procured . . . preachers to blatter against me, . . . so thatthey had place and time to belie me shamefully. Latimer.
One who blatters; a babbler; a noisy, blustering boaster.
A senseless babbler or boaster. [Obs.] "I hate suchblatteroons." Howell.
The blue buck. See Blue buck, under Blue.
A white spot on the forehead of a horse.
One who spreads reports or blazes matters abroad. "Blazers ofcrime." Spenser.

Burning with a blaze; as, a blazing fire; blazing torches. SirW. Scott. Blazing star. (a) A comet. [Obs.] (b) A brilliant center ofattraction. (c) (Bot.) A name given to several plants; as, toChamælirium luteum of the Lily family; Liatris squarrosa; and Aletrisfarinosa, called also colicroot and star grass.
To describe in proper terms (the figures of heraldic devices);also, to delineate (armorial bearings); to emblazon.The coat of , arms, which I am not herald enough to blazon intoEnglish. Addison.
One who gives publicity, proclaims, or blazons; esp., one whoblazons coats of arms; a herald. Burke.
The act or blazoning; blazoning; emblazonment.
The part of a tree which lies immediately under the bark; thealburnum or sapwood.

To make white, or whiter; to remove the color, or stains, from;to blanch; to whiten.The destruction of the coloring matters attached to the bodies to bebleached is effected either by the action of the air and light, ofchlorine, or of sulphurous acid. Ure.Immortal liberty, whose look sublime Hath bleached the tyrant's cheekin every varying clime. Smollett.
Whitened; make white.Let their bleached bones, and blood's unbleaching stain, Long markthe battlefield with hideous awe. Byron.
One who whitens, or whose occupation is to whiten, bybleaching.
A place or an establishment where bleaching is done.

The act or process of whitening, by removing color or stains;esp. the process of whitening fabrics by chemical agents. Ure.Bleaching powder, a powder for bleaching, consisting of chloride oflime, or some other chemical or chemicals.
A small European river fish (Leuciscus alburnus), of the familyCyprinidæ; the blay. [Written also blick.]

To make somewhat sore or watery, as the eyes; to dim, or blur,as the sight. Figuratively: To obscure (mental or moral perception);to blind; to hoodwink.That tickling rheums Should ever tease the lungs and blear the sight.Cowper.To blear the eye of, to deceive; to impose upon. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Dimmed, as by a watery humor; affected with rheum.-- Blear"ed*ness (, n.Dardanian wives, With bleared visages, come forth to view The issueof the exploit. Shak.
A disease of the eyelids, consisting in chronic inflammation ofthe margins, with a gummy secretion of sebaceous matter. Dunglison.

To make the noise of, or one like that of, a sheep; to cry likea sheep or calf.Then suddenly was heard along the main, To low the ox, to bleat thewoolly train. PopeThe ewe that will not hear her lamb when it baas, will never answer acalf when he bleats. Shak.
One who bleats; a sheep.In cold, stiff soils the bleaters oft complain Of gouty ails. Dyer.
Crying as a sheep does.Then came the shepherd back with his bleating flocks from theseaside. Longfellow.
A large vesicle or bulla, usually containing a serous fluid; ablister; a bubble, as in water, glass, etc.Arsenic abounds with air blebs. Kirwan.
Containing blebs, or characterized by blebs; as, blebby glass.
Complexion; color; hue; likeness; form. [Archaic]For him which is so bright of blee. Lament. of Mary Magd.That boy has a strong blee of his father. Forby.
Emitting, or appearing to emit, blood or sap, etc.; also,expressing anguish or compassion.

Any mark of deformity or injury, whether physical or moral;anything; that diminishes beauty, or renders imperfect that which isotherwise well formed; that which impairs reputation.He shall take two he lambs without blemish, and one ewe lamb of thefirst year without blemish. Lev. xiv. 10.The reliefs of an envious man are those little blemishes andimperfections that discover themselves in an illustrious character.Spectator.
Without blemish; spotless.A life in all so blemishless. Feltham.
The state of being blemished; blemish; disgrace; damage;impairment.For dread of blame and honor's blemishment. Spenser.
A looking aside or askance. [Obs.]These blenches gave my heart another youth. Shak.
To mingle; to mix; to unite intimately; to pass or shadeinsensibly into each other, as colors.There is a tone of solemn and sacred feeling that blends with ourconviviality. Irving.
One who, or that which, blends; an instrument, as a brush, usedin blending.
The method of laying on different tints so that they may mingletogether while wet, and shade into each other insensibly. Weale.
Pertaining to, consisting of, or containing, blende.
A distemper incident to cattle, in which their livers areaffected. Crabb.
A small variety of spaniel, kept as a pet.
To blink; to shine; to look. [Obs.]
A marine fish of the genus Blennius or family Blenniidæ; -- socalled from its coating of mucus. The species are numerous.
Mingled; mixed; blended; also, polluted; stained.Rider and horse, friend, foe, in one red burial blent. Byron.
Inflammation of the eyelids. -- Bleph`a*rit"ic (#), a.
A South African antelope (Alcelaphus albifrons), having a largewhite spot on the forehead.
Happily; fortunately; joyfully.We shall blessedly meet again never to depart. Sir P. Sidney.

The state of being blessed; happiness; felicity; bliss;heavenly joys; the favor of God.The assurance of a future blessedness. Tillotson.Single blessedness, the unmarried state. "Grows, lives, and dies insingle blessedness." Shak.
One who blesses; one who bestows or invokes a blessing.
Blessed. "This patriarch blest." Milton.White these blest sounds my ravished ear assail. Trumbull.
A form of decay in fruit which is overripe.
The supposed faculty of perceiving subterraneous springs andcurrents by sensation; -- so called from one Bleton, of France.
A form of decay seen in fleshy, overripe fruit. Lindley.
An inflammation in the foot of a horse, between the sole andthe bone. [Obs.]
A tin dinner pail. [Local, U. S.] Bartlett.
To be affected by blight; to blast; as, this vine neverblights.
To stop; to cease; to desist. [Obs.] Spenser.

Abortive; failing to produce flowers or fruit; as, blind buds;blind flowers. Blind alley, an alley closed at one end; a cul-de-sac.-- Blind axle, an axle which turns but does not communicate motion.Knight.-- Blind beetle, one of the insects apt to fly against people, esp.at night.-- Blind cat (Zoöl.), a species of catfish (Gronias nigrolabris),nearly destitute of eyes, living in caverns in Pennsylvania.-- Blind coal, coal that burns without flame; anthracite coal.Simmonds.-- Blind door, Blind window, an imitation of a door or window,without an opening for passage or light. See Blank door or window,under Blank, a.-- Blind level (Mining), a level or drainage gallery which has avertical shaft at each end, and acts as an inverted siphon. Knight.-- Blind nettle (Bot.), dead nettle. See Dead nettle, under Dead.-- Blind shell (Gunnery), a shell containing no charge, or one thatdoes not explode.-- Blind side, the side which is most easily assailed; a weak orunguarded side; the side on which one is least able or disposed tosee danger. Swift.-- Blind snake (Zoöl.), a small, harmless, burrowing snake, of thefamily Typhlopidæ, with rudimentary eyes.-- Blind spot (Anat.), the point in the retina of the eye where theoptic nerve enters, and which is insensible to light.-- Blind tooling, in bookbinding and leather work, the indentedimpression of heated tools, without gilding; -- called also blanktooling, and blind blocking.-- Blind wall, a wall without an opening; a blank wall.
A post-office clerk whose duty is to decipher obscureaddresses.
A cover or protection for an advanced trench or approach,formed of fascines and earth supported by a framework.
One of the leather screens on a bridle, to hinder a horse fromseeing objects at the side; a blinker.
A small fish (Amblyopsis spelæus) destitute of eyes, found inthe waters of the Mammoth Cave, in Kentucky. Related fishes fromother caves take the same name.
To cover the eyes of, as with a bandage; to hinder from seeing.And when they had blindfolded him, they struck him on the face. Lukexxii. 64.
Making blind or as if blind; depriving of sight or ofunderstanding; obscuring; as, blinding tears; blinding snow.
Without sight, discernment, or understanding; without thought,investigation, knowledge, or purpose of one's own.By his imperious mistress blindly led. Dryden.
State or condition of being blind, literally or figuratively.Darwin. Color blindness, inability to distinguish certain color. SeeDaltonism.
The triforium as opposed to the clearstory.

A small, burrowing, snakelike, limbless lizard (Anguisfragilis), with minute eyes, popularly believed to be blind; theslowworm; -- formerly a name for the adder.Newts and blindworms do no wrong. Shak.
The dazzling whiteness about the horizon caused by thereflection of light from fields of ice at sea; ice blink.
Beer kept unbroached until it is sharp. Crabb.
A kind of goggles, used to protect the eyes form glare, etc.
A gust of wind and rain. Ham. Nav. Encyc.
Orig., blithesomeness; gladness; now, the highest degree ofhappiness; blessedness; exalted felicity; heavenly joy.An then at last our bliss Full and perfect is. Milton.
Full of, characterized by, or causing, joy and felicity; happyin the highest degree. "Blissful solitude." Milton.-- Bliss"ful*ly, adv.-- Bliss"ful*ness, n.
Destitute of bliss. Sir P. Sidney.
To be lustful; to be lascivious. [Obs.]
To be affected with a blister or blisters; to have a blisterform on.Let my tongue blister. Shak.
A genus of herbs (Blitum) with a fleshy calyx. Blitum capitatumis the strawberry blite.
Gay; merry; sprightly; joyous; glad; cheerful; as, a blithespirit.The blithe sounds of festal music. Prescott.A daughter fair, So buxom, blithe, and debonair. Milton.
The state of being blithe. Chaucer.
Cheery; gay; merry.The blithesome sounds of wassail gay. Sir W. Scott.-- Blithe"some*ly, adv.-- Blithe"some*ness, n.
A gale of piercingly cold wind, usually accompanied with fineand blinding snow; a furious blast. [U. S.]
To grow turgid as by effusion of liquid in the cellular tissue;to puff out; to swell. Arbuthnot.
Distended beyond the natural or usual size, as by the presenceof water, serum, etc.; turgid; swollen; as, a bloated face. Also,puffed up with pride; pompous.
The common herring, esp. when of large size, smoked, and halfdried; -- called also bloat herring.
A small fresh-water fish (Uranidea Richardsoni); the miller'sthumb.
A bubble; blubber. [Low] T. Carew. Blobber lip, a thick,protruding lip.His blobber lips and beetle brows commend. Dryden.
Having thick lips. "A blobber-lipped shell." Grew.
The roughest and cheapest sort of rubblework, in masonry.
The perch on which a bird of prey is kept.
A book printed from engraved wooden blocks instead of movabletypes.
A chain in which the alternate links are broad blocks connectedby thin side links pivoted to the ends of the blocks, used withsprocket wheels to transmit power, as in a bicycle.

One of the danger signals or safety signals which guide themovement of trains in a block system. The signal is often so coupledwith a switch that act of opening or closing the switch operates thesignal also.

A system by which the track is divided into short sections, asof three or four miles, and trains are so run by the guidance ofelectric, or combined electric and pneumatic, signals that no trainenters a section or block until the preceding train has left it, asin absolute blocking, or that a train may be allowed to followanother into a block as long as it proceeds with excessive caution,as in permissive blocking.
The act of blocking up; the state of being blocked up.
A stupid fellow; a dolt; a person deficient in understanding.The bookful blockhead, ignorantly read, With loads of learned lumberin his head. Pope.
That which characterizes a blockhead; stupidity. Carlyle.

An edifice or structure of heavy timbers or logs for militarydefense, having its sides loopholed for musketry, and often an upperstory projecting over the lower, or so placed upon it as to have itssides make an angle wit the sides of the lower story, thus enablingthe defenders to fire downward, and in all directions; -- formerlymuch used in America and Germany.
The finishing course of a wall showing above a cornice.
Like a block; deficient in understanding; stupid; dull."Blockish Ajax." Shak.-- Block"ish*ly, adv.-- Block"ish*ness, n.
A hydrous sulphate of magnesium and sodium.
A variety of clay ironstone, in Staffordshire, England, usedfor making tools.
A kind of silk lace originally of the color of raw silk, nowsometimes dyed; -- called also blond lace.
The state of being blond. G. Eliot.
Descent from parents of recognized breed; excellence or purityof breed.
Any vessel or canal in which blood circulates in an animal, asan artery or vein.
Having the hair matted with clotted blood. [Obs. & R.]The blood-boltered Banquo smiles upon me. Shak.
An Australian honeysucker (Myzomela sanguineolata); -- socalled from the bright red color of the male bird.
Having pure blood, or a large admixture or pure blood; ofapproved breed; of the best stock.
A genus of bulbous plants, natives of Southern Africa, namedHæmanthus, of the Amaryllis family. The juice of H. toxicarius isused by the Hottentots to poison their arrows.
Guilty of murder or bloodshed. "A bloodguilty life." Fairfax.-- Blood"guilt`i*ness (, n.-- Blood"guilt`less, a.

A breed of large and powerful dogs, with long, smooth, andpendulous ears, and remarkable for acuteness of smell. It is employedto recover game or prey which has escaped wounded from a hunter, andfor tracking criminals. Formerly it was used for pursuing runawayslaves. Other varieties of dog are often used for the same purposeand go by the same name. The Cuban bloodhound is said to be a varietyof the mastiff.
In a bloody manner; cruelly; with a disposition to shed blood.
One who, or that which, lets blood; a phlebotomist.
The act or process of letting blood or bleeding, as by openinga vein or artery, or by cupping or leeches; -- esp. applied tovenesection.

A plant (Sanguinaria Canadensis), with a red root and red sap,and bearing a pretty, white flower in early spring; -- called alsopuccoon, redroot, bloodwort, tetterwort, turmeric, and Indian paint.It has acrid emetic properties, and the rootstock is used as astimulant expectorant. See Sanguinaria.
The shedding or spilling of blood; slaughter; the act ofshedding human blood, or taking life, as in war, riot, or murder.
One who sheds blood; a manslayer; a murderer.
Red and inflamed; suffused with blood, or having the vesselsturgid with blood, as when the conjunctiva is inflamed or irritated.His eyes were bloodshot, . . . and his hair disheveled. Dickens.
A piece of hard wood loaded at one end with lead, and used tostrike the fleam into the vein. Youatt.
Loss of sensation and motion from hemorrhage or congestion inthe brain. Dunglison.
Any animal that sucks blood; esp., the leech (Hirudomedicinalis), and related species.
Eager to shed blood; cruel; sanguinary; murderous.-- Blood"thirst`i*ness (n.
A tree having the wood or the sap of the color of blood.

A plant, Rumex sanguineus, or bloody-veined dock. The name isapplied also to bloodroot (Sanguinaria Canadensis), and to anextensive order of plants (Hæmodoraceæ), the roots of many species ofwhich contain a red coloring matter useful in dyeing.
The dysentery, a disease in which the flux or discharge fromthe bowels has a mixture of blood. Arbuthnot.
A red hand, as in the arms of Ulster, which is now thedistinguishing mark of a baronet of the United Kingdom.
A sweat accompanied by a discharge of blood; a disease, calledsweating sickness, formerly prevalent in England and other countries.
Having a cruel, ferocious disposition; bloodthirsty. Dryden.
A popular term for a bright-hued variety of some minerals; as,the rose-red cobalt bloom.
A furnace and forge in which wrought iron in the form of bloomsis made directly from the ore, or (more rarely) from cast iron.
The process of making blooms from the ore or from cast iron.
Bloom; a blossoming. [Prov. Eng.]All that blooth means heavy autumn work for him and his hands. T.Hardy.
The act of blowing; a roaring wind; a blast. [Obs.]A most tempestuous blore. Chapman.
To take a blot; as, this paper blots easily.
A large pustule, or a coarse eruption.Foul scurf and blotches him defile. Thomson.
Marked or covered with blotches.To give their blotched and blistered bodies ease. Drayton.
To cure, as herrings, by salting and smoking them; to bloat.[Obs.]
A wastebook, in which entries of transactions are made as theytake place.
Characterized by blots or heavy touches; coarsely depicted;wanting in delineation. Ruskin.
A kind of thick, bibulous, unsized paper, used to absorbsuperfluous ink from freshly written manuscript, and thus preventblots.
A light, loose over-garment, like a smock frock, wornespecially by workingmen in France; also, a loose coat of anymaterial, as the undress uniform coat of the United States army.
To flower; to blossom; to bloom.How blows the citron grove. Milton.
as, a blow-off cock or pipe.
The cleaning of the flues of a boiler from scale, etc., by ablast of steam.
The downy seed head of a dandelion, which children delight toblow away. B. Jonson.

A device for producing a current of air; as: (a) A metal platetemporarily placed before the upper part of a grate or open fire. (b)A machine for producing an artificial blast or current of air bypressure, as for increasing the draft of a furnace, ventilating abuilding or shaft, cleansing gram, etc.
Any species of fly of the genus Musca that deposits its eggs oryoung larvæ (called flyblows and maggots) upon meat or other animalproducts.

A tube, as of cane or reed, sometimes twelve feet long, throughwhich an arrow or other projectile may be impelled by the force ofthe breath. It is a weapon much used by certain Indians of Americaand the West Indies; -- called also blowpipe, and blowtube. SeeSumpitan.
An air hole in a casting.
Opened; in blossom or having blossomed, as a flower. Shak.
A blossoming; a bloom. [Obs. or Archaic] "In the blowth andbud." Sir W. Raleigh.
A long wrought iron tube, on the end of which the workmangathers a quantity of "metal" (melted glass), and through which heblows to expand or shape it; -- called also blowing tube, andblowpipe.
Windy; as, blowy weather; a blowy upland.
A ruddy, fat-faced woman; a wench. [Obs.] Shak.
Having high color from exposure to the weather; ruddy-faced;blowzy; disordered.Huge women blowzed with health and wind. Tennyson.
Coarse and ruddy-faced; fat and ruddy; high colored; frowzy.
To swell; to puff out, as with weeping. [Obs.]
A large sea nettle or medusa.
Swollen; turgid; as, a blubbered lip. Spenser.
The act of weeping noisily.He spake well save that his blubbering interrupted him. Winthrop.
A kind of half boot, named from the Prussian general Blücher.Thackeray.
A short stick, with one end loaded, or thicker and heavier thatthe other, used as an offensive weapon.
Low spirits; a fit of despondency; melancholy. [Colloq.] Berlinblue, Prussian blue.-- Mineral blue. See under Mineral.-- Prussian blue. See under Prussian.

A species of grass (Poa compressa) with bluish green stems,valuable in thin gravelly soils; wire grass. Kentucky blue grass, aspecies of grass (Poa pratensis) which has running rootstocks andspreads rapidly. It is valuable as a pasture grass, as it enduresboth winter and drought better than other kinds, and is verynutritious.

The State of Delaware; -- a popular sobriquet. It is said,though the story lacks proof, to have taken its origin from theinsistence of a Delaware Revolutionary captain, named Caldwell, thatno cock could be truly game unless the mother was a blue hen, whenceBlue Hen's Chickens came to be a nickname for the people of Delaware.
The common jay of the United States (Cyanocitta, or Cyanura,cristata). The predominant color is bright blue.
a grasslike plant (Sisyrinchium anceps), with small flowers ofa delicate blue color.
The Sate of Kentucky; -- a nickname alluding to the blue-grassregion, where fine horses are bred.
A name given to fluor spar in Derbyshire, where it is used forornamental purposes.

A law enacted to provide for the regulation and supervision ofinvestment companies in order to protect the public against companiesthat do not intend to do a fair and honest business and that offerinvestments that do not promise a fair return; -- so called becausethe promises made by some investment companies are as boundless oralluring as the blue sky, or, perhaps, because designed to clear awaythe clouds and fogs from the simple investor's horizon. [Colloq.]
Having blue veins or blue streaks.

The hero of a mediæval French nursery legend, who, leavinghome, enjoined his young wife not to open a certain room in hiscastle. She entered it, and found the murdered bodies of his formerwives.-- Also used adjectively of a subject which it is forbidden toinvestigate.The Bluebeard chamber of his mind, into which no eye but his own mustlook. Carlyle.

The berry of several species of Vaccinium, and ericaceousgenus, differing from the American huckleberries in containingnumerous minute seeds instead of ten nutlets. The commonest speciesare V. Pennsylvanicum and V. vacillans. V. corymbosum is the tallblueberry.
A duck of the genus Fuligula. Two American species (F. marilaand F. affinis) are common. See Scaup duck.

A small song bird (Sialia sialis), very common in the UnitedStates, and, in the north, one of the earliest to arrive in spring.The male is blue, with the breast reddish. It is related to theEuropean robin. Pairy bluebird (Zoöl.), a brilliant Indian or EastIndian bird of the genus Irena, of several species.
A plant (Centaurea cyanus) which grows in grain fields. Itreceives its name from its blue bottle-shaped flowers.
A small European bird; the blue-throated warbler.
One dressed in blue, as a soldier, a sailor, a beadle, etc.
A species of whitefish (Coregonus nigripinnis) found in LakeMichigan.
One of a class of paupers or pensioners, or licensed beggars,in Scotland, to whim annually on the king's birthday were distributedcertain alms, including a blue gown; a beadsman.
The quality of being blue; a blue color. Boyle.
A nickname for a Nova Scotian.
A kind of salmon (Salmo Cambricus) found in Wales.
The character or manner of a bluestocking; female pedantry.[Colloq.]
A singing bird of northern Europe and Asia (Cyanecula Suecica),related to the nightingales; -- called also blue-throated robin andblue-throated warbler.
A name given to several different species of plants having blueflowers, as the Houstonia coerulea, the Centaurea cyanus orbluebottle, and the Vaccinium angustifolium.
To deter (an opponent) from taking the risk of betting on hishand of cards, as the bluffer does by betting heavily on his own handalthough it may be of less value. [U. S.]
Built with the stem nearly straight up and down.
Built with the stem nearly straight up and down.
The quality or state of being bluff.
Somewhat blue; as, bluish veins. "Bluish mists." Dryden.-- Blu"ish*ly, adv.-- Blu"ish*ness, n.
One who is apt to blunder.
To amalgamate and blend; to beat up or mix in water, as clay.
A wooden blade with a cross handle, used for mi Tomlinson.
The process of mixing clay in potteries with a blunger.Tomlinson.
Dull; stupid.Blunt-witted lord, ignoble in demeanor! Shak.

In a blunt manner; coarsely; plainly; abruptly; withoutdelicacy, or the usual forms of civility.Sometimes after bluntly giving his opinions, he would quietly layhimself asleep until the end of their deliberations. Jeffrey.

To utter suddenly and unadvisedly; to divulge inconsiderately;to ejaculate; -- commonly with out.Others . . . can not hold, but blurt out, those words which afterwardthey forced to eat. Hakewill.To blurt at, to speak contemptuously of. [Obs.] Shak.
Full of blushes.While from his ardent look the turning Spring Averts her blushfulface. Thomson.
Showing blushes; rosy red; having a warm and delicate colorlike some roses and other flowers; blooming; ruddy; roseate.The dappled pink and blushing rose. Prior.
In a blushing manner; with a blush or blushes; as, to answer orconfess blushingly.
Free from blushes; incapable of blushing; shameless; impudent.Vice now, secure, her blushless front shall raise. Dodsley.
Like a blush; having the color of a blush; rosy. [R.] "A blushycolor." Harvey.

To utter, or do, with noisy violence; to force by blustering;to bully.He bloweth and blustereth out . . . his abominable blasphemy. Sir T.More.As if therewith he meant to bluster all princes into a perfectobedience to his commands. Fuller.
One who, or that which, blusters; a noisy swaggerer.
Inclined to bluster; given to blustering; blustering. Motley.
An exclamation used to startle or frighten. [Spelt also boh andboo.]

The peepul tree; esp., the very ancient tree standing atAnurajahpoora in Ceylon, grown from a slip of the tree under whichGautama is said to have received the heavenly light and so to havebecome Buddha.The sacred bo tree of the Buddhists (Ficus religiosa), which isplanted close to every temple, and attracts almost as much venerationas the status of the god himself. . . . It differs from the banyan(Ficus Indica) by sending down no roots from its branches. Tennent.
A genus of large American serpents, including the boaconstrictor, the emperor boa of Mexico (B. imperator), and thechevalier boa of Peru (B. eques).
A large and powerful serpent of tropical America, sometimestwenty or thirty feet long. See Illustration in Appendix.
Any declamatory and vociferous preacher or orator.
The uncastrated male of swine; specifically, the wild hog.
The stage in a theater; as, to go upon the boards, to enterupon the theatrical profession.
That can be boarded, as a ship.
One who boards a ship; one selected to board an enemy's ship.Totten.
