Coupled without intermediate connections, as an engine and adynamo.
One who directs; a director. Directer plane (Geom.), the planeto which all right-lined elements in a warped surface are parallel.
The pointing of a piece with reference to an imaginary verticalaxis; -- distinguished from elevation. The direction is given whenthe plane of sight passes through the object. Wilhelm.
The quality of being direct; straightness; straightforwardness;immediateness.
A style of dress prevalent at the time of the French Directory,characterized by great extravagance of design and imitating the Greekand Roman costumes.
A part of a machine or instrument which directs its motion oraction.
The office of director; also, a body of directors takenjointly.
The condition or office of a director; directorate.
A woman who directs. Bp. Hurd.
Dire; dreadful; terrible; calamitous; woeful; as, a direfulfiend; a direful day.-- Dire"ful*ly, adv.-- Dire"ful*ness, n.
A tearing apart; violent separation. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.
The act of plundering, despoiling, or snatching away. [R.]Speed.
With plundering violence; by violent injustice. [R.] Strype.
A piece of music of a mournful character, to accompany funeralrites; a funeral hymn.The raven croaked, and hollow shrieks of owls Sung dirges at herfuneral. Ford.
Funereal; moaning.Soothed sadly by the dirgeful wind. Coleridge.

A service for the dead, in the Roman Catholic Church, being thefirst antiphon of Matins for the dead, of which Dirige is the firstword; a dirge.Evensongs and placebo and dirige. Wyclif.Resort, I pray you, unto my sepulture To sing my dirige with greatdevotion. Lamentation of Mary Magdalene.
Capable of being directed; steerable; as, a dirigible balloon.
Absolute. Diriment impediment (R. C. Ch.), an impediment thatnullifies marriage.
A kind of dagger or poniard; -- formerly much used by theScottish Highlander. Dirk knife, a clasp knife having a large,dirklike blade.
To thrill; to vibrate; to penetrate. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.
To make foul of filthy; to dirty. Swift.
In a dirty manner; foully; nastily; filthily; meanly; sordidly.
The state of being dirty; filthiness; foulness; nastiness;baseness; sordidness.
Lacking ability; unable. [Obs.] "Our disable and unactiveforce." Daniel.

To set free from mistakes; to undeceive; to disengage fromfallacy or deception; to set right.To undeceive and disabuse the people. South.If men are now sufficiently enlightened to disabuse themselves orartifice, hypocrisy, and superstition, they will consider this eventas an era in their history. J. Adams.
To put to inconvenience; to incommode. [R.] Bp. Warburton.
A state of being unaccommodated or unsuited. [R.] Sir M. Hale.
To destroy the force of habit in; to wean from a custom.Johnson.
To refuse to acknowledge; to deny; to disown. [Obs.] South.
To render unacquainted; to make unfamiliar. [Obs.]While my sick heart With dismal smart Is disacquainted never.Herrick.
Neglect of disuse of familiarity, or familiar acquaintance.[Obs.] South.
A white amorphous substance obtained as a polymericmodification of acrolein.
To draw back, or cause to draw back. [Obs.] Spenser.
To injure the interest of; to be detrimental to.

Attended with disadvantage; unfavorable to success orprosperity; inconvenient; prejudicial; -- opposed to advantageous;as, the situation of an army is disadvantageous for attack ordefense.Even in the disadvantageous position in which he had been placed, hegave clear indications of future excellence. Prescott.-- Dis*ad`van*ta"geous*ly, adv.-- Dis*ad`van*ta"geous*ness, n.
To advise against; to dissuade from. [R.] Boyle.
Alienated in feeling; not wholly loyal. J. H. Newman.-- Dis`af*fect"ed*ly, adv.-- Dis`af*fect"ed*ness, n.
Not disposed to affection; unfriendly; disaffected. [R.]Blount.
To refuse to confirm; to annul, as a judicial decision, by acontrary judgment of a superior tribunal.
Overthrow or annulment by the decision of a superior tribunal;as, disaffirmance of judgment.
The act of disaffirming; negation; refutation.
To reduce from the privileges of a forest to the state ofcommon ground; to exempt from forest laws.By charter 9 Henry III. many forests were disafforested. Blackstone.
To destroy the aggregation of; to separate into componentparts, as an aggregate mass.
The separation of an aggregate body into its component parts.
The state or quality of being; disagreeable; unpleasantness.
In a disagreeable manner; unsuitably; offensively.
To alienate from allegiance. [Obs. & R.] Milton.

To refuse to allow; to deny the force or validity of; to disownand reject; as, the judge disallowed the executor's charge.To whom coming, as unto a living stone, disallowed indeed of men, butchosen of God. 1 Pet. ii. 4.That the edicts of Cæsar we may at all times disallow, but thestatutes of God for no reason we may reject. Milton.
Not allowable; not to be suffered. Raleigh.-- Dis`al*low"a*ble*ness, n.
The act of disallowing; refusal to admit or permit; rejection.
To part, as an alliance; to sunder. [R.] "Disallied theirnuptials." Milton.
To raise the anchor of, as a ship; to weigh anchor. [Obs.]Heywood.
To disunite; to undo or repeal the annexation of. State Trials(1608).
To annul completely; to render void or of no effect.For the Lord of hosts hath purposed, and who shall disannul Isaiahxiv. 27.
To invalidate the consecration of; as, to disanoint a king.[Obs.] Milton.
To disrobe; to strip of apparel; to make naked.Drink disapparels the soul. Junius (1635).
The act of disappearing; cessation of appearance; removal fromsight; vanishing. Addison.
p. pr. & vb. n. of Disappear.
A detachment or separation from a former connection. [R.]
Freed from a former connection or dependence; disconnected.[R.]
To undervalue; not to esteem.-- Dis`ap*pre`ci*a"tion, n.
The act of disapproving; mental condemnation of what is judgedwrong, unsuitable, or inexpedient; feeling of censure.We have ever expressed the most unqualified disapprobation of all thesteps. Burke.
Severed from the appropriation or possession of a spiritualcorporation.The appropriation may be severed, and the church becomedisappropriate, two ways. Blackstone.
The act of divesting of armature. [R.]
Deprived of claws, and teeth or beaks. Cussans.
To unsettle or disturb the order or due arrangement of; tothrow out of order.
The act of disarranging, or the state of being disarranged;confusion; disorder. Cowper.
To sunder; to separate, as joints.-- Dis`ar*tic`u*la"tion, n.
One who disarticulates and prepares skeletons.
One who disassents; a dissenter. [Obs.] State Trials (1634).
Want of as siduity or care. [R.] Sir H. Wotton.

The decomposition of complex substances, within the organism,into simpler ones suitable only for excretion, with evolution ofenergy, -- a normal nutritional process the reverse of assimilation;downward metabolism.The breaking down of already existing chemical compounds into simplerones, sometimes called disassimilation. Martin.
Having power to disassimilate; of the nature ofdisassimilation.Disassimilative processes constitute a marked feature in the life ofanimal cells. McKendrick.
To disconnect from things associated; to disunite; todissociate. Florio.
To deprive of credit or authority; to discredit. [R.] W.Wotton.
To retard; to repel; to do damage to. [Obs.] Chaucer.
The act of disavowing, disclaiming, or disowning; rejection anddenial.An earnest disavowal of fear often proceeds from fear. Richardson.
To become separated, broken up, dissolved, or scattered;especially, to quit military service by breaking up organization.
To expel from the bar, or the legal profession; to deprive (anattorney, barrister, or counselor) of his status and privileges assuch. Abbott.
To debase or degrade. [Obs.]Nor you nor your house were so much as spoken of before I disbasedmyself. B. Jonson.

The act of disbelieving;; a state of the mind in which one isfully persuaded that an opinion, assertion, or doctrine is not true;refusal of assent, credit, or credence; denial of belief.Our belief or disbelief of a thing does not alter the nature of thething. Tillotson.No sadder proof can be given by a man of his own littleness thatdisbelief in great men. Carlyle.

Not to believe; to refuse belief or credence to; to hold not tobe true or actual.Assertions for which there is abundant positive evidence are oftendisbelieved, on account of what is called their improbability orimpossibility. J. S. Mill.
One who disbelieves, or refuses belief; an unbeliever.Specifically, one who does not believe the Christian religion. I.Watts.
To deprive (a bencher) of his privileges. Mozley & W.
Converting forest land into cleared or arable land; removal ofa forest. Sir W. Scott.
To divest of a branch or branches; to tear off. Shak.
To deprive of buds or shoots, as for training, or economizingthe vital strength of a tree.

To rid of a burden; to free from a load borne or from somethingoppressive; to unload; to disencumber; to relieve.He did it to disburden a conscience. Feltham.My mediations . . . will, I hope, be more calm, being thusdisburdened. Hammond.
To strip of burgeons or buds; to disbud. [R.] Holland.

To pay out; to expend; -- usually from a public fund ortreasury.The duty of collecting and disbursing his revenues. Macaulay.Disbursing officer, an officer in any department of the publicservice who is charged with the duty of paying out public money.
To disburden; to relieve of a load. [Archaic]
Pertaining to, or resembling, a disk; as, discal cells.
To pull off shoes or sandals from. [Obs.] Cockeram.
Deprived off shoes or sandals; unshod; discalced.
The act of pulling off the shoes or sandals. [Obs.] Sir T.Browne.
Unshod; barefooted; -- in distinction from calced. "Thefoundation of houses of discalced friars." Cardinal Manning's St.Teresa.
To drive from a camp. [Obs.] Holland.
To melt; to dissolve; to thaw. [Obs.]
To deprive of capacity; to incapacitate. [R.]
To throw out of one's hand, as superfluous cards; to lay aside(a card or cards).
To yield or give up; to depart. [Obs.]I dare not discede from my copy a tittle. Fuller.
To debate; to discuss. [R.]One dissertates, he is candid; Two must discept, -- hasdistinguished. R. Browning.
Controversy; disputation; discussion. [Archaic]Verbose janglings and endless disceptations. Strype.
One who arbitrates or decides. [R.] Cowley.
One who, or that which, discerns, distinguishes, perceives, orjudges; as, a discerner of truth, of right and wrong.A great observer and discerner of men's natures. Clarendon.

Capable of being discerned by the eye or the understanding; as,a star is discernible by the eye; the identity of difference of ideasis discernible by the understanding.The effect of the privations and sufferings . . . was discernible tothe last in his temper and deportment. Macaulay.
In a manner to be discerned; perceptibly; visibly. Hammond.
In a discerning manner; with judgment; judiciously; acutely.Garth.
Capability or liableness to be discerped. [R.] Wollaston.
The act of pulling to pieces, or of separating the parts. Bp.Hall.
Tending to separate or disunite parts. Encys. Dict.

To throw off or deliver a load, charge, or burden; to unload;to emit or give vent to fluid or other contents; as, the water pipedischarges freely.The cloud, if it were oily or fatty, would not discharge. Bacon.
One who, or that which, discharges. Specifically, inelectricity, an instrument for discharging a Leyden jar, orelectrical battery, by making a connection between the two surfaces;a discharging rod.
To deprive of status as a church, or of membership in a church.Bp. Hall.
To divide; to cleave in two. [Obs.] Spenser.
A genus of Branchiopoda, having a disklike shell, attached byone valve, which is perforated by the peduncle.
Ungirded; loosely dressed. [R.] Sir W. Scott.

One who receives instruction from another; a scholar; alearner; especially, a follower who has learned to believe in thetruth of the doctrine of his teacher; an adherent in doctrine; as,the disciples of Plato; the disciples of our Savior. The disciples,or The twelve disciples, the twelve selected companions of Jesus; --also called the apostles.-- Disciples of Christ. See Christian, n., 3, and Campbellite.
The state of being a disciple or follower in doctrines andprecepts. Jer. Taylor.
The quality of being improvable by discipline. Sir M. Hale.

Pertaining to discipline; intended for discipline; corrective;belonging to a course of training.Those canons . . . were only disciplinary. Bp. Ferne.The evils of the . . . are disciplinary and remedial. Buckminster.
The enforcement of methods of correction against one guilty ofecclesiastical offenses; reformatory or penal action toward a churchmember.
To relinquish or deny having a claim; to disavow another'sclaim; to decline accepting, as an estate, interest, or office.Burrill.
A denial, disavowal, or renunciation, as of a title, claim,interest, estate, or trust; relinquishment or waiver of an interestor estate. Burrill.
A disavowing or disowning. Bp. Hall.
To disclaim; to expel. [Obs.] "Money did love disclame."Spenser.
To injure one's good name; to slander. [Obs.]
To take off a cloak from; to uncloak. [Obs.] B. Jonson.
Represented with wings expanded; -- applied to doves and otherbirds not of prey. Cussans.
A shutting off; exclusion. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

To depart; to quit the coast (that is, the side or border) ofanything; to be separated. [Obs.]As far as heaven and earth discoasted lie. G. Fletcher.To discoast from the plain and simple way of speech. Barrow.
Applied to a form of egg cleavage seen in osseous fishes, whichoccurs only in a small disk that separates from the rest of the egg.
A division of amphibians having suctorial disks on the toes, asthe tree frogs.
Having sucking disks on the toes, as the tree frogs.

Having the form of a disk, as those univalve shells which havethe whorls in one plane, so as to form a disk, as the pearlynautilus. Discoid flower (Bot.), a compound flower, consisting oftubular florets only, as a tansy, lacking the rays which are seen inthe daisy and sunflower.
One of a species of coccoliths, having an oval discoidal body,with a thick strongly refracting rim, and a thinner central portion.One of them measures about

The act of discomfiting, or the state of being discomfited;rout; overthrow; defeat; frustration; confusion and dejection.Every man's sword was against his fellow, and there was a very greatdiscomfiture. 1 Sam. xiv. 20.A hope destined to end . . . in discomfiture and disgrace. Macaulay.
Deserving, disapprobation or blame.-- Dis`com*mend"a*ble*ness, n.
One who discommends; a dispraiser. Johnson.
To deprive of a commission or trust. [R.] Laud.
To put inconvenience; to incommode; to trouble. [R.]
Inconvenient; troublesome; incommodious. [R.] Spenser.-- Dis`com*mo"di*ous*ly, adv.-- Dis`com*mo"di*ous*ness, n.
To deprive of commonable quality, as lands, by inclosing orappropriating. Burrill.

A lack of common possessions, properties, or relationship.Community of embryonic structure reveals community of descent; butdissimilarity of embryonic development does not prove discommunity ofdescent. Darwin.
To free from company; to dissociate. [R.]It she be alone now, and discompanied. B. Jonson.
To change the complexion or hue of. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.
Failure or refusal to comply; noncompliance.A compliance will discommend me to Mr. Coventry, and a discomplianceto my lord chancellor. Pepys.
Disordered; disturbed; disquieted.-- Dis`com*pos"ed*ly, adv.-- Dis`com*pos"ed*ness, n.
Want of concert; disagreement. Sir W. Temple.
The act of disconcerting, or state of being disconcerted;discomposure; perturbation. [R.] State Trials (1794).
Not conformable.Disconformable in religion from us. Stow (1603).

Want of conformity or correspondence; inconsistency;disagreement.Those . . . in some disconformity to ourselves. Milton.Disagreement and disconformity betwixt the speech and the conceptionof the mind. Hakewill.
Incongruity; disagreement; unsuitableness. Sir M. Hale.

To dissolve the union or connection of; to disunite; to sever;to separate; to disperse.The commonwealth itself would . . . be disconnected into the dust andpowder of individuality. Burke.This restriction disconnects bank paper and the precious metals.Walsh.
The act of disconnecting, or state of being disconnected;separation; want of union.Nothing was therefore to be left in all the subordinate members butweakness, disconnection, and confusion. Burke.
To deprive of consecration or sacredness. [R.]
To differ; to disagree; to dissent. [Obs.] Milton.
The state of being disconsolate. [Obs.] Barrow.
Disconsolate. [Obs.]A poor, disconsolated, drooping creature. Sterne.
Not content; discontented; dissatisfied. Jer. Taylor.Passion seemed to be much discontent, but Patience was very quiet.Bunyan.

Dissatisfied; uneasy in mind; malcontent.And every one that was in distress, and every one that was in debt,and every one that was discontented, gathered themselves unto him. 1Sam. xxii. 2.-- Dis`con*tent"ed*ly, adv.-- Dis`con*tent"ed*ness, n.
Relating or tending to discontent. [R.] "Pride is everdiscontentive." Feltham.
The state of being discontented; uneasiness; inquietude. Bacon.

Breach or interruption of continuity; separation of parts in aconnected series; discontinuance.Upon any discontinuation of parts, made either by bubbles or byshaking the glass, the whole mercury falls. Sir I. Newton.

To interrupt the continuance of; to intermit, as a practice orhabit; to put an end to; to cause to cease; to cease using, to stop;to leave off.Set up their conventicles again, which had been discontinued. Bp.Burnet.I have discontinued school Above a twelvemonth. Shak.Taught the Greek tongue, discontinued before in these parts the spaceof seven hundred years. Daniel.They modify and discriminate the voice, without appearing todiscontinue it. Holder.
One whose possession of an estate is broken off, ordiscontinued; one whose estate is subject to discontinuance.
One who discontinues, or breaks off or away from; an absentee.He was no gadder abroad, not discontinuer from his convent for a longtime. Fuller.
Want of continuity or cohesion; disunion of parts."Discontinuity of surface." Boyle.
One who deprives another of the possession of an estate bydiscontinuance. See Discontinuance, 2.
Not convenient or congruous; unsuitable; ill-adapted. [Obs.]Bp. Reynolds.
A division of acalephs or jellyfishes, including most of thelarge disklike species.-- Dis*coph"o*rous, a.

Union of musical sounds which strikes the ear harshly ordisagreeably, owing to the incommensurability of the vibrations whichthey produce; want of musical concord or harmony; a chord demandingresolution into a concord.For a discord itself is but a harshness of divers sounds mBacon.Apple of discord. See under Apple.
That may produce discord; disagreeing; discordant. [R.]Halliwell.
Dissonant; not in harmony or musical concord; harsh; jarring;as, discordant notes or sounds.For still their music seemed to start Discordant echoes in eachheart. Longfellow.
Full of discord; contentious. [Obs.] "His discordful dame."Spenser.
Deprived of the privileges or form of a body corporate. [Obs.]Jas. II.
To lend, or make a practice of lending, money, abating thediscount; as, the discount for sixty or ninety days.
Capable of being, or suitable to be, discounted; as, certainforms are necessary to render notes discountable at a bank.
Unfavorable aspect; unfriendly regard; cold treatment;disapprobation; whatever tends to check or discourage.He thought a little discountenance on those persons would suppressthat spirit. Clarendon.
One who discountenances; one who disfavors. Bacon.
One who discounts; a discount broker. Burke.
Capable of being discouraged; easily disheartened. Bp. Hall.
One who discourages.The promoter of truth and the discourager of error. Sir G. C. Lewis.
Causing or indicating discouragement.-- Dis*cour"a*ging*ly, adv.
To discover. [Obs.]That none might her discoure. Spenser.
The state or quality of being discoursive or able to reason.[R.] Feltham.
Uncivil; rude; wanting in courtesy or good manners;uncourteous.-- Dis*cour"te*ous*ly, adv.-- Dis*cour"te*ous*ness, n.
Rudeness of behavior or language; ill manners; manifestation ofdisrespect; incivility.Be calm in arguing; for fierceness makes Error a fault, and truthdiscourtesy. Herbert.
To discover or show one's self. [Obs.]This done, they discover. DeckeNor was this the first time that they discovered to be followers ofthis world. Milton.
The quality of being discoverable. [R.] Carlyle.
Capable of being discovered, found out, or perceived; as, manyminute animals are discoverable only by the help of the microscope;truths discoverable by human industry.
Not covert; not within the bonds of matrimony; unmarried; --applied either to a woman who has never married or to a widow.
A state of being released from coverture; freedom of a womanfrom the coverture of a husband.
To take from a cradle. [R.]This airy apparition first discradled From Tournay into Portugal.Ford.
Not creditable; injurious to reputation; disgraceful;disreputable.-- Dis*cred"it*a*bly, adv.

The state or quality of being discrepant; disagreement;variance; discordance; dissimilarity; contrariety.There hath been ever a discrepance of vesture of youth and age, menand women. Sir T. Elyot.There is no real discrepancy between these two genealogies. G. S.Faber.
Discordant; at variance; disagreeing; contrary; different.The Egyptians were . . . the most oddly discrepant from the rest intheir manner of worship. Cudworth.

Separate; not coalescent; -- said of things usually coalescent.Discrete movement. See Concrete movement of the voice, underConcrete, a.-- Discrete proportion, proportion where the ratio of the means isdifferent from that of either couplet; as, 3:6::8:16, 3 bearing thesame proportion to 6 as 8 does to 16. But 3 is not to 6 as 6 to 8. Itis thus opposed to continued or continual proportion; as, 3:6::12:24.-- Discrete quantity, that which must be divided into units, asnumber, and is opposed to continued quantity, as duration, orextension.
Left to discretion; unrestrained except by discretion orjudgment; as, an ambassador with discretionary powers.

Marking distinction or separation; disjunctive. Discretiveproposition (Logic & Gram.), one that expresses distinction,opposition, or variety, by means of discretive particles, as but,though, yet, etc.; as, travelers change their climate, but not theirtemper.
In palmistry, applied to the line which marks the separationbetween the hand and the arm.
The eliminant of the n partial differentials of any homogenousfunction of n variables. See Eliminant.
Having the difference marked; distinguished by certain tokens.Bacon.
The state of being discriminated; distinctness.
Marking a difference; distinguishing.-- Dis*crim"i*na`ting*ly, adv.And finds with keen discriminating sight, Black's not so black; --nor white so very white. Canning.

The arbitrary imposition of unequal tariffs for substantiallythe same service.A difference in rates, not based upon any corresponding difference incost, constitutes a case of discrimination. A. T. Hadley.
With discrimination or distinction. J. Foster.
To deprive of a crown.The end had crowned the work; it not unreasonably discrowned theworkman. Motley.
To torture; to excruciate. [Obs.]Discruciate a man in deep distress. Herrick.
Leaning; fitted for a reclining posture. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.
To free from blame or the imputation of a fault; to exculpate.I almost fear you think I begged it, but I can disculpate myself.Walpole.
The act of reclining at table according to the manner of theancients at their meals. Sir T. Browne.
To free from that which cumbers or impedes; to disencumber.[Archaic] Pope.
To discover; to reveal; to discoure. [Obs.]I will, if please you it discure, assay To ease you of that ill, sowisely as I may. Spenser.
Not current or free to circulate; not in use. [Obs.] Sir E.Sandys.
The act of discoursing or reasoning; range, as from thought tothought. Coleridge.
To examine or search thoroughly; to exhaust a remedy against,as against a principal debtor before proceeding against the surety.Burrill.
One who discusses; one who sifts or examines. Wood.
Able or tending to discuss or disperse tumors or coagulatedmatter.
Serving to disperse morbid matter; discussive; as, a discutientapplication.-- n.
To be filled with scorn; to feel contemptuous anger; to behaughty.And when the chief priests and scribes saw the marvels that he did .. . they disdained. Genevan Testament (Matt. xxi. 15).
Disdainful. [Obs.]Revenge the jeering and disdained contempt Of this proud king. Shak.
Full of disdain; expressing disdain; scornful; contemptuous;haughty.From these Turning disdainful to an equal good. Akenside.-- Dis*dain"ful*ly, adv.-- Dis*dain"ful*ness, n.
To divest or deprive of deity or of a deific rank or condition.Feltham.
To disdain. [Obs.]Guyon much disdeigned so loathly sight. Spenser.
One of the dark particles forming the doubly refracting disksof muscle fibers.
An interval of two octaves, or a fifteenth; -- called alsobisdiapason.
Afflicted with disease.It is my own diseased imagination that torments me. W. Irving.
The state of being diseased; a morbid state; sickness. [R.] T.Burnet.
The quality of being diseaseful; trouble; trial. [R.] Sir P.Sidney.
To deprive of an edge; to blunt; to dull.Served a little to disedge The sharpness of that pain about herheart. Tennyson.
To fail of edifying; to injure. [R.]
To deprive of an elder or elders, or of the office of an elder.[Obs.] Fuller.
A selenide containing two atoms of selenium in each molecule.
To remove from on board a vessel; to put on shore; to land; todebark; as, the general disembarked the troops.
To free from embarrassment, or perplexity; to clear; toextricate.To disembarrass himself of his companion. Sir W. Scott.
Freedom or relief from impediment or perplexity.
To clear from a bay. Sherburne.
To deprive of embellishment; to disadorn. Carlyle.
Divested of a body; ceased to be corporal; incorporeal.The disembodied spirits of the dead. Bryant.
The act of disembodying, or the state of being disembodied.
To disarm and disband, as a body of soldiers,-Wilhelm.
To become discharged; to flow put; to find vent; to pour outcontents.Volcanos bellow ere they disembogue. Young.
The act of disemboguing; discharge. Mease.
To separate from the bosom. [R.] Young.
The act of disemboweling, or state of being disemboweled;evisceration.
Deprived of, or removed from, a bower. [Poetic] Bryant.
To free from wrangling or litigation. [Obs.] Berkeley.
To disentangle; to free from perplexity; to extricate fromconfusion.Vaillant has disembroiled a history that was lost to the world beforehis time. Addison.
To throw out of employment. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor.
The state of being disemployed, or deprived of employment.This glut of leisure and disemployment. Jer. Taylor.
To deprive of power; to divest of strength. H. Bushnell.
To disable; to disqualify.The sight of it might damp me and disenable me to speak. State Trials(1640).
To free from the captivity of love. Shelton.
Freed from restraint; unrestrained. [Archaic] E. A. Poe.

To free from enchantment; to deliver from the power of charmsor spells; to free from fascination or delusion.Haste to thy work; a noble stroke or two Ends all the charms, anddisenchants the grove. Dryden.
One who, or that which, disenchants.
The act of disenchanting, or state of being disenchanted.Shelton.
To free from the influence of a charm or spell; to disenchant.[R.] Jer. Taylor.
To free from encumbrance, or from anything which clogs,impedes, or obstructs; to disburden. Owen.I have disencumbered myself from rhyme. Dryden.
Freedom or deliverance from encumbrance, or anything burdensomeor troublesome. Spectator.
To deprive of an endowment, as a church. Gladstone.
The act of depriving of an endowment or endowments.[The] disendowment of the Irish Church. G. B. Smith.
To disfranchise; to deprive of the rights of a citizen.-- Dis`en*fran"chise*ment, n.

To release from that with which anything is engaged, engrossed,involved, or entangled; to extricate; to detach; to set free; toliberate; to clear; as, to disengage one from a party, from broilsand controversies, from an oath, promise, or occupation; to disengagethe affections a favorite pursuit, the mind from study.To disengage him and the kingdom, great sums were to be borrowed.Milton.Caloric and light must be disengaged during the process. Transl. ofLavoisier.
Not engaged; free from engagement; at leisure; free fromoccupation or care; vacant.-- Dis`en*ga"ged*ness, n.
Loosing; setting free; detaching. Disengaging machinery. Seeunder Engaging.
To deprive of that which ennobles; to degrade.An unworthy behavior degrades and disennobles a man. Guardian.
To erase from a roll or list. [Written also disenrol.] Donne.
Insanity; folly. [Obs.]What tediosity and disensanity Is here among! Beau. & Fl.
Freed from a shroudlike covering; unveiled.The disenshrouded statue. R. Browning.
To free from bondage or slavery; to disenthrall.He shall disenslave and redeem his soul. South.
The act of disentangling or clearing from difficulties. Warton.
To release from thralldom or slavery; to give freedom to; todisinthrall. [Written also disenthral.] Milton.
Liberation from bondage; emancipation; disinthrallment.[Written also disenthralment.]
To dethrone; to depose from sovereign authority. Milton.
To deprive of title or claim.Every ordinary offense does not disentitle a son to the love of hisfather. South.
To take out from a tomb; a disinter.
To disembowel; to let out or draw forth, as the entrails.[Obs.]As if he thought her soul to disentrail. Spenser.
To awaken from a trance or an enchantment. Hudibras.
To free from being entwined or twisted. Shelley.
To release from espousal or plighted faith. [Poetic] Milton.
To unsettle; to break up (anything established); to deprive, asa church, of its connection with the state. M. Arnold.
Want of esteem; low estimation, inclining to dislike; disfavor;disrepute.Disesteem and contempt of the public affairs. Milton.
To deprive of exercise; to leave untrained. [Obs.]By disexercising and blunting our abilities. Milton.
To deprive of features; to mar the features of. [R.]
To exclude from fellowship; to refuse intercourse with, as anassociate.An attempt to disfellowship an evil, but to fellowship the evildoer.Freewill Bapt. Quart.
The act of disfiguring, or the state of being disfigured;defacement; deformity; disfigurement. Gauden.
To mar the figure of; to render less complete, perfect, orbeautiful in appearance; to deface; to deform.Disfiguring not God's likeness, but their own. Milton.
To reduce the flesh or obesity of. [Obs.] Shelton.
The act of clearing land of forests. Daniel.
Discordance or diversity of form; unlikeness in form.Uniformity or disformity in comparing together the respective figuresof bodies. S. Clarke.

To deprive of a franchise or chartered right; to dispossess ofthe rights of a citizen, or of a particular privilege, as of voting,holding office, etc.Sir William Fitzwilliam was disfranchised. Fabyan (1509).He was partially disfranchised so as to be made incapable of takingpart in public affairs. Thirlwall.

The act of disfranchising, or the state disfranchised;deprivation of privileges of citizenship or of chartered immunities.Sentenced first to dismission from the court, and then todisfranchisement and expulsion from the colony. Palfrey.
To depose or withdraw from the condition of a friar. [Obs.]Many did quickly unnun and disfriar themselves. Fuller.

To deprive of that with which anything is furnished (furniture,equipments, etc.); to strip; to render destitute; to divest.I am a thing obscure, disfurnished of All merit, that can raise mehigher. Massinger.
The act of disfurnishing, or the state of being disfurnished.Daniel.
The act of disfurnishing, or the state of being disfurnished.[Obs.]
To free from a gage or pledge; to disengage. [Obs.] Holland.
To deprive of gallantry. [Obs.] B. Jonson.
To strip of a garland. [Poetic] "Thy locks disgarland."Drummond.
To divest of garniture; to disfurnish; to dismantle. Bp. Hall.
To deprive of a garrison. Hewyt.
To deprive of that principal quality of gavelkind tenure bywhich lands descend equally among all the sons of the tenant; -- saidof lands. Burrill.
To deprive of glory; to treat with indignity. [R.]Disglorified, blasphemed, and had in scorn. Milton.
Dishonor. [Obs.]To the disglory of God's name. Northbrooke.
To vomit forth what anything contains; to discharge; to makerestitution.See where it flows, disgorging at seven mouths Into the sea. Milton.
The act of disgorging; a vomiting; that which is disgorged. Bp.Hall.
To be inconsistent with, or act contrary to, the precepts ofthe gospel; to pervert the gospel. [Obs.] Milton.

Bringing disgrace; causing shame; shameful; dishonorable;unbecoming; as, profaneness is disgraceful to a man.-- Dis*grace"ful*fy, adv.-- Dis*grace"ful*ness, n.The Senate have cast you forth disgracefully. B. Jonson.
Degradation; a stripping of titles and honors.
To degrade; to reduce in rank. [Obs.] Tyndale.
To disperse; to scatter; -- opposite of congregate. [Obs.]
The process of separation, or the condition of being separate,as of the molecules of a body.
To dissatisfy; to disaffect; to anger. [Colloq.]

To provoke disgust or strong distaste in; to cause (any one)loathing, as of the stomach; to excite aversion in; to offend themoral taste of; -- often with at, with, or by.To disgust him with the world and its vanities. Prescott.Ærius is expressly declared . . . to have been disgusted at failing.J. H. Newman.Alarmed and disgusted by the proceedings of the convention. Macaulay.
Provoking disgust; offensive to the taste; exciting aversion;disgusting.That horrible and disgustful situation. Burke.
That causes disgust; sickening; offensive; revolting.-- Dis*gust"ing*ly, adv.
An undress; a loose, negligent dress; deshabille.They breakfast in dishabille. Smollett.
To dislodge. [Obs.]Those sleeping stones . . . from their fixed beds of lime Had beendishabited. Shak.
To make unholy; to profane. Tennyson.Nor can the unholiness of the priest dishallow the altar. T. Adams.
Want of harmony; discord; incongruity. [R.]A disharmony in the different impulses that constitute it [ournature]. Coleridge.
To leave; to quit; to cease to haunt. Halliwell.
A cloth used for washing dishes.
To discourage; to deprive of courage and hope; to depress thespirits of; to deject.Regiments . . . utterly disorganized and disheartened. Macaulay.
To deprive of the helmet. [Poetic]Lying stark, Dishelmed and mute, and motionlessly pale. Tennyson.
The act of disheriting, or debarring from inheritance;disinhersion. Bp. Hall.
To disinherit; to cut off, or detain, from the possession orenjoyment of an inheritance. [Obs.] Spenser.
The act of disinheriting or state of being disinherited;disinheritance. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.
One who puts another out of his inheritance.
To be spread in disorder or hang negligently, as the hair. [R.]Sir T. Herbert.
Disheveled. [Obs.]Dishevele, save his cap, he rode all bare. Chaucer.
As much as a dish holds when full.
To disgrace; to dishonor; as, to dishonest a maid. [Obs.]I will no longer dishonest my house. Chapman.
The nonpayment or nonacceptance of commercial paper by theparty on whom it is drawn.
Bringing dishonor on; tending to disgrace; lesseningreputation. Holmes.
One who dishonors or disgraces; one who treats anotherindignity. Milton.
To deprive of horns; as, to dishorn cattle. "Dishorn thespirit." Shak.
To deprive of house or home. "Dishoused villagers." JamesWhite.
Water in which dishes have been washed. "Suds and dishwater."Beau. & Fl.
The act or process of freeing from an illusion, or the state ofbeing freed therefrom. Lowell.
To disenchant; to free from illusion. "The bitterdisillusionizing experience of postnuptial life." W. Black.
The act of freeing from an illusion, or the state of beingfreed therefrom.
To free from the barriers or restrictions of a park. [R.]Spectator.
Free from warmth of passion or feeling.
To make worse; -- the opposite of improve. [R.] Jer. Taylor.
Reduction from a better to a worse state; as, disimprovement ofthe earth.

The state of being disinclined; want of propensity, desire, oraffection; slight aversion or dislike; indisposition.Disappointment gave him a disinclination to the fair sex. Arbuthnot.Having a disinclination to books or business. Guardian.

To incline away the affections of; to excite a slight aversionin; to indispose; to make unwilling; to alienate.Careful . . . to disincline them from any reverence or affection tothe Queen. Clarendon.To social scenes by nature disinclined. Cowper.
Separated from, or not included in, a corporation;disincorporated. Bacon.
Deprivation of the rights and privileges of a corporation. T.Warton.

To free from infectious or contagious matter; to destroyputrefaction; to purify; to make innocuous.When the infectious matter and the infectious matter and theodoriferous matter are one . . . then to deodorize is to disinfect.Ure.
That which disinfects; an agent for removing the causes ofinfection, as chlorine.
The act of disinfecting; purification from infecting matter.
One who, or that which, disinfects; an apparatus for applyingdisinfectants.
To divest of flame or ardor. Chapman.
The act of disinheriting, or the condition of being;disinherited; disherison.
To render insecure; to put in danger. [Obs.] Fanshawe.
Capable of being disintegrated, or reduced to fragments orpowder.Argillo-calcite is readily disintegrable by exposure. Kirwan.

To separate into integrant parts; to reduce to fragments or topowder; to break up, or cause to fall to pieces, as a rock, by blowsof a hammer, frost, rain, and other mechanical or atmosphericinfluences.Marlites are not disintegrated by exposure to the atmosphere, atleast in six years. Kirwan.
A machine for grinding or pulverizing by percussion.
To deprive or rid of interest in, or regard for; to disengage.[Obs.]
Disinterested. [Obs.]The measures they shall walk by shall be disinterest and even. Jer.Taylor.

Not influenced by regard to personal interest or advantage;free from selfish motive; having no relation of interest or feeling;not biased or prejudiced; as, a disinterested decision or judge.The happiness of disinterested sacrifices. Channing.
In a disinterested manner; without bias or prejudice.
The state or quality of being disinterested; impartiality.That perfect disinterestedness and self-devotion of which man seemsto be incapable, but which is sometimes found in woman. Macaulay.
The act of disinterring, or taking out of the earth;exhumation.
To free from thralldom; to disenthrall. [Written alsodisinthral.]
A releasing from thralldom or slavery; disenthrallment.[Written also disinthralment.]
To disentangle. [R.] "To disintricate the question." Sir W.Hamilton.
To render unaccustomed or unfamiliar.We are hindered and disinured . . . towards the true knowledge.Milton.
The act of depriving of investiture. [Obs.] Ogilvie.
To enervate; to weaken. [R.] Sydney Smith.
To uncover; to unfold or unroll; to disentangle. [R.] Dr. H.More.

To part; to disunite; to separate; to sunder.That marriage, therefore, God himself disjoins. Milton.Never let us lay down our arms against France, till we have utterlydisjoined her from the Spanish monarchy. Addison.Windmill Street consisted of disjoined houses. Pennant.
Disjointed; unconnected; -- opposed to conjoint. Milton.
Separated at the joints; disconnected; incoherent.-- Dis*joint"ed*ly, adv.-- Dis*joint"ed*ness, n.

Having the head, thorax, and abdomen separated by a deepconstriction. Disjunct tetrachords (Mus.), tetrachords so disposed toeach other that the gravest note of the upper is one note higher thanthe acutest note of the other.

Pertaining to disjunct tetrachords. "Disjunctive notes." Moore(Encyc. of Music). Disjunctive conjunction (Gram.), one connectinggrammatically two words or clauses, expressing at the same time anopposition or separation inherent in the notions or thoughts; as,either, or, neither, nor, but, although, except, lest, etc.-- Disjunctive proposition, one in which the parts are connected bydisjunctive conjunctions; as it is either day or night.-- Disjunctive syllogism (Logic), one in which the major propositionis disjunctive; as, the earth moves in a circle or an ellipse; but indoes not move in a circle, therefore it moves in an ellipse.
In a disjunctive manner; separately. Dr. H. More.
The act of disjoining, or state of being disjoined; separation.Fuller.
The circular figure of a celestial body, as seen projected ofthe heavens.
A friction clutch in which the gripping surfaces are disks ormore or less resemble disks.
Having no disk; appearing as a point and not expanded into adisk, as the image of a faint star in a telescope.
To deprive of leaves. [R.]The cankerworms that annually that disleaved the elms. Lowell.
Full of dislike; disaffected; malign; disagreeable. [Obs.]Spenser.
The want of likelihood; improbability. Sir W. Scott.
To make unlike; to disguise. [Obs.] Shak.
To tear limb from limb; to dismember. [Obs.] Bailey.
To efface, as a picture. [Obs.] Shak.
To unlink; to disunite; to separate. [R.] Tennyson.
To deprive of life. [Obs.]Telemachus dislived Amphimedon. Chapman.

To displace; to put out of its proper place. Especially, of abone: To remove from its normal connections with a neighboring bone;to put out of joint; to move from its socket; to disjoint; as, todislocate your bones. Shak.After some time the strata on all sides of the globe were dislocated.Woodward.And thus the archbishop's see, dislocated or out of joint for a time,was by the hands of his holiness set right again. Fuller.
The displacement of parts of rocks or portions of strata fromthe situation which they originally occupied. Slips, faults, and thelike, are dislocations.
To go from a place of rest. [R.]Where Light and Darkness in perpetual round Lodge and dislodge byturns. Milton.
The act or process of dislodging, or the state of beingdislodged.
To put at a distance; to remove. [Obs.]Low-looking dales, disloigned from common gaze. Spenser.

Not loyal; not true to a sovereign or lawful superior, or tothe government under which one lives; false where allegiance is due;faithless; as, a subject disloyal to the king; a husband disloyal tohis wife.Without a thought disloyal. Mrs. Browning.
Want of loyalty; lack of fidelity; violation of allegiance.
To divest of coat of mail. Spenser.
In a dismal manner; gloomily; sorrowfully; uncomfortably.
The quality of being dismal; gloominess.
To free from the bonds of marriage; to divorce. [Obs.] Ld.Berners.
To disarrange; to derange; to put in disorder. [R.] Drummond.
To divest of a mask. Shak.
To deprive of a mast of masts; to break and carry away themasts from; as, a storm dismasted the ship.
The act of dismasting; the state of being dismasted. [R.]Marshall.
To eject from the maw; to disgorge. [R.] Shelton.
To take dismay or fright; to be filled with dismay. [Obs.]Shak.
A state of being dismayed; dejection of courage;dispiritedness.
A tenth; a tenth part; a tithe. Ayliffe.

The act of dismembering, or the state of being dismembered;cutting in piece; mThe Castilians would doubtless have resented the dismemberment of theunwieldy body of which they formed the head. Macaulay.
Destitute of mettle, that is, or fire or spirit. [R.]Llewellyn.
Dismission; discharge.Officeholders were commanded faithfully to enforce it, upon pain ofimmediate dismissal. Motley.
To take down, or apart, as a machine.
To make alien; to deprive of the privileges of birth. Locke.
Deprived or destitute of natural feelings; unnatural. [Obs.]Shak.
Neglect or refusal to obey; violation of a command orprohibition.He is undutiful to him other actions, and lives in open disobedience.Tillotson.

Not to obey; to neglect or refuse to obey (a superior or hiscommands, the laws, etc.); to transgress the commands of (one inauthority); to violate, as an order; as, refractory children disobeytheir parents; men disobey their Maker and the laws.Not to disobey her lord's behest. Tennyson.
Releasing from obligation. "Disobligatory power." Charles I.
To turn away from the west; to throw out of reckoning as tolongitude. [Obs.] Marvell.
The state of being unemployed; want of occupation. [R.]
Want or difference of belief; disbelief. [Obs.] Bp. Reynolds.
To throw out of the proper orbit; to unsphere. Shak.
Offensive to good morals and public decency; notoriouslyoffensive; as, a disorderly house.
The state of being in disorder; derangement; confusion. [Obs.]Bacon.

To destroy the organic structure or regular system of (agovernment, a society, a party, etc.); to break up (what isorganized); to throw into utter disorder; to disarrange.Lyford . . . attempted to disorganize the church. Eliot (1809).
One who disorganizes or causes disorder and confusion.
To turn away from the cast; to confuse as to which way is east;to cause to lose one's bearings. [R.] Bp. Warburton.
To turn away from the east, or (figuratively) from the right orthe truth. [R.]
To deprive of oxygen; to deoxidize. [R.]
To roam. [Obs.]In this fair plot dispacing to and fro. Spenser.
To separate (a pair). [R.]I have . . . dispaired two doves. Beau. & Fl.
To spread out; to expand. [Obs.] Bailey.
Act of dispanding, or state of being dispanded. [Obs.]
Inequality in marriage; marriage with an inferior. [Obs.]Chaucer.Dissuaded her from such a disparage. Spenser.
One who disparages or dishonors; one who vilifies or disgraces.
In a manner to disparage or dishonor; slightingly.
Pertaining to two coördinate species or divisions.
Things so unequal or unlike that they can not be compared witheach other.
Act of disappearing; disappearance. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

Inequality; difference in age, rank, condition, or excellence;dissimilitude; -- followed by between, in, of, as to, etc.; as,disparity in, or of, years; a disparity as to color.The disparity between God and his intelligent creatures. I. Taylor.The disparity of numbers was not such as ought to cause anyuneasiness. Macaulay.

To part asunder; to divide; to separate; to sever; to rend; torive or split; as, disparted air; disparted towers. [Archaic]Them in twelve troops their captain did dispart. Spenser.The world will be whole, and refuses to be disparted. Emerson.
Freedom from passion; an undisturbed state; apathy. Sir W.Temple.
To make haste; to conclude an affair; to finish a matter ofbusiness.They have dispatched with Pompey. Shak.
Bent on haste; intent on speedy execution of business or anytask; indicating haste; quick; as, dispatchful looks. Milton.
The act of dispatching. [Obs.] State Trials (1529).
Lack of sympathy; want of passion; apathy. [R.]Many discrepancies and some dispathies between us. Southey.
To deprive of the claim of a pauper to public support; todeprive of the privilege of suing in forma pauperis.
To free a state of pauperism, or from paupers. J. S. Mill.
To send off with speed; to dispatch. [Obs.] Knolles.Then they dispeeded themselves of the Cid and of their mother-in-law,DoSouthey.

To drive away by scattering, or so to cause to vanish; to clearaway; to banish; to dissipate; as, to dispel a cloud, vapors, cares,doubts, illusions.[Satan] gently raised their fainting courage, and dispelled theirfears. Milton.I saw myself the lambent easy light Gild the brown horror, and dispelthe night. Dryden.
To spend; to lay out; to expend. [Obs.] Spenser.Able to dispend yearly twenty pounds and above. Fuller.
One who dispends or expends; a steward. [Obs.] Wyclif (1 Cor.iv. 1).

a system of principles, promises, and rules ordained andadministered; scheme; economy; as, the Patriarchal, Mosaic, andChristian dispensations.Neither are God's methods or intentions different in hisdispensations to each private man. Rogers.
In the way of dispensation; dispensatively.
Granting, or authorized to grant, dispensations. "Dispensatorypower." Bp. Rainbow.
One who, or that which, dispenses; a distributer; as, adispenser of favors.
To deprive of inhabitants; to depopulate.Leave the land dispeopled and desolate. Sir T. More.A certain island long before dispeopled . . . by sea rivers. Milton.
One who, or that which, dispeoples; a depopulator. Gay.
To scatter; to sprinkle. [Obs.]Odorous water was Disperpled lightly on my head and neck. Chapman.
The act or result of dispersing or scattering; dispersion.Darwin.
Scattered.-- Dis*pers"ed*ly, adv.-- Dis*pers"ed*ness, n. Dispersed harmony (Mus.), harmony in whichthe tones composing the chord are widely separated, as by an octaveor more.

The separation of light into its different colored rays,arising from their different refrangibilities. Dispersion of theoptic axes (Crystallog.), the separation of the optic axes in biaxialcrystals, due to the fact that the axial angle has different valuesfor the different colors of the spectrum.

Tending to disperse. Dispersive power (Opt.), the relativeeffect of a material in separating the different rays of light byrefraction, as when the substance is formed into a prism.-- Dis*pers"ive*ness, n.
To deprive of personality or individuality. [R.]We multiply; we dispersonate ourselves. Hare.
Depressed in spirits; disheartened; daunted.-- Dis*pir"it*ed*ly, adv.-- Dis*pir"it*ed, n.
Depression of spirits; discouragement. [R.]Procter, in evident distress and dispiritment, was waiting the slowconclusion of this. Carlyle.
Full of despite; cruel; spiteful; pitiless. Spenser.-- Dis*pit"e*ous*ly, adv. [Obs.]

The process of extracting soluble substances from organicmaterial and the like, whereby a quantity of saturated solvent isdisplaced, or removed, for another quantity of the solvent. Pistondisplacement (Mech.), the volume of the space swept through, orweight of steam, water, etc., displaced, in a given time, by thepiston of a steam engine or pump.
Want of complacency or gratification; envious displeasure;dislike. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.
The funnel part of the apparatus for solution by displacement.
The act of displanting; removal; displacement. Sir W. Raleigh.
To untwist; to uncurl; to unplat. [Obs.] Hakewill.
To extend the front of (a column), bringing it into line.Farrow.
With wings expanded; -- said of a bird of pray, esp. an eagle.
One who, or that which, displays.
To discipline; to correct. [Obs.]And bitter Penance, with an iron whip, Was wont him once to displeevery day. Spenser.
Unpleasing; offensive; unpleasant. [Obs.] Speed.-- Dis*pleas"ant*ly, adv. [Obs.] Strype.-- Dis*pleas"ant*ness, n. [Obs.]
Causing displeasure or dissatisfaction; offensive;disagreeable.-- Dis*pleas"ing*ly, adv.-- Dis*pleas"ing*ness, n. Locke.
To deprive or strip, as a house of furniture, or a barn ofstock. [Scot.]
To discharge; to explode.In posture to displode their second tire Of thunder. Milton.
Explosion.The vast displosion dissipates the clouds. Young.
To strip of, or as of, a plume, or plumes; to deprive ofdecoration; to dishonor; to degrade.Displumed, degraded, and metamorphosed. Burke.
One of several isomeric organic bases of the quinoline seriesof alkaloids.
A double spondee; a foot consisting of four long syllables.
The person to whom any property is legally conveyed.
One who legally transfers property from himself to another.
To sprinkle, as with water from a sponge. [Poetic & Rare][Written also dispunge.]O sovereign mistress of true melancholy, The poisonous damp of nightdisponge upon me. Shak.
To refuse to consider as pope; to depose from the popedom.One whom they disposed. Tennyson.
Play; sport; pastime; diversion; playfulness. Milton.
Act of disporting; diversion; play. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.
Subject to disposal; free to be used or employed as occasionmay require; not assigned to any service or use.The great of this kingdom . . . has easily afforded a disposablesurplus. Burke.
To bargain; to make terms. [Obs.]She had disposed with Cæsar. Shak.
The state of being disposed or inclined; inclination;propensity. [R.]
One who, or that which, disposes; a regulator; a director; abestower.Absolute lord and disposer of all things. Barrow.
Having (such) a disposition; -- used in compounds; as, well-dispositioned.
In a dispositive manner; by natural or moral disposition.[Obs.] Sir T. Browne.Do dispositively what Moses is recorded to have done literally, . . .break all the ten commandments at once. Boyle.
The planet which is lord of the sign where another planet is.[Obs.] Crabb.

To put out of possession; to deprive of the actual occupancyof, particularly of land or real estate; to disseize; to eject; --usually followed by of before the thing taken away; as, to dispossessa king of his crown.Usurp the land, and dispossess the swain. Goldsmith.
The putting out of possession, wrongfully or otherwise, of onewho is in possession of a freehold, no matter in what title; --called also ouster.
To eject from a post; to displace. [R.] Davies (Holy Roode).

To withdraw praise from; to notice with disapprobation or somedegree of censure; to disparage; to blame.Dispraising the power of his adversaries. Chaucer.I dispraised him before the wicked, that the wicked might not fall inlove with him. Shak.
To spread abroad, or different ways; to spread apart; to open;as, the sun dispreads his beams. Spenser.
One who spreads abroad.Dispreaders both of vice and error. Milton.
To free from prejudice. [Obs.] W. Montagu.
To make unlike a prince. [R.]For I was drench'd with ooze, and torn with briers, . . . And, allone rag, disprinced from head to heel. Tennyson.
To let loose from prison, to set all liberty. [R.] Bulwer.
To deprive of a privilege or privileges. [R.]
To do preciate. [R.] Cotton (Ode to Lydia).
To renounce the profession or pursuit of.His arms, which he had vowed to disprofess. Spenser.
A proving to be false or erroneous; confutation; refutation;as, to offer evidence in disproof of a statement.I need not offer anything farther in support of one, or in disproofof the other. Rogers.
To cause to be no longer property; to dispossess of. [R.] Shak.

To make unsuitable in quantity, form, or fitness to an end; toviolate symmetry in; to mismatch; to join unfitly.To shape my legs of an unequal size; To disproportion me in everypart. Shak.A degree of strength altogether disproportioned to the extent of itsterritory. Prescott.
Disproportional; unsuitable in form, size, quantity, oradaptation; disproportionate; inadequate.-- Dis`pro*por"tion*a*ble*ness, n. Hammond.-- Dis`pro*por"tion*a*bly, adv.

Not having due proportion to something else; not havingproportion or symmetry of parts; unsuitable in form, quantity orvalue; inadequate; unequal; as, a disproportional limb constitutesdeformity in the body; the studies of youth should not bedisproportional to their understanding.
The state of being disproportional. Dr. H. More.
In a disproportional manner; unsuitably in form, quantity, orvalue; unequally.

Not proportioned; unsymmetrical; unsuitable to something elsein bulk, form, value, or extent; out of proportion; inadequate; as,in a perfect body none of the limbs are disproportionate; it iswisdom not to undertake a work disproportionate means.-- Dis`pro*por"tion*ate*ly, adv.-- Dis`pro*por"tion*ate*ness, n.
To cancel the appropriation of; to disappropriate. [R.]
Capable of being disproved or refuted. Boyle.
Not to provide; to fail to provide. [Obs.] Boyle.
Wanting in punctilious respect; discourteous. [Obs.]That were dispunct to the ladies. B. Jonson.
Without penal restraint; not punishable. [R.] Swift.
To dissuade; to frustrate; as, to dispurpose plots. [R.] A.Brewer.

Inclined to dispute; apt to civil or controvert; characterizedby dispute; as, a disputatious person or temper.The Christian doctrine of a future life was no recommendation of thenew religion to the wits and philosophers of that disputationsperiod. Buckminster.-- Dis`pu*ta"tious*ly, adv.-- Dis`pu*ta"tious*ness, n.
Disposed to dispute; inclined to cavil or to reason inopposition; as, a disputative temper. I. Watts.

To contend in argument; to argue against something maintained,upheld, or claimed, by another; to discuss; to reason; to debate; toaltercate; to wrangle.Therefore disputed [reasoned, Rev. Ver.] he in synagogue with the Jews. Acts xvii. 17.
One who disputes, or who is given to disputes; a controvertist.Where is the disputer of this world 1 Cor. i. 20.
To diminish the quantity of; to lessen. [Obs.] Shak.
Deprived of quiet; impatient; restless; uneasy. [R.] Shak.
The act of disquieting; a state of disquiet. [Obs.][It] roars and strives 'gainst its disquietal. Dr. H. More.
One who, or that which, disquiets, or makes uneasy; adisturber.
In a disquiet manner; uneasily; as, he rested disquietly thatnight. [R.] Wiseman.
State of being disquieted; uneasiness; harassment. [R.]Hopkins.
Disturbance of quiet in body or mind; restlessness; uneasiness.Hooker.
Causing uneasiness. [R.]So distasteful and disquietous to a number of men. Milton.
Want of peace or tranquility; uneasiness; disturbance;agitation; anxiety.Fears and disquietude, and unavoidable anxieties of mind. Abp. Sharp.

A formal or systematic inquiry into, or discussion of, anysubject; a full examination or investigation of a matter, with thearguments and facts bearing upon it; elaborate essay; dissertation.For accurate research or grave disquisition he was not wellqualified. Macaulay.
Pertaining to disquisition; of the nature of disquisition.
Relating to disquisition; fond discussion or investigation;examining; inquisitive.
Of or pertaining to disquisition; disquisitive. Ed. Rev.
To reduce to a lower rating or rank; to degrade. Marryat.
To divest of reality; to make uncertain. [Obs.] Udall.

Not to regard; to pay no heed to; to omit to take notice of; toneglect to observe; to slight as unworthy of regard or notice; as, todisregard the admonitions of conscience.Studious of good, man disregarded fame. Blackmore.
To fail to remember; to forget. [Obs. or Archaic]
A state of being in bad condition, and wanting repair.The fortifications were ancient and in disrepair. Sir W. Scott.

Not reputable; of bad repute; not in esteem; dishonorable;disgracing the reputation; tending to bring into disesteem; as, it isdisreputable to associate familiarly with the mean, the lewd, and theprofane.Why should you think that conduct disreputable in priests which youprobably consider as laudable in yourself Bp. Watson.
Loss or want of reputation or good name; dishonor; disrepute;disesteem. "A disreputation of piety." Jer. Taylor.
Loss or want of reputation; ill character; disesteem;discredit.At the beginning of the eighteenth century astrology fell intogeneral disrepute. Sir W. Scott.
Want of respect or reverence; disesteem; incivility;discourtesy.Impatience of bearing the least affront or disrespect. Pope.
Wanting in respect; manifesting disesteem or lack of respect;uncivil; as, disrespectful behavior.-- Dis`re*spect"ful*ly, adv.-- Dis`re*spect"ful*ness, n.
Showing want of respect; disrespectful. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.
To treat irreverently or with disrespect. [Obs.] Sir T. More.

To divest of a robe; to undress; figuratively, to strip ofcovering; to divest of that which clothes or decorates; as, autumndisrobes the fields of verdure.Two great peers were disrobed of their glory. Sir H. Wotton.
One who, or that which, disrobes.
To tear up the roots of, or by the roots; hence, to tear from afoundation; to uproot.A piece of ground disrooted from its situation by subterraneousinundations. Goldsmith.
To deprive of the rudder, as a ship.
In a disorderly manner. [Obs.] Rom. of R.
Rent off; torn asunder; severed; disrupted.
The act or rending asunder, or the state of being rent asunderor broken in pieces; breach; rent; dilaceration; rupture; as, thedisruption of rocks in an earthquake; disruption of a state.
Causing, or tending to cause, disruption; caused by disruption;breaking through; bursting; as, the disruptive discharge of anelectrical battery. Nichol.

The state of being dissatisfied, unsatisfied, or discontented;uneasiness proceeding from the want of gratification, or fromdisappointed wishes and expectations.The ambitious man has little happiness, but is subject to muchuneasiness and dissatisfaction. Addison.

Causing dissatisfaction; unable to give content;unsatisfactory; displeasing.To have reduced the different qualifications in the different Statesto one uniform rule, would probably have been as dissatisfactory tosome of the States, as difficult for the Convention. A. Hamilton.-- Dis*sat`is*fac"to*ri*ness, n.

To render unsatisfied or discontented; to excite uneasiness inby frustrating wishes or expectations; to displease by the want ofsomething requisite; as, to be dissatisfied with one's fortune.The dissatisfied factions of the autocracy. Bancroft.
To divide into separate parts; to cut in pieces; to separateand expose the parts of, as an animal or a plant, for examination andto show their structure and relations; to anatomize.
Cut deeply into many lobes or divisions; as, a dissected leaf.
Capable of being dissected, or separated by dissection. Paley.

To deprive of seizin or possession; to dispossess or oustwrongfully (one in freehold possession of land); -- followed by of;as, to disseize a tenant of his freehold. [Written also disseise.]Which savage beasts strive as eagerly to keep and hold those goldenmines, as the Arimaspians to disseize them thereof. Holland.
A person disseized, or put out of possession of an estateunlawfully; -- correlative to disseizor. [Written also disseisee.]
The act of disseizing; an unlawful dispossessing and ouster ofa person actually seized of the freehold. [Written also disseisin.]Blackstone.
One who wrongfully disseizes, or puts another out of possessionof a freehold. [Written also disseisor.] Blackstone.
To conceal the real fact, motives,He that hateth dissembleth with his lips. Prov. xxvi. 24.He [an enemy] dissembles when he assumes an air of friendship. C. J.Smith.

One who dissembles; one who conceals his opinions ordispositions under a false appearance; a hypocrite.It is the weakest sort of politicians that are the greatestdissemblers. Bacon.Priests, princes, women, no dissemblers here. Pope.
That dissembles; hypocritical; false.-- Dis*sem"bling*ly, adv.
Occurring in small portions scattered through some othersubstance.

The act of disseminating, or the state of being disseminated;diffusion for propagation and permanence; a scattering or spreadingabroad, as of ideas, beliefs, etc.The universal dissemination of those writings. Wayland.
Tending to disseminate, or to become disseminated.The effect of heresy is, like the plague, infectious anddisseminative. Jer. Taylor.
One who, or that which, disseminates, spreads, or propagates;as, disseminators of disease.

Disagreement in opinion, usually of a violent character,producing warm debates or angry words; contention in words; partisanand contentious divisions; breach of friendship and union; strife;discord; quarrel.Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and disputation with them.Acts xv. 2.Debates, dissension, uproars are thy joy. Dryden.A seditious person and raiser-up of dissension among the people.Robynson (More's Utopia).
Disposed to discord; contentious; dissentious. [R.] Ascham.-- Dis*sen"sious*ly, adv. Chapman.
To differ from an established church in regard to doctrines,rites, or government.
Disagreeing; contrary; differing; -- opposed to consentaneous.[R.] Barrow.

One who separates from the service and worship of anestablished church; especially, one who disputes the authority ortenets of the Church of England; a nonconformist.Dissenters from the establishment of their several countries. Burke.Robert Brown is said to have the first formal dissenter. Shipley.
The spirit or principles of dissenters. Ed. Rev.
To throw into a state of dissent. [R.] Feltham.
Marked by dissensions; apt to breed discord; quarrelsome;contentious; factious.-- Dis*sen"tious*ly, adv.
One of the partitions which divide a compound ovary into cells.
To discourse or dispute; to discuss. [R.]We have disserted upon it a little longer than was necessary.Jeffrey.
To deal in dissertation; to write dissertations; to discourse.[R.] J. Foster.
A formal or elaborate argumentative discourse, oral or written;a disquisition; an essay; a discussion; as, Dissertations on theProphecies.
Relating to dissertations; resembling a dissertation.
One who writers a dissertation; one who discourses. Boyle.
To fail to serve; to do injury or mischief to; to damage; tohurt; to harm.Have neither served nor disserved the interests of any party. Jer.Taylor.
Injury; mischief.We shall rather perform good offices unto truth than any disserviceunto their relators. Sir T. Browne.
Calculated to do disservice or harm; not serviceable;injurious; harmful; unserviceable. Shaftesbury.-- Dis*serv"ice*a*ble*ness, n. Norris.-- Dis*serv"ice*a*bly, adv.
The act of unsettling, or the state of being unsettled.Marvell.

To part in two; to sever thoroughly; to sunder; to disunite; toseparate; to disperse.The storm so dissevered the company . . . that most of therm nevermet again. Sir P. Sidney.States disserved, discordant, belligerent. D. Webster.
To free from shadow or shade. [Obs.] G. Fletcher.
To become unsheathed. [Obs.] Sir W. Raleigh.
To dismiss from service on board ship. [Obs.] Hakluyt.
To shiver or break in pieces. [Obs.]
Disagreement; dissent; separation from the establishedreligion. I. Taylor.It is the dissidence of dissent. Burke.
No agreeing; dissenting; discordant; different.Our life and manners be dissident from theirs. Robynson (More'sUtopia).
Starting asunder; bursting and opening with an elastic force;dehiscing explosively; as, a dissilient pericarp.
The act of bursting or springing apart. [R.] Boyle.
Not similar; unlike; heterogeneous; as, the tempers of men areas dissimilar as their features.This part very dissimilar to any other. Boyle.
Want of resemblance; unlikeness; dissimilitude; variety; as,the dissimilarity of human faces and forms. Sir W. Jones.
In a dissimilar manner; in a varied style.With verdant shrubs dissimilarly gay. C. Smart.
The act of making dissimilar. H. Sweet.
A comparison by contrast; a dissimile.

The act of dissembling; a hiding under a false appearance;concealment by feigning; false pretension; hypocrisy.Let love be without dissimulation. Rom. xii. 9.Dissimulation . . . when a man lets fall signs and arguments that heis not that he is. Bacon.Simulation is a pretense of what is not, and dissimulation aconcealment of what is. Tatler.
Capable of being scattered or dissipated. [R.]The heat of those plants is very dissipable. Bacon.

Tending to dissipate. Dissipative system (Mech.), an assumedsystem of matter and motions in which forces of friction andresistances of other kinds are introduced without regard to the heator other molecular actions which they generate; -- opposed toconservative system.
The rate at which palpable energy is dissipated away into otherforms of energy.
Lying apart. [Obs.]Lands far dissite and remote asunder. Holland.
Want of sociability; unsociableness. Bp. Warburton.
Unfriendly to society; contracted; selfish; as, dissocialfeelings.

To separate from fellowship or union; to disunite; to disjoin;as, to dissociate the particles of a concrete substance.Before Wyclif's death in 1384, John of Gaunt had openly dissociatedhimself from the reformer. A. W. Ward.

The process by which a compound body breaks up into simplerconstituents; -- said particularly of the action of heat on gaseousor volatile substances; as, the dissociation of the sulphurmolecules; the dissociation of ammonium chloride into hydrochloricacid and ammonia.
The quality of being dissoluble; capacity of being dissoluble;capacity of being dissolved by heat or moisture, and converted into afluid.
The quality of being dissoluble; dissolubility. Boyle.
State or quality of being dissolute; looseness of morals andmanners; addictedness to sinful pleasures; debauchery; dissipation.Chivalry had the vices of dissoluteness. Bancroft.
Capacity of being dissolved; solubility. Richardson.

Capable of being dissolved, or separated into component parts;capable of being liquefied; soluble.-- Dis*solv"a*ble*ness, n.Though everything which is compacted be in its own naturedissolvable. Cudworth.Such things as are not dissolvable by the moisture of the tongue. SirI. Newton.
Having the power to dissolve anything; solvent. [Obs.]Frampton.
To annul; to rescind; to discharge or release; as, to dissolvean injunction.
Having power to dissolve power to dissolve a solid body; as,the dissolvent juices of the stomach. Ray.
One who, or that which, has power to dissolve or dissipate.Thou kind dissolver of encroaching care. Otway.
Melting; breaking up; vanishing.-- Dis*solv"ing*ly, adv. Dissolving view, a picture which grows dimand is gradually replaced by another on the same field; -- an effectproduced by magic lanterns.
Tending to dissuade or divert from a measure or purpose;dehortatory; as, dissuasive advice.-- n.
A dissuasive. [R.]This virtuous and reasonable person, however, has ill luck in all hisdissuasories. Jeffrey.
To separate; to sunder; to destroy. [R.] Chapman.
To deprive of sweetness. [R.] Bp. Richardson.
Consisting of two syllabas, a dissyllabic foot in poetry. B.Jons
To form into two syllables. Ogilvie.
To form into two syllables; to dyssyllabify.
A word of two syllables; as, pa-per.
Absence or defect of symmetry; asymmetry.
Lack of sympathy; want of interest; indifference. [R.]
Toward a distal part; on the distal side of; distally.

To tinge with a different color from the natural or proper one;to stain; to discolor; to sully; to tarnish; to defile; -- usedchiefly in poetry. "Distained with dirt and blood." Spenser.[She] hath . . . distained her honorable blood. Spenser.The worthiness of praise distains his worth. Shak.
A space marked out in the last part of a race course.The horse that ran the whole field out of distance. L'Estrange.
Distant. [Obs.]More distantial from the eye. W. Montagu.
At a distance; remotely; with reserve.
To be distasteful; to taste ill or disagreeable. [Obs.]Dangerous conceits are, in their natures, poisons, Which at the arescarce found to distaste. Shak.
Something which excites distaste or disgust. [Obs.] Speed.
To mix (colors) in the way of distemper; as, to distempercolors with size. [R.]
To become expanded or inflated; to swell. "His heart distendswith pride." Milton.
The quality or capacity of being distensible. [R.]
Capable of being distended or dilated.
Distending, or capable of being distended.
To banish or drive from a country. [Obs.] Howell.
Cyanite or kyanite; -- so called in allusion to its unequalhardness in two different directions. See Cyanite.
A couple of verses or poetic lines making complete sense; anepigram of two verses.
Capable of being distilled; especially, capable of beingdistilled without chemical change or decomposition; as, alcohol isdistillable; olive oil is not distillable.
The product of distillation; as, the distillate from molasses.

The separation of the volatile parts of a substance from themore fixed; specifically, the operation of driving off gas or vaporfrom volatile liquids or solids, by heat in a retort or still, andthe condensation of the products as far as possible by a coolreceiver, alembic, or condenser; rectification; vaporization;condensation; as, the distillation of illuminating gas and coal, ofalcohol from sour mash, or of boric acid in steam.
Belonging to, or used in, distilling; as, distillatory vessels.-- n.
Distillation; the substance obtained by distillation. [Obs.]Shak.

Constituting difference, or distinction from everything else;distinctive; peculiar; characteristic.The distinguishing doctrines of our holy religion. Locke.Distinguishing pennant (Naut.), a special pennant by which anyparticular vessel in a fleet is recognized and signaled. Simmonds.
With distinction; with some mark of preference. Pope.
To deprive of title or right. [R.] B. Jonson.
A genus of parasitic, trematode worms, having two suckers forattaching themselves to the part they infest. See 1st Fluke,
Distorted; misshapen. [Obs.]Her face was ugly and her mouth distort. Spenser.
One who, or that which, distorts.
An unnatural deviation of shape or position of any part of thebody producing visible deformity.
Mentally disordered; unsettled; mad.My distracted mind. Pope.
A state of being distracted; distraction. Bp. Hall.
One who, or that which, distracts away.
Capable of being drawn aside or distracted.
Tending or serving to draw apart.
To levy a distress.Upon whom I can distrain for debt. Camden.
Capable of being, or liable to be, distrained. Blackstone.
One who distrains; the party distraining goods or chattels.Blackstone.
The act or proceeding of seizing personal property by distress.Abbott.
To flow. [Poetic]Yet o'er that virtuous blush distreams a tear. Shenstone.
To seize for debt; to distrain.
A state of being distressed or greatly pained.
Full of distress; causing, indicating, or attended with,distress; as, a distressful situation. "Some distressful stroke."Shak. "Distressful cries." Pope.-- Dis*tress"ful*ly, adv.
Capable of being distributed. Sir W. Jones.
Tending to distribute or be distributed; that distributes;distributive.

To employ (a term) in its whole extent; to take as universal inone premise.A term is said to be distributed when it is taken universal, so as tostand for everything it is capable of being applied to. Whately.
One who, or that which, distributes or deals out anything; adispenser. Addison.
That distributes; dealing out. Distributing past office, anoffice where the mails for a large district are collected to beassorted according to their destination and forwarded.
A resolving a whole into its parts.
Of or pertaining to distribution. Huxley.
Assigning the species of a general term.
By distribution; singly; not collectively; in a distributivemanner.
Rigorous; stringent; harsh. [Obs.]Punishing with the rod of district severity. Foxe.
Sudden display; flash; glitter. [R.]A smile . . . breaks out with the brightest distriction. Collier.
A writ commanding the sheriff to distrain a person by his goodsor chattels, to compel a compliance with something required of him.

To feel absence of trust in; not to confide in or rely upon; todeem of questionable sufficiency or reality; to doubt; to besuspicious of; to mistrust.Not distrusting my health. 2 Mac. ix. 22.To distrust the justice of your cause. Dryden.He that requireth the oath doth distrust that other. Udall.Of all afraid, Distrusting all, a wise, suspicious maid. Collins.
That distrusts; suspicious; lacking confidence in.-- Dis*trust"ing*ly, adv.

The hindering or disquieting of a person in the lawful andpeaceable enjoyment of his right; the interruption of a right; as,the disturbance of a franchise, of common, of ways, and the like.Blackstone.
One who interrupts or incommodes another in the peaceableenjoyment of his right.
Having two columns in front; -- said of a temple, portico, orthe like. Distyle in antis, having columns between two antæ. SeeAnta.
A binary compound of sulphur containing two atoms of sulphur ineach molecule; -- formerly called disulphuret. Cf. Bisulphide.

Applied to an acid having in each molecule two atoms of sulphurin the higher state of oxidation. Disulphuric acid, a thick oilyliquid, H2S2O7, called also Nordhausen acid (from Nordhausen in theHarts, where it was originally manufactured), fuming sulphuric acid,and especially pyrosulphuric acid. See under Pyrosulphuric.
An advocate of disunion, specifically, of disunion of theUnited States.
To part; to fall asunder; to become separated.The joints of the body politic do separate and disunite. South.
One who, or that which, disjoins or causes disunion.
A state of separation or disunion; want of unity. Dr. H. More.
Gradual cessation of use or custom; neglect of use; disuse.[R.] Hooker.

Cessation of use, practice, or exercise; inusitation;desuetude; as, the limbs lose their strength by disuse.The disuse of the tongue in the only . . . remedy. Addison.Church discipline then fell into disuse. Southey.
To deprive of utility; to render useless. [R.] Mrs. Browning.
To dissuade from by previous warning. [Obs.]
Deprived of wits or understanding; distracted. [Obs.] Drayton.
To deprive of wonted usage; to disaccustom. [R.] Bp. Hall.
To refuse to worship; to treat as unworthy. [Obs.] Sir T. More.
To deprive of worth; to degrade. [Obs.] Feltham.
To unyoke; to free from a yoke; to disjoin. [Poetic] R.Browning.
To close up. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.
The act of making rich; enrichment. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.
To dig a ditch or ditches. Swift.
To prepare for action or use; to make ready; to dight. [Obs.]His hideous club aloft he dites. Spenser.
The doctrine of those who maintain the existence of two gods orof two original principles (as in Manicheism), one good and one evil;dualism.
One who holds the doctrine of ditheism; a dualist. Cudworth.
Containing two equivalents of sulphur; as, dithionic acid.Dithionic acid (Chem.), an unstable substance, H2S2O6, known only inits solutions, and in certain well-defined salts.
A kind of lyric poetry in honor of Bacchus, usually sung by aband of revelers to a flute accompaniment; hence, in general, a poemwritten in a wild irregular strain. Bentley.
Pertaining to, or resembling, a dithyramb; wild and boisterous."Dithyrambic sallies." Longfellow.-- n.
A white, crystalline, aromatic hydrocarbon, C14H14, consistingof two radicals or residues of toluene.
The Greek major third, which comprehend two major tones (themodern major third contains one major and one minor whole tone).
Dividing into double or treble ramifications; -- said of a leafor stem. [R.] Loudon.
A double trochee; a foot made up of two trochees.
An igneous rock composed of orthoclase, elæolite, and sodalite.
Set, sung, or composed as a ditty; -- usually in composition.Who, with his soft pipe, and smooth-dittied song. Milton.

The aforesaid thing; the same (as before). Often contracted todo., or to two "turned commas" ("), or small marks. Used in bills,books of account, tables of names, etc., to save repetition.A spacious table in the center, and a variety of smaller dittos inthe corners. Dickens.
A double reading, or twofold interpretation, as of a Scripturetext. [R.]
To sing; to warble a little tune.Beasts fain would sing; birds ditty to their notes. Herbert.
A sailor's small bag to hold thread, needles, tape, etc.; --also called sailor's housewife.
A small box to hold a sailor's thread, needless, comb, etc.
One of a series of complex nitrogenous substances regarded ascontaining two molecules of urea or their radicals, as uric acid orallantoin. Cf. Ureide.
Tending to increase the secretion and discharge of urine.-- n.
The quality of being diuretical; diuretic property.
A division of Lepidoptera, including the butterflies; -- socalled because they fly only in the daytime.
Opening during the day, and closing at night; -- said offlowers or leaves.
The condition of sleeping or becoming dormant by day, as is thecase of the bats.
Long duration; lastingness. [R.] Sir T. Browne.
A wandering about or going astray; digression.Let us be set down at Queen's Crawley without further divagation.Thackeray.
Having two units of combining power; bivalent. Cf. Valence.
To divide into two branches; to cause to branch apart.
A divergence of lines of color sculpture, or of fibers atdifferent angles.
One of the muscles which open the shell of brachiopods; acardinal muscle. See Illust. of Brachiopoda.
A water fowl; the didapper. See Dabchick.
To rend apart. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.
To pull in pieces. [Obs. or R.]
Any bird of certain genera, as Urinator (formerly Colymbus), orthe allied genus Colymbus, or Podiceps, remarkable for their agilityin diving.
A saying in which two members of the sentence are contrasted;an antithetical proverb. [Obs.]Italy, a paradise for horses, a hell for women, as the diverb goes.Burton.
To strike or sound through. [R.] Davies (Holy Roode).
Causing divergence of rays; as, a divergent lens.
