Tending in different directions from a common center; spreadingapart; divergent. Diverging series (Math.), a series whose terms arelarger as the series is extended; a series the sum of whose termsdoes not approach a finite limit when the series is extendedindefinitely; -- opposed to a converging series.
The quality or capacity of being diversifiable. Earle.
Capable of being diversified or varied. Boyle.
Distinguished by various forms, or by a variety of aspects orobjects; variegated; as, diversified scenery or landscape.
One who, or that which, diversifies.
Of a different form; of varied forms.

To make diverse or various in form or quality; to give varietyto; to variegate; to distinguish by numerous differences or aspects.Separated and diversified on from another. Locke.Its seven colors, that diversify all the face of nature. I. Taylor.
The act of drawing the attention and force of an enemy from thepoint where the principal attack is to be made; the attack, alarm, orfeint which diverts.
Serving or tending to divert; also, distinguishing. [Obs.]
To turn aside; to digress. [Obs.]I diverted to see one of the prince's palaces. Evelyn.
One who, or that which, diverts, turns off, or pleases.
A blind tube branching out of a longer one.
Amusing; entertaining.-- Di*vert"ing*ly, adv.-- Di*vert"ing*ness, n.
A short ballet, or other entertainment, between the acts of aplay. Smart.
Tending to divert; diverting; amusing; interesting.Things of a pleasant and divertive nature. Rogers.
The name popularly given to the rich man in our Lord's parableof the "Rich Man and Lazarus" (Luke xvi. 19-31). Hence, a name for arich worldling.
The act of stripping, or depriving; the state of beingdivested; the deprivation, or surrender, of possession of property,rights, etc.
A small tree of tropical America (Cæsalpinia coriaria), whoselegumes contain a large proportion of tannic and gallic acid, and areused by tanners and dyers.
Cut into distinct parts, by incisions which reach the midrib; -- said of a leaf.
A number or quantity which is to be divided.
An instrument for dividing lines, describing circles, etc.,compasses. See Compasses.

That divides; separating; marking divisions; graduating.Dividing engine, a machine for graduating circles (as forastronomical instruments) or bars (as for scales); also, for spacingoff and cutting teeth in wheels.-- Dividing sinker. (Knitting Mach.). See under Sinker.
Divided, shared, or participated in, in common with others.[R.] Milton.
Divided; dividual. [R.]He so often substantiates distinctions into dividuous,selfsubsistent. Coleridge.
One who practices or pretends to divination; a diviner. [R.]Burton.
Professing, or relating to, divination. "A natural divinatoryinstinct." Cowley.
The quality of being divine; superhuman or supreme excellence.Shak.

That dives or is used or diving. Diving beetle (Zoöl.), anybeetle of the family Dytiscidæ, which habitually lives under water; -- called also water tiger.-- Diving bell, a hollow inverted vessel, sometimes bell-shaped, inwhich men may descend and work under water, respiration beingsustained by the compressed air at the top, by fresh air pumped inthrough a tube from above.-- Diving dress. See Submarine armor, under Submarine.-- Diving stone, a kind of jasper.
To render divine; to deify. [Obs.] "Blessed and divinifiedsoul." Parth. Sacra (1633).
That divines; for divining. Divining rod, a rod, commonly ofwitch hazel, with forked branches, used by those who pretend todiscover water or metals under ground.
A diviner. [Obs.] " I am no divinistre." Chaucer.
Calf stained dark brown and worked without gilding, often usedfor theological books.
To invest with a divine character; to deify. [R.] M. Arnold.Man had divinized all those objects of awe. Milman.
The quality of being divisible; the property of bodies by whichtheir parts are capable of separation.Divisibility . . . is a primary attribute of matter. Sir W. Hamilton.

Capable of being divided or separated.Extended substance . . . is divisible into parts. Sir W. Hamilton.Divisible contract (Law), a contract containing agreements one ofwhich can be separated from the other.-- Divisible offense (Law), an offense containing a lesser offensein one of a greater grade, so that on the latter there can be anacquittal, while on the former there can be a conviction.-- Di*vis"i*ble*ness, n.-- Di*vis"i*bly, adv.
The process of finding how many times one number or quantity iscontained in another; the reverse of multiplication; also, the ruleby which the operation is performed.
That divides; pas, a divisional line; a divisional general; adivisional surgeon of police. Divisional planes (Geol.), planes ofseparation between rock masses. They include joints.
One who divides or makes division. [Obs.] Sheldon.
The number by which the dividend is divided. Common divisor.(Math.) See under Common, a.
Incapable of being divorced or separated; free from divorce.
Dissolution of the marriage tie; divorce; separation.Let him write her a divorcement. Deut. xxiv. 1.The divorcement of our written from our spoken language. R. Morris.
The person or cause that produces or effects a divorce.Drummond.
Having power to divorce; tending to divorce. "This divorcivelaw." Milton.
A thin, oblong turf used for covering cottages, and also forfuel. [Scot.] Simmonds.
The act of divulging or publishing. [R.]Secrecy hath no use than divulgation. Bp. Hall.
To become publicly known. [R.] "To keep it from divulging."Shak.
Tending to pull asunder, tear, or rend; distracting.
A colloquial name for the Southern portion of the UnitedStates, esp. during the Civil War. [U.S.]
To make dizzy; to astonish; to puzzle. [Obs.] Gayton.
A blockhead. [Obs.] [Written also dizard, and disard.] --Diz"zard*ly, adv. [Obs.]
In a dizzy manner or state.
Giddiness; a whirling sensation in the head; vertigo.
To make dizzy or giddy; to give the vertigo to; to confuse.If the jangling of thy bells had not dizzied thy understanding. SirW. Scott.

A syllable attached to the first tone of the major diatonicscale for the purpose of solmization, or solfeggio. It is the firstof the seven syllables used by the Italians as manes of musicaltones, and replaced, for the sake of euphony, the syllable Ut,applied to the note C. In England and America the same syllables areused by mane as a scale pattern, while the tones in respect toabsolute pitch are named from the first seven letters of thealphabet.
General manager; factotum.Under him, Dunstan was the do-all at court, being the king'streasurer, councilor, chancellor, confessor, all things. Fuller.
One who performs little though professing much. [Colloq.]Great talkers are commonly dolittles. Bp. Richardson.
Doing nothing; inactive; idle; lazy; as, a do-nothing policy.
A tongue or tract of land included between two rivers; as, thedoab between the Ganges and the Jumna. [India] Am. Cyc.
An apparatus resembling a Jacquard for weaving small figures(usually about 12 - 16 threads, seldom more than 36 - 40 threads).
The aquatic larva of a large neuropterous insect (Corydaluscornutus), used as bait in angling. See Hellgamite.
Ancient heretics who held that Christ's body was merely aphantom or appearance.
Pertaining to, held by, or like, the Docetæ. "DoceticGnosticism." Plumptre.
Pertaining to, or containing, the dochmius.
Easily taught or managed; teachable. Milton.
The art or practice of applying tests to ascertain the nature,quality, etc., of objects, as of metals or ores, of medicines, or offacts pertaining to physiology.

Proving by experiments or tests. Docimastic art, metallurgy, orthe art of assaying metals; the art of separating metals from foreignmatters, and determining the nature and quantity of metallicsubstances contained in any ore or mineral.
A treatise on the art of testing, as in assaying metals, etc.
A genus of plants (Rumex), some species of which are well-knownweeds which have a long taproot and are difficult of extermination.
A charge for the use of a dock.
A yard or storage place for all sorts of naval stores andtimber for shipbuilding.
An order of gastropods, including the true limpets, and havingthe teeth on the odontophore or lingual ribbon.

The friar skate. [Prov. Eng.] Doctors' Commons. See underCommons.-- Doctor's stuff, physic, medicine. G. Eliot.-- Doctor fish (Zoöl.), any fish of the genus Acanthurus; thesurgeon fish; -- so called from a sharp lancetlike spine on each sideof the tail. Also called barber fish. See Surgeon fish.
Of or relating to a doctor, or to the degree of doctor.Doctoral habit and square cap. Wood.
In the manner of a doctor.[R.]
The degree, title, or rank, of a doctor.
Like a doctor or learned man. [Obs.] "Doctorly prelates." Foxe.
Of the nature of, or constituting, doctrine. [Obs.] Sir P.Sidney.

One who would apply to political or other practical concernsthe abstract doctrines or the theories of his own philosophicalsystem; a propounder of a new set of opinions; a dogmatic theorist.Used also adjectively; as, doctrinaire notions.
A matter of doctrine; also, a system of doctrines. T. Goodwin.Sir T. Elyot.
In a doctrinal manner or for; by way of teaching or positivedirection.
The principles or practices of the Doctrinaires.
Pertaining to written evidence; contained or certified inwriting. "Documentary evidence." Macaulay.
A game much like hockey, played in an open field; also, the,bent stick for playing the game. [Local, Eng.] Halliwell.
Without horns; as, dodded cattle; without beards; as, doddedcorn. Halliwell.

A plant of the genus Cuscuta. It is a leafless parasitical vinewith yellowish threadlike stems. It attaches itself to some otherplant, as to flax, goldenrod, etc., and decaying at the root. isnourished by the plant that supports it.
Shattered; infirm. "A laurel grew, doddered with age." Dryden.
A figure or polygon bounded by twelve sides and containingtwelve angles.
A Linnæan order of plants having twelve styles.
Pertaining to, or like, a dodecahedion; consisting of twelveequal sides. Dodecahedral cleavage. See under Cleavage.
A Linnæan class of plants including all that have any number ofstamens between twelve and nineteen.
Any one of a group of thick oily hydrocarbons, C12H26, of theparaffin series.
Having twelve columns in front.-- n.
A word consisting of twelve syllables.
A tern applied to the twelve houses, or parts, of the zodiac ofthe primum mobile, to distinguish them from the twelve signs; also,any one of the twelve signs of the zodiac.

The act of evading by some skillful movement; a sudden startingaside; hence, an artful device to evade, deceive, or cheat; a cunningtrick; an artifice. [Colloq.]Some, who have a taste for good living, have many harmless arts, bywhich they improve their banquet, and innocent dodges, if we may bepermitted to use an excellent phrase that has become vernacular sincethe appearance of the last dictionaries. Thackeray.
A doit; a small coin. Shelton.
Any shellfish which casts its shell, as a lobster. [Prov. Eng.]

A large, extinct bird (Didus ineptus), formerly inhabiting theIsland of Mauritius. It had short, half-fledged wings, like those ofthe ostrich, and a short neck and legs; -- called also dronte. It wasrelated to the pigeons.
A female deer or antelope; specifically, the female of thefallow deer, of which the male is called a buck. Also applied to thefemale of other animals, as the rabbit. See the Note under Buck.
Pertaining to, or obtained from, the doegling; as, doeglic acid(Chem.), an oily substance resembling oleic acid.
The beaked whale (Balænoptera rostrata), from which doeglingoil is obtained.
An agent or attorney; a factor. Burrill.
The 3d pers. sing. pres. of Do.
To put off dress; to take off the hat.
A revolving cylinder, or a vibrating bar with teeth, in acarding machine, which doffs, or strips off, the cotton from thecards. Ure.
A quadruped of the genus Canis, esp. the domestic dog (C.familiaris).
A male or drone bee. Halliwell.

A period of from four to six weeks, in the summer, variouslyplaced by almanac makers between the early part of July and the earlypart of September; canicular days; -- so called in reference to therising in ancient times of the Dog Star (Sirius) with the sun.Popularly, the sultry, close part of the summer.
One who has an unusual fancy for, or interest in, dogs; also,one who deals in dogs.
Sirius, a star of the constellation Canis Major, or the GreaterDog, and the brightest star in the heavens; -- called also Canicula,and, in astronomical charts, a Canis Majoris. See Dog days.
Having the corners of the leaves turned down and soiled bycareless or long-continued usage; -- said of a book.Statute books before unopened, not dog-eared. Ld. Mansfield.
Having a face resembling that of a dog. Dog-faced baboon(Zoöl.), any baboon of the genus Cynocephalus. See Drill.
Having a head shaped like that of a dog; -- said of certainbaboons.
Noting a flight of stairs, consisting of two or more straightportions connected by a platform (landing) or platforms, and runningin opposite directions without an intervening wellhole.
A common European wild rose, with single pink or white flowers.
Of or pertaining to a doge.[R.]
The office or dignity of a doge.
A small genus of perennial herbaceous plants, with poisonousmilky juice, bearing slender pods pods in pairs.
The berry of the dogwood; -- called also dogcherry. Dr. Prior.Dogberry tree (Bot.), the dogwood.
The bolt of the cap-square over the trunnion of a cannon.Knight.
A light one-horse carriage, commonly two-wheeled, patternedafter a cart. The original dogcarts used in England by sportsmen hada box at the back for carrying dogs.
The act of drawing after, or pursuing, deer with a dog. Cowell.
The chief magistrate in the republics of Venice and Genoa.
In a dogged manner; sullenly; with obstinate resolution.
A two-masted fishing vessel, used by the Dutch.
Low in style, and irregular in measure; as, doggerel rhymes.This may well be rhyme doggerel, quod he. Chaucer.
A sailor belonging to a dogger.
Like a dog; having the bad qualities of a dog; churlish;growling; brutal.-- Dog"*gish*ly, adv.-- Dog"gish*ness, n.
A place fit only for dogs; a vile, mean habitation orapartment. Dryden.
One of an ancient sect of physicians who went by generalprinciples; -- opposed to the Empiric.
In a dogmatic manner; positively; magisterially.
The quality of being dogmatical; positiveness.
The science which treats of Christian doctrinal theology.
The manner or character of a dogmatist; arrogance orpositiveness in stating opinion.The self-importance of his demeanor, and the dogmatism of hisconversation. Sir W. Scott.

One who dogmatizes; one who speaks dogmatically; a bold andarrogant advancer of principles.I expect but little success of all this upon the dogmatist; hisopinioned assurance is paramount to argument. Glanvill.
To assert positively; to teach magisterially or with bold andundue confidence; to advance with arrogance.The pride of dogmatizing schools. Blackmore.
One who dogmatizes; a bold asserter; a magisterial teacher.Hammond.
The character, or individuality, of a dog.
One of several shores used to hold a ship firmly and preventher moving while the blocks are knocked away before launching.
Sick as a dog sometimes is very sick. [Colloq.]
The skin of a dog, or leather made of the skin. Also usedadjectively.
The fitful naps taken when all hands are kept up by stress.

An ornament common in Gothic architecture, consisting ofpointed projections resembling teeth; -- also called tooth ornament.Dogtooth spar (Min.), a variety of calcite, in acute crystals,resembling the tooth of a dog. See Calcite.-- Dogtooth violet (Bot.), a small, bulbous herb of the Lily family(genus Erythronium). It has two shining flat leaves and commonly onelarge flower. [Written also dog's-tooth violet.]
A gentle trot, like that of a dog.
A small vane of bunting, feathers, or any other light material,carried at the masthead to indicate the direction of the wind.Totten.
A half watch; a watch of two hours, of which there are two, thefirst dogwatch from 4 to 6 o'clock, p.m., and the second dogwatchfrom 6 to 8 o'clock, P. M. Totten.
The Cornus, a genus of large shrubs or small trees, the wood ofwhich is exceedingly hard, and serviceable for many purposes.
Anything done; a deed; an action good or bad; hence, in theplural, conduct; behavior. See Do.To render an account of his doings. Barrow.
A very small coin; a doit.
A rude ancient ax or hatchet, seen in museums.
Shaped like the head of an ax or hatchet, as some leaves, andalso certain organs of some shellfish.

A part of the ocean near the equator, abounding in calms,squalls, and light, baffling winds, which sometimes prevent allprogress for weeks; -- so called by sailors. To be in the doldrums,to be in a state of listlessness ennui, or tedium.
grief; sorrow; lamentation. [Archaic]And she died. So that day there was dole in Astolat. Tennyson.
Full of dole or grief; expressing or exciting sorrow;sorrowful; sad; dismal.With screwed face and doleful whine. South.Regions of sorrow, doleful shades. Milton.
A dark-colored, basic, igneous rock, composed essentially ofpyroxene and a triclinic feldspar with magnetic iron. By many authorsit is considered equivalent to a coarse-grained basalt.
Of the nature of dolerite; as, much lava is doleritic lava.Dana.
Doleful; dismal; gloomy; sorrowful.-- Dole"some*ly, adv.-- Dole"some*ness, n.
Barrel-shaped, or like a cask in form.
A genus of freeswimming oceanic tunicates, allied to Salpa, andhaving alternate generations.
A genus of large univalve mollusks, including the partridgeshell and tun shells.
A child's puppet; a toy baby for a little girl.
A species of sunfish (Lepomis pallidus), common in the UnitedStates; -- called also blue sunfish, and copper-nosed bream.
A contrivance, turning on a vertical axis by a handle or winch,and giving a circular motion to the ore to be washed; a stirrer.
A cromlech. See Cromlech. [Written also tolmen.]

A mineral consisting of the carbonate of lime and magnesia invarying proportions. It occurs in distinct crystals, and in extensivebeds as a compact limestone, often crystalline granular, either whiteor clouded. It includes much of the common white marble. Also calledbitter spar.
To convert into dolomite.-- Dol`o*mi*za"tion, n.
Pain; grief; distress; anguish. [Written also dolour.] [Poetic]Of death and dolor telling sad tidings. Spenser.
Plaintive; pathetic; -- used adverbially as a musicaldirection.
A mass of iron or lead hung from the yardarm, in readiness tobe dropped on the deck of an enemy's vessel.
A heavy, stupid fellow; a blockhead; a numskull; an ignoramus;a dunce; a dullard.This Puck seems but a dreaming dolt. Drayton.
Doltlike; dull in intellect; stupid; blockish; as, a doltishclown.-- Dolt"ish*ly, adv.-- Dolt"ish*ness, n.
Evil intent, embracing both malice and fraud. See Culpa.Wharton.

Ownership of land; an estate or patrimony which one has in hisown right; absolute proprietorship; paramount or sovereign ownership.Public domain, the territory belonging to a State or to the generalgovernment; public lands. [U.S.]in the public domain may be used byanyone wihout restriction.-- Right of eminent domain, that superior dominion of the sovereignpower over all the property within the state, including thatpreviously granted by itself, which authorizes it to appropriate anypart thereof to a necessary public use, reasonable compensation beingmade.
Of or relating to a domain or to domains.
A cupola formed on a large scale.

A book said to have been compiled under the direction of KingAlfred. It is supposed to have contained the principal maxims of thecommon law, the penalties for misdemeanors, and the forms of judicialproceedings. Domebook was probably a general name for book ofjudgments. Burrill.
Furnished with a dome; shaped like a dome.

A day of judgment. See Doomsday. [Obs.] Domesday Book, theancient record of the survey of most of the lands of England, made byorder of William the Conqueror, about 1086. It consists of twovolumes, a large folio and a quarto, and gives the proprietors'tenures, arable land, woodland, etc. [Written also Doomsday Book.]
Articles of home manufacture, especially cotton goods. [U. S.]
Domestic. [Obs.]Our private and domestical matter. Sir. P. Sidney.
In a domestic manner; privately; with reference to domesticaffairs.
Forming part of the same family. [Obs.] Sir E. Dering.
The act of domesticating, or accustoming to home; the action oftaming wild animals.
The state of being domestic; domestic character; householdlife.
A kind of baize of which the ward is cotton and the weftwoolen. Blakely.
A massive mineral of tin-white or steel-gray color, an arsenideof copper.
Relating to, or shaped like, a dome.
A residence at a particular place accompanied with an intentionto remain there for an unlimited time; a residence accepted as afinal abode. Wharton.
A member of a household; a domestic.

Of or pertaining to a domicile, or the residence of a person orfamily.The personal and domiciliary rights of the citizen scrupulouslyguarded. Motley.Domiciliary visit (Law), a visit to a private dwelling, particularlyfor searching it, under authority.
The act of domiciliating; permanent residence; inhabitancy.Milman.
The art of house-keeping, cookery, etc. [R.] R. Park.
To divide, as the heavens, into twelve houses. See House, inastrological sense. [Obs.]
Lady; a lady; -- a title formerly given to noble ladies whoheld a barony in their own right. Burrill.

Ruling; governing; prevailing; controlling; predominant; as,the dominant party, church, spirit, power.The member of a dominant race is, in his dealings with the subjectrace, seldom indeed fraudulent, . . . but imperious, insolent, andcruel. Macaulay.Dominant estate or tenement (Law), the estate to which a servitude oreasement is due from another estate, the estate over which theservitude extends being called the servient estate or tenement.Bouvier. Wharton's Law Dict.-- Dominant owner (Law), one who owns lands on which there is aneasement owned by another.
To predominate over; to rule; to govern. "A city dominated bythe ax." Dickens.We everywhere meet with Slavonian nations either dominant ordominated. W. Tooke.
A high order of angels in the celestial hierarchy; -- a meaninggiven by the schoolmen.Thrones, dominations, princedoms, virtues, powers. Milton.
Governing; ruling; imperious. Sir E. Sandys.
A ruler or ruling power. "Sole dominator of Navarre." Shak.Jupiter and Mars are dominators for this northwest part of the world.Camden.
A West Indian fish (Epinula magistralis), of the familyTrichiuridæ. It is a long-bodied, voracious fish.

To rule with insolence or arbitrary sway; to play the master;to be overbearing; to tyrannize; to bluster; to swell with conscioussuperiority or haughtiness; -- often with over; as, to domineer overdependents.Go to the feast, revel and domineer. Shak.His wishes tend abroad to roam, And hers to domineer at home. Prior.
Ruling arrogantly; overbearing.A violent, brutal, domineering old reprobate. Blackw. Mag.
The Lord's day or Sunday; also, the Lord's prayer. [Obs.]

Of or pertaining to St. Dominic (Dominic de Guzman), or to thereligions communities named from him. Dominican nuns, an order ofnuns founded by St. Dominic, and chiefly employed in teaching.-- Dominican tertiaries (the third order of St. Dominic). SeeTertiary.
A supposed high order of angels; dominations. See Domination,3. Milton.By him were all things created . . . whether they be thrones, ordominions, or principalities, or powers. Col. i. 16.
In Canada, a legal holiday, July lst, being the anniversary ofthe proclamation of the formation of the Dominion in 1867.

A game played by two or more persons, with twenty-eight piecesof wood, bone, or ivory, of a flat, oblong shape, plain at the back,but on the face divided by a line in the middle, and either leftblank or variously dotted after the manner of dice. The game isplayed by matching the spots or the blank of an unmatched half of adomino already played Hoyle.
A game of cards in which the suits are played in sequence,beginning with a 5 or 9, the player who gets rid of his cards firstbeing the winner.
Master; sir; -- a title of respect formerly applied to a knightor a clergyman, and sometimes to the lord of a manor. Cowell.
That can be tamed. [R.] Sir M. Hale.
A grayish variety of trachyte; -- so called from the Puy-de-Dôme in Auvergne, France, where it is found.
To put on; to dress in; to invest one's self with.Should I don this robe and trouble you. Shak.At night, or in the rain, He dons a surcoat which he doffs at morn.Emerson.
Capable of being donated or given. [R.]
A thing given to a sacred use. [R.] Burton.
To give; to bestow; to present; as, to donate fifty thousanddollars to a college.

The act or contract by which a person voluntarily transfers thetitle to a thing of which be is the owner, from himself to another,without any consideration, as a free gift. Bouvier. Donation party, aparty assembled at the house of some one, as of a clergyman, each onebringing some present. [U.S.] Bartlett.
A follower of Donatus, the leader of a body of North Africanschismatics and purists, who greatly disturbed the church in the 4thcentury. They claimed to be the true church.
A benefice conferred on a person by the founder or patron,without either presentation or institution by the ordinary, orinduction by his orders. See the Note under Benefice, n.,
One who makes a gift; a donor; a giver.
A donee of the crown; one the whom, upon certain condition,escheated property is made over.
A canelike grass of southern Europe (Arundo Donax), used forfishing rods, etc.
A handsome fish of Florida and the West Indies (Platyglossusradiatus). The name is applied also to the ladyfish (Harpe rufa) ofthe same region.
p. p. from Do, and formerly the infinitive.

Anciently, one to whom lands were given; in later use, one towhom lands and tenements are given in tail; in modern use, one onwhom a power is conferred for execution; -- sometimes called theappointor.
A clumsy craft, having one mast with a long sail, used fortrading purposes on the coasts of Coromandel and Ceylon. [Writtenalso dhony, doney, and done.]
The chief tower, also called the keep; a massive tower inancient castles, forming the strongest part of the fortifications.See Illust. of Castle.
A lady; madam; mistress; -- the title given a lady in Italy.
Lit., given; hence, in a literary work, as a drama or tale,that which is assumed as to characters, situation, etc., as a basisfor the plot or story.  W. E. Henley.

One who grants an estate; in later use, one who confers apower; -- the opposite of donee. Kent.Touching, the parties unto deeds and charters, we are to consider aswell the donors and granters as the donees or grantees. Spelman.
The quality or rank of a don, gentleman, or knight. Hudibras.
A young squire, or knight's attendant; a page. [Obs.] Beau. &Fl.
A perennial, creeping grass (Cynodon dactylon), highly prized,in Hindostan, as food for cattle, and acclimated in the UnitedStates. [Written also doub grass.]

A kind of litter suspended from men's shoulders, for carryingpersons or things; a palanquin. [Written also doolee and doolie.][East Indies]Having provided doolies, or little bamboo chairs slung on four men'sshoulders, in which I put my papers and boxes, we next morningcommenced the ascent. J. D. Hooker.
A species of palm tree (Hyphæne Thebaica), highly valued forthe fibrous pulp of its fruit, which has the flavor of gingerbread,and is largely eaten in Egypt and Abyssinia. [Written also doumpalm.]
A penalty or fine for neglect. [Local, New England]
Full of condemnation or destructive power. [R.] "That doomfuldeluge." Drayton.
The surrounding frame into which a door shuts.
The jamb or sidepiece of a door. Ex. xii. 22 (Douay version).
A Hindoo divinity, the consort of Siva, represented with tenarms. [Written also Durga.] Malcom.
The frame of a door. Milton.
One who guards the entrance of a house or apartment; a porter;a janitor.
The nail or knob on which in ancient doors the knocker struck;-- hence the old saying, "As dead as a doornail."
A plane on a door, giving the name, and sometimes theemployment, of the occupant.
The jamb or sidepiece of a doorway.
The sill or threshold of a door.
Entrance or place of a door. [Obs. or Local] Bp. Warburton.
The stone or plank forming a step before an outer door.
The block or strip of wood or similar material which stops, atthe right place, the shutting of a door.
The passage of a door; entrance way into a house or a room.
A yard in front of a house or around the door of a house.
A chart of previous performances, etc., of race horses. [Race-track Slang]
Affected by "dope"; esp., sluggish or dull as though under theinfluence of a narcotic. [Slang]
A spiritual or ghostly double or counterpart; esp., anapparitional double of a living person; a cowalker.
An Anabaptist or Baptist. [Contemptuous] B. Jonson.
A brownish black native hydrocarbon occurring in elastic orjellylike masses.

A large European scaraboid beetle (Geotrupes stercorarius),which makes a droning noise while flying. The name is also applied toallied American species, as the June bug. Called also dorr,dorbeetle, or dorrbeetle, dorbug, dorrfly, and buzzard clock.
A southern constellation, within which is the south pole of theecliptic; -- called also sometimes Xiphias, or the Swordfish.
A European marine fish (Zeus faber), of a yellow color. SeeIllust. of John Doree.
A doorpost. [Obs.] "As dead as a doretree." Piers Plowman.
The European goatsucker; -- so called because it eats the dorbeetle. See Goatsucker. [Written also dorrhawk.] Booth.
Same as Doric, 3. "Dorian mood." Milton. Dorian mode (Mus.),the first of the authentic church modes or tones, from D to D,resembling our D minor scale, but with the B natural. Grove.
Belonging to, or resembling, the oldest and simplest of thethree orders of architecture used by the Greeks, but ranked as secondof the five orders adopted by the Romans. See Abacus, Capital, Order.
A genus of nudibranchiate mollusks having a wreath of branchi¯n the back.
One of a breed of large-bodied domestic fowls, having fivetoes, or the hind toe double. There are several strains, as thewhite, gray, and silver-gray. They are highly esteemed for the table.
The state of being dormant; quiescence; abeyance.

In a sleeping posture; as, a lion dormant; -- distinguishedfrom couchant. Dormant partner (Com.), a partner who takes no sharein the active business of a company or partnership, but is entitledto a share of the profits, and subject to a share in losses; --called also sleeping or silent partner.-- Dormant window (Arch.), a dormer window. See Dormer.-- Table dormant, a stationary table. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Causing sleep; as, the dormitive properties of opium. Clarke.-- n. (Med.)
A small European rodent of the genus Myoxus, of severalspecies. They live in trees and feed on nuts, acorns, etc.; -- socalled because they are usually torpid in winter.
Up, or ahead, as many holes as remain to be played; -- said ofa player or side.
A hamlet. "A mean fishing dorp." Howell.
The dorbeetle; also, a drone or an idler. See 1st Dor. Robynson(More's Utopia).
Toward the dorsum or back; on the dorsal side; dorsally.
Pertaining to, or situated near, the back, or dorsum, of ananimal or of one of its parts; notal; tergal; neural; as, the dorsalfin of a fish; the dorsal artery of the tongue; -- opposed toventral.
On, or toward, the dorsum, or back; on the dorsal side of;dorsad.
The Baltic or variable cod (Gadus callarias), by some believedto be the young of the common codfish.
A division of chætopod annelids in which the branchiæ are alongthe back, on each side, or on the parapodia. [See Illusts. underAnnelida and Chætopoda.]
Having branchiæ along the back; belonging to theDorsibranchiata.-- n.

Bearing, or producing, on the back; -- applied to ferns whichproduce seeds on the back of the leaf, and to certain Batrachia, theova of which become attached to the skin of the back of the parent,where they develop; dorsiparous.
Having distinct upper and lower surfaces, as most commonleaves. The leaves of the iris are not dorsiventral.
From the dorsal to the ventral side of an animal; as, thedorsoventral axis.
The back or dorsal region of an animal; the upper side of anappendage or part; as, the dorsum of the tongue.
A European fish. See Doree, and John Doree.
A genus of plant-eating beetles, including the potato beetle.See Potato beetle.
A spear bearer; a statue of a man holding a spear or in theattitude of a spear bearer. Several important sculptures of thissubject existed in antiquity, copies of which remain to us.
Back to back; as, to sit dos-à-dos in a dogcart; to dance dos-à-dos, or so that two dancers move forward and pass back to back.
The administration of medicine in doses; specif., a scheme orsystem of grading doses of medicine according to age, etc.
Measurement of doses; specif., a system of therapeutics whichuses but few remedies, mostly alkaloids, and gives them in dosesfixed by certain rules. --Do`si*met"ric (#), a. --Do*sim"e*trist (#),n.
A place to sleep in; a bed; hence, sleep. [Slang]
A bundle containing the papers in reference to some matter.
A small ovoid or cylindrical roil or pledget of lint, forkeeping a sore, wound, etc., open; a tent.
Pertaining to dower, or a woman's marriage portion;constituting dower, or comprised in it. Garth.
One whose mind is impaired by age; one in second childhood.The sickly dotard wants a wife. Prior.
The acts or speech of a dotard; drivel. [R.]
That dotes; silly; excessively fond.-- Dot"ing*ly, adv.-- Dot"ing*ness, n.
Foolish; weak; imbecile. Sir W. Scott.

Marked with, or made of, dots or small spots; diversified withsmall, detached objects. Dotted note (Mus.), a note followed by a dotto indicate an increase of length equal to one half of its simplevalue; thus, a dotted semibreve is equal to three minims, and adotted quarter to three eighth notes.-- Dotted rest, a rest lengthened by a dot in the same manner as adotted note.
Half-rotten; as, doty timber. [Local, U. S.]
An officer of the French customs. [Anglicized form douaneer.]
A village composed of Arab tents arranged in streets.

A translation of the Scriptures into the English language forthe use of English-speaking Roman Catholics; -- done from the LatinVulgate by English scholars resident in France. The New Testamentportion was published at Rheims, A. D. 1582, the Old Testament atDouai, A. D. 1609-10. Various revised editions have since beenpublished. [Written also Doway Bible. Called also the Rheims andDouay version.]

Having the petals in a flower considerably increased beyond thenatural number, usually as the result of cultivation and the expenseof the stamens, or stamens and pistils. The white water lily and someother plants have their blossoms naturally double.
One who practices double dealing; a deceitful, trickish person.L'Estrange.
False or deceitful dealing. See Double dealing, under Dealing.Shak.
Acting or operating in two directions or with both motions;producing a twofold result; as, a double-acting engine or pump.
To row by rowers sitting side by side in twos on a bank orthwart. To double-bank an oar, to set two men to pulling one oar.
Applied to a kind of rowing in which the rowers sit side byside in twos, a pair of oars being worked from each bank or thwart.
Folding or lapping over on the breast, with a row of buttonsand buttonholes on each side; as, a double-breasted coat.
A man-of-war having two gun decks.
To dye again or twice over.To double-dye their robes in scarlet. J. Webster.
Dyed twice; thoroughly or intensely colored; hence; firmlyfixed in opinions or habits; as, a double-dyed villain.
A locomotive with pilot at each end. Knight.
A word or expression admitting of a double interpretation, oneof which is often obscure or indelicate.
Having a deceitful look. [R.] "Deceitful meanings is double-eyed." Spenser.
Having two heads; bicipital. Double-headed rail (Railroad), arail whose flanges are duplicates, so that when one is worn the othermay be turned uppermost.
Having both sashes hung with weights and cords; -- said of awindow.
To lock with two bolts; to fasten with double security. Tatler.
Twice milled or fulled, to render more compact or fine; -- saidof cloth; as, double-milled kerseymere.
Of, or performed in, the fastest time or step in marching, nextto the run; as, a double-quick step or march.
A kind of coasting sled, made of two sleds fastened togetherwith a board, one before the other. [Local, U. S.]
To double the natural darkness of (a place). Milton.
Having two surfaces; -- said specif. of aëroplane wings oraërocurves which are covered on both sides with fabric, etc., thuscompletely inclosing their frames.
Deceit; duplicity.Now cometh the sin of double-tongue, such as speak fair before folkand wickedly behind. Chaucer.
Making contrary declarations on the same subject; deceitful.Likewise must the deacons be grave, not double-tongued. 1 Tim. iii.8.
A peculiar action of the tongue by flute players inarticulating staccato notes; also, the rapid repetition of notes incornet playing.
An apparition or double of a living person; a doppelgänger.
Having a false heart; deceitful; treacherous. Sandys.
Having different minds at different times; unsettled;undetermined.A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways. Jas. i. 8.
An instrument for augmenting a very small quantity ofelectricity, so as to render it manifest by sparks or theelectroscope.
A word or words unintentionally doubled or set up a secondtime.
Having two screw threads instead of one; -- said of a screw inwhich the pitch is equal to twice the distance between the centers ofadjacent threads.
The bar, or crosspiece, of a carriage, to which the singletreesare attached.
The lining of the mantle borne about the shield or escutcheon.
A Spanish gold coin, no longer issued, varying in value atdifferent times from over fifteen dollars to about five. See Doblonin Sup.
State of being in doubt; uncertainty; doubt. [Obs.] Chaucer.
One who doubts; one whose opinion is unsettled; one whoscruples.
In a doubtful manner.Nor did the goddess doubtfully declare. Dryden.
That is uncertain; that distrusts or hesitates; having doubts.-- Doubt"ing*ly, adv.
Free from fear or suspicion. [Obs.]Pretty child, sleep doubtless and secure. Shak.
A monkey (Semnopithecus nemæus), remarkable for its varied andbrilliant colors. It is a native of Cochin China.
One of the twelve peers of France, companions of Charlemagne inwar. [Written also douzepere.] [Obs.]Big-looking like a doughty doucepere. Spenser.
A grebe or diver; -- applied also to the golden-eye, pochard,scoter, and other ducks. [Written also ducker.] [Prov. Eng.]
Imperfectly baked; hence, not brought to perfection;unfinished; also, of weak or dull understanding. [Colloq.] Halliwell.
Like dough; soft.He demeans himself . . . like a dough-kneaded thing. Milton.
The Eskimo curlew (Numenius borealis). See Curlew.
A contemptuous nickname for a timid, yielding politician, orone who is easily molded. [Political cant, U. S.]
The character of a doughface; truckling pliability.
The quality or state of being doughy.
A small cake (usually sweetened) fried in a kettle of boilinglard.
The quality of being doughty; valor; bravery.

Able; strong; valiant; redoubtable; as, a doughty hero.Sir Thopas wex [grew] a doughty swain. Chaucer.Doughty families, hugging old musty quarrels to their hearts, buffeteach other from generation to generation. Motley.
Like dough; soft and heavy; pasty; crude; flabby and pale; as,a doughy complexion.
A government by slaves. [Written also dulocracy.] Hare.
The carrion crow. [Written also dob.] [Prov. Eng.]
Hard; inflexible; obstinate; sour in aspect; hardy; bold.[Scot.]A dour wife, a sour old carlin. C. Reade.
A kind of millet. See Durra.
To strike or lower in haste; to slacken suddenly; as, douse thetopsail.
One of several pieces fayed across the apron and lapped in theknightheads, or inside planking above the upper deck. Ham. Nav.Encyc.
To put out. [Obs.] "It douts the light." Sylvester.
A pigeon of the genus Columba and various related genera. Thespecies are numerous.

A Central American orchid (Peristeria elata), having a flowerstem five or six feet high, with numerous globose white fragrantflowers. The column in the center of the flower resembles a dove; --called also Holy Spirit plant.
Having eyes like a dove; meekeyed; as, dove-eyed Peace.
A guillemot (Uria grylle), of the arctic regions. Also appliedto the little auk or sea dove. See under Dove.
A young or small dove. Booth.
Mild as a dove; gentle; pure and lovable. Longfellow.
The possession of dovelike qualities, harmlessness andinnocence. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

A flaring tenon, or tongue (shaped like a bird's tail spread),and a mortise, or socket, into which it fits tightly, making aninterlocking joint between two pieces which resists pulling a part inall directions except one. Dovetail molding (Arch.), a molding of anyconvex section arranged in a sort of zigzag, like a series ofdovetails.-- Dovetail saw (Carp.), a saw used in dovetailing.
Like a dove; harmless; innocent. "Joined with dovishsimplicity." Latimer.
A kind of vessel. See Dhow.
Capable of being endowed; entitled to dower. Blackstone.

A widow endowed, or having a jointure; a widow who eitherenjoys a dower from her deceased husband, or has property of her ownbrought by her to her husband on marriage, and settled on her afterhis decease. Blount. Burrill.
The rank or condition of a dowager; formality, as that of adowager. Also used figuratively.Mansions that have passed away into dowagerism. Thackeray.
One of the testicles of a hart or stag. [Spelt also doucet.] B.Jonson.
Showing a vulgar taste in dress; awkward and slovenly in dress;vulgar-looking.-- Dow"di*ly, adv.-- Dow"di*ness, n.
To fasten together by dowels; to furnish with dowels; as, acooper dowels pieces for the head of a cask.
That portion of the real estate of a man which his widow enjoysduring her life, or to which a woman is entitled after the death ofher husband. Blackstone.
Furnished with, or as with, dower or a marriage portion. Shak.
Destitute of dower; having no marriage portion. Shak.
The red-breasted or gray snipe (Macrorhamphus griseus); --called also brownback, and grayback.
A coarse linen cloth made in the north of England and inScotland, now nearly replaced by calico. Shak.
Feathery or wool-like down; filament of a feather. Shak.No feather, or dowle of a feather. De Quincey.
To cover, ornament, line, or stuff with down. [R.] Young.
A breastplow used in paring off turf on downs. [Eng.] Knight.

Cast downward; directed to the ground, from bashfulness,modesty, dejection, or guilt.'T is love, said she; and then my downcast eyes, And guilty dumbness,witnessed my surprise. Dryden.- Down"cast`ly, adv.-- Down"cast`ness, n.
A pipe for leading combustible gases downward from the top ofthe blast furnace to the hot-blast stoves, boilers, etc., where theyare burned.
Hanging down like gyves or fetters. [Poetic & Rare] Shak.
A rope to haul down, or to assist in hauling down, a sail; as,a staysail downhaul; a trysail downhaul.
Towards the bottom of a hill; as, water runs downhill.
The quality or state of being downy.
Having a downcast countenance; dejected; gloomy; sullen. [R.]Dryden.
The time of retiring to rest; time of repose. Cavendish. At thedownlying, at the travail in childbirth. [Scot.]
A pouring or streaming downwards; esp., a heavy or continuousshower.
The act of sitting down; repose; a resting.Thou knowest my downsitting and my uprising. Ps. cxxxix. 2.
Down the stairs; to a lower floor.-- a.
Down the stream; as, floating downstream.
A stroke made with a downward motion of the pen or pencil.
The sudden drop or depression of the strata of rocks on oneside of a fault. See Throw, n.
To weigh or press down.A different sin downweighs them to the bottom. Longfellow.
Of or relating to a dower. [R.]
A woman entitled to dower. Bouvier.
To beat or thrash. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.
Pertaining to doxology; giving praise to God. Howell.
To give glory to God, as in a doxology; to praise God withdoxologies.

In Christian worship: A hymn expressing praise and honor toGod; a form of praise to God designed to be sung or chanted by thechoir or the congregation.David breaks forth into these triumphant praises and doxologies.South.
A loose wench; a disreputable sweetheart. Shak.
Lit., a dean; the senior member of a body or group; as, thedoyen of French physicians. "This doyen of newspapers."  A. R.Colquhoun.
To slumber; to sleep lightly; to be in a dull or stupefiedcondition, as if half asleep; to be drowsy.If he happened to doze a little, the jolly cobbler waked him.L'Estrange.
The state of being dozy; drowsiness; inclination to sleep.
Drowsy; inclined to doze; sleepy; sluggish; as, a dozy head.Dryden.
Stupid; heavy. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.
To associate with strumpets; to wench. Beau. & Fl.
One who associates with drabs; a wencher. Massinger.
A coarse linen fabric, or duck.
To draggle; to wet and befoul by draggling; as, to drabble agown or cloak. Halliwell.
A piece of canvas fastened by lacing to the bonnet of a sail,to give it a greater depth, or more drop.
A genus of liliaceous plants with woody stems and funnel-shapedflowers.
A kind of gum; -- called also gum tragacanth, or tragacanth.See Tragacanth.
The Dragon, a northern constellation within which is the northpole of the ecliptic.

Pertaining to Draco, a famous lawgiver of Athens, 621 b. c.Draconian code, or Draconian laws, a code of laws made by Draco.Their measures were so severe that they were said to be written inletters of blood; hence, any laws of excessive rigor.
Relating to Draco, the Athenian lawgiver; or to theconstellation Draco; or to dragon's blood.
A red resin forming the essential basis of dragon's blood; --called also dracin.
Belonging to that space of time in which the moon performs onerevolution, from ascending node to ascending node. See Dragon's head,under Dragon. [Obs.] "Dracontic month." Crabb.
Inferior ore, separated from the better by cobbing. Raymond.

Refuse; lees; dregs; the wash given to swine or cows; hogwash;waste matter.Prodigals lately come from swine keeping, from eating draff andhusks. Shak.The draff and offal of a bygone age. Buckle.Mere chaff and draff, much better burnt. Tennyson.
Dreggy; waste; worthless.The dregs and draffy part. Beau. & Fl.
A confection; a comfit; a drug. [Obs.] Chaucer.
A mucilage obtained from, or containing, gun tragacanth.
Same as Drawbar (b). Called also draglink, and drawlink. [U.S.]
A coupling pin. See under Coupling. [U. S.]
To wet and soil by dragging on the ground, mud, or wet grass;to drabble; to trail. Gray.With draggled nets down-hanging to the tide. Trench.
A slattern who suffers her gown to trail in the mire; adrabble-tail.
A fisherman who uses a dragnet. Sir M. Hale.
A net to be drawn along the bottom of a body of water, as infishing.
An interpreter; -- so called in the Levant and other parts ofthe East.

A fabulous animal, generally represented as a monstrous wingedserpent or lizard, with a crested head and enormous claws, andregarded as very powerful and ferocious.The dragons which appear in early paintings and sculptures areinvariably representations of a winged crocodile. Fairholt.
A small British marine fish (Callionymuslyra); -- called alsoyellow sculpin, fox, and gowdie.

The severe persecution of French Protestants under Louis XIV.,by an armed force, usually of dragoons; hence, a rapid anddevastating incursion; dragoonade.He learnt it as he watched the dragonnades, the tortures, themassacres of the Netherlands. C. Kingsley.
Formerly, a soldier who was taught and armed to serve either onhorseback or on foot; now, a mounted soldier; a cavalry man.

The grain from the mashing tub; as, brewers' drains. [Eng.]Halliwell. Box drain, Counter drain. See under Box, Counter.-- Right of drain (Law), an easement or servitude by which one manhas a right to convey water in pipes through or over the estate ofanother. Kent.
The system of drains and their operation, by which superfluouswater is removed from towns, railway beds, mines, and other works.
One who, or that which, drains.
The art of carrying off surplus water, as from land. Drainingtile. Same as Draintile.
A pipe used for carrying off surplus water.
A hollow tile used in making drains; -- called also drainingtile.
The drake fly.The drake will mount steeple height into the air. Walton.Drake fly, a kind of fly, sometimes used in angling.The dark drake fly, good in August. Walton.

A flat stone so thrown along the surface of water as to skipfrom point to point before it sinks; also, the sport of so throwingstones; -- sometimes called ducks and drakes.Internal earthquakes, that, not content with one throe, run alongspasmodically, like boys playing at what is called drakestone. DeQuincey.
A Persian daric. Ezra ii. 69. Fluid dram, or Fluid drachm. Seeunder Fluid.
Of or pertaining to the drama; appropriate to, or having thequalities of, a drama; theatrical; vivid.The emperor . . . performed his part with much dramatic effect.Motley.
In a dramatic manner; theatrically; vividly.
The actors in a drama or play.
The author of a dramatic composition; a writer of plays.

To compose in the form of the drama; to represent in a drama;to adapt to dramatic representation; as, to dramatize a novel, or anhistorical episode.They dramatized tyranny for public execration. Motley.
The art of dramatic composition and representation.
One who sells distilled liquors by the dram or glass.
A shop or barroom where spirits are sold by the dram.
One who sells cloths; a dealer in cloths; as, a draper andtailor.
Covered or supplied with drapery. [R.] Byron.
Acting rapidly and violently; efficacious; powerful; -- opposedto bland; as, drastic purgatives.-- n. (Med.)
The act of selecting or detaching soldiers; a draft (see Draft,n., 2)(g) The act of drawing up, marking out, or delineating;representation. Dryden.
A checkered board on which draughts are played. SeeCheckerboard.
A house for the reception of waste matter; a privy. [Obs.] 2Kings x. 27.
A mild vesicatory. See Draught, n., 3 (c).
The office, art, or work of a draughtsman.
Pertaining to a draught, or current of air; as, a draughtly,comfortless room.
A race Hindostan, believed to be the original people whooccupied the land before the Hindoo or Aryan invasion.

Of or pertaining to the Dravida. Dravidian languages, a groupof languages of Southern India, which seem to have been the idioms ofthe natives, before the invasion of tribes speaking Sanskrit. Ofthese languages, the Tamil is the most important.
To have efficiency as an epispastic; to act as a sinapism; --said of a blister, poultice, etc.
A single cut with a knife.

Money paid back or remitted; especially, a certain amount ofduties or customs, sometimes the whole, and sometimes only a part,remitted or paid back by the government, on the exportation of thecommodities on which they were levied. M
A machine in which strips of metal are drawn through adrawplate; especially, one in which wire is thus made; -- also calleddrawing bench.
A coupling pin. See under Coupling.

A hole bored through a tenon nearer to the shoulder than theholes through the cheeks are to the edge or abutment against whichthe shoulder is to rest, so that a pin or bolt, when driven into it,will draw these parts together. Weale.
A boy who operates the harness cords of a hand loom; also, apart of power loom that performs the same office.

A bridge of which either the whole or a part is made to beraised up, let down, or drawn or turned aside, to admit or hindercommunication at pleasure, as before the gate of a town or castle, orover a navigable river or canal.
A blustering, bullying fellow; a pot-valiant braggart; a bully.The leader was of an ugly look and gigantic stature; he acted like adrawcansir, sparing neither friend nor foe. Addison.
The person on whom an order or bill of exchange is drawn; --the correlative of drawer.
An under-garment worn on the lower limbs. Chest of drawers. Seeunder Chest.
The process of smooth filing by working the file sidewiseinstead of lengthwise.
The means or parts by which cars are connected to be drawn.
An old game, played by holding up the fingers. Herrick.
The flanged outer end of a drawbar; also, a name applied to thedrawgear.
The process of pulling out and elongating the sliver from thecarding machine, by revolving rollers, to prepare it for spinning.
To utter in a slow, lengthened tone.
A housebreaker or thief. [Obs.] Old Play (1631).
The act of speaking with a drawl; a drawl.-- Drawl"ing*ly, adv. Bacon.

See Draw, v. t. & i. Drawn butter, butter melter and preparedto be used as a sort of gravy.-- Drawn fowl, an eviscerated fowl.-- Drawn game or battle, one in which neither party wins; oneequally contested.-- Drawn fox, one driven from cover. Shak.-- Drawn work, ornamental work made by drawing out threads from finecloth, and uniting the cross threads, to form a pattern.
A net for catching the larger sorts of birds; also, a dragnet.Crabb.
A hardened steel plate having a hole, or a gradation of conicalholes, through which wires are drawn to be reduced and elongated.
A rod which unites the drawgear at opposite ends of the car,and bears the pull required to draw the train.
The spring to which a drawbar is attached.
A man who attends a dray.
A slut; a vagabond wench. Same as Drossel. [Obs.] Hudibras.

To fear in a great degree; to regard, or look forward to, withterrific apprehension.When at length the moment dreaded through so many years came close,the dark cloud passed away from Johnson's mind. Macaulay.
One who fears, or lives in fear.
In a dreadful manner; terribly. Dryden.

To have a dream of; to see, or have a vision of, in sleep, orin idle fancy; -- often followed by an objective clause.Your old men shall dream dreams. Acts ii. 17.At length in sleep their bodies they compose, And dreamt the futurefight. Dryden.And still they dream that they shall still succeed. Cowper.To dream away, out, through, etc., to pass in revery or inaction; tospend in idle vagaries; as, to dream away an hour; to dream throughlife. " Why does Antony dream out his hours" Dryden.
Full of dreams. " Dreamful ease." Tennyson.-- Dream"ful*ly, adv.
As if in a dream; softly; slowly; languidly. Longfellow.
An unreal, delightful country such as in sometimes pictured indreams; region of fancies; fairyland.[He] builds a bridge from dreamland for his lay. Lowell.
Free from, or without, dreams. Camden.-- Dream"less*ly, adv.
Abounding in dreams or given to dreaming; appropriate to, orlike, dreams; visionary. "The dreamy dells." Tennyson.
Dismal; gloomy with solitude. "A drear and dying sound."Milton.
Very fine mineral matter held in suspension in water. Raymond.
A box with holes in its lid; -- used for sprinkling flour, ason meat or a breadboard; -- called also dredging box, drudger, anddrudging box.

Corrupt or defiling matter contained in a liquid, orprecipitated from it; refuse; feculence; lees; grounds; sediment;hence, the vilest and most worthless part of anything; as, the dregsof society.We, the dregs and rubbish of mankind. Dryden.
Fullness of dregs or lees; foulness; feculence.
Containing dregs or lees; muddy; foul; feculent. Boyle.
A triple alliance; specif., the alliance of Germany, Austria,and Italy, formed in 1882.
A genus of bivalve shells of which one species (D. polymorpha)is often so abundant as to be very troublesome in the fresh waters ofEurope.
A drink; a draught; specifically, a potion of medicine pouredor forced down the throat; also, a potion that causes purging. "Adrench of wine." Dryden.Give my roan horse a drench. Shak.
To drown. [Obs.]In the sea he drenched. Chaucer.
The tenure by which a drench held land. [Obs.] Burrill.
Drenched; drowned. [Obs.] "Condemned to be drent." Spenser.
A superior kind of decorated porcelain made near Dresden inSaxony.
To arrange in exact continuity of line, as soldiers; commonlyto adjust to a straight line and at proper distance; to align; as, todress the ranks.
A gallery or circle in a theater, generally the first above thefloor, in which originally dress clothes were customarily worn.

A coat with skirts behind only, as distinct from the frockcoat, of which the skirts surround the body. It is worn on occasionsof ceremony. The dress coat of officers of the United States army isa full-skirted frock coat.
A term applied to fabrics for the gowns of women and girls; --most commonly to fabrics of mixed materials, but also applicable tosilks, printed linens, and calicoes.
A kind of pick for shaping large coal.
An application (a remedy, bandage, etc.) to a sore or wound.Wiseman.
A maker of gowns, or similar garments; a mantuamaker.
The art, process, or occupation, of making dresses.
Showy in dress; attentive to dress.A dressy flaunting maidservant. T. Hook.A neat, dressy gentleman in black. W. Irving.
A fool; a drudge. See Drivel.
To do by little and little; as:(a) To cut off by a little at a time; to crop.(b) To appropriate unlawfully; to filch; to defalcate.He who drives their bargain dribs a part. Dryden.
One who dribs; one who shoots weakly or badly. [Obs.] Ascham.
To let fall in drops.Let the cook . . . dribble it all the way upstairs. Swift.
To endure. [Obs.]So causeless such drede for to drie. Chaucer.
of Day. Also adj.; as, dried apples.
Drying oil; a substance mingled with the oil used in oilpainting to make it dry quickly.
The horizontal thrust or pressure of an arch or vault upon theabutments. [R.] Knight.
A bolt for driving out other bolts.
Having no drift or direction; without aim; purposeless.
An upright or curved piece of timber connecting the plank sheerwith the gunwale; also, a scroll terminating a rail.
A smooth drift. See Drift, n., 9.
Seaweed drifted to the shore by the wind. Darwin.
A driving wind; a wind that drives snow, sand, etc., intoheaps. Beau. & Fl.
Full of drifts; tending to form drifts, as snow, and the like.
To practice an exercise or exercises; to train one's self.
A machine for drilling holes in metal, the drill being pressedto the metal by the action of a screw.
One who, or that which, drills.
The act of using a drill in sowing seeds.
One who teaches drill, especially in the way of gymnastics.Macaulay.
A contrivance for holding and turning a drill. Knight.
A genus of magnoliaceous trees. Drimys aromatica furnishesWinter's bark.
Capable of being drunk; suitable for drink; potable. Macaulay.Also used substantively, esp. in the plural. Steele.
One who drinks; as, the effects of tea on the drinker; also,one who drinks spirituous liquors to excess; a drunkard. Drinker moth(Zoöl.), a large British moth (Odonestis potatoria).
To let fall in drops.Which from the thatch drips fast a shower of rain. Swift.
A drip, when made of stone. See Drip, 2.
To dig Horizontally; to cut a horizontal gallery or tunnel.Tomlinson.
A drift; a tool for setting bolts home.
To be weak or foolish; to dote; as, a driveling hero; drivelinglove. Shak. Dryden.
A slaverer; a slabberer; an idiot; a fool. [Written alsodriveller.]
of Drive. Also adj. Driven well, a well made by driving a tubeinto the earth to an aqueous stratum; -- called also drive well.
A pipe for forcing into the earth.

A part that transmits motion to another part by contact withit, or through an intermediate relatively movable part, as a gearwhich drives another, or a lever which moves another through a link,etc. Specifically:(a) The driving wheel of a locomotive.(b) An attachment to a lathe, spindle, or face plate to turn acarrier.(c) A crossbar on a grinding mill spindle to drive the upper stone.
A passage or way along or through which a carriage may bedriven.
To rain slightly in very small drops; to fall, as water fromthe clouds, slowly and in fine particles; as, it drizzles; drizzlingdrops or rain. "Drizzling tears." Spenser.
Characterized by small rain, or snow; moist and disagreeable."Winter's drizzly reign." Dryden.

A small craft used in the West India Islands to take offsugars, rum, etc., to the merchantmen; also, a vessel fortransporting lumber, cotton, etc., coastwise; as, a lumber drogher.[Written also droger.] Ham. Nar. Encyc.
To work sluggishly or slowly; to plod. [Obs.]

A right; law in its aspect of the foundation of rights; also,in old law, the writ of right. Abbott. Droit d'aubaine. See underAubaine.-- Droits of the Admiralty (Eng. Law), rights or perquisites of theAdmiralty, arising from seizure of an enemy's ships in port on thebreaking out of war, or those coming into port in ignorance ofhostilities existing, or from such ships as are taken bynoncommissioned captors; also, the proceeds of wrecks, and derelictproperty at sea. The droits of admiralty are now paid into theExchequer for the public benefit.
relating to the mere right of property, as distinguished fromthe right of possession; as, droitural actions. [Obs.] Burrill.
Queer, and fitted to provoke laughter; ludicrous from oddity;amusing and strange.
Having the structure of the palate like that of the ostrich andemu.
A small extinct triassic mammal from North Carolina, theearliest yet found in America.
The crab plover (Dromas ardeola), a peculiar North Africanbird, allied to the oyster catcher.
The Arabian camel (Camelus dromedarius), having one hump orprotuberance on the back, in distinction from the Bactrian camel,which has two humps.
The male of bees, esp. of the honeybee. It gathers no honey.See Honeybee.All with united force combine to drive The lazy drones from thelaborious hive. Dryden.
The male of the honeybee; a drone.
A dipterous insect (Eristalis tenax), resembling the drone bee.See Eristalis.
One of the low-toned tubes of a bagpipe.
A passerine bird of the family Dicruridæ. They are usuallyblack with a deeply forked tail. They are natives of Asia, Africa,and Australia; -- called also drongo shrikes.
Like a drone; indolent; slow. Burke.-- Dron"ish*ly, adv.-- Dron"ish*ness, n.
To drivel, or drop saliva; as, the child drools.His mouth drooling with texts. T. Parker.
To let droop or sink. [R.] M. Arnold.Like to a withered vine That droops his sapless branches to theground. Shak.
One who, or that which, droops.
Any medicine the dose of which is measured by drops; as,lavender drops.
A little drop; a tear. Shak.
An apparatus for bringing artificial light down from achandelier nearer to a table or desk; a pendant.
A branch vein which drops off from, or leaves, the main lode.

That which falls in drops; the excrement or dung of animals.Dropping bottle, an instrument used to supply small quantities of afluid to a test tube or other vessel.-- Dropping fire, a continued irregular discharge of firearms.-- Dropping tube, a tube for ejecting any liquid in drops.
An unnatural collection of serous fluid in any serous cavity ofthe body, or in the subcutaneous cellular tissue. Dunglison.
imp. & p. p. of Drop, v. G. Eliot.
After the manner of a drop; in the form of drops.Trickling dropwise from the cleft. Tennyson.
The larva of any geometrid moth, which drops from trees bymeans of a thread of silk, as the cankerworm.
An Old World species of Spiræa (S. filipendula), with finelycut leaves.
A genus of low perennial or biennial plants, the leaves ofwhich are beset with gland-tipped bristles. See Sundew. Gray.

A low, four-wheeled, open carriage, used in Russia, consistingof a kind of long, narrow bench, on which the passengers ride as on asaddle, with their feet reaching nearly to the ground. Other kinds ofvehicles are now so called, esp. a kind of victoria drawn by one ortwo horses, and used as a public carriage in German cities. [Writtenalso droitzschka, and droschke.]

An instrument for measuring the quantity of dew on the surfaceof a body in the open air. It consists of a balance, having a plateat one end to receive the dew, and at the other a weight protectedfrom the deposit of dew.
A slut; a hussy; a drazel. [Obs.] Warner.
Of, pertaining to, resembling, dross; full of dross; impure;worthless. " Drossy gold." Dryden. "Drossy rhymes." Donne.-- Dross"i*ness, n.
A state of dryness of the weather; want of rain.

Same as Drought. Sandys.Another ill accident is drouth at the spindling of corn. Bacon.One whose drouth [thirst], Yet scarce allayed, still eyes the currentstream. Milton.In the dust and drouth of London life. Tennyson.
To be suffocated in water or other fluid; to perish in water.Methought, what pain it was to drown. Shak.
One who, or that which, drowns.
To sleep imperfectly or unsoundly; to slumber; to be heavy withsleepiness; to doze. "He drowsed upon his couch." South.In the pool drowsed the cattle up to their knees. Lowell.
To beat with a stick; to thrash; to cudgel.Soundly Drubbed with a good honest cudgel. L'Estrange.
One who drubs. Sir W. Scott.
To perform menial work; to labor in mean or unpleasant officeswith toil and fatigue.He gradually rose in the estimation of the booksellers for whom hedrudged. Macaulay.

The act of drudging; disagreeable and wearisome labor; ignobleor slavish toil.The drudgery of penning definitions. Macaulay.Paradise was a place of bliss . . . without drudgery and with outsorrow. Locke.
Courtship; gallantry; love; an object of love. [Obs.] Chaucer.
To drudge; to toil laboriously. [Obs.] "To drugge and draw."Chaucer.
One who deals in drugs; especially, one who buys and sellsdrugs without compounding them; also, a pharmaceutist or apothecary.
The system of religion, philosophy, and instruction, receivedand taught by the Druids; the rites and ceremonies of the Druids.

An instrument of percussion, consisting either of a hollowcylinder, over each end of which is stretched a piece of skin orvellum, to be beaten with a stick; or of a metallic hemisphere(kettledrum) with a single piece of skin to be so beaten; the commoninstrument for marking time in martial music; one of the pair oftympani in an orchestra, or cavalry band.The drums cry bud-a-dub. Gascoigne.
A method of armature winding in which the wire is wound uponthe outer surface of a cylinder or drum from end to end of thecylinder; -- distinguished from ring winding, etc.

The sound of a beaten drum; drum music.Whose morning drumbeat, following the sun, and keeping company withthe hours, circles the earth with one continuous and unbroken strainof the martial airs of England. D. Webster.
any fish of the family Sciænidæ, which makes a loud noise bymeans of its air bladder; -- called also drum.
A hill of compact, unstratified, glacial drift or till, usuallyelongate or oval, with the larger axis parallel to the former localglacial motion.
Turbid; muddy. [Scot. & Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Wodroephe (1623).Burns.
A fish that makes a sound when caught; as:(a) The squeteague.(b) A California sculpin.
The act of beating upon, or as if upon, a drum; also, the noisewhich the male of the ruffed grouse makes in spring, by beating hiswings upon his sides.

A very intense light, produced by turning two streams of gas,one oxygen and the other hydrogen, or coal gas, in a state ofignition, upon a ball of lime; or a stream of oxygen gas through aflame of alcohol upon a ball or disk of lime; -- called alsooxycalcium light, or lime light.
One who habitually drinks strong liquors immoderately; onewhose habit it is to get drunk; a toper; a sot.The drunkard and glutton shall come to poverty. Prov. xxiii. 21.
The state of being drunk; drunkenness. [Obs.] Gower.
Producing, or pertaining to, drupes; having the form of drupes;as, drupaceous trees or fruits.

A fruit consisting of pulpy, coriaceous, or fibrous exocarp,without valves, containing a nut or stone with a kernel. The exocarpis succulent in the plum, cherry, apricot, peach, etc.; dry andsubcoriaceous in the almond; and fibrous in the cocoanut.
A cavity in a rock, having its interior surface studded withcrystals and sometimes filled with water; a geode.
Of certain morbid conditions, in which there is entire orcomparative absence of moisture; as, dry gangrene; dry catarrh.
A commercial name for textile fabrics, cottons, woolens, linen,silks, laces, etc., -- in distinction from groceries. [U.S.]
A nurse who attends and feeds a child by hand; -- indistinction from a wet nurse, who suckles it.
Having dry bones, or bones without flesh.
Not having tears in the eyes.
To rub and cleanse without wetting. Dodsley.
Constructed of uncemented stone. "Dry-stone walls." Sir W.Scott.
A wood nymph; a nymph whose life was bound up with that of hertree.
A genus of shrubs growing in Australia, having beautiful, hard,dry, evergreen leaves.
The scent of the game, as far as it can be traced. [Obs.] Shak.
In a dry manner; not succulently; without interest; withoutsympathy; coldly.
The state of being dry. See Dry.
To feed, attend, and bring up without the breast. Hudibras.
The genus to which belongs the single species D. Camphora, alofty resinous tree of Borneo and Sumatra, yielding Borneo camphorand camphor oil.

A dealer in salted or dried meats, pickles, sauces, etc., andin the materials used in pickling, salting, and preserving variouskinds of food Hence drysalters usually sell a number of salinesubstances and miscellaneous drugs. Brande & C.
The articles kept by a drysalter; also, the business of adrysalter.
A union of two; duality. [R.] Harris.
Expressing, or consisting of, the number two; belonging to two;as, the dual number of nouns, etc. , in Greek.Here you have one half of our dual truth. Tyndall.
An explosive substance consisting essentially of sawdust orwood pulp, saturated with nitroglycerin and other similar nitrocompounds. It is inferior to dynamite, and is more liable toexplosion.

State of being dual or twofold; a twofold division; any systemwhich is founded on a double principle, or a twofold distinction; as:(a) (Philos.) A view of man as constituted of two original andindependent elements, as matter and spirit. (Theol.)(b) A system which accepts two gods, or two original principles, onegood and the other evil.(c) The doctrine that all mankind are divided by the arbitrary decreeof God, and in his eternal foreknowledge, into two classes, the electand the reprobate.(d) (Physiol.) The theory that each cerebral hemisphere actsindependently of the other.An inevitable dualism bisects nature, so that each thing is a half,and suggests another thing to make it whole. Emerson.

Consisting of two; pertaining to dualism or duality. Dualisticsystem or theory (Chem.), the theory, originated by Lavoisier anddeveloped by Berzelius, that all definite compounds are binary intheir nature, and consist of two distinct constituents, themselvessimple or complex, and possessed of opposite chemical or electricalaffinities.
The quality or condition of being two or twofold; dualcharacter or usage.
A division of a poem corresponding to a canto; a poem or song.[R.]
To make a noise by brisk drumbeats. "Now the drum dubs." Beau.& Fl.
The Syrian bear. See under Bear. [Written also dhubb, and dub.]
One who, or that which, dubs.
Doubtfulness; uncertainty; doubt. [R.] Lamb. "The dubiety ofhis fate." Sir W. Scott.
The state of being doubtful; a doubtful statement or thing.[R.]Men often swallow falsities for truths, dubiosities for certainties,possibilities for feasibilities. Sir T. Browne.
Liable to be doubted; uncertain. [R.] Dr. H. More.-- Du"bi*ta*bly, adv. [R.]
To doubt. [R.]If he . . . were to loiter dubitating, and not come. Carlyle.
Act of doubting; doubt. [R.] Sir T. Scott.
Tending to doubt; doubtful. [R.] -- Du"bi*ta*tive*ly, adv. [R.]. Eliot.
An alkaloid obtained from the leaves of an Australian tree(Duboisia myoporoides), and regarded as identical with hyoscyamine.It produces dilation of the pupil of the eye.
Of or pertaining to a duke.His ducal cap was to be exchanged for a kingly crown. Motley.
In the manner of a duke, or in a manner becoming the rank of aduke.
A coin, either of gold or silver, of several countries inEurope; originally, one struck in the dominions of a duke.
A silver coin of several countries of Europe, and of differentvalues.
A judicial process commanding a person to appear in court andbring with him some piece of evidence or other thing to be producedto the court.
The wife or widow of a duke; also, a lady who has thesovereignty of a duchy in her own right.

A beautiful variety of Brussels pillow lace made originally inBelgium and resembling Honiton guipure. It is worked with fine threadin large sprays, usually of the primrose pattern, with much raisedwork.
The territory or dominions of a duke; a dukedom.
Having a bill like that of a duck..
Having short legs, like a waddling duck; short-legged. Dryden.
See Duck mole, under Duck, n.

, from Duck, v. t. & i. Ducking stool, a stool or chair inwhich common scolds were formerly tied, and plunged into water, as apunishment. See Cucking stool. The practice of ducking began in thelatter part of the 15th century, and prevailed until the early partof the 18th, and occasionally as late as the 19th century.Blackstone. Chambers.
A young or little duck. Gay.
A genus (Lemna) of small plants, seen floating in greatquantity on the surface of stagnant pools fresh water, and supposedto furnish food for ducks; -- called also duckmeat.
One of the vessels of an animal body by which the products ofglandular secretion are conveyed to their destination.
Capable of being drawn out [R.] Feltham.
An instrument for accurately determining the ductility ofmetals.
Having to duct or outlet; as, a ductless gland.
A contrivance for removing superfluous ink or coloring matterfrom a roller. See Doctor, 4. Knight. Ductor roller (Printing), theroller which conveys or supplies ink to another roller. Knight.
To confuse or confound with noise. Jennings.
A place where rags are bought and kept for sale. [Eng.]
A kind of dandy; especially, one characterized by anultrafashionable style of dress and other affectations. [Recent]The social dude who affects English dress and English drawl. TheAmerican.
A short tobacco pipe. [Written also dudheen.] [Irish]
Resentment; ill will; anger; displeasure.I drink it to thee in dudgeon and hostility.Sir T. Scott.
Like, or characterized of, a dude.
Directly; exactly; as, a due east course.
A brief written acknowledgment of a debt, not made payable toorder, like a promissory note. Burrill.

A combat between two persons, fought with deadly weapons, byagreement. It usually arises from an injury done or an affront givenby one to the other. Trial by duel (Old Law), a combat between twopersons for proving a cause; trial by battel.
One who engages in a duel. [R.] [Written also dueller.] South.
e act or practice of fighting in single combat. Also adj.[Written also duelling.]
One who fights in single combat. [Written also duellist.]A duelist . . . always values himself upon his courage, his sense ofhonor, his fidelity and friendship. Hume.
A duel; also, the rules of dueling. [Obs.] Shak.
Quality of being due; debt; what is due or becoming. T.Goodwin.
A composition for two performers, whether vocal orinstrumental.
A duet of short extent and concise form.
A kind of coarse woolen cloth, having a thick nap or frieze.[Written also duffle.]Good duffel gray and flannel fine. Wordsworth.
A sack to hold miscellaneous articles, as tools, supplies, orthe like.
A mineral of a blackish green color, commonly massive or innodules. It is a hydrous phosphate of iron.
A teat, pap, or nipple; -- formerly that of a human mother, nowthat of a cow or other beast.With mother's dug between its lips. Shak.

An aquatic herbivorous mammal (Halicore dugong), of the orderSirenia, allied to the manatee, but with a bilobed tail. It inhabitsthe Red Sea, Indian Ocean, East Indies, and Australia. [Written alsoduyong.]
A way or road dug through a hill, or sunk below the surface ofthe land. [U.S.]
To play the duke. [Poetic]Lord Angelo dukes it well in his absence. Shak.
A little or insignificant duke. Ford.
The quality or condition of being a duke; also, the personalityof a duke. Massinger.
A plant (Solanum Dulcamara). See Bittersweet, n.,
A glucoside extracted from the bittersweet (Solanum Dulcamara),as a yellow amorphous substance. It probably occasions the compoundtaste. See Bittersweet, 3(a).
A sweet-toned stop of an organ.
The act of dulcifying or sweetening. Boyle.
Sweetened; mollified. Dulcified spirit or spirits, a compoundof alcohol with mineral acids; as, dulcified spirits of niter.
To sweeten; to free from acidity, saltness, or acrimony.Wiseman.
A mistress; a sweetheart.I must ever have some Dulcinea in my head. Sterne.
A white, sugarlike substance, C6H8.(OH)2, occurring naturallyin a manna from Madagascar, and in certain plants, and producedartificially by the reduction of galactose and lactose or milk sugar.
To sweeten; to make less acrimonious. [R.] Bacon.
One of the dowels joining the ends of the fellies which formthe circle of the wheel of a gun carriage. Wilhelm.
An inferior kind of veneration or worship, given to the angelsand saints as the servants of God.
To become dull or stupid. Rom. of R.
Having eyes wanting brightness, liveliness, or vivacity. Shak.
A stupid person; a dunce. Shak.-- a.
One who, or that which, dulls.
Somewhat dull; uninteresting; tiresome. "A series of dullishverses." Prof. Wilson.

The state of being dull; slowness; stupidity; heaviness;drowsiness; bluntness; obtuseness; dimness; want of luster; want ofvividness, or of brightness. [Written also dulness.]And gentle dullness ever loves a joke. Pope.
In a dull manner; stupidly; slowly; sluggishly; without life orspirit.Supinely calm and dully innocent. G. Lyttelton.

A seaweed of a reddish brown color, which is sometimes eaten,as in Scotland. The true dulse is Sarcophyllis edulis; the common isRhodymenia. [Written also dillisk.]The crimson leaf of the dulse is seen To blush like a banner bathedin slaughter. Percival.
In a due, fit, or becoming manner; as it (anything) ought tobe; properly; regularly.
Pertaining to, or set with, briers or bushes; brambly. [R.]
A weight, consisting of two spheres or spheroids, connected bya short bar for a handle; used (often in pairs) for gymnasticexercise.
A framework on which dishes, food, etc., are passed from oneroom or story of a house to another; a lift for dishes, etc.; also, apiece of furniture with movable or revolving shelves.
A bumblebee; also, a cockchafer. [Prov. Eng.]
The quality or state of being dumb; muteness; silence;inability to speak.
A kind of manstopping bullet; -- so named from Dumdum, inIndia, where bullets are manufactured for the Indian army.
To strike dumb; to confuse with astonishment. [Written alsodumbfound.] Spectator.
To dumfound; to confound. [Written also dumbfounder.]
One who plays a merely nominal part in any action; a shamcharacter.
A thick, ill-shapen piece; a clumsy leaden counter used by boysin playing chuck farthing. [Eng.] Smart.
Dull; stupid; sad; moping; melancholy. " A . . . dumpish andsour life." Lord Herbert.-- Dump"ish*ly, adv.-- Dump"ish*ness, n.
To make dumpy; to fold, or bend, as one part over another. [R.]He was a little man, dumpled up together. Sir W. Scott.
A roundish mass of dough boiled in soup, or as a sort ofpudding; often, a cover of paste inclosing an apple or other fruit,and boiled or baked; as, an apple dumpling.

A level having a short telescope (hence its name) rigidly fixedto a table capable only of rotatory movement in a horizontal plane.The telescope is usually an inverting one. It is sometimes called theTroughton level, from the name of the inventor, and a varietyimproved by one Gavatt is known as the Gavatt level.
One backward in book learning; a child or other person dull orweak in intellect; a dullard; a dolt.I never knew this town without dunces of figure. Swift.
The realm or domain of dunces. [Jocose] Carlyle.
Like a dunce; duncish.The most dull and duncical commissioner. Fuller.
To make stupid in intellect. [R.] Bp. Warburton.
Somewhat like a dunce. [R.] -- Dun"cish*ness, n. [R.]
