A channel of curved section; -- usually applied to one of avertical series of such channels used to decorate columns andpilasters in classical architecture. See Illust. under Base, n.
A beak flute, an older form of the flute, played with amouthpiece resembling a beak, and held like a flageolet.
A fish of the genus Aulostoma, having a much elongated tubularsnout.

Decoration by means of flutes or channels; a flute, or flutescollectively; as, the fluting of a column or pilaster; the fluting ofa lady's ruffle. Fluting iron, a laundry iron for fluting ruffles; --called also Italian iron, or gaufering iron. Knight.-- Fluting lathe, a machine for forming spiral flutes, as onbalusters, table legs, etc.
A performer on the flute; a flautist. Busby.
One who, or that which, flutters.
Soft and clear in tone, like a flute.
Belonging to rivers; growing or living in streams or ponds; as,a fluvial plant.
One who exlpains geological phenomena by the action of streams.[R.]
Belonging to rivers or streams; fluviatile. Johnson.
Belonging to rivers or streams; existing in or about rivers;produced by river action; fluvial; as, fluviatile starta, plants.Lyell.
Formed by the joint action of a river and the sea, as depositsat the mouths of rivers.
An instrument for measuring and recording automatically therise and fall of a river.
An instrument for measuring the height of water in a river; ariver gauge.
Any substance or mixture used to promote the fusion of metalsor minerals, as alkalies, borax, lime, fluorite.
The quality of being fluxible. Hammond.
Capable of being melted or fused, as a mineral. Holland.-- Flux"i*ble*ness, n.
Pertaining to, or having the nature of, fluxion or fluxions;variable; inconstant.The merely human,the temporary and fluxional. Coleridge.Fluxional structure (Geol.), fluidal structure.
Pertaining to, or caused by, an increased flow of blood to apart; congestive; as, a fluxionary hemorrhage.
Flowing; also, wanting solidity. B. Jonson.
That part of a compass on which the points are marked; thecompass card. Totten.
Marked by, or as if by, the bite of flies. Shak.
The covering of an insect, esp. the elytra of beetles.
Having the habit of catching insects on the wing.
To angle, using flies for bait. Walton.
Disposed to fly away; flighty; unrestrained; light and free; --used of both persons and things. -- n.
The hair grass (Agrostis scabra). So called from its lightpanicle, which is blown to great distances by the wind.
A kind of catchfly of the genus Silene; also, a poisonousmushroom (Agaricus muscarius); fly agaric.
To deposit eggs upon, as a flesh fly does on meat; to cause tobe maggoty; hence, to taint or contaminate, as if with flyblows. Bp.Srillingfleet.
Tainted or contaminated with flyblows; damaged; foul.Wherever flyblown reputations were assembled. Thackeray.
A large Dutch coasting vessel.Captain George Weymouth made a voyage of discovery to the northwestwith two flyboats. Purchas.
One of numerous species of birds that feed upon insects, whichthey take on the wing.
One in a flight of steps which are parallel to each other(as inordinary stairs), as distinguished from a winder.
A California scorpænoid fish (Sebastichthys rhodochloris),having brilliant colors.
Moving in the air with, or as with, wings; moving lightly orrapidly; intended for rapid movement.
A compact form of hydro-aëroplane having one central body, orhull.

A fish which is able to leap from the water, and fly aconsiderable distance by means of its large and long pectoral fins.These fishes belong to several species of the genus Exocoetus, andare found in the warmer parts of all the oceans.
One of a group of squirrels, of the genera Pteromus andSciuropterus, having parachute-like folds of skin extending from thefore to the hind legs, which enable them to make very long leaps.
The driver of a fly, or light public carriage.
A name given to the series of sandstones and schists overlyingthe true nummulitic formation in the Alps, and included in the EoceneTertiary.
A speck or stain made by the excrement of a fly; hence, anyinsignificant dot.
To breathe heavily; to snort. [Obs.] Chaucer.

The young of any animal of the Horse family (Equidæ); a colt; afilly. Foal teeth (Zoöl.), the first set of teeth of a horse.-- In foal, With foal, being with young; pregnant; -- said of a mareor she ass.

The white substance, consisting of an aggregation of bubbles,which is formed on the surface of liquids,or in the mouth of ananimal, by violent agitation or fermentation; froth; spume; scum; as,the foam of the sea. Foam cock, in steam boilers, a cock at the waterlevel, to blow off impurities.
Covered with foam; frothy; spumy.Behold how high the foamy billows ride! Dryden.
A little pocket for a watch. Fob chain, a short watch chainworn a watch carried in the fob.

Belonging to,or concerning, a focus; as, a focal point. Focaldistance, or length,of a lens or mirror (Opt.), the distance of thefocus from the surface of the lens or mirror, or more exactly, in thecase of a lens, from its optical center. --Focal distance of atelescope, the distance of the image of an object from the objectglass.
The act of focalizing or bringing to a focus, or the state ofbeing focalized.
To bring to a focus; to focus; to concentrate.Light is focalized in the eye, sound in the ear. De Quincey.
(Photog.) An assisting instrument for focusing an object in orbefore a camera. Knight.
A point in which the rays of light meet, after being reflectedor refrcted, and at which the image is formed; as, the focus of alens or mirror.
A weight by which lead and some other metals were formerlysold, in England, varying from 19 [Obs.]
Fitted for, or pertaining to, digging.
A group of African edentates including the aard-vark.
See Fiend, and cf. Feud a quarrel.
An enemy in war.And the stern joy which warriors feel In foemen worthy of theirsteel. Sir W. Scott
(Agric.) To pasture cattle on the fog, or aftergrass, of; toeat off the fog from.
A region of the ocean where fogs are of marked frequency, asnear the coast of Newfoundland.
A nebulous arch, or bow, of white or yellowish light sometimesseen in fog, etc.
The Cornish name for a forge used for smelting tin. Raymond
One who fogs; a pettifogger. [Obs.]A beggarly fogger. Terence in English(1614)
In a foggy manner; obscurely. Johnson.
The state of being foggy. Johnson.
A dull old fellow; a person behind the times, over-conservative, or slow; -- usually preceded by old. [Written alsofogie and fogey.] [Colloq.]Notorious old bore; regular old fogy. Thackeray.
The principles and conduct of a fogy. [Colloq.]
An exclamation of abhorrence or contempt; poh; fle. Shak.
One who foils or frustrates. Johnson.
The beech marten (Mustela foina). See Marten.
Thrusting with the foil; fencing with the point, asdistinguished from broadsword play. [Obs.] Marston.
Rich harvest; plenty; abundance. [Archaic] Lowell.That from the seedness the bare fallow brings To teeming foison.Shak.
A light and fast-sailing ship. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.
One who foists something surreptitiously; a falsitier. Mir. forMag.
To become folded, plaited, or doubled; to close over another ofthe same kind; to double together; as, the leaves of the door fold. 1Kings vi. 34.
One who, or that which, folds; esp., a flat, knifelikeinstrument used for folding paper.

The keepig of sheep in inclosures on arable land, etc. Foldingboat, a portable boat made by stretching canvas, etc., over jointedframework, used in campaigning, and by tourists, etc. Ham. Nav.Encyc. Folding chairFolding door, one of two or more doors filling asingle and hung upon hinges.
Belonging to, or having the texture or nature of, a leaf;having leaves intermixed with flowers; as, a foliaceous spike.
To adorn with foliage or the imitation of foliage; to form intothe representation of leaves. [R.] Drummond.
Furnished with foliage; leaved; as, the variously foliagedmulberry.

Consisting of, or pertaining to, leaves; as, foliar appendages.Foliar gap (Bot.), an opening in the fibrovascular system of a stemat the point of origin of a leaf.-- Foliar trace (Bot.), a particular fibrovascular bundle passingdown into the stem from a leaf.
Furnished with leaves; leafy; as, a foliate stalk. Foliatecurve. (Geom.) Same as Folium.
Containing, or consisting of, foils; as, a foliated arch.
The enrichment of an opening by means of foils, arranged intrefoils, quatrefoils, etc.; also, one of the ornaments. See Tracery.
The page number. The even folios are on the left-hand pages andthe odd folios on the right-hand.
Of or pertaining to leaflets; -- used in composition; as, bi-foliolate. Gray.
One of the distinct parts of a compound leaf; a leaflet.
The ponderousness or bulk of a folio; voluminousness. [R.] DeQuincey.
A curve of the third order, consisting of two infinitebranches, which have a common asymptote. The curve has a doublepoint, and a leaf-shaped loop; whence the name. Its equation is x3 +y3 = axy.
The lower house of the Danish Rigsdag, or Parliament. SeeLegislature, below.

Land held in villenage, being distributed among the folk, orpeople, at the pleasure of the lord of the manor, and resumed at hisdiscretion. Not being held by any assurance in writing, it wasopposed to bookland or charter land, which was held by deed. Mozley &W.
An assembly of the people; esp. (Sax. Law),
One who takes part in a folkmote, or local court. [Obs.]Milton.
A simple podlike pericarp which contains several seeds andopens along the inner or ventral suture, as in the peony, larkspurand milkweed.
Affecting the follicles; as, follicular pharyngitis.
To go or come after; -- used in the various senses of thetransitive verb: To pursue; to attend; to accompany; to be a result;to imitate.
1. One who follows; a pursuer; an attendant; a disciple; adependent associate; a retainer.

(In the field of a telescope) In the direction from which starsare apparently moving (in consequence of the erth's rotation); as, asmall star, north following or south following. In the directiontoward which stars appear to move is called preceding.
A star of the first magnitude, in the constellation PiscisAustralis, or Southern Fish.
One who foments; one who encourages or instigates; as, afomenter of sedition.
Any substance supposed to be capable of absorbing, retaining,and transporting contagious or infectious germs; as, woolen clothesare said to be active fomites.
A kind of soft sweetmeat made by boiling solutions to the pointof crystallization, usually molded; as, cherry fondant.
To endeavor; to strive; to try. [Obs.] Chaucer.
To treat or handle with tenderness or in a loving manner; tocaress; as, a nurse fondles a child.
The act of caressing; manifestation of tenderness.Cyrus made no . . . amorous fondling To fan her pride, or melt herguardless heart. Mickle.
A large copper vessel used for hot amalgamation.
Blended; passing into each other by subtle gradations; -- saidof colors or of the surface or material on which the colors are laid.
A style of printing calico, paper hangings, etc., in which thecolors are in bands and graduated into each other. Ure.

A complete assortment of printing type of one size, including adue proportion of all the letters in the alphabet, large and small,points, accents, and whatever else is necessary for printing withthat variety of types; a fount.
Pertaining to a font, fountain, source, or origin; original;primitive. [R.]From the fontal light of ideas only can a man draw intellectualpower. Coleridge.
An issue or artificial ulcer for the discharge of humors fromthe body.[Obs.] Wiseman.
A kind of tall headdress formerly worn. Addison.
Full of food; supplying food; fruitful; fertile. "The foodfulearth." Dryden.Bent by its foodful burden [the corn]. Glover.
A compound of gooseberries scalded and crushed, with cream; --commonly called gooseberry fool.
Lucky, without judgment or contrivance. [Obs.] Spenser.
The state of being foolhardy; foolhardiness.
Courage without sense or judgment; foolish rashness;recklessness. Dryden.
Daring without judgment; foolishly adventurous and bold.Howell.
To make a fool of; to befool. [R.] Holland.
A writing paper made in sheets, ordinarily 16 x 13 inches, andfolded so as to make a page 13 x 8 inches. See Paper.
The terminal part of the leg of man or an animal; esp., thepart below the ankle or wrist; that part of an animal upon which itrests when standing, or moves. See Manus, and Pes.
The amount of illumination produced by a standard candle at adistance of one foot.
Infantry soldiers belonging to select regiments called theGuards. [Eng.]
A unit of energy, or work, being equal to the work done inraising one pound avoirdupois against the force of gravity the heightof one foot.
A unit of energy or work, equal to the work done in moving abody through one foot against the force of one poundal.
A unit of energy or work, being equal to the work done inraising one ton against the force of gravity through the height ofone foot.
A suction valve or check valve at the lower end of a pipe;esp., such a valve in a steam-engine condenser opening to the airpump.
Having sore or tender feet, as by reason of much walking; as,foot-sore cattle.
An inflated ball to be kicked in sport, usually made in Indiarubber, or a bladder incased in Leather. Waller.
A bath for the feet; also, a vessel used in bathing the feet.
A page; an attendant in livery; a lackey. Shak.
The breadth of a foot; -- used as a measure. Longfellow.Not so much as a footbreadth. Deut. ii. 5.
A narrow bridge for foot passengers only.
Formerly, a housing or caparison for a horse. Sir W. Scott.
A setting down of the foot; a footstep; the sound of afootstep. Shak.Seraphim, whose footfalls tinkled on the tufted floor. Poe
A conflict by persons on foot; -- distinguished from a fight onhorseback. Sir P. Sidney.
A disease affecting the feet of sheep.
A low hill at the foot of highe
A holding with the feet; firm L'Estrange.
Hastily; immediately; instantly; on the spot; hotfloot. Gower.Custance have they taken anon, foothot. Chaucer.

The thickened or sloping portion of a wall, or of an embankmentat its foot. Footing course (Arch.), one of the courses of masonry atthe foot of a wall, broader than the courses above.-- To pay one's footing, to pay a fee on first doing anything, asworking at a trade or in a shop. Wright.-- Footing beam, the tie beam of a roof.
A sycophant; a fawner; a toady. Cf. Bootlick. Shak.
One of a row of lights in the front of the stage in a theater,etc., and on a level therewith. Before the footlights, upon thestage; -- hence, in the capacity of an actor.
A moth of the family Lithosidæ; -- so called from its livery-like colors.
Art or skill of a footman.
A footprint; a track or vestige. Coleridge.
A note of reference or comment at the foot of a page.
A highwayman or robber on foot.
A narrow path or way for pedestrains only; a footway.
The impression of the foot; a trace or footmark; as,"Footprints of the Creator."
The settlings of oil, molasses, etc., at the bottom of a barrelor hogshead. Simmonds.
The stalk of a leaf or of flower; a petiole, pedicel, orreduncle.
The plinth or base of a pillar.
The stone at the foot of a grave; -- opposed to headstone.
A low stool to support the feet of one when sitting.
Worn by, or weared in, the feet; as, a footworn path; afootworn traveler.
To bungle; to manage awkwardly; to treat or play unskillfully;as, to foozle a stroke in golf.
One whose ambition it is to gain admiration by showy dress; acoxcomb; an inferior dandy.
A stupid or insignaficant fellow; a fool; a simpleton. [R.]Hudibras.
Foplike; characteristic of a top in dress or manners; making anostentatious display of gay clothing; affected in manners.
In the most general sense, indicating that in consideration of,in view of, or with reference to, which anything is done or takesplace.

A prefix to verbs, having usually the force of a negative orprivative. It often implies also loss, detriment, or destruction, andsometimes it is intensive, meaning utterly, quite thoroughly, as inforbathe.

To wander or rove in search of food; to collect food, esp.forage, for horses and cattle by feeding on or stripping the country;to ravage; to feed on spoil.His most mighty father on a hill Stood smiling to behold his lion'swhelp Forage in blood of French nobility. Shak.Foraging ant (Zoöl.), one of several species of ants of the genusEciton, very abundant in tropical America, remarkable for marching invast armies in search of food.-- Foraging cap, a forage cap.-- Foraging party, a party sent out after forage.
A tubelike marking, occuring in sandstone and other strata.

A small opening, perforation, or orifice; a fenestra. Foramenof Monro (Anat.), the opening from each lateral into the thirdventricle of the brain.-- Foramen of Winslow (Anat.), the opening connecting the sac of theomentum with the general cavity of the peritoneum.

An extensive order of rhizopods which generally have achambered calcareous shell formed by several united zooids. Many ofthem have perforated walls, whence the name. Some species are coveredwith sand. See Rhizophoda.
Having foramina; full of holes; porous. Bacon.
In consideration that; seeing that; since; because that; --followed by as. See under For, prep.
A sudden or irregular incursion in border warfare; hence, anyirregular incursion for war or spoils; a raid. Spenser.The huge Earl Doorm, . . . Bound on a foray, rolling eyes of prey.Tennyson.
One who makes or joins in a foray.They might not choose the lowand road, For the Merse forayers wereabroad. Sir W. Scott.
An ancestor; a forefather; -- usually in the plural. [Scot.]"Your forbears of old." Sir W. Scott.
The act of forbearing or waiting; the exercise of patience.He soon shall findForbearance no acquittance ere day end. Milton.
Disposed or accustomed to forbear; patient; long-suffering.-- For*bear"ing*ly, adv.
To utter a prohibition; to prevent; to hinder. "I did not orforbid." Milton.
The act of forbidding; prohibition; command or edict against athing. [Obs.]ow hast thou yield to transgress The strict forbiddance. Milton.

Prohibited; interdicted.I kniw no spells, use no forbidden arts. Milton.Forbidden fruit. (a) Any coveted unlawful pleasure, -- so called withreference to the forbidden fruit of the Garden of Eden. (b) (Bot.) Asmall variety of shaddock (Citrus decumana). The name is given indifferent places to several varieties of Citrus fruits.
In a forbidden or unlawful manner. Shak.
Repelling approach; repulsive; raising abhorrence, aversion, ordislike; disagreeable; prohibiting or interdicting; as, a forbiddingaspect; a forbidding formality; a forbidding air.
Very black. [Obs.]As any raven's feathers it shone forblack. Chaucer.
To bruise sorely or exceedingly. [Obs.]All forbrosed, both back and side. Chaucer.
Near; hard by; along; past. [Obs.]To tell her if her child went ought forby. Chaucer.To the intent that ships may pass along forby all the sides of thecity without let. Robynson (More's Utopia).
To cut completely; to cut off. [Obs.] Chaucer.
To stuff; to lard; to farce. [R.]Wit larded with malice, and malice forced with wit. Shak.

Done or produced with force or great labor, or by extraordinaryexertion; hurried; strained; produced by unnatural effort orpressure; as, a forced style; a forced laugh. Forced draught. Seeunder Draught.-- Forced march (Mil.), a march of one or more days made with allpossible speed.-- For"ced*ly, adv.-- For"ced*ness, n.
Full of or processing force; exerting force; mighty.-- Force"ful*ly, adv.Against the steed he threw His forceful spear. Dryden.
Having little or no force; feeble.These forceless flowers like sturdy trees support me. Shak.
Meat chopped fine and highly seasoned, either served up alone,or used as a stuffing. [Written also forced meat.]
The act of forcing; compulsion. [Obs.]It was imposed upon us by constraint; And will you count suchforcement treachery J. Webster.
The caudal forceps-shaped appendage of earwigs and some otherinsects. See Earwig. Dressing forceps. See under Dressing.

Seemingly vigorous, but really weak or insipid.He [Prof. Ayton] would purge his book of much offensive matter, if hestruck out epithets which are in the bad taste of the forcible-feebleschool. N. Brit. Review.

The art of raising plants, flowers, and fruits at an earlierseason than the natural one, as in a hitbed or by the use ofartificial heat. Forcing bed or pit, a plant bed having an underlayer of fermenting manure, the fermentation yielding bottom heat forforcing plants; a hotbed.-- Forcing engine, a fire engine.-- Forcing fit (Mech.), a tight fit, as of one part into a hole inanother part, which makes it necessary to use considerable force inputting the two parts together.-- Forcing house, a greenhouse for the forcing of plants, fruittrees, etc.-- Forcing machine, a powerful press for putting together orseparating two parts that are fitted tightly one into another, as forforcing a crank on a shaft, or for drawing off a car wheel from theaxle.-- Forcing pump. See Force pump (b).
Forked or branched like a pair of forceps; constructed so as toopen and shut like a pair of forceps. Sir T. Browne.
Torture by pinching with forceps or pinchers. Bacon.
A gelatin dynamite in which the dope is composed largely ofsodium nitrate.
To cut completely; to cut off. [Obs.] Chaucer.
To pass or cross, as a river or other water, by wading; to wadethrough.His last section, which is no deep one, remains only to be forted.Milton.
Capable of being forded.-- Ford"a*ble*ness, n.
Without a ford.A deep and fordless river. Mallock.
To drive about; to drive here and there. [Obs.] Rom. of R.
Entirely dry; withered. [Obs.] "A tree fordry." Chaucer.
To dwindle away; to disappear. [Obs.] Rom of R.
Journey; way; method of proceeding. [Obs.] "Follow him and hisfore." Chaucer.
One of the teeth in the forepart of the mouth; an incisor.
The evening between twilight and bedtime. [Scot.]
Designating the mast, sail, yard, etc., above the topmast; as,the fore-topgallant sail. See Sail.
The mast erected at the head of the foremast, and at the headof which stands the fore-topgallant mast. See Ship.
To admonish beforehand, or before the act or event. Bp. Hall.
To advise or counsel before the time of action, or before theevent. Shak.
To allege or cite before. Fotherby.
To set, order, or appoint, beforehand. Sherwood.
To arm or prepare for attack or resistance before the time ofneed. South.
The breast beam of a loom.
To fortell; to presage; to augur.If I forebode aright. Hawthorne.
The act of foreboding; the thing foreboded.
Presage of coming ill; expectation of misfortune.
A rope applied to the fore yardarm, to change the position ofthe foresail.
The anterior of the three principal divisions of the brain,including the prosencephalon and thalamencephalon. Sometimesrestricted to the prosencephalon only. See Brain.
Near; hard by; along; past. See Forby. Spenser.
To contrive or plan beforehand.If it happen as I did forecast. Milton.
Cited or quoted before or above. Arbuthnot.

To shut up or out; to preclude; to stop; to prevent; to bar; toexclude.The embargo with Spain foreclosed this trade. Carew.To foreclose a mortgager (Law), to cut him off by a judgment of courtfrom the power of redeeming the mortgaged premises, termed his equityof redemption.-- To foreclose a mortgage, (not technically correct, but often usedto signify) the obtaining a judgment for the payment of an overduemortgage, and the exposure of the mortgaged property to sale to meetthe mortgage debt. Wharton.
The act or process of foreclosing; a proceeding which bars orextinguishes a mortgager's right of redeeming a mortgaged estate.
To preconceive; to imagine beforehand. [Obs.] Bacon.
To date before the true time; to antendate.
The fore part of a deck, or of a ship.
To recognize or judge in advance; to forebode. [Obs.] Udall.Laugh at your misery, as foredeeming you An idle meteor. J. Webster.
To plan beforehand; to intend previously. Cheyne.
To determine or decree beforehand. Bp. Hopkins.
To bestow beforehand. [R.]King James had by promise foredisposed the place on the Bishop ofMeath. Fuller.
To doom beforehand; to predestinate.Thou art foredomed to view the Stygian state. Dryden.

One who precedes another in the line of genealogy in anydegree, but usually in a remote degree; an ancestor.Respecting your forefathers, you would have been taught to respectyourselves. Burke.Forefathers' Day, the anniversary of the day (December 21) on whichthe Pilgrim Fathers landed at Plymouth, Massachusetts (1620). Onaccount of a mistake in reckoning the change from Old Style to NewStyle, it has generally been celebrated on the 22d.
To feel beforehand; to have a presentiment of. [Obs.]As when, with unwieldy waves, the great sea forefeels winds. Chapman.

To hinder; to fend off; to avert; to prevent the approach of;to forbid or prohibit. See Forfend.God forefend it should ever be recorded in our history. Landor.It would be a far better work . . . to forefend the cruelty. I.Taylor.
The finger next to the thumb; the index.
A piece of timber which terminates the keel at the fore end,connecting it with the lower end of the stem.

Foremost part or place.Set ye Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle. 2 Sam. xi. 15.Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, standing in the forefront for all time,the masters of those who know. J. C. Shairp.
A first game; first plan. [Obs.] Whitlock.
A short rope grafted on a harpoon, to which a longer linTotten.
An antecedent or premonitory gleam; a dawning light.The foregleams of wisdom. Whittier.

To go before; to precede; -- used especially in the present andpast participles.Pleasing remembrance of a thought foregone. Wordsworth.For which the very mother's face forewent The mother's specialpatience. Mrs. Browning.Foregone conclusion, one which has preceded argument or examination;one predetermined.

On a painting, and sometimes in a bas-relief, mosaic picture,or the like, that part of the scene represented, which is nearest tothe spectator, and therefore occupies the lowest part of the work ofart itself. Cf. Distance, n., 6.
The anterior part of the alimentary canal, from the mouth tothe intestine, o
Done beforehand; anticipative.And so extenuate the forehand sin. Shak.
The forward extension of the hearth of a blast furnace underthe tymp.
To hew or cut in front. [Obs.] Sackville.
The forward part of the hold of a ship.
A piece of timber placed across the stem, to unite the bows andstrengthen the fore part of the ship; a breast hook.

A person belonging to or owning allegiance to a foreigncountry; one not native in the country or jurisdiction underconsideration, or not naturalized there; an alien; a stranger.Joy is such a foreigner, So mere a stranger to my thoughts. Denham.Nor could the majesty of the English crown appear in a greaterluster, either to foreigners or subjects. Swift.
Anything peculiar to a foreign language or people; a foreignidiom or custom.It is a pity to see the technicalities of the so-called liberalprofessions distigured by foreignisms. Fitzed. Hall.

The quality of being foreign; remoteness; want of relation orappropriateness.Let not the foreignness of the subject hinder you from endeavoring toset me right. Locke.A foreignness of complexion. G. Eliot.
To judge beforehand, or before hearing the facts and proof; toprejudge.
A judgment by which one is deprived or put of a right or thingin question.
To have previous knowledge of; to know beforehand.Who would the miseries of man foreknow Dryden.
That may be foreknown. Dr. H. More.
With foreknowledge.He who . . . foreknowingly loses his life. Jer. Taylor.
Knowledge of a thing before it happens, or of whatever is tohappen; prescience.If I foreknew, Foreknowledge had no influence on their fault. Milton.
A kind of parchment for book covers. See Forrill.
A piece of ground between the wall of a place and the moat.Farrow.
One who leads others by his example; aguide.
See Forlend. [Obs.]As if that life to losse they had forelent. Spenser.
To lie in front of. [Obs.]Which forelay Athwart her snowy breast. Spenser.

A cotter or split pin, as in a slot in a bolt, to preventretraction; a linchpin; a pin fastening the cap-square of a gun.Forelock bolt, a bolt retained by a key, gib, or cotter passingthrough a slot.-- Forelock hook (Rope Making), a winch or whirl by which a bunch ofthree yarns is twisted into a standard. Knight.-- To take time, or occasion, by the forelock, to make prompt use ofanything; not to let slip an opportunity.Time is painted with a lock before and bald behind, signifyingthereby that we must take time by the forelock; for when it is oncepast, there is no recalling it. Swift.On occasion's forelock watchful wait. Milton.
To look beforehand or forward. [Obs.] Spenser.
The first or chief man; as:(a) The chief man of a jury, who acts as their speaker.(b) The chief of a set of hands employed in a shop, or on works ofany kind, who superintends the rest; an overseer.
The mast nearest the bow. Foremast hand or man (Naut.), acommon sailor; also, a man stationed to attend to the gear of theforemast.
Mentioned before; already cited; aforementioned. Addison.
The milk secreted just before, or directly after, the birth ofa child or of the young of an animal; colostrum.
First in time or place; most advanced; chief in rank ordignity; as, the foremost troops of an army.THat struck the foremost man of all this world. Shak.
In the foremost place or order; among the foremost. J. Webster.
A name that precedes the family name or surname; a first name.Selden.
Over against; opposite to. [Now dialectic]The land forenenst the Greekish shore. Fairfax.
The early part of the day, from morning to meridian, or noon.
Notice or information of an event before it happens;forewarning. [R.] Rymer.

Belonging to courts of judicature or to public discussion anddebate; used in legal proceedings, or in public discussions;argumentative; rhetorical; as, forensic eloquence or disputes.Forensic medicine, medical jurisprudence; medicine in its relationsto law.
To ordain or appoint beforehand; to preordain; to predestinate;to predetermine. Hooker.
To prize or rate beforehand. [Obs.] Hooker.
Cited before; quoted in a foregoing part of the treatise oressay.
To advance or gain upon; -- said of a vessel that gains uponanother when sailing closehauled.
To tell beforehand; to signify by tokens; to predestine. [Obs.]Spenser.
Named or recited before. "The forerecited practices." Shak.
Called to mind previously. Bp. Montagu.
Ready; directly forward; going before. [Obs.] "A forerightwind." Chapman.
A piece of rag terminating the log line.
To foretell. [Obs.]Her danger nigh that sudden change foresaid. Fairfax.

, or (strictly) p. p. Provided; in case that; on conditionthat. [Obs.]One manner of meat is most sure to every complexion, foreseen that itbe alway most commonly in conformity of qualities, with the personthat eateth. Sir T. Elyot.
The fore part of a ship. [Obs.]
To represent on a plane surface, as if extended in a directiontoward the spectator or nearly so; to shorten by drawing inperspective.
Representation in a foreshortened mode or way.
In distillation of low wines, the first portion of spirit thatcomes over, being a fluid abounding in fusel oil. Knight.

To show or exhibit beforehand; to give foreknowledge of; toprognosticate; to foretell.Your looks foreshow You have a gentle heart. Shak.Next, like Aurora, Spenser rose, Whose purple blush the dayforeshows. Denham.
Any sight or reading of the leveling staff, except thebacksight; any sight or bearing taken by a compass or theodolite in aforward direction.
Sagacious; prudent; provident for the future. Bartram.
To signify beforehand; to foreshow; to typify. Milton.
The fold of skin which covers the glans of the penis; theprepuce.
The front skirt of a garment, in distinction from the train.Honor's train Is longer than his foreskirt. Shak.
To make slow; to hinder; to obstruct. [Obs.] See Forslow, v. t.No stream, no wood, no mountain could foreslow Their hasty pace.Fairfax.
A prediction; also, a preface. [Obs.] Camden. Huloet.
Already spent; gone by; past. [Obs.] Shak.
One who rides before; a harbinger. [Obs.] Shak.

A large extent or precinct of country, generally waste andwoody, belonging to the sovereign, set apart for the keeping of gamefor his use, not inclosed, but distinguished by certain limits, andprotected by certain laws, courts, and officers of its own. Burrill.
An instrument formerly used at sea for taking the altitudes ofheavenly bodies, now superseded by the sextant; -- called also cross-staff. Brande & C.
Of or pertaining to forests; as, forestal rights.

To obstruct or stop up, as a way; to stop the passage of onhighway; to intercept on the road, as goods on the way to market. Toforestall the market, to buy or contract for merchandise or provisionon its way to market, with the intention of selling it again at ahigher price; to dissuade persons from bringing their goods orprovisions there; or to persuade them to enhance the price whenthere. This was an offense at law in England until 1844. Burrill.
One who forestalls; esp., one who forestalls the market. Locke.
A large, strong rope, reaching from the foremast head to thebowsprit, to support the mast. See Illust. under Ship.
A lepidopterous insect belonging to Alypia and allied genera;as, the eight-spotted forester (A. octomaculata), which in the larvalstate is injurious to the grapevine.
Front stick of a hearth fire.
The art of forming or of cultivating forests; the management ofgrowing timber.
A taste beforehand; enjoyment in advance; anticipation.
One who tastes beforehand, or before another.
To predict; to tell before occurence; to prophesy; to foreshow.Deeds then undone my faithful tongue foretold. Pope.Prodigies, foretelling the future eminence and luster of hischaracter. C. Middleton.
Thought of, or planned, beforehand; aforethought; prepense;hence, deliberate. "Forethought malice." Bacon.
The past; the time before the present. "A very dim foretime."J. C. Shairp.
Prognostic; previous omen. Sir P. Sidney.
The platform at the head of the foremast.
Formerly vouched or avowed; affirmed in advance. [R.] Shak.
The van; the front. [Obs.]My foreward shall be drawn out all in length, Consisting equally ofhorse and foot. Shak.
To warn beforehand; to give previous warning, admonition,information, or notice to; to caution in advance.We were forewarned of your coming. Shak.
A woman who is chief; a woman who has charge of the work orworkers in a shop or other place; a head woman. Tatler. W. Besant.
Worn out; wasted; used up. [Archaic]Old foreworn stories almost forgotten. Brydges.
The lowermost yard on the foremast.
Lost or alienated for an offense or crime; liable to penalseizure.Thy wealth being forfeit to the state. Shak.To tread the forfeit paradise. Emerson.
Liable to be forfeited; subject to forfeiture.For the future, uses shall be subject to the statutes of mortmain,and forfeitable, like the lands themselves. Blackstone.
One who incurs a penalty of forfeiture.
To prohibit; to forbid; to avert. [Archaic]Which peril heaven forefend! Shak.
Excessively alarmed; in great fear. [Obs.] "Forfered of hisdeath." Chaucer.
To incur a penalty; to transgress. [Obs.]And all this suffered our Lord Jesus Christ that never forfeted.Chaucer.
Deeply forked, as the tail of certain birds.
A genus of insects including the earwigs. See Earwig, 1.
To convene; to gossip; to meet accidentally. [Scot.] Jamieson.Within that circle he forgathered with many a fool. Wilson.

To move heavily and slowly, as a ship after the sails arefurled; to work one's way, as one ship in outsailing another; -- usedespecially in the phrase to forge ahead. Totten.And off she [a ship] forged without a shock. De Quincey.
A skilled smith, who has a hammerer to assist him.
One who forges, makes, of forms; a fabricator; a falsifier.
A small herb, of the genus Myosotis (M. palustris, incespitosa,etc.), bearing a beautiful blue flower, and extensively consideredthe emblem of fidelity.
Liable to be, or that may be, forgotten. Carlyle.
One who forgets; a heedless person. Johnson.
A piece of forged work in metal; -- a general name for a pieceof hammered iron or steel.There are very few yards in the world at which such forgings could beturned out. London Times.
Capable of being forgiven; pardonable; venial. Sherwood.
Disposed to forgive; inclined to overlook offenses; mild;merciful; compassionate; placable; as, a forgiving temper.-- For*giv"ing*ly, adv.-- For*giv"ing*ness, n. J. C. Shairp.
To pass by; to leave. See 1st Forego.For sith [since] I shall forgoon my liberty At your request. Chaucer.And four [days] since Florimell the court forwent. Spenser.
To harass; to torment; to distress. [Obs.] Spenser.
Literally, to put out of a family; hence, to portion off, so asto exclude further claim of inheritance; to emancipate (as a with hisown consent) from paternal authority. Blackstone.

To raise, or pitch with a fork, as hay; to dig or turn overwith a fork, as the soil.Forking the sheaves on the high-laden cart. Prof. Wilson.To fork over or out, to hand or pay over, as money. [Slang] G. Eliot.

Having the outer tail feathers longer than the median ones;swallow-tailed; -- said of many birds. Fork-tailed flycatcher(Zoöl.), a tropical American flycatcher (Milvulus tyrannus).-- Fork-tailed gull (Zoöl.), a gull of the genus Xema, of twospecies, esp. X. Sabinii of the Arctic Ocean.-- Fork-tailed kite (Zoöl.), a graceful American kite (Elanoidesforficatus); -- called also swallow-tailed kite.
The quality or state or dividing in a forklike manner.
Opening into two or more parts or shoots; forked; furcated."Forky tongues." Pope.
To lie in wait for; to ambush.An ambushed thief forlays a traveler. Dryden.
To give up; to leave; to abandon. [Obs.] "To forlet sin."Chaucer.
oForlese. [Obs.]The beasts their caves, the birds their neforlore. Fairfax.
A suffix used to denote in the form or shape of, resembling,etc.; as, valiform; oviform.
A colorless, volatile liquid, H2CO, resembling acetic or ethylaldehyde, and chemically intermediate between methyl alcohol andformic acid.
An aqueous solution of formaldehyde, used as a preservative inmuseums and as a disinfectant.
The practice or the doctrine of strict adherence to, ordependence on, external forms, esp. in matters of religion.Official formalism. Sir H. Rawlinson.

One overattentive to forms, or too much confined to them; esp.,one who rests in external religious forms, or observes strictly theoutward forms of worship, without possessing the life and spirit ofreligion.As far a formalist from wisdom sits, In judging eyes, as libertinesfrom wits. Young.
The dress prescribed for any body of men, academical,municipal, or sacerdotal. [Obs.]The doctors attending her in their formalities as far as Shotover.Fuller.

In a formal manner; essentially; characteristically; expressly;regularly; ceremoniously; precisely.That which formally makes this [charity] a Christian grace, is thespring from which it flows. Smalridge.You and your followers do stand formally divided against theauthorized guides of the church and rest of the people. Hooker.
The shape and size of a book; hence, its external form.
A salt of formic acid. [Written also formiate.]
The arrangement of a body of troops, as in a square, column,etc. Farrow.
Serving to form; derivative; not radical; as, a terminationmerely formative.
Arranged, as stars in a constellation; as, formed stars. [R.]
A writ of right for a tenant in tail in case of adiscontinuance of the estate tail. This writ has been abolished.
The female of a hawk or falcon.
One of the half ribs against the walls in a ceiling vaultedwith ribs.
In time past, either in time immediately preceding or at anyindefinite distance; of old; heretofore.

Pertaining to, or derived from, ants; as, formic acid; in anextended sense, pertaining to, or derived from, formic acid; as,formic ether. Amido formic acid, carbamic acid.-- Formic acid, a colorless, mobile liquid, HCO.OH, of a sharp, acidtaste, occurring naturally in ants, nettles, pine needles, etc., andproduced artifically in many ways, as by the oxidation of methylalcohol, by the reduction of carbonic acid or the destructivedistillation of oxalic acid. It is the first member of the fattyacids in the paraffin series, and is homologous with acetic acid.
A Linnæan genus of hymenopterous insects, including the commonants. See Ant.
Like or pertaining to the family Formicaridæ or ant thrushes.
The nest or dwelling of a swarm of ants; an ant-hill.
Resembling, or pertaining to, an ant or ants.
A sensation resembling that made by the creeping of ants on theskin. Dunglison.

Exciting fear or apprehension; impressing dread; adapted toexcite fear and deter from approach, encounter, or undertaking;alarming.They seemed to fear the formodable sight. Dryden.I swell my preface into a volume, and make it formidable, when yousee so many pages behind. Drydn.
The quality of being formidable, or adapted to excite dread.Boyle.
The act or process of giving form or shape to anything; as, inshipbuilding, the exact shaping of partially shaped timbers.
Shapeless; without a determinate form; wanting regularity ofshape.-- Form"less*ly, adv.-- Form"less*ness, n.
A written confession of faith; a formal statement of foctrines.
Pertaining to, or exhibiting, formularization. Emerson.
The act of formularizing; a formularized or formulatedstatement or exhibition. C. Kingsley.
To reduce to a forula; to formulate.
To reduce to, or express in, a formula; to put in a clear anddefinite form of statement or expression. G. P. Marsh.
The act, process, or result of formulating or reducing to aformula.
A set or prescribed model; a formula. [Obs.] Johnson.
The act or process of reducing to a formula; the state of beingformulized.
To reduce to a formula; to formulate. Emerson.
To commit fornication; to have unlawful sexual intercourse.
An unmarried person, male or female, who has criminalintercourse with the other sex; one guilty of fornication.
A woman guilty of fornication. Shak.
Very old. [Obs.]A bear's skin, coal-black, forold. Chaucer.
To pass by or along; to pass over. [Obs.] Spenser.
To waste away completely by suffering or torment. [Archaic]"Pale as a forpined ghost." Chaucer.
To foray; to ravage; to pillage.For they that morn had forrayed all the land. Fairfax.
To forbid; to renounce; to forsake; to deny. [Obs.] Spenser.
To neglect by idleness; to delay or to waste by sloth. [Obs.]Spenser.
To lose by sloth or negligence. [Obs.] Chaucer.
To delay; to hinder; to neglect; to put off. [Obs.] Bacon.
To lsoe by idleness or slotch. [Obs.] Chaucer.

In truth; in fact; certainly; very well; -- formerly used as anexpression of deference or respect, especially to woman; now usedironically or contemptuously.A fit man, forsooth, to govern a realm! Hayward.Our old English word forsooth has been changed for the French madam.Guardian.
Wasted in strength; tired; exhausted. [Archaic]A gentleman almost forspent with speed. Shak.
Spent with heat; covered with sweat. [Obs.] P. Sidney.
To swear falsely; to commit perjury. Shak.
One who rejects of renounces upon oath; one who swears a falseoath.
A shrub of the Olive family, with yellow blossoms.

A strong or fortified place; usually, a small fortified place,occupied only by troops, surrounded with a ditch, rampart, andparapet, or with palisades, stockades, or other means of defense; afortification.Detached works, depending solely on their own strength, belong to theclass of works termed forts. Farrow.
A small outwork of a fortification; a fortilage; -- called alsofortelace.
Furnished with, or guarded by, forts; strengthened or defended,as by forts. [R.] Shak.
Forth from; out of. [Archaic]Some forth their cabins peep. Donne.
Ready or about to appear; making appearance.
A going forth; an utterance. A. Chalmers.
To repent; to regret; to be sorry for; to cause regret. [Obs.]"Let it forthink you." Tyndale.That me forthinketh, quod this January. Chaucer.
Straight forward; in a straight direction. [Archaic] Sir P.Sidney.
Straightforwardness; explicitness; directness. [Archaic]Dante's concise forthrightness of phrase. Hawthorne.
As soon as the thing required may be done by reasonableexertion confined to that object. Bouvier.
One of forty equal parts into which one whole is divided; thequotient of a unit divided by forty; one next in order after thethirty-ninth.
One who, or that which, fortifies, strengthens, supports, orupholds.
A little fort; a blockhouse. [Obs.] Spenser.
Very loud; with the utmost strength or loudness.
Casual choice; fortuitous selection; hazard. [R.]No mode of election operating in the spirit of fortition or rotationcan be generally good. Burke.
The space of fourteen days; two weeks.
Occurring or appearing once in a fortnight; as, a fortnightlymeeting of a club; a fortnightly magazine, or other publication.-- adv.
To tread down; to trample upon. [Obs.]In hell shall they be all fortroden of devils. Chaucer.
A fortified place; a large and permanent fortification,sometimes including a town; a fort; a castle; a stronghold; a placeof defense or security.
Happening independently of human will or means of foresight;resulting from unavoidable physical causes. Abbott.
In a fortunate manner; luckily; successfully; happily.
The condition or quality of being fortunate; good luck;success; happiness.
To fall out; to happen.It fortuned the same night that a Christian, serving a Turk in thecamp, secretely gave the watchmen warning. Knolles.
Luckless; also, destitute of a fortune or portion. Spenser.
To regulate the fortune of; to make happy. [Obs.] Spenser.
Four times ten; thirtynine and one more.
One of those who went to California in the rush for gold in1849; an argonaut. [Colloq., U. S.]
Tired out with excessive waking or watching. [Obs.] Chaucer.
To wander away; to go astray; to wander far and to weariness.[Obs.]
An agreement; a covenant; a promise. [Obs.]Tell us a tale anon, as forward is. Chaucer.
The process of putting a book into its cover, and making itready for the finisher.
The quality of being forward; cheerful readiness; promtness;as, the forwardness of Christians in propagating the gospel.
To desolate or lay waste utterly. [Obs.] Spenser.
To weary extremely; to dispirit. [Obs.] Spenser.
Much worn. [Obs.]A silly man, in simple weeds forworn. Spenser.
pres. indic. 1st & 3d pers. sing. of Forwete. [Obs.] Chaucer.
To wrap up; to conceal. [Obs.]All mote be said and nought excused, nor hid, nor forwrapped.Chaucer.
A pit, groove, cavity, or depression, of greater or less depth;as, the temporal fossa on the side of the skull; the nasal fossæcontaining the nostrils in most birds.
A species of civet (Viverra fossa) resembling the genet.
A small, deep-centered ulcer of the transparent cornea.
One of the great military roads constructed by the Romans inEngland and other parts of Europe; -- so called from the fosse orditch on each side for keeping it dry.
To search for gold by picking at stone or earth or among rootsin isolated spots, picking over abandoned workings, etc.; hence, tosteal gold or auriferous matter from another's claim. [Australia]

Like or pertaining to fossils; contained in rocks. whetherpetrified or not; as, fossil plants, shells. Fossil copal, a resinoussubstance, first found in the blue clay at Highgate, near London, andapparently a vegetable resin, partly changed by remaining in theearth.-- Fossil cork, flax, paper, or wood, varieties of amianthus.-- Fossil farina, a soft carbonate of lime.-- Fossil ore, fossiliferous red hematite. Raymond.
One who is versed in the science of fossils; a paleontologist.Joseph Black.
The process of converting, or of being converted, into afossil.
Converted into a fossil; antiquated; firmly fixed in views oropinions.A fossilized sample of confused provincialism. Earle.

A group of hymenopterous insects including the sand wasps. Theyexcavate cells in earth, where they deposit their eggs, with thebodies of other insects for the food of the young when hatched.[Written also Fossoria.]
Fitted for digging, adapted for burrowing or digging; as, afossorial foot; a fossorial animal.
Adapted for digging; -- said of the legs of certain insects.
Having, or surrounded by, long, narrow depressions or furrows.
To be nourished or trained up together. [Obs.] Spenser.
The care of a foster child; the charge of nursing. Sir W.Raleigh.
One who, or that which, fosters.
A woman who feeds and cherishes; a nurse. B. Jonson.
To stop (a leak in a ship at sea) by drawing under its bottom athrummed sail, so that the pressure of the water may force it intothe crack. Totten.
Using language scurrilous, opprobrious, obscene, or profane;abusive.So foul-mouthed a witness never appeared in any cause. Addison.
Using profane, scurrilous, slanderous, or obscene language.Shak.
A thin, washable material of silk, or silk and cotton,originally imported from India, but now also made elsewhere.
To flash, as lightning; to lighten; to gleam; to thunder.[Obs.] "Flames of fouldering heat." Spenser.
In a foul manner; filthily; nastily; shamefully; unfairly;dishonorably.I foully wronged him; do forgive me, do. Gay.
The quality or condition of being foul.
The European polecat; -- called also European ferret, andfitchew. See Polecat. [Written also foulmart, foulimart, andfulimart.]
The lowest and supporting part or member of a wall, includingthe base course (see Base course (a), under Base, n.) and footingcourses; in a frame house, the whole substructure of masonry.
One who derives support from the funds or foundation of acollege or school. [Eng.]
One who founds, establishes, and erects; one who lays afoundation; an author; one from whom anything originates; one whoendows.
Difficult to travel; likely to trip one up; as, a founderousroad. [R.] Burke.
The art of smelting and casting metals.
A deserted or exposed infant; a child found without a parent orowner. Foundling hospital, a hospital for foundlings.
A female founder; a woman who founds or establishes, or whoendows with a fund.
Having no fountain; destitute of springs or sources of water.Barren desert, fountainless and dry. Milton.
One more than three; twice two.
A four-stroke cycle, as the Otto cycle, for an internal-combustion engine. -- Four"-cy`cle, a.
Consisting of four horses controlled by one person; as, a four-in-hand team; drawn by four horses driven by one person; as, a four-in-hand coach.-- n.
A large bedstead with tall posts at the corners to supportcurtains. [Colloq.]

Allowing passage in either of four directions; as, a four-waycock, or valve. Francis. Four-way cock, a cock connected with fourpipes or ports, and having two or more passages in the plug, by whichthe adjacent pipes or ports may be made to communicate; formerly usedas a valve in the steam engine, and now for various other purposes.In the illustration, a leads to the upper end of a steam enginecylinder, and b to the lower end; c is the steam pipe, and d theexhaust pipe.
Having the ends forked or branched, and the ends of thebranches terminating abruptly as if cut off; -- said of an ordinary,especially of a cross.
An instrument used to raise and support the tongue during thecutting of the frænum.
A machine used in making paper; -- so named from an earlyinventor of improvements in this class of machinery.
Four times; quadruple; as, a fourfold division.He snall restore the lamb fourfold. 2 Sam. xii. 6.
Having four feet; quadruped; as, fourfooted beasts.
The coöperative socialistic system of Charles Fourier, aFrenchman, who recommended the reorganization of society into smallcommunities, living in common.
A compound or twin crystal consisting of four individuals.
The chamber of a mine in which the powder is placed.
Consisting of four; requiring four participants. [Scot. orGolf]
Having four sides and four equal angles. Sir W. Raleigh.
Four and ten more; twice seven.

The interval of two tones and a semitone, embracing fourdiatonic degrees of the scale; the subdominant of any key. TheFourth, specifically, un the United States, the fourth day of July,the anniversary of the declaration of American independence; as, tocelebrate the Fourth.
A viverrine animal of Madagascar (Cryptoprocta ferox). Itresembles a cat in size and form, and has retractile claws.
A fig; -- a word of contempt. [Obs.]A foutra for the world and wordlings base! Shak.
A slight depression or pit; a fossa.
A small depression or pit; a fovea.
Having small pits or depression, as the receptacle in somecomposite flowers.
One of the fine granules contained in the protoplasm of apollen grain.

To catch or kill wild fowl, for game or food, as by shooting,or by decoys, nets, etc.Such persons as may lawfully hunt, fish, or fowl. Blackstone.Fowling piece, a light gun with smooth bore, adapted for the use ofsmall shot in killing birds or small quadrupeds.
A sportsman who pursues wild fowl, or takes or kills for food.
A variety of rhodonite, from Franklin Furnace, New Jersey,containing some zinc.

A carnivorous animal of the genus Vulpes, family Canidæ, ofmany species. The European fox (V. vulgaris or V. vulpes), theAmerican red fox (V. fulvus), the American gray fox (V. Virginianus),and the arctic, white, or blue, fox (V. lagopus) are well-knownspecies.
Pertaining to or engaged in the hunting of foxes; fond ofhunting foxes.
A hole in the earth to which a fox resorts to hide himself.
Behavior like that of a fox; [Obs.] Chaucer.

Any plant of the genus Digitalis. The common English foxglove(Digitalis purpurea) is a handsome perennial or biennial plant, whoseleaves are used as a powerful medicine, both as a sedative anddiuretic. See Digitalis.Pan through the pastures oftentimes hath run To pluck the speckledfoxgloves from their stem. W. Browne.
One of a special breed of hounds used for chasing foxes.
Resembling a fox in his characteristic qualities; cunning;artful; foxy.
The name of several kinds of grass having a soft dense head offlowers, mostly the species of Alopecurus and Setaria.
The state of being fozy; spiritlessness; dullness. [Scot.][The Whigs'] foziness can no longer be concealed. Blackwood's.
An uproar; a noisy quarrel; a disturbance; a brawl.
A shallow iron pan to hold glass ware while being annealed.
Rotten from being too ripe; overripe. [Obs.] Blount.
Having a part displaced, as if broken; -- said of an ordinary.Macaulay.

One or more aliquot parts of a unit or whole number; anexpression for a definite portion of a unit or magnitude. Common, orVulgar, fraction, a fraction in which the number of equal parts intowhich the integer is supposed to be divided is indicated by figuresor letters, called the denominator, written below a line, over whichis the numerator, indicating the number of these parts included inthe fraction; as -- Complex fraction, a fraction having a fraction ormixed number in the numerator or denominator, or in both. Davies &Peck.-- Compound fraction, a fraction of a fraction; two or morefractions connected by of.-- Continued fraction, Decimal fraction, Partial fraction, etc. Seeunder Continued, Decimal, Partial, etc.-- Improper fraction, a fraction in which the numerator is greaterthan the denominator.-- Proper fraction, a fraction in which the numerator is less thanthe denominator.
By fractions or separate portions; as, to distill a liquidfractionally, that is, so as to separate different portions.
To separate into different portions or fractions, as in thedistillation of liquids.
Apt to break out into a passion; apt to scold; cross; snappish;ugly; unruly; as, a fractious man; a fractious horse.
Pertaining to, or consequent on, a fracture. [R.]
Easily broken; brittle; frail; delicate; easily destroyed.The state of ivy is tough, and not fragile. Bacon.
A part broken off; a small, detached portion; an imperfectpart; as, a fragment of an ancient writing.Gather up the fragments that remain. John vi. 12.
Consisting of the pulverized or fragmentary material of rock,as conglomerate, shale, etc.
The quality or property of being in fragnebts, or brokenpieces, incompleteness; want of continuity. G. Eliot.
Composed of the fragments of other rocks.
A writer of fragments; as, the fragmentist of Wolfenbüttel.[R.]
A strong or sweet scent. [Obs. & Illegitimate.] Sir T. Herbert.

[fragrans. -antis, p.pr. of fragrare to emit a smell offragrance: cf. OF. fragrant. Affecting the olfactory nervesagreeably; sweet of smell; odorous; having or emitting an agreeableperfume.Fragrant the fertile earth After soft showers. Milton.
A basket made of rushes, used chiefly for containing figs andraisins.
A large and thick pancake, with slices of bacon in it. [Obs.]Johnson.
A freckle. [Obs.]A few fraknes in his face. Chaucer.

To construct by fitting and uniting the several parts of theskeleton of any structure; specifically, in woodwork, to put togetherby cutting parts of one member to fit parts of another. See Dovetail,Halve, v. t., Miter, Tenon, Tooth, Tusk, Scarf, and Splice.
A conspiracy or plot, esp. for a malicious or evil purpose, asto incriminate a person on false evidence. [Slang]
One who frames; as, the framer of a building; the framers ofthe Constitution.
A framework, or a sy Framing chisel (Carp.), a heavy chiselwith a socket shank for making mortises.

A silver coin of France, and since 1795 the unit of the Frenchmonetary system. It has been adopted by Belgium and Swizerland. It isequivalent to about nineteen cents, or ten pence, and is divided into100 centimes.
A French partisan soldier, or one belonging to a corps ofdetached light troops engaged in forays, skirmishes, scouting, etc.

A particular privilege conferred by grant from a sovereign or agovernment, and vested in individuals; an imunity or exemption fromordinary jurisdiction; a constitutional or statutory right orprivilege, esp. the right to vote.Election by universal suffrage, as modified by the Constitution, isthe one crowning franchise of the American people. W. H. Seward.
Pertaining to the Franks, or their language; Frankish.

Belonging to the Order of St. Francis of the Franciscans.Franciscan Brothers, pious laymen who devote themselves to usefulworks, such as manual labor schools, and other educationalinstitutions; -- called also Brothers of the Third Order of St.Francis.-- Franciscan Nuns, nuns who follow the rule of t. Francis, esp.those of the Second Order of St. Francis, -- called also Poor Claresor Minoresses.-- Franciscan Tertiaries, the Third Order of St. Francis.
A spurred partidge of the genus Francolinus and allied genera,of Asia and Africa. The common species (F. vulgaris) was formerlycommon in southern Europe, but is now nearly restricted to Asia.
A variety of apatite from Wheal Franco in Devonshire.
The state or quality of being frangible. Fox.
Capable of being broken; brittle; fragile; easily broken.
A perfume derived from, or imitating the odor of, the flower ofthe red jasmine, a West Indian tree of the genus Plumeria.
A yellow crystalline dyestuff, regarded as a glucoside,extracted from a species (Rhamnus Frangula) of the buckthorn; --called also rhamnoxanthin.
A paramour; a loose woman; also, a gay, idle fellow. [Obs.]Spenser.
The liberty or franchise of having a chase; free chase.Burrill.
A species of tenure in fee simple, being the opposite ofancient demesne, or copyhold. Burrill.

The liberty of being sworn in courts, as a juror or witness;one of the ancient privileges of a freeman; free and common law; --an obsolete expression signifying substantially the same as theAmerican expression civil rights. Abbot.

A certain tenure in tail special; an estate of inheritancegiven to a man his wife (the wife being of the blood of the donor),and descendible to the heirs of their two bodies begotten. [Obs.]Blackstone.

A tenure by which a religious corporation holds lands given tothem and their successors forever, usually on condition of prayingfor the soul of the donor and his heirs; -- called also tenure byfree alms. Burrill.
. A black pigment used in copperplate printing, prepared byburning vine twigs, the lees of wine, etc. McElrath.

A fragrant, aromatic resin, or gum resin, burned as an incensein religious rites or for medicinal fumigation. The best kinds nowcome from East Indian trees, of the genus Boswellia; a commoner sort,from the Norway spruce (Abies excelsa) and other coniferous trees.The frankincense of the ancient Jews is still unidentified.
A method of forming a joint at the intersection of window-sashbars, by cutting away only enough wood to show a miter.
Like, or pertaining to, the Franks.
An English freeholder, or substantial householder. [Obs.]Chaucer.The franklin, a small landholder of those days. Sir J. Stephen.

. A kind of open stove introduced by Benjamin Franklin, thepeculiar feature of which was that a current of heated air wasdirectly supplied to the room from an air box; -- now applied toother varieties of open stoves.
Of or pertaining to Benjamin Franklin. Franklinic electricity,electricity produced by friction; called also statical electricity.
A kind of mineral of the spinel group.
In a frank manner; freely.Very frankly he confessed his treasons. Shak.
The quality of being frank; candor; openess; ingenuousness;fairness; liberality.

Mad; raving; furious; violent; wild and disorderly; distracted.Die, frantic wretch, for this accursed deed! Shak.Torrents of frantic abuse. Macaulay.-- Fran"tic*al*ly, adv.-- Fran"tic*ly, adv. Shak.-- Fran"tic*ness, n. Johnson.
To draw together; to bind with a view to secure and strengthen,as a vessel by passing cables around it; to tighten; as a tackle bydrawing the lines together. Tottem.
A blusterer; a rowdy. [Obs.]Unpolished, a frapler, and base. B. Jonson.
Iced; frozen; artificially cooled; as, wine frappé. -- n.
A lashing binding a thing tightly or binding things together.
A monk; also, a frater house. [R.] Shipley. Frater house, anapartament in a convent used as an eating room; a refectory; --called also a fratery.

Pf, pertaining to, or involving, brethren; becoming tobrothers; brotherly; as, fraternal affection; a fraternal embrace.-- Fra*ter"nal*ly, adv.An abhorred, a cursed, a fraternal war. Milton.Fraternal love and friendship. Addison.
To fraternize; to hold fellowship. Jefferson.
The act of fraternizing or uniting as brothers.I hope that no French fraternization . . . could so change the heartsof Englishmen. Burke.
To associate or hold fellowship as brothers, or as men of likeoccupation or character; to have brotherly feelings.
A frater house. See under Frater.
A sharing among brothers, or brothers' kin. [Obs.] Crabb.
Of or pertaining to fratricide; of the nature of fratricide.
One who murders or kills his own brother.
In Germany, a woman; a married woman; a wife; -- as a title,equivalent to Mrs., Madam.
An intentional perversion of truth for the purpose of obtainingsome valuable thing or promise from another.
Full of fraud, deceit, or treachery; trickish; treacherous;fraudulent; -- applied to persons or things. I. Taylor.-- Fraud"ful*ly, adv.
Free from fraud.-- Fraud"less*ly, adv.-- Fraud"less*ness, n.
Constituting the freight or cargo. [Obs.] "The fraughting soulswithin her." Shak.
In Germany, a young lady; an unmarried woman; -- as a title,equivalent to Miss.
The lines of the spectrun; especially and properly, the darklines of the solar spectrum, so called because first accuratelyobserved and interpreted by Fraunhofer, a German physicist.

A colorless crystalline substance, regarded as a glucoside, andfound in the bark of the ash (Fraxinus) and along with esculin in thebark of the horse-chestnut. It shows a delicate fluorescence inalkaline solutions; -- called also paviin.
A genus of deciduous forest trees, found in the north temperatezone, and including the true ash trees.
Affray; broil; contest; combat.Who began this bloody fray Shak.
The skin which a deer frays from his horns. B. Jonson.
To fray; to wear or pull into tatters or tag ends; to tatter; --used literally and figuratively. [Prov. Eng. & U. S.]
To variegate; to checker; to streak. [R.]Freaked with many a mingled hue. Thomson.

Apt to change the mind suddenly; whimsical; capricious.It may be a question whether the wife or the woman was the morefreakish of the two. L'Estrange.Freakish when well, and fretful when she's sick. Pope.-- Freak"ish*ly, adv.-- Freak"ish*ness, n.
To checker; to diversify. [R. & Poet.]The painted windows, frecking gloom with glow. Lowell.
To spinkle or mark with freckle or small discolored spots; tospot.
Marked with freckles; spotted. "The freckled trout." Dryden.The freckled cowslip, burnet, and green clover. Shak.
Full of or marked with freckles; sprinkled with spots;freckled.
Peace; -- a word used in composition, especially in propernames; as, Alfred; Frederic.
Certain or honorable; the opposite of base; as, free service;free socage. Burrill.

In the fullest sense, the conversion of bullion (of anyspecified metal) into legal-tender coins for any person who choosesto bring it to the mint; in a modified sense, such coinage when doneat a fixed charge proportionate to the cost of the operation.

The free coinage of silver; often, specif., the free coinage ofsilver at a fixed ratio with gold, as at the ratio of 16 to 1, whichratio for some time represented nearly or exactly the ratio of themarket values of gold and silver respectively.
Done by the hand, without support, or the guidance ofinstruments; as, free-hand drawing. See under Drawing.
Open; frank; unreserved; liberal; generous; as, free-heartedmirth.-- Free"-heart`ed*ly, adv.-- Free"-heart`ed*ness, n.
One who gratifies his appetites without stint; one given toindulgence in eating and drinking.
The doctrine or practice of consorting with the opposite sex,at pleasure, without marriage.
One who believes in or practices free-love.
An imperfect female calf, twinborn with a male.
Yielding free gold or silver; -- said of certain ores which canbe reduced by crushing and amalgamation, without roasting or otherchemical treatment. Raymond.
Not perplexed; having a mind free from care. Bacon.
Pertaining to, or advocating, the non-extension of slavery; --esp. applied to a party which was active during the period 1846-1856.[U.S.] -- Free"soil`er, n. [U.S.] -- Free"-soil`ism, n. [U.S.]
Accustomed to speak without reserve. Bacon.-- Free"-spo`ken-ness, n.
Swimming in the open sea; -- said of certain marine animals.
One who plunders or pillages without the authority of nationalwarfare; a member of a predatory band; a pillager; a buccaneer; a searobber. Bacon.
The act, practice, or gains of a freebooter; freebooting.Booth.
Born free; not born in vasssalage; inheriting freedom.
A man who has been a slave, and has been set free.
An estate in real property, of inheritance (in fee simple orfee tail) or for life; or the tenure by which such estate is held.Kent. Burrill. To abate into a freehold. See under Abate.

In a free manner; without restraint or compulsion; abundantly;gratuitously.Of every tree of the garden thou mayst freely eat. Gen. ii. 16.Freely ye have received, freely give. Matt. x. 8.Freely they stood who stood, and fell who fell. Milton.Freely we serve Because we freely love. Milton.

One of an ancient and secret association or fraternity, said tohave been at first composed of masons or builders in stone, but nowconsisting of persons who are united for social enjoyment and mutualassistance.
Pertaining to, or resembling, the institutions or the practicesof freemasons; as, a freemasonic signal.
The institutions or the practices of freemasons.
The state or quality of being free; freedom; liberty; openness;liberality; gratuitousness.
One who frees, or sets free.
A stone composed of sand or grit; -- so called because it iseasily cut or wrought.

One who speculates or forms opinions independently of theauthority of others; esp., in the sphere or religion, one who formsopinions independently of the authority of revelation or of thechurch; an unbeliever; -- a term assumed by deists and skeptics inthe eighteenth century.Atheist is an old-fashioned word: I'm a freethinker, child. Addison.
Undue boldness of speculation; unbelief. Berkeley.-- a.

A clutch fitted in the rear hub of a cycle, which engages therear sprocket with the rear wheel when the pedals are rotatedforwards, but permits the rear wheel to run on free from the rearsprocket when the pedals are stopped or rotated backwards.Freewheelcycles are usually fitted with hub brakes or rim brakes,operated by back pedaling.
Of or pertaining to free will; voluntary; spontaneous; as, afreewill offering. Frewill Baptists. See under Baptist.
One who, or that which, cools or freezes, as a refrigerator, orthe tub and can used in the process of freezing ice cream.

Tending to freeze; for freezing; hence, cold or distant inmanner.-- Frrez"ing*ly, adv. Freezing machine. See Ice machine, under Ice.-- Freezing mixture, a mixture (of salt and snow or of chemicalsalts) for producing intense cold.-- Freezing point, that degree of a thermometer at which a fluidbegins to freeze; -- applied particularly to water, whose freezingpoint is at 32º Fahr., and at 0º Centigrade.
A sulphide of antimony, lead, and silver, occuring inmonoclinic crystals.

Employed in the transportation of freight; having to do withfreight; as, a freight car. Freight agent, a person employed by atransportation company to receive, forward, or deliver goods.-- Freight car. See under Car.-- Freight train, a railroad train made up of freight cars; --called in England goods train.
In Germany and Austria, a baron.
Becoming murmurous, roaring. "Fremescent clangor." Carlyle. --Fre*mes"cence (#), n.
Palpable vibration or thrill; as, the rhonchial fremitus.

Of or pertaining to France or its inhabitants. French bean(Bot.), the common kidney bean (Phaseolus vulgaris).-- French berry (Bot.), the berry of a species of buckthorn (Rhamnuscatharticus), which affords a saffron, green or purple pigment.-- French casement (Arch.) See French window, under Window.-- French chalk (Min.), a variety of granular talc; -- used fordrawing lines on cloth, etc. See under Chalk.-- French cowslip (Bot.) The Primula Auricula. See Bear's-ear.-- French fake (Naut.), a mode of coiling a rope by running itbackward and forward in parallel bends, so that it may run freely.-- French honeysuckle (Bot.) a plant of the genus Hedysarum (H.coronarium); -- called also garland honeysuckle.-- French horn, a metallic wind instrument, consisting of a longtube twisted into circular folds and gradually expanding from themouthpiece to the end at which the sound issues; -- called in Francecor de chasse.-- French leave, an informal, hasty, or secret departure; esp., theleaving a place without paying one's debts.-- French pie Etym: [French (here used in sense of "foreign") + piea magpie (in allusion to its black and white color)] (Zoöl.), theEuropean great spotted woodpecker (Dryobstes major); -- called alsowood pie.-- French polish. (a) A preparation for the surface of woodwork,consisting of gums dissolved in alcohol, either shellac alone, orshellac with other gums added. (b) The glossy surface produced by theapplication of the above.-- French purple, a dyestuff obtained from lichens and used forcoloring woolen and silken fabrics, without the aid of mordants. Ure.-- French red rouge.-- French rice, amelcorn.-- French roof (Arch.), a modified form of mansard roof having anearly flat deck for the upper slope.-- French tub, a dyer's mixture of protochloride of tin and logwood;-- called also plum tub. Ure.-- French window. See under Window.
To make French; to infect or imbue with the manners or tastesof the French; to Gallicize. Burke.
A French mode or characteristic; an idiom peculiar to theFrench language. Earle.
A native or one of the people of France.
Affected with frenzy; frantic; maddened.-- Fren"zied-ly, adv.The people frenzied by centuries of oppression. Buckle.Up starting with a frenzied look. Sir W Scott.

Any violent agitation of the mind approaching to distraction;violent and temporary derangement of the mental faculties; madness;rage.All else is towering frenzy and distraction. Addison.The poet's eye in a fine frenzy rolling. Shak.
The practice or habit of frequenting. [R.] Southey.
The act or habit of frequenting or visiting often; resort.Chesterfield.
Serving to express the frequent repetition of an action; as, afrequentative verb.-- n.
One who frequents; one who often visits, or resorts tocustomarily.
At frequent or short intervals; many times; often; repeatedly;commonly.
A cool walk; shady place. [R.] Maunder.
To paint in fresco, as walls.
To refresh; to freshen. [Obs.] Rom. of R.
A lantern having a lamp surrounded by a hollow cylindricalFresnel lens.

To relieve, as a rope, by change of place where friction wearsit; or to renew, as the material used to prevent chafing; as, tofreshen a hawse. Totten. To freshen ballast (Naut.), to shift Orrestore it.-- To freshen the hawse, to pay out a little more cable, so as tobring the chafe on another part.-- To freshen the way, to increase the speed of a vessel. Ham. Nav.Encyc.
In a fresh manner; vigorously; newly, recently; brightly;briskly; coolly; as, freshly gathered; freshly painted; the windblows freshly.Looks he as freshly as he did Shak.

novice; one in the rudiments of knowledge; especially, astudent during his fist year in a college or university.He drank his glass and cracked his joke, And freshmen wondered as hespoke. Goldsmith.Freshman class, the lowest of the four classes in an Americancollege. [ U. S.]
The state of being a freshman.

The state of being fresh.The Scots had the advantage both for number and freshness of men.Hayward.And breathe the freshness of the open air. Dryden.Her cheeks their freshness lose and wonted grace. Granville.
Disposed to fret; ill-humored; peevish; angry; in a state ofvexation; as, a fretful temper.-- Fret"ful-ly, adv.-- Fret"ful-ness, n.
The worn side of the bank of a river. See 4th Fret, n., 4.
Interlaced one with another; -- said of charges and ordinaries.
Rubbed; marked; as, pock-fretten, marked with the smallpox.[Obs.] Wright.
One who, or that which, frets.
A strait, or arm of the sea.

Work adorned with frets; ornamental openwork or work in relief,esp. when elaborate and minute in its parts. Heuce, any minute playof light andshade, dark and light, or the like.Banqueting on the turf in the fretwork of shade and sunshine.Macaulay.
The daughter of Njörd, aud goddess of love and beauty; theScandinavian Venus; -- in Teutonic myths confounded with Frigga, butin Scandinavian, distinct. [Written also Frea, Fraying, and Ereyja.]
The quality of being friable; friableness. Locke.

[friabilis, fr. friare to rub, break, or crumble into smallpieces, cf. fricare to rub, E. fray. cf. F. friable.) Easilycrumbled, pulverized, or reduced to powder. "Friable ground." Evelyn."Soft and friable texture." Paley.-- Fri'a-ble-ness, n.

A brother or member of any religious order, but especially ofone of the four mendicant orders, viz: (a) Minors, Gray Friars, orFranciscans. (b) Augustines. (c) Dominicans or Black Friars. (d)White Friars or Carmelites. See these names in the Vocabulary.
Like a friar; pertaining to friars or to a convent. [Obs.]Camden.
The act of breaking up or pulverizing.
A ragout or fricassee of veal; a fancy dish of veal or of bonedturkey, served as an entrée, -- called also fricandel. A. J. Cooley.
A dish made of fowls, veal, or other meat of small animals cutinto pieces, and stewed in a gravy.

Produced by the friction or rustling of the breath, intonatedor unintonated, through a narrow opening between two of the mouthorgans; uttered through a close approach, but not with a completeclosure, of the organs of articulation, and hence capable of beingcontinued or prolonged; -- said of certain consonantal sounds, as f,v, s, z, etc.-- n.
A lewd woman; a harlot. [Obs.] B. Jonson.
The resistance which a body meets with from the surface onwhich it moves. It may be resistance to sliding motion, or to rollingmotion.

Relating to friction; moved by friction; produced by friction;as, frictional electricity. Frictional gearing, wheels which transmitmotion by surface friction instead of teeth. The faces are sometimesmade more or less V-shaped to increase or decrease friction, asrequired.
The sixth day of the week, following Thursday and precedingSaturday.
To act as the friend of; to favor; to countenance; to befriend.[Obs.]Fortune friends the bold. Spenser.
Destitute of friends; forsaken.-- Friend"less*ness, n.
The condition or quality of being friendly. Sir P. Sidney.
In the manner of friends; amicably; like friends. [Obs.] Shak.In whom all graces that can perfect beauty Are friendly met. Beau. &Fl.
Of or pertaining to Friesland, a province in the northern partof the Netherlands.
A kind of coarse woolen cloth or stuff with a shaggy or tufted(friezed) nap on one side. "Robes of frieze." Goldsmith.
Gathered, or having the map gathered, into little tufts, knots,or protuberances. Cf. Frieze, v. t., and Friz, v. t.,
One who, or that which, friezes or frizzes.
Built like a frigate with a raised quarter-deck and forecastle.
A Venetian vessel, with a square stern, having only a mainmast,jigger mast, and bowsprit; also a sloop of war ship-rigged.
To alarm suddenly; to shock by causing sudden fear; to terrify;to scare.Nor exile or danger can fright a brave spirit. Dryden.
To disturb with fear; to throw into a state of alarm or fright;to affright; to terrify.More frightened than hurt. Old Proverb.
In a frightful manner; to a frightful dagree.
The cooling room of the Roman thermæ, furnished with a coldbath.
In a frigid manner; coldly; dully; without affection.
The state of being frigid; want of heat, vigor, or affection;coldness; dullness.
To wrinkle; -- said of the gelatin film.
Furnished with a frill or frills. Frilled lizard (Zoöl.), alarge Australian lizard (Chlamydosaurus Kingii) about three feetlong, which has a large, erectile frill on each side of the neck.
Flourishing; thriving; fresh; in good case; vigorous. [Obs.]"Frim pastures." Drayton.
The third month of the French republican calendar. It commencedNovember 21, and ended December 20., See Vendémiaire.
One of a number of light or dark bands, produced by theinterference of light; a diffraction band; -- called alsointerference fringe.
A small oleaceous tree (Chionanthus virginica), of the southernUnited States, having clusters of white flowers with slender petals.It is often cultivated.
Furnished with a fringe. Fringed lear (Bot.), a leaf edged withsoft parallel hairs.
Encircling like a fringe; bordering. [R.] "The fringent air."Emerson.
A genus of birds, with a short, conical, pointed bill. Itformerly included all the sparrows and finches, but is now restrictedto certain European finches, like the chaffinch and brambling.
Pertaining to the family Fringillidæ; characteristic offinches; sparrowlike.
One who deals in frippery or in old clothes. [Obs.] Bacon.
Of or pertaining to Friesland, a province of the Netherlands;Friesic.
Lively; brisk; frolicsome; frisky. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.
A leap or caper. [Obs.] B. Jonson.
One who frisks; one who leaps of dances in gayety; a wanton; aninconstant or unsettled person. Camden.
The light frame which holds the sheet of paper to the tympan inprinting.
State or quality of being frisky.
Inclined to frisk; frolicsome; gay.He is too frisky for an old man. Jeffrey.
[Fraise a kind of defense; also Friz.) A kind of small ruffle.Halliwell.
To sell upon credit, as goods. [R.] Crabb.
The dressing of the hair by crisping or curling. Smollett.
The material of which glass is made, after having been calcinedor partly fused in a furnace, but before vitrification. It is acomposition of silex and alkali, occasionally with other ingredients.Ure.
A small dipterous fly of the genus Oscinis, esp. O. vastator,injurious to grain in Europe, and O. Trifole, injurious to clover inAmerica.
A narrow arm of the sea; an estuary; the opening of a riverinto the sea; as, the Frith of Forth.
