A group of acalephs, including the naked-eyed medusæ; thehydromedusæ. Most of them are known to be the free-swimming progeny(gonophores) of hydroids.
A cell or mass of protoplasm devoid of an envelope, as a whiteblood corpuscle.
Having unfeathered nostrils, as certain birds.
One of the orders of Pteropoda. They have no shell.

One of a sect of philosophers, said to have been found in Indiaby Alexander the Great, who went almost naked, denied themselves theuse of flesh, renounced bodily pleasures, and employed themselves inthe contemplation of nature.
The doctrines of the Gymnosophists. Good.
A plant that bears naked seeds (i. e., seeds not inclosed in anovary), as the common pine and hemlock. Cf. Angiosperm.

A genus of South American fresh-water fishes, including theGymnotus electricus, or electric eel. It has a greenish, eel-likebody, and is possessed of electric power.One fearful shock, fearful but momentary, like from the electric blowof the gymnotus. De Quincey.
A ventral canal or groove, in which the males of some dioecioustrematodes carry the female. See Illust. of Hæmatozoa.
A plant having the stamens inserted in the pistil.
A class of plants in the Linnaean system, whose stamens growout of, or are united with, the pistil.
An abnormal condition of certain animals, in which one side hasthe external characters of the male, and the other those of thefemale.
Pertaining to an abnormal condition of the flower, in which thestamens are converted into pistils. A. Brown.
Government by a woman, female power; gyneocracy. Bailey.
The science which treats of the structure and diseases ofwomen.-- Gyn`e*col"o*gist.
The adoration or worship of woman.The sentimental gyneolatry of chivalry, which was at best but skin-deep. Lowell.
Hatred of women; repugnance to the society of women. Holmes.
A dilated base or receptacle, supporting a multilocular ovary.
Pertaining to, or having, a gynobase.

Female government; gynecocracy.The aforesaid state has repeatedly changed from absolute despotism torepublicanism, not forgetting the intermediate stages of oligarchy,limited monarchy, and even gynocracy; for I myself remember Alsatiagoverned for nearly nine months by an old fishwoman. Sir H. Scott.
Dioecious, but having some hermaphrodite or perfect flowers onan individual plant which bears mostly pistillate flowers.
The pistils of a flower, taken collectively. See Illust. ofCarpophore.
The pedicel raising the pistil or ovary above the stamens, asin the passion flower. Lindley.
A college servant; -- so called in Cambridge, England; atOxford called a scout. [Cant]
Resembling or containing gypsum; partaking of the qualities ofgypsum.
The act or art of engraving on gypsum.
A cast taken in plaster of Paris, or in white lime.
A mineral consisting of the hydrous sulphate of lime (calcium).When calcined, it forms plaster of Paris. Selenite is a transparent,crystalline variety; alabaster, a fine, white, massive variety.

Pertaining to, or suitable for, gypsies. Gypsy hat, a woman'sor child's broad-brimmed hat, usually of straw or felt.-- Gypsy winch, a small winch, which may be operated by a crank, orby a ratchet and pawl through a lever working up and down.

A tussock moth (Ocneria dispar) native of the Old World, butaccidentally introduced into eastern Massachusetts about 1869, whereits caterpillars have done great damage to fruit, shade, and foresttrees of many kinds. The male gypsy moth is yellowish brown, thefemale white, and larger than the male. In both sexes the wings aremarked by dark lines and a dark lunule. The caterpillars, when full-grown, have a grayish mottled appearance, with blue tubercles on theanterior and red tubercles on the posterior part of the body, allgiving rise to long yellow and black hairs. They usually pupate inJuly and the moth appears in August. The eggs are laid on treetrunks, rocks, etc., and hatch in the spring.
A labiate plant (the Lycopus Europæus). Gypsies are said tostain their skin with its juice.
A genus of fossil fishes, found in Devonian and carboniferousstrata; -- so named from their round, sculptured spines.
Pertaining to a gyrus, or convolution.
Winding or coiled round; curved into a circle; taking acircular course.
One of the whorls of a spiral univalve shell. Center ofgyration. (Mech.) See under Center.-- Radius of gyration the distance between the axis of a rotatingbody and its center of gyration. Rankine.
Moving in a circle, or spirally; revolving; whirling around.
A circular motion, or a circle described by a moving body; aturn or revolution; a circuit.Quick and more quick he spins in giddy gyres. Dryden.Still expanding and ascending gyres. Mrs. Browning.
The higher orders of Mammalia, in which the cerebrum isconvoluted.-- Gyr"en*ceph"a*lous, a.

One of several species and varieties of large Arctic falcons,esp. Falco rusticolus and the white species F. Islandicus, both ofwhich are circumpolar. The black and the gray are varieties of theformer. See Illust. of Accipiter. [Written also gerfalcon,gierfalcon, and jerfalcon.]
A genus of extinct oölitic fishes, having rounded teeth inseveral rows adapted for crushing.
The petrified fruit of the Chara hispida, a species ofstonewort. See Stonewort. Lyell.
Having the planes arranged spirally, so that they incline allto the right (or left) of a vertical line; -- said of certainhemihedral forms.
A genus of ganoid fishes, found in strata of the new redsandetone, and the lias bone beds. Agassiz.
A kind of divination performed by drawing a ring or circle, andwalking in or around it. Brande & C.

A subordinary of triangular form having one of its angles atthe fess point and the opposite aide at the edge of the escutcheon.When there is only one gyron on the shield it is bounded by two lineadrawn from the fess point, one horizontally to the dexter side, andone to the dexter chief corner.
Covered with gyrons, or divided so as to form several gyrons; -- said of an escutcheon.
Pertaining to the gyroscope; resembling the motion of thegyroscope.
Turned round like a crook, or bent to and fro. Loudon.

A modification of the gyroscope, consisting essentially of afly wheel fixed inside a rigid case to which is attached a thinflange of metal for supporting the instrument. It is used in studyingthe dynamics of rotating bodies.
Of or pertaining to the gyrostat or to gyrostatics.
The doctrine or theory of the gyrostat, or of the phenomena ofrotating bodies.
A convoluted ridge between grooves; a convolution; as, the gyriof the brain; the gyri of brain coral. See Brain.
Delirious; senselessly extravagant; as, the man is clean gyte.[Scot.] Sir W. Scott.
A shackle; especially, one to confine the legs; a fetter.[Written also give.]Like a poor prisoner in his twisted gyves. Shak.With gyves upon his wrist. Hood.

the eighth letter of the English alphabet, is classed among theconsonants, and is formed with the mouth organs in the same positionas that of the succeeding vowel. It is used with certain consonantsto form digraphs representing sounds which are not found in thealphabet, as sh, th, th, as in shall, thing, thine (for zh see §274);also, to modify the sounds of some other letters, as when placedafter c and p, with the former of which it represents a compoundsound like that of tsh, as in charm (written also tch as in catch),with the latter, the sound of f, as in phase, phantom. In some words,mostly derived or introduced from foreign languages, h following cand g indicates that those consonants have the hard sound before e,i, and y, as in chemistry, chiromancy, chyle, Ghent, Ghibelline,etc.; in some others, ch has the sound of sh, as in chicane. SeeGuide to Pronunciation, §§ 153, 179, 181-3, 237-8.

An exclamation denoting surprise, joy, or grief. Both asuttered and as written, it expresses a great variety of emotions,determined by the tone or the context. When repeated, ha, ha, it isan expression of laughter, satisfaction, or triumph, sometimes ofderisive laughter; or sometimes it is equivalent to "Well, it is so."Ha-has, and inarticulate hootings of satirical rebuke. Carlyle.
A sunk fence; a fence, wall, or ditch, not visible till one isclose upon it. [Written also haw-haw.]
The deepsea fishing for cod, ling, and tusk, off the ShetlandIsles.
A sea fish. See Hake. Ash.
A fog; esp., a fog or mist with a chill wind. [Scot.] T.Chalmers.

A writ having for its object to bring a party before a court orjudge; especially, one to inquire into the cause of a person'simprisonment or detention by another, with the view to protect theright to personal liberty; also, one to bring a prisoner into courtto testify in a pending trial. Bouvier.
That part of a deed which follows the part called the premises,and determines the extent of the interest or estate granted; -- socalled because it begins with the word Habendum. Kent.
To deal in small wares. [R.]To haberdash in earth's base ware. Quarles.
The goods and wares sold by a haberdasher; also (Fig.),trifles. Burke.
A cod salted and dried. Ainsworth.
Properly, a short hauberk, but often used loosely for thehauberk. Chaucer.
Of or pertaining to clothing; wearing clothes. Ld. Lytton.
The general appearance and manner of life of a living organism.
Capable of being inhabited; that may be inhabited or dwelt in;as, the habitable world.-- Hab"it*a*ble*ness, n.-- Hab"it*a*bly, adv.
Same as Habitant, 2.General met an emissary . . . sent . . . to ascertain the feelings ofthe habitans or French yeomanry. W. Irwing.

An inhabitant or resident; -- a name applied to and denotingfarmers of French descent or origin in Canada, especially in theProvince of Quebec; -- usually in plural.The habitants or cultivators of the soil. Parkman.
The natural abode, locality or region of an animal or plant.
A dweller; an inhabitant. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.
Firmly established by custom; formed by habit; habitual. [R.]Hammond.
The act of habituating, or accustoming; the state of beinghabituated.
One who habitually frequents a place; as, an habitué of atheater.
Habitude; mode of life; general appearance.
A short line used in drawing and engraving, especially inshading and denoting different surfaces, as in map drawing. SeeHatching.

A large estate where work of any kind is done, as agriculture,manufacturing, mining, or raising of animals; a cultivated farm, witha good house, in distinction from a farming establishment with rudehuts for herdsmen, etc.; -- a word used in Spanish-American regions.1.
To cough faintly and frequently, or in a short, broken manner;as, a hacking cough.
A halter consisting of a long leather or rope strap andheadstall, -- used for leading or tieing a pack animal. [WesternU.S.]
A genus of trees (Celtis) related to the elm, but bearingdrupes with scanty, but often edible, pulp. C. occidentalis is commonin the Eastern United States. Gray.
The greater shearwater or hagdon. See Hagdon.
The chipmunk; also, the chickaree or red squirrel. [U.S.]
One who, or that which, hacks. Specifically: A cuttinginstrument for making notches; esp., one used for notching pine treesin collecting turpentine; a hack.
A cart with wooden wheels, drawn by bullocks. [Bengal] Malcom.
Having fine, short, and sharp points on the surface; as, thehackly fracture of metallic iron.
The driver of a hack or carriage for public hire.
The American larch (Larix Americana), a coniferous tree withslender deciduous leaves; also, its heavy, close-grained timber.Called also tamarack.
Let out for hire; devoted to common use; hence, much used;trite; mean; as, hackney coaches; hackney authors. "Hackney tongue."Roscommon.
A man who lets horses and carriages for hire.
A bully; a bravo; a ruffian; an assassin. [Obs.] Milton.

See Have. Had as lief, Had rather, Had better, Had as soon,etc., with a nominative and followed by the infinitive without to,are well established idiomatic forms. The original construction wasthat of the dative with forms of be, followed by the infinitive. SeeHad better, under Better.And lever me is be pore and trewe. [And more agreeable to me it is tobe poor and true.] C. Mundi (Trans. ).Him had been lever to be syke. [To him it had been preferable to besick.] Fabian.For him was lever have at his bed's head Twenty bookes, clad in blackor red, . . . Than robes rich, or fithel, or gay sawtrie. Chaucer.

A marine food fish (Melanogrammus æglefinus), allied to thecod, inhabiting the northern coasts of Europe and America. It has adark lateral line and a black spot on each side of the body, justback of the gills. Galled also haddie, and dickie. Norway haddock, amarine edible fish (Sebastes marinus) of Northern Europe and America.See Rose fish.
The inclination or deviation from the vertical of any mineralvein.

The nether world (according to classical mythology, the abodeof the shades, ruled over by Hades or Pluto); the invisible world;the grave.And death and Hades gave up the dead which were in them. Rev. xx. 13(Rev. Ver. ).Neither was he left in Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption. Actsii. 31 (Rev. Ver.).And in Hades he lifted up his eyes, being in torments. Luke xvi.23(Rev. Ver.).
The pilgrimage to Mecca, performed by Mohammedans.
An American herbivorous dinosaur of great size, allied to theiguanodon. It is found in the Cretaceous formation.
Literally, this-ness. A scholastic term to expressindividuality or singleness; as, this book.
A substance found in the blood of the octopus, which gives toit its blue color.
An apparatus for determining the number of corpuscles in agiven quantity of blood.
Toward the hæmal side; on the hæmal side of; -- opposed toneurad.
An instrument for registering the velocity of the blood.
Pertaining to the blood or blood vessels; also, ventral. SeeHemal.
A brownish substance sometimes found in the blood, in cases ofjaundice.
Having the limbs on, or directed toward, the ventral or hemalside, as in vertebrates; -- opposed to neuropodous.
Bloodforming; as, the hæmapoietic function of the spleen.
A form of apparatus (somewhat different from the hemadrometer)for measuring the velocity of the blood.
The measurement of the velocity of the blood.

Of or pertaining to the blood; sanguine; brownish red. Hæmaticacid (Physiol.), a hypothetical acid, supposed to be formed fromhemoglobin during its oxidation in the lungs, and to have the powerof freeing carbonic acid from the sodium carbonate of the serum.Thudichum.
Of a blood-red color; crimson; (Bot.) brownish red.

One of the very minute, disk-shaped bodies found in blood withthe ordinary red corpuscles and white corpuscles; a third kind ofblood corpuscle, supposed by some to be an early stage in thedevelopment of the red corpuscles; -- called also blood plaque, andblood plate.
The cold-blooded vertebrates. Same as Hematocrya.

A substance formed from the hematin of blood, by removal of theiron through the action of concentrated sulphuric acid. Two likebodies, called respectively hæmatoporphyrin and hæmatolin, are formedin a similar manner.
The science which treats of the blood. Same as Hematology.
Dissolution of the red blood corpuscles with diminishedcoagulability of the blood; hæmolysis. -- Hæm`a*to*lyt"ic (#), a.
A division of Cheiroptera, including the bloodsucking bats. SeeVampire.
Blood formative; -- applied to a substance in early fetal life,which breaks up gradually into blood vessels.
A vascular sac connected, beneath the brain, in many fishes,with the infundibulum.
The coloring principle of logwood. It is obtained as a yellowcrystalline substance, C16H14O6, with a sweetish taste. Formerlycalled also hematin.
A genus of leguminous plants containing but a single species,the H. Campechianum or logwood tree, native in Yucatan.
A body obtained from hemoglobin, by the action of reducingagents in the absence of oxygen.
An apparatus for measuring the amount of hemoglobin in a fluid,by comparing it with a solution of known strength and of normalcolor.
A breaking up of the blood corpuscles, as by pressure, indistinction from solution of the corpuscles, or hæmcytolysis.
A dark brown powder containing iron, prepared by the action ofzinc dust as a reducing agent upon the coloring matter of the blood,used medicinally as a hematinic.
A plant described by Milton as "of sovereign use against allenchantments."
An instrument devised by Hermann, for regulating and measuringthe thickness of a layer of blood for spectroscopic examination.
To stammer; to speak unintelligibly; to prevaricate.[Prov.Eng.] Halliwell.
To set in, or furnish with, a haft; as, to haft a dagger.

An eel-like marine marsipobranch (Myxine glutinosa), allied tothe lamprey. It has a suctorial mouth, with labial appendages, and asingle pair of gill openings. It is the type of the orderHyperotpeta. Called also hagfish, borer, slime eel, sucker, andsleepmarken.
Ridden by a hag or witch; hence, afflicted with nightmare.Beattie. Cheyne.
A plant of the genus Prunus (P. Padus); the bird cherry.[Scot.]
Born of a hag or witch. Shak.
A harquebus, of which the but was bent down or hooked forconvenience in taking aim. [Written also haguebut and hackbuss.]
A soldier armed with a hagbut or arquebus. [Written alsohackbutter.] Froude.

One of several species of sea birds of the genus Puffinus;esp., P. major, the greater shearwarter, and P. Stricklandi, theblack hagdon or sooty shearwater; -- called also hagdown, haglin, andhag. See Shearwater.
A story, anecdote, or legend in the Talmud, to explain orillustrate the text of the Old Testament. [Written also hadaga.]

Having the expression of one wasted by want or suffering;hollow-eyed; having the features distorted or wasted, or anxious inappearance; as, haggard features, eyes.Staring his eyes, and haggard was his look. Dryden.

A Scotch pudding made of the heart, liver, lights, etc., of asheep or lamb, minced with suet, onions, oatmeal, etc., highlyseasoned, and boiled in the stomach of the same animal; minced headand pluck. [Written also haggiss, haggess, and haggies.]
Like a hag; ugly; wrinkled.But on both did haggish age steal on. Shak.
In the manner of a hag.

To cut roughly or hack; to cut into small pieces; to notch orcut in an unskillful manner; to make rough or mangle by cutting; as,a boy haggles a stick of wood.Suffolk first died, and York, all haggled o'er, Comes to him, wherein gore he lay insteeped. Shak.
A sacred government; by holy orders of men. Southey.
The lives of the saints. Brande & C.
, Pertaining to the hagiographa, or to sacred writings.
One of the writers of the hagiographa; a writer of lives of thesaints. Shipley.
The invocation or worship of saints.
One who treats of the sacred writings; a writer of the lives ofthe saints; a hagiographer. Tylor.Hagiologists have related it without scruple. Southey.
The history or description of the sacred writings or of sacredpersons; a narrative of the lives of the saints; a catalogue ofsaints. J. H. Newman.
An opening made in the interior walls of a cruciform church toafford a view of the altar to those in the transepts; -- called, inarchitecture, a squint. Hook.
The offspring of a hag. Shak.
The state or title of a hag. Middleton.

The permanent court of arbitration created by the"International Convention for the Pacific Settle of InternationalDisputes.", adopted by the International Peace Conference of 1899. Itis composed of persons of known competency in questions ofinternational law, nominated by the signatory powers. From thesepersons an arbitration tribunal is chosen by the parties to adifference submitted to the court. On the failure of the parties toagree directly on the arbitrators, each chooses two arbitrators, anumpire is selected by them, by a third power, or by two powersselected by the parties.
A mineral consisting of the arseniate of lime; -- so named inhonor of W. Haidinger, of Vienna.
Formerly, a mercenary foot soldier in Hungary, now, ahalberdier of a Hungarian noble, or an attendant in German orHungarian courts. [Written also hayduck, heiduc, heiduck, andheyduk.]
A large piece of woolen or cotton cloth worn by Arabs as anouter garment. [Written also hyke.] Heyse.
The central chapel of the three forming the sanctuary of aCoptic church. It contains the high altar, and is usually closed byan embroidered curtain.
A Chinese weight ( 1/10 catty) equivalent to 1 1/3 oz. or37.801 g.

Small roundish masses of ice precipitated from the clouds,where they are formed by the congelation of vapor. The separatemasses or grains are called hailstones.Thunder mixed with hail, Hail mixed with fire, must rend the Egyptiansky. Milton.
An intimate companion.Hail-fellow well met. Lyly.
To greet; to salute. [Obs.] P. Plowman.
Small shot which scatter like hailstones. [Obs.] Hayward.
A single particle of ice falling from a cloud; a frozenraindrop; a pellet of hail.
A storm accompanied with hail; a shower of hail.
To inclose for mowing; to set aside for grass. "A ground . . .hained in." Holland.

A slender outgrowth from the chitinous cuticle of insects,spiders, crustaceans, and other invertebrates. Such hairs are totallyunlike those of vertebrates in structure, composition, and mode ofgrowth.
A grass with very slender leaves or branches; as the Agrostisscabra, and several species of Aira or Deschampsia.
Of a clear tint of brown, resembling brown human hair. It iscomposed of equal proportions of red and green.
A variety of native Epsom salt occurring in silky fibers.
Having the breadth of a hair; very narrow; as, a hairbreadthescape.
A brush for cleansing and smoothing the hair.
Stuff or cloth made wholly or in part of hair.
One who dresses or cuts hair; a barber.
Hairy. [Obc.]His hairen shirt and his ascetic diet. J. Taylor.
The state of abounding, or being covered, with hair. Johnson.
A pin, usually forked, or of bent wire, for fastening the hairin place, -- used by women.
One who makes excessively nice or needless distinctions inreasoning; one who quibbles. "The caviling hairsplitter." De Quincey.
Making excessively nice or trivial distinctions in reasoning;subtle.-- n.
The slender recoil spring which regulates the motion of thebalance in a timepiece.
A butterfly of the genus Thecla; as, the green hairstreak (T.rubi).
Any species of marine fishes of the genus Trichiurus; esp., T.lepterus of Europe and America. They are long and like a band, with aslender, pointed tail. Called also bladefish.
A nematoid worm of the genus Gordius, resembling a hair. SeeGordius.
Bearing or covered with hair; made of or resembling hair; roughwith hair; rough with hair; rough with hair; hirsute.His mantle hairy, and his bonnet sedge. Milton.

The Egyptian asp or cobra (Naja haje.) It is related to thecobra of India, and like the latter has the power of inflating itsneck into a hood. Its bite is very venomous. It is supposed to be thesnake by means of whose bite Cleopatra committed suicide, and henceis sometimes called Cleopatra's snake or asp. See Asp.
A drying shed, as for unburned tile.
A wise man; a physician, esp. a Mohammedan. [India]
The general term for the Hebrew oral or traditional law; one oftwo branches of exposition in the Midrash. See Midrash.
An appearance as of a halo of light, surround the edges of darkobject

An ancient long-handled weapon, of which the head had a pointand several long, sharp edges, curved or straight, and sometimesadditional points. The heads were sometimes of very elaborate form.[Written also halbert.]
One who is armed with a halberd. Strype.

A kingfisher. By modern ornithologists restricted to a genusincluding a limited number of species having omnivorous habits, asthe sacred kingfisher (Halcyon sancta) of Australia.Amidst our arms as quiet you shall be As halcyons brooding on awinter sea. Dryden.
Sound; entire; healthy; robust; not impaired; as, a hale body.Last year we thought him strong and hale. Swift.
A genus of American shrubs containing several species, calledsnowdrop trees, or silver-bell trees. They have showy, white flowers,drooping on slender pedicels.

In an equal part or degree; in some paas, half-colored, halfdone, half-hearted, half persuaded, half conscious. "Half loth andhalf consenting." Dryden.Their children spoke halfin the speech of Ashdod. Neh. xiii. 24
A hold in which one arm is thrust under the corresponding armof the opponent, generally behind, and the hand placed upon the backof his neck. In the full nelson both hands are so placed.
Half drunk. [Slang: used only predicatively.] Spectator.
A mixture of two malt liquors, esp. porter and ale, in aboutequal parts. Dickens.
A boot with a short top covering only the ankle. See Cocker,and Congress boot, under Congress.
Having only the back and corners in leather, as a book.
A brother by one parent, but not by both.
One born of a European parent on the one side, and of a Hindooor Mohammedan on the other. Also adjective; as, half-caste parents.
Half-filled. [Obs.]Lions' half-clammed entrails roar food. Marston.
A shell of the genus Crepidula; a boat shell. See Boat shell.
Partially decked.The half-decked craft . . . used by the latter Vikings. Elton.
Showing only part of the face; wretched looking; meager. Shak.
A salmon in its fifth year of growth. [Prov. Eng.]
Imperfectly hatched; as, half-hatched eggs. Gay.
Imperfectly or partly heard to the end.And leave half-heard the melancholy tale. Pope.
Done or happening at intervals of half an hour.
Of half the whole or ordinary length, as a picture.
A point some distance below the top of a mast or staff; as, aflag a half-mast (a token of mourning, etc.).
An outwork composed of two faces, forming a salient angle whosegorge resembles a half-moon; -- now called a ravelin.
An English coin of the value of half a penny; also, the valueof half a penny.
A short pike, sometimes carried by officers of infantry,sometimes used in boarding ships; a spontoon. Tatler.
One half of a shutter made in two parts for closing a porthole.
A straight line considered as drawn from a center to anindefinite distance in one direction, the complete ray being thewhole line drawn to an indefinite distance in both directions.
Informed by insufficient reading; superficial; shallow. Dryden.
Seeing imperfectly; having weak discernment. Bacon.
A sister by one parent only.
Half the length of a sword; close fight. "At half-sword." Shak.
Constructed of a timber frame, having the spaces filled in withmasonry; -- said of buildings.
Having, consisting of, or pertaining to, half tones; specif.(Photo-engraving),
A jury, for the trial of a fore foreigner, composed equally ofcitizens and aliens.
A foolish; a dolt; a blockhead; a dunce. Dryden.
Two in a year; semiannual.-- adv. Twice in a year; semiannually.
Any slender, marine fish of the genus Hemirhamphus, having theupper jaw much shorter than the lower; -- called also balahoo.

To set the cock of (a firearm) at the first notch. To go offhalfcocked. (a) To be discharged prematurely, or with the trigger athalf cock; -- said of a firearm. (b) To do or say something withoutdue thought or care. [Colloq. or Low]
Wanting half its due qualities. [Obs.] Spencer.
Half; by the part. [Obs.] Chaucer.-- n.
The quality of being half; incompleteness. [R.]As soon as there is any departure from simplicity, and attempt athalfness, or good for me that is not good for him, my neighbor feelsthe wrong. Emerson.
A platform of a staircase where the stair turns back in exactlythe reverse direction of the lower flight. See Quarterpace.
In the middle; at half the distance; imperfectly; partially;as, he halfway yielded.Temples proud to meet their gods halfway. Young.

A large, northern, marine flatfish (Hippoglossus vulgaris), ofthe family Pleuronectidæ. It often grows very large, weighing morethan three hundred pounds. It is an important food fish. [Writtenalso holibut.]
An order of sponges, having simple siliceous spicules andkeratose fibers; -- called also Keratosilicoidea.
A treatise upon fish or the art of fishing; ichthyology.
One who writes about or describes the sea.
Description of the sea; the science that treats of the sea.
A genus of marine shells; the ear-shells. See Abalone.
Like or pertaining to the genus Haliotis; ear-shaped.
Produced by, or like, breath; vaporous. Boyle.

The official stamp of the Goldsmiths' Company and other assayoffices, in the United Kingdom, on gold and silver articles,attesting their purity. Also used figuratively; -- as, a word orphrase lacks the hall-mark of the best writers.
A fee or toll paid for goods sold in a hall.
A kind of net for catching birds.
A loud exclamation; a call to invite attention or to incite aperson or an animal; a shout.List! List! I hear Some far off halloo break the silent air. Milton.

To make holy; to set apart for holy or religious use; toconsecrate; to treat or keep as sacred; to reverence. "Hallowed bethy name." Matt. vi. 9.Hallow the Sabbath day, to do no work therein. Jer. xvii. 24.His secret altar touched with hallowed fire. Milton.In a larger sense . . . we can not hallow this ground [Gettysburg].A. Lincoln.
The evening preceding Allhallows or All Saints' Day. [Scot.]Burns.
The feast of All Saints, or Allhallows.To speak puling, like a beggar at Hallowmas. Shak.
A claylike mineral, occurring in soft, smooth, amorphousmasses, of a whitish color.
Of or pertaining to the hallux.
To wander; to go astray; to err; to blunder; -- used of mentalprocesses. [R.] Byron.

The perception of objects which have no reality, or ofsensations which have no corresponding external cause, arising fromdisorder or the nervous system, as in delirium tremens; delusion.Hallucinations are always evidence of cerebral derangement and arecommon phenomena of insanity. W. A. Hammond.
One whose judgment and acts are affected by hallucinations; onewho errs on account of his hallucinations. N. Brit. Rev.
Partaking of, or tending to produce, hallucination.
The first, or preaxial, digit of the hind limb, correspondingto the pollux in the fore limb; the great toe; the hind toe of birds.
The long jump, with weights in the hands, -- the most importantof the exercises of the Pentathlon.
To form, or surround with, a halo; to encircle with, or aswith, a halo.The fire That haloed round his saintly brow. Sothey.
Surrounded with a halo; invested with an ideal glory;glorified.Some haloed face bending over me. C. Bronté.

An electro-negative element or radical, which, by combinationwith a metal, forms a haloid salt; especially, chlorine, bromine, andiodine; sometimes, also, fluorine and cyanogen. See Chlorine family,under Chlorine.
Of the nature of a halogen.

Resembling salt; -- said of certain binary compounds consistingof a metal united to a negative element or radical, and now chieflyapplied to the chlorides, bromides, iodides, and sometimes also tothe fluorides and cyanides.-- n.
An instrument for measuring the forms and angles of salts andcrystals; a goniometer.
Alternating transparent and opaque white rings which are seenoutside the blastoderm, on the surface of the developing egg of thehen and other birds.
A plant found growing in salt marshes, or in the sea.
An instrument for exhibition or illustration of the phenomenaof halos, parhelia, and the like.
An iron alum occurring in silky fibrous aggregates of ayellowish white color.
An explosive mixture, consisting of sawdust, charcoal, niter,and ferrocyanide of potassium, used as a substitute for gunpowder.
The neck or throat. [Obs.]Do me hangen by the hals. Chaucer.
Sounding harshly in the throat; inharmonious; rough. [Obs.]Carew.
3d pers. sing. pres. of Hold, contraction for holdeth. [Obs.]Chaucer.
A term of reproach, implying that one is fit to be hanged.[Obs.] Beau. & Fl.
Balancers; the rudimentary hind wings of Diptera.
In a halting or limping manner.
Appearing as if one side, or one half, were cut away;dimidiate.
pl. of Half. By halves, by one half at once; halfway;fragmentarily; partially; incompletely.I can not believe by halves; either I have faith, or I have it not.J. H. Newman.To go halves. See under Go.
A genus of Silurian fossil corals; the chain corals. See Chaincoral, under Chain.
A tree nymph whose life ended with that of the particular tree,usually an oak, which had been her abode.
The sacred baboon of Egypt (Cynocephalus Hamadryas).
In Turkey and other Oriental countries, a porter or burdenbearer; specif., in Western India, a palanquin bearer.
A genus of plants which includes the witch-hazel (HamamelisVirginica), a preparation of which is used medicinally.
Hooked; bent at the end into a hook; hamous.
Hooked, or set with hooks; hamate. Swift.

A commercial city of Germany, near the mouth of the Elbe. BlackHamburg grape. See under Black.-- Hamburg , a kind of embroidered work done by machinery on cambricor muslin; -- used for trimming.-- Hamburg lake, a purplish crimson pigment resembling cochineal.
A low-grade actor or performer. [Theatrical Slang]
A subdivision of the Devonian system of America; -- so namedfrom Hamilton, Madison Co., New York. It includes the Marcellus,Hamilton, and Genesee epochs or groups. See the Chart of Geology.
A large edible river fish (Erythrinus macrodon) of Guiana.
A fossil cephalopod of the genus Hamites, related to theammonites, but having the last whorl bent into a hooklike form.
Pertaining to Ham or his descendants. Hamitic languages, thegroup of languages spoken mainly in the Sahara, Egypt, Galla, andSomâli Land, and supposed to be allied to the Semitic. Keith Johnson.
A small village; a little cluster of houses in the country.The country wasted, and the hamlets burned. Dryden.

That part of a gunlock which strikes the percussion cap, orfiring pin; the cock; formerly, however, a piece of steel coveringthe pan of a flintlock musket and struck by the flint of the cock toignite the priming.(e) Also, a person of thing that smites or shatters; as, St.Augustine was the hammer of heresies.He met the stern legionaries [of Rome] who had been the "massive ironhammers" of the whole earth. J. H. Newman.Atmospheric hammer, a dead-stroke hammer in which the spring isformed by confined air.-- Drop hammer, Face hammer, etc. See under Drop, Face, etc.-- Hammer fish. See Hammerhead.-- Hammer hardening, the process of hardening metal by hammering itwhen cold.-- Hammer shell (Zoöl.), any species of Malleus, a genus of marinebivalve shells, allied to the pearl oysters, having the wings narrowand elongated, so as to give them a hammer-shaped outline; -- calledalso hammer oyster.-- To bring to the hammer, to put up at auction.
An interrupter in which contact is broken by the movement of anautomatically vibrating hammer between a contact piece and anelectromagnet, or of a rapidly moving piece mechanically driven.
A hold in which an arm of one contestant is held twisted andbent behind his back by his opponent.

A member of one description of roof truss, called hammer-beamtruss, which is so framed as not to have a tiebeam at the top of thewall. Each principal has two hammer-beams, which occupy thesituation, and to some extent serve the purpose, of a tiebeam.
Having the surface roughly shaped or faced with thestonecutter's hammer; -- said of building stone.
To harden, as a metal, by hammering it in the cold state.
Without a visible hammer; -- said of a gun having a cock orstriker concealed from sight, and out of the way of an accidentaltouch.
Capable of being formed or shaped by a hammer. Sherwood.
The cloth which covers a coach box.
One who works with a hammer.

A shark of the genus Sphyrna or Zygæna, having the eyes set onprojections from the sides of the head, which gives it a hammershape. The Sphyrna zygæna is found in the North Atlantic. Called alsohammer fish, and balance fish.
A bird of the Heron family; the umber.
A stone with spangles of gold color in it.
Having the end hooked or curved.
A large basket, usually with a cover, used for the packing andcarrying of articles; as, a hamper of wine; a clothes hamper; anoyster hamper, which contains two bushels.
To fasten (an animal) by a rope binding the head to one of thefore legs; as, to hamshackle a horse or cow; hence, to bind orrestrain; to curb.
A small European rodent (Cricetus frumentarius). It isremarkable for having a pouch on each side of the jaw, under theskin, and for its migrations.
One of the great tendons situated in each side of the ham, orspace back of the knee, and connected with the muscles of the back ofthe thigh.
Hooked; hooklike; hamate; as, the hamular process of thesphenoid bone.
Furnished with a small hook; hook-shaped. Gray.
Bearing a small hook at the end. Gray.
To have; have. [Obs.] Piers Plowman.Him thanken all, and thus they han an end. Chaucer.
A rich goblet, esp. one used on state occasions. [Obs.]

A kind of basket, usually of wickerwork, and adapted for thepacking and carrying of articles; a hamper. Hanaper office, an officeof the English court of chancery in which writs relating to thebusiness of the public, and the returns to them, were anciently keptin a hanaper or hamper. Blackstone.
The small part of a gunstock near the lock, which is grasped bythe hand in taking aim.
A small hole in a boiler for the insertion of the hand incleaning, etc. Hand-hole plate, the cover of a hand-hole.
As tight as can be made by the hand. Totten.
Having wings that are like hands in the structure andarrangement of their bones; -- said of bats. See Cheiroptera.
A frame or barrow, without a wheel, carried by hand.
A book of reference, to be carried in the hand; a manual; aguidebook.
A space equal to the breadth of the hand; a palm. Ex. xxxvii.12.
A cart drawn or pushed by hand.
A fastening, consisting of an iron ring around the wrist,usually connected by a chain with one on the other wrist; a manacle;-- usually in the plural.
One who hands over or transmits; a conveyer in succession.Dryden.
Fast by contract; betrothed by joining hands. [Obs.] Bale.
In a handfast or publicly pledged manner. [Obs.] Holinshed.
To encumber with a handicap in any contest; hence, in general,to place at disadvantage; as, the candidate was heavily handicapped.
One who determines the conditions of a handicap.
A man skilled or employed in handcraft. Bacon.
In a handy manner; skillfully; conveniently.
The quality or state of being handy.
Work done by the hands; hence, any work done personally.The firmament showeth his handiwork. Ps. xix. 1.
A handkerchief. [Obs. or Colloq.] Chapman (1654). Shak.
To use the hands.They have hands, but they handle not. Ps. cxv. 7.
The mode of using the pencil or brush, etc.; style of touch.Fairholt.
Manufactured by hand; as, handmade shoes.
A saw used with one hand.
The quality of being handsome.Handsomeness is the mere animal excellence, beauty the mereimaginative. Hare.
A bar or lever, generally of wood, used in a windlass orcapstan, for heaving anchor, and, in modified forms, for variouspurposes.
A somersault made with the assistance of the hands placed uponthe ground.
Any wheel worked by hand; esp., one the rim of which serves asthe handle by which a valve, car brake, or other part is adjusted.
Easily managed; obedient to the helm; -- said of a vessel.
A child's play, one child guessing in which closed hand theother holds some small object, winning the object if right andforfeiting an equivalent if wrong; hence, forfeit. Piers Plowman.
A fight with the hands; boxing. "Pollux loves handyfights." B.Jonson.
Seizure by, or grasp of, the hand; also, close quarters infighting. Hudibras.
A dependent; a hanger-on; -- so called in contempt. B. Jonson.
The Baltimore oriole (Icterus galbula); -- so called becauseits nest is suspended from the limb of a tree. See Baltimore oriole.
A base, degraded person; a sneak; a gallows bird.
One who hangs on, or sticks to, a person, place, or service; adependent; one who adheres to others' society longer than he iswanted. Goldsmith.
One who hangs another; esp., one who makes a business ofhanging; a public executioner; -- sometimes used as a term ofreproach, without reference to office. Shak.
The office or character of a hangman.
A small piece or silver of skin which hangs loose, near theroot of finger nail. Holloway.
A ring or eye of rope, wood, or iron, attached to the edge of asail and running on a stay.
Professional cant; the chatter of conjurers to divert attentionfrom their tricks; hence, jugglery. [Colloq.]
Of or pertaining to Hanover or its people, or to the House ofHanover in England.
An official report of proceedings in the British Parliament; --so called from the name of the publishers.
That part of an elliptical or many-centered arch which has theshorter radius and immediately adjoins the impost.
Pertaining to the Hanse towns, or to their confederacy.Hanseatic league. See under 2d Hanse.
To clothe; to wrap.The surgeon happed her up carefully. Dr. J. Brown.
Extra hazard; chance; accident; random.We take our principles at haphazard, upon trust. Locke.

One of the lessons from the Nebiim (or Prophets) read in theJewish synagogue on Sabbaths, feast days, fasts, and the ninth of Ab,at the end of the service, after the parashoth, or lessons from theLaw. Such a practice is evidenced in Luke iv.17 and Acts xiii.15.
Without hap or luck; luckless; unfortunate; unlucky; unhappy;as, hapless youth; hapless maid. Dryden.
An order of freshwater fishes, including the true pikes,cyprinodonts, and blindfishes.
Having but one series of stamens, and that equal in number tothe proper number of petals; isostemonous.
By hap, chance, luck, or accident; perhaps; it may be.Lest haply ye be found even to fight against God. Acts v. 39.
Wrapped; covered; cloaked. [Scot.]All happed with flowers in the green wood were. Hogg.
A large and valuable food fish (Polyprion prognathus) of NewZealand. It sometimes weighs one hundred pounds or more.

Suicide, by slashing the abdomen, formerly practiced in Japan,and commanded by the government in the cases of disgraced officials;disembowelment; -- also written, but incorrectly, hari-kari. W. E.Griffis.

A speech addressed to a large public assembly; a popularoration; a loud address a multitude; in a bad sense, a noisy orpompous speech; declamation; ranting.Gray-headed men and grave, with warriors mixed, Assemble, andharangues are heard. Milton.
One who harangues, or is fond of haranguing; a declaimer.With them join'd all th' harangues of the throng, That thought to getpreferment by the tongue. Dryden.

To fatigue; to tire with repeated and exhausting efforts; esp.,to weary by importunity, teasing, or fretting; to cause to endureexcessive burdens or anxieties; -- sometimes followed by out.[Troops] harassed with a long and wearisome march. Bacon.Nature oppressed and harass'd out with care. Addison.Vext with lawyers and harass'd with debt. Tennyson.
The act of harassing, or state of being harassed; worry;annoyance; anxiety.Little harassments which I am led to suspect do occasionally molestthe most fortunate. Ld. Lytton.
Harborous. [Obs.]A bishop must be faultless, the husband of one wife, honestlyappareled, harberous. Tyndale (1 Tim. iii. 2)
To usher in; to be a harbinger of. "Thus did the star ofreligious freedom harbinger the day." Bancroft.
The mansion of a heavenly body. [Obs.]
An officer charged with the duty of executing the regulationsrespecting the use of a harbor.
Shelter; entertainment.[R.]Where can I get me harborage for the night Tennyson.
One who, or that which, harbors.Geneva was . . . a harborer of exiles for religion. Strype.
To harden; to make hard. [Obs.] Chaucer.
A name given to several different grasses, especially to theRoltböllia incurvata, and to the species of Ægilops, from one ofwhich it is contended that wheat has been derived.
Steel hardened by the addition of other elements, as manganese,phosphorus, or (usually) carbon.
Hard-featured; ill-looking; as, Vulcan was hard-favored.Dryden.
Having coarse, unattractive or stern features. Smollett.
Having hard hands, as a manual laborer.Hard-handed men that work in Athens here. Shak.
Having sound judgment; sagacious; shrewd.-- Hard"-head`ed*ness, n.
Unsympathetic; inexorable; cruel; pitiless.-- Hard"-heart`ed*ness, n.
Wrought with severe labor; elaborate; studied. Swift.
Not sensible to the bit; not easily governed; as, a hard-mouthed horse.
Unyielding; insensible to argument; uncompromising; strict.[Collog., U.S.]
A name given by soldiers and sailors to a kind of hard biscuitor sea bread.
Of a harsh or stern countenance; hard-featured. Burke.
A sweetmeat of boiled brown sugar or molasses made withalmonds, and flavored with orange or lemon juice, etc. Thackeray.
A tree of the genus Carpinus, of compact, horny texture;hornbeam.
Made hard, or compact; made unfeeling or callous; madeobstinate or obdurate; confirmed in error or vice.
One who, or that which, hardens; specif., one who temperstools.
A South African mullet, salted for food.
A term applied to a lachrymal gland on the inner side of theorbit of many animals which have a third eyelid, or nictitatingmembrane. See Nictitating membrane, under Nictitate.
A species of fern (Lomaria borealis), growing in Europe andNorthwestern America.
A very astringent shrub (Spiræa tomentosa), common in pastures.The Potentilla fruticosa in also called by this name.

Boldness, united with firmness and constancy of mind; bravery;intrepidity; also, audaciousness; impudence.A bound of graceful hardihood. Wordsworth.It is the society of numbers which gives hardihood to iniquity.Buckminster.
Hardihood; boldness; courage; energetic action. [Obs.]Changing hardiment with great Glendower. Shak.

The cohesion of the particles on the surface of a body,determined by its capacity to scratch another, or be itselfscratched;-measured among minerals on a scale of which diamond andtalc form the extremes.
The hard substratum. Same as Hard pan, under Hard, a.
The refuse or coarse part of fiax; tow.
That which is hard to hear, as toil, privation, injury,injustice, etc. Swift.
Ware made of metal, as cutlery, kitchen utensils, and the like;ironmongery.
One who makes, or deals in, hardware.
A blacksmith's fuller or chisel, having a square shank forinsertion into a square hole in an anvil, called the hardy hole.
To excite; to tease, or worry; to harry. [Obs.] Locke.

A small, slender, branching plant (Campanula rotundifolia),having blue bell-shaped flowers; also, Scilla nutans, which hassimilar flowers; -- called also bluebell. [Written also hairbell.]E'en the light harebell raised its head. Sir W. Scott .
A long, narrow foot, carried (that is, produced or extending)forward; -- said of dogs.
The long-tailed duck. See Old Squaw.
A lip, commonly the upper one, having a fissure ofperpendicular division like that of a hare.-- Hare"lipped`, a.
The East Indian name of the Cynodon Dactylon; dog's-grass.

To listen; to hearken. [Now rare, except in the imperative formused as an interjection, Hark! listen.] Hudibras. Hark away! Harkback! Hark forward! (Sporting), cries used to incite and guide houndsin hunting.-- To hark back, to go back for a fresh start, as when one haswandered from his direct course, or made a digression.He must have overshot the mark, and must hark back. Haggard. Heharked back to the subject. W. E. Norris.
A minor subdivision at the base of the Cambrian system inWales.

A buffoon, dressed in party-colored clothes, who plays tricks,often without speaking, to divert the bystanders or an audience; amerry-andrew; originally, a droll rogue of Italian comedy. PercySmith.As dumb harlequin is exhibited in our theaters. Johnson.Harlequin bat (Zoöl.), an Indian bat (Scotophilus ornatus), curiouslyvariegated with white spots.-- Harlequin beetle (Zoöl.), a very large South American beetle(Acrocinus longimanus) having very long legs and antennæ. The elytraare curiously marked with red, black, and gray.-- Harlequin cabbage bug. (Zoöl.) See Calicoback.-- Harlequin caterpillar. (Zoöl.), the larva of an American bombycidmoth (Euchætes egle) which is covered with black, white, yellow, andorange tufts of hair.-- Harlequin duck (Zoöl.), a North American duck (Histrionicushistrionicus). The male is dark ash, curiously streaked with white.-- Harlequin moth. (Zoöl.) See Magpie Moth.-- Harlequin opal. See Opal.-- Harlequin snake (Zoöl.), a small, poisonous snake (Elapsfulvius), ringed with red and black, found in the Southern UnitedStates.
A play or part of play in which the harlequin is conspicuous;the part of a harlequin. Macaulay.
Probably a corruption either of charlock or hardock. Drayton.
To hurt; to injure; to damage; to wrong.Though yet he never harmed me. Shak.No ground of enmity between us known Why he should mean me ill orseek to harm. Milton.
An alkaloid found in the plant Peganum harmala. It formsbitter, yellow salts.
A dry, hot wind, prevailing on the Atlantic coast of Africa, inDecember, January, and February, blowing from the interior or Sahara.It is usually accompanied by a haze which obscures the sun.
A kind of rue (Ruta sylvestris) growing in India. At Lahore theseeds are used medicinally and for fumigation.
Full of harm; injurious; hurtful; mischievous. " Most harmfulhazards." Strype. --Harm"ful*ly, adv.-- Harm"ful*ness, n.
An alkaloid accompanying harmaline (in the Peganum harmala),and obtained from it by oxidation. It is a white crystallinesubstance.

Relating to harmony, -- as melodic relates to melody;harmonious; esp., relating to the accessory sounds or overtones whichaccompany the predominant and apparent single tone of any string orsonorous body.
A musical note produced by a number of vibrations which is amultiple of the number producing some other; an overtone. SeeHarmonics.
A small, flat, wind instrument of music, in which the notes areproduced by the vibration of free metallic reeds.

Secondary and less distinct tones which accompany anyprincipal, and apparently simple, tone, as the octave, the twelfth,the fifteenth, and the seventeenth. The name is also applied to theartificial tones produced by a string or column of air, when theimpulse given to it suffices only to make a part of the string orcolumn vibrate; overtones.
An obsolete wind instrument with a keyboard, in which thesound, which resembled the oboe, was produced by the vibration ofthin metallic plates, acted upon by blowing through a tube.
One who understands the principles of harmony or is skillful inapplying them in composition; a musical composer.

A musical instrument, resembling a small organ and especiallydesigned for church music, in which the tones are produced by forcingair by means of a bellows so as to cause the vibration of freemetallic reeds. It is now made with one or two keyboards, and haspedals and stops.
To accompany with harmony; to provide with parts, as an air, ormelody.
An instrument for measuring the harmonic relations of sounds.It is often a monochord furnished with movable bridges.
See Harmonic suture, under Harmonic. Close harmony, Dispersedharmony, etc. See under Close, Dispersed, etc.-- Harmony of the spheres. See Music of the spheres, under Music.
A governor or prefect appointed by the Spartans in the citiessubjugated by them.
A hydrous silicate of alumina and baryta, occurring usually inwhite cruciform crystals; cross-stone.
A tub lashed to a vessel's deck and containing saltedprovisions for daily use; -- called also harness tub. W. C. Russell.
A constellation; Lyra, or the Lyre.
A genus of marine univalve shells; the harp shells; -- socalled from the form of the shells, and their ornamental ribs.
Pertaining to the harp; as, harping symphonies. Milton.
The fore parts of the wales, which encompass the bow of avessel, and are fastened to the stem. [Written also harpins.] Totten.
A player on the harp; a harper. W. Browne.

A spear or javelin used to strike and kill large fish, aswhales; a harping iron. It consists of a long shank, with a broad,fiat, triangular head, sharpened at both edges, and is thrown byhand, or discharged from a gun. Harpoon fork, a kind of hayfork,consisting of bar with hinged barbs at one end a loop for a rope atthe other end, used for lifting hay from the load by horse power.-- Harpoon gun, a gun used in the whale fishery for shooting theharpoon into a whale.
A female harper. [R.] Sir W. Scott.

A harp-shaped instrument of music set horizontally on legs,like the grand piano, with strings of wire, played by the fingers, bymeans of keys provided with quills, instead of hammers, for strikingthe strings. It is now superseded by the piano.

A fabulous winged monster, ravenous and filthy, having the faceof a woman and the body of a vulture, with long claws, and the facepale with hunger. Some writers mention two, others three.Both table and provisions vanished guite. With sound of harpies'wings and talons heard. Milton.
To harass; to plunder from. [Obs.] Fuller.
A worn-out strumpet; a vixenish woman; a hag.Such a weak, watery, wicked old harridan, substituted for the prettycreature I had been used to see. De Quincey.
One of a small breed of hounds, used for hunting hares.[Written also harier.]

An obstacle formed by turning an ordinary harrow upside down,the frame being buried. Bush harrow, a kind of light harrow made ofbushes, for harrowing grass lands and covering seeds, or to finishthe work of a toothed harrow.-- Drill harrow. See under 6th Drill.-- Under the harrow, subjected to actual torture with a toothedinstrument, or to great affliction or oppression.
To make a predatory incursion; to plunder or lay waste. [Obs.]Beau. & Fl.
Having violent contrasts of color, or of light and shade;lacking in harmony.
In a harsh manner; gratingly; roughly; rudely.'T will sound harshly in her ears. Shak.

The quality or state of being harsh.O, she is Ten times more gentle than her father 's crabbed, And he'scomposed of harshness. Shak.'Tis not enough no harshness gives offense, The sound must seem anecho to the sense. Pope.
A stag; the male of the red deer. See the Note under Buck.Goodliest of all the forest, hart and hind. Milton.
A large South African antelope (Alcelaphus caama), formerlymuch more abundant than it is now. The face and legs are marked withblack, the rump with white. [Written also hartebeest, and hartebest.]
To hearten; to encourage; to incite. [Obs.] Spenser.
The Hartford grape, a variety of grape first raised atHartford, Connecticut, from the Northern fox grape. Its large dark-colored berries ripen earlier than those of most other kinds.
A coarse umbelliferous plant of Europe (Tordylium maximum).
Wild; giddy; flighty; rash; thoughtless. [Colloq.]They had a quarrel with Sir Thomas Newcome's own son, a harum-scarumlad. Thackeray.
A diviner of ancient Rome. Same as Aruspice.
The art or practices of haruspices. See Aruspicy.
To reap or gather, as any crop.
, from Harvest, v. t. Harvesting ant (Zoöl.), any species ofant which gathers and stores up seeds for food. Many species areknown.
Without harvest; lacking in crops; barren. "Harvestlessautumns." Tennyson.
The act of harvesting; also, that which is harvested.Swinburne.

A process of hardening the face of steel, as armor plates,invented by Hayward A. Harvey of New Jersey, consisting in theadditional carburizing of the face of a piece of low carbon steel bysubjecting it to the action of carbon under long-continued pressureat a very high heat, and then to a violent chilling, as by a spray ofcold water. This process gives an armor plate a thick surface ofextreme hardness supported by material gradually decreasing inhardness to the unaltered soft steel at the back.
To draw; to drag; to carry off by vio [Obs.] Chaucer.
To as, to hash meat. Hudibras.
A basket made of rushes or flags, as for carrying fish. [Obs.]Spenser.
The edible viscera, as the heart, liver, etc., of a beast, esp.of a hog. [Written also harslet.]
To shut or fasten with a hasp.
, 2d pers. sing. pres. of. Fave, contr. of havest. [Archaic]
To hasten; to hurry. [Archaic]I 'll haste the writer. Shak.They were troubled and hasted away. Ps. xlviii. 5.
To press; to drive or urge forward; to push on; to precipitate;to accelerate the movement of; to expedite; to hurry.I would hasten my escape from the windy storm. Ps. lv. 8.
The quality or state of being hasty; haste; precipitation;rashness; quickness of temper.
Early fruit or vegetables; especially, early pease. Mortimer.
The lower group of the Wealden formation; -- so called from itsdevelopment around Hastings, in Sussex, England.
Proceeding from, or indicating, a quick temper.Take no unkindness of his hasty words. Shak
Capable of being, or deserving to be, hated; odious;detestable.
A band round the crown of a hat; sometimes, a band of blackcloth, crape, etc., worn as a badge of mourning.
To produce young; -- said of eggs; to come forth from the egg;-- said of the young of birds, fishes, insects, etc.
A vessel whose deck consists almost wholly of movable hatches;-- used mostly in the fisheries.
An instrument with long iron teeth set in a board, forcleansing flax or hemp from the tow, hards, or coarse part; a kind oflarge comb; -- called also hackle and heckle.
A house for hatching fish, etc.
1. A person hired to murder or physically attack another; a hitman.
A mode of execution in engraving, drawing, and miniaturepainting, in which shading is produced by lines crossing each otherat angles more or less acute; -- called also crosshatching.

A sort of panel, upon which the arms of a deceased person aretemporarily displayed, -- usually on the walls of his dwelling. It islozenge-shaped or square, but is hung cornerwise. It is used inEngland as a means of giving public notification of the death of thedeceased, his or her rank, whether married, widower, widow, etc.Called also achievement.His obscure funeral; No trophy, sword, or hatchment o'er his bones.Shak.
A square or oblong opening in a deck or floor, affordingpassage from one deck or story to another; the entrance to a cellar.
To love less, relatively. Luke xiv. 26.
One who hates.An enemy to God, and a hater of all good. Sir T. Browne.
Strong aversion; intense dislike; hate; an affection of themind awakened by something regarded as evil.
A stand of wood or iron, with hooks or pegs upon which to hanghats, etc.
pres. & imp. sing. & pl. of Hote, to be called. See Hote.[Obs.] Chaucer.A full perilous place, purgatory it hatte. Piers Plowman.
To tire or worry; -- out. [Obs.] Dryden.

A New Zealand lizard, which, in anatomical character, differswidely from all other existing lizards. It is the only livingrepresentative of the order Rhynchocephala, of which many Mesozoicfossil species are known; -- called also Sphenodon, and Tuatera.
A irrevocable Turkish decree countersigned by the sultan.
The business of making hats; also, stuff for hats.

A coat of mail; especially, the long coat of mail of theEuropean Middle Ages, as contrasted with the habergeon, which isshorter and sometimes sleeveless. By old writers it is often usedsynonymously with habergeon. See Habergeon. [Written variouslyhauberg, hauberque, hawberk, etc.] Chaucer.Helm, nor hawberk's twisted mail. Gray.
Native sulphide of manganese a reddish brown or brownish blackmineral.
A low-lying meadow by the side of a river. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.]On a haugh or level plain, near to a royal borough. Sir W. Scott.
High; elevated; hence, haughty; proud. [Obs.] Shak.
The quality of being haughty; disdain; arrogance.
To change the direction of a ship by hauling the wind. Seeunder Haul, v. t.I . . . hauled up for it, and found it to be an island. Cook.
A bargelike vessel with steel hull, large hatchways, and coaltransporters, for coaling war vessels from its own hold or from othercolliers.
Act of hauling; as, the haulage of cars by an engine; chargefor hauling.
The denuded stems or stalks of such crops as buckwheat and thecereal grains, beans, etc.; straw.
Lofty; haughty. [Obs.]Through support of countenance proud and hault. Spenser.
To persist in staying or visiting.I've charged thee not to haunt about my doors. Shak.
Inhabited by, or subject to the visits of, apparitions;frequented by a ghost.All houses wherein men have lived and died Are haunted houses.Longfellow.
One who, or that which, haunts.
In pale, with the head in chief; -- said of the figure of afish, as if rising for air.
A large sturgeon (Acipenser huso) from the region of the BlackSea. It is sometimes twelve feet long.
A kind of graduated breech sight for a small arm, or a cannon.
An artificial division of insects, including all those with asucking proboscis.
Provided with a haustellum, or sucking proboscis.-- n.
The sucking proboscis of various insects. See Lepidoptera, andDiptera.
One of the suckerlike rootlets of such plants as the dodder andivy. R. Brown.
A wind instrument, sounded through a reed, and similar in shapeto the clarinet, but with a thinner tone. Now more commonly calledoboe. See Illust. of Oboe.
Haughty manner or spirit; haughtiness; pride; arrogance.
High relish or flavor; high seasoning.
A raised part of the floor of a large room; a platform for araised table or throne. See Dais.
A blue isometric mineral, characteristic of some volcani
Of or pertaining to Havana, the capital of the island of Cuba;as, an Havana cigar; -- formerly sometimes written Havannah.-- n.
Of or pertaining to Havana, in Cuba.-- n. sing. & pl.
A light cloth covering for the head and neck, used by soldiersas a protection from sunstroke.
To shelter, as in a haven. Keats.
Sheltered in a haven.Blissful havened both from joy and pain. Keats.
Pertaining to, or discovered by, Clopton Havers, an Englishphysician of the seventeenth century. Haversian canals (Anat.), thesmall canals through which the blood vessels ramify in bone.
In the British Indian armies, a noncommissioned officer ofnative soldiers, corresponding to a sergeant. Havildar major, anative sergeant major in the East Indian army.
Possession; goods; estate.I 'll lend you something; my having is not much. Shak.
Wide and general destruction; devastation; waste.As for Saul, he made havoc of the church. Acts viii. 3.Ye gods, what havoc does ambition make Among your works! Addison.
The third eyelid, or nictitating membrane. See Nictitatingmembrane, under Nictitate.
Belonging to Hawaii or the Sandwich Islands, or to the peopleof Hawaii.-- n.
Probably, the baked berry of the hawthorn tree, that is, coarsefare. See 1st Haw, 2. [Obs.] Chaucer.
The common European grosbeak (Coccothraustes vulgaris); --called also cherry finch, and coble.
To laugh boisterously. [Colloq. U. S.]We haw-haw'd, I tell you, for more than half an hour. Major JackDowning.

One of numerous species and genera of rapacious birds of thefamily Falconidæ. They differ from the true falcons in lacking theprominent tooth and notch of the bill, and in having shorter and lesspointed wings. Many are of large size and grade into the eagles.Some, as the goshawk, were formerly trained like falcons. In a moregeneral sense the word is not infrequently applied, also, to truefalcons, as the sparrow hawk, pigeon hawk, duck hawk, and prairiehawk.

Any moth of the family Sphingidæ, of which there are numerousgenera and species. They are large, handsome moths, which fly mostlyat twilight and hover about flowers like a humming bird, sucking thehoney by means of a long, slender proboscis. The larvæ are large,hairless caterpillars ornamented with green and other bright colors,and often with a caudal spine. See Sphinx, also Tobacco worm, andTomato worm. Tobacco Hawk Moth (Macrosila Carolina), and its Larva,the Tobacco Worm.
Having a keen eye; sharpsighted; discerning.
A sea turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata), which yields the bestquality of tortoise shell; -- called also caret.
Curved like a hawk's bill; crooked.
One who sells wares by crying them in the street; hence, apeddler or a packman.
Iowa; -- a nickname of obscure origin.
A large rope made of three strands each containing many yarns.
Made in the manner of a hawser. Cf. Cable-laid, and see Illust.of Cordage.

A thorny shrub or tree (the Cratægus oxyacantha), having deeplylobed, shining leaves, small, roselike, fragrant flowers, and a fruitcalled haw. It is much used in Europe for hedges, and for standardsin gardens. The American hawthorn is Cratægus cordata, which has theleaves but little lobed.Gives not the hawthorn bush a sweeter shade To shepherds Shak.
To lay snares for rabbits. Huloet.
A machine in which hay is chopped short, as fodder for cattle.
An allowance of wood to a tenant for repairing his hedges orfences; hedgebote. See Bote. Blackstone.
A conical pile or hear of hay in the field.The tanned haycock in the mead. Milton.
A field where grass for hay has been cut; a meadow. Cowper.
A fork for pitching and tedding hay. Horse hayfork, acontrivance for unloading hay from the cart and depositing it in theloft, or on a mow, by horse power.
A loft or scaffold for hay.
The operation or work of cutting grass and curing it for hay.
A frame mounted on the running gear of a wagon, and used inhauling hay, straw, sheaves, etc.; -- called also hay rigging.
A rake for collecting hay; especially, a large rake drawn by ahorse or horses.
A heap or pile of hay, usually covered with thatch forpreservation in the open air.
A stack or conical pile of hay in the open air.
An officer who is appointed to guard hedges, and to keep cattlefrom breaking or cropping them, and whose further duty it is toimpound animals found running at large.
Holing a ball, whether the object ball (winning hazard) or theplayer's ball (losing hazard).
A hazardous attempt or situation; hazard. [Obs.]Herself had run into that hazardize. Spenser.
Exposed to hazard; dangerous; risky.To enterprise so hazardous and high! Milton.

Light vapor or smoke in the air which more or less impedesvision, with little or no dampness; a lack of transparency in theair; hence, figuratively, obscurity; dimness.O'er the sky The silvery haze of summer drawn. Tennyson.Above the world's uncertain haze. Keble.

A shrub or small tree of the genus Corylus, as the C. avellana,bearing a nut containing a kernel of a mild, farinaceous taste; thefilbert. The American species are C. Americana, which produces thecommon hazelnut, and C. rostrata. See Filbert. Gray.
Of the color of the hazelnut; of a light brown. Mortimer.
The nut of the hazel. Shak.
In a hazy manner; mistily; obscurely; confusedly.
The quality or state of being hazy.
Tiles laid at the eaves of a house. Knight.
A dish made of portions of the head, or head and feet, ofswine, cut up fine, seasoned, and pressed into a cheeselike mass.

A member of any tribe or race of savages who have the custom ofdecapitating human beings and preserving their heads as trophies. TheDyaks of Borneo are the most noted head-hunters.-- Head"-hunt`ing, n.
Lugged or dragged by the head. [R.] "The head-lugged bear."Shak.
Pain in the head; ceph "Headaches and shivering fits."Macaulay.
A board or boarding which marks or forms the head of anything;as, the headboard of a bed; the headboard of a grave.
In a heady or rash manner; hastily; rashly; obstinately.
A gallery, drift, or adit in a mine; also, the end of a driftor gallery; the vein above a drift.
A light, with a powerful reflector, placed at the head of alocomotive, or in front of it, to throw light on the track at night,or in going through a dark tunnel.
The line at the head or top of a page.
A head or leading man, especially of a village community.
Most advanced; most forward; as, the headmost ship in a fleet.
A note at the head of a page or chapter; in law reports, anabstract of a case, showing the principles involved and the opinionof the court.

The quarters or place of residence of any chief officer, as thegeneral in command of an army, or the head of a police force; theplace from which orders or instructions are issued; hence, the centerof authority or order.The brain, which is the headquarters, or office, of intelligence.Collier.
That part of a boltrope which is sewed to the upper edge orhead of a sail.
Any sail set forward of the foremast. Totten.
A significant shake of the head, commonly as a signal ofdenial. Shak.
An executioner who cuts off heads. Dryden.
Fountain; source.The headspring of our belief. Stapleton.
That part of a bridle or halter which encompasses the head.Shak.

A part (usually separate from the bed or frame) for supportingsome of the principal working parts of a machine; as:(a) The part of a lathe that holds the revolving spindle and itsattachments; -- also called poppet head, the opposite correspondingpart being called a tailstock.(b) The part of a planing machine that supports the cutter, etc.
The source and upper part of a stream; -- commonly used in theplural; as, the headwaters of the Missouri.
Clear space under an arch, girder, and the like, sufficient toallow of easy passing underneath.
To cover, as a roof, with tiles, slate, lead, or the like.[Obs.]
A common herb of the Mint family (Brunela vulgaris), destituteof active properties, but anciently thought a panacea.
One who, or that which, heals.
Tending or serving to heal; healing. [Obs.] Ecclus. xv. 3.
Tending to cure; soothing; mollifying; as, the healing art; ahealing salve; healing words.Here healing dews and balms abound. Keble.
So as to heal or cure.
The state of being healthy or healthful; freedom from disease.
In the direction of health; as, a healthward tendency.
The afterbirth or secundines of a beast.
One who heaps, piles, or amasses.

Report; rumor; fame; common talk; something heard from another.Much of the obloquy that has so long rested on the memory of ourgreat national poet originated in frivolous hearsays of his life andconversation. Prof. Wilson.Hearsay evidence (Law), that species of testimony which consists in aa narration by one person of matters told him by another. It is, witha few exceptions, inadmissible as testimony. Abbott.
A hind in the year of its age. [Eng.] Wright.
A cloth for covering a coffin when on a bier; a pall. Bp.Sanderson.
Suitable to a funeral.If you listen to David's harp, you shall hear as many hearselike airsas carols. Bacon.
A hollow, muscular organ, which, by contracting rhythmically,keeps up the circulation of the blood.Why does my blood thus muster to my heart! Shak.
A species of violet (Viola tricolor); -- called also pansy.
A part of the breastbone. [Obs.]He feeleth through the herte-spon the pricke. Chaucer.
Wounded to the heart with love or grief. Pope.
Sorrow; anguish of mind; mental pang. Shak.
Crushing sorrow or grief; a yielding to such grief. Shak.
Overcome by crushing sorrow; deeply grieved.
An uneasy, burning sensation in the stomach, often attendedwith an inclination to vomit. It is sometimes idiopathic, but isoften a symptom of often complaints.
One who, or that which, heartens, animates, or stirs up. W.Browne.

The floor of a furnace, on which the material to be heatedlies, or the lowest part of a melting furnace, into which the meltedmaterial settles. Hearth ends (Metal.), fragments of lead ore ejectedfrom the furnace by the blast.-- Hearth money, Hearth penny Etym: [AS. heoredhpening], a taxformerly laid in England on hearths, each hearth (in all housespaying the church and poor rates) being taxed at two shillings; --called also chimney money, etc.He had been importuned by the common people to relieve them from the. . . burden of the hearth money. Macaulay.
Stone forming the hearth; hence, the fireside; home.Chords of memory, stretching from every battlefield and patriot graveto every living heart and hearthstone. A. Lincoln.
The quality of being hearty; as, the heartiness of a greeting.
An exclamation used in addressing a familiar acquaintance.[Obs.] Shak.
Trembling of the heart; trepidation; fear.In many an hour of danger and heartquake. Hawthorne.
Causing intense grief; overpowering with anguish; verydistressing.
A climbing plant of the genus Cardiospermum, having round seedswhich are marked with a spot like a heart. Loudon.
Having the shape of a heart; cordate.
Sick at heart; extremely depressed in spirits; very despondent.
To affect at heart; to shock. [R.] "The seek to heartstrikeus." B. Jonson.
A nerve or tendon, supposed to brace and sustain the heart.Shak.Sobbing, as if a hearstring broke. Moore.
Rankling in, or swelling, the heart. "Heartswelling hate."Spenser.

The hard, central part of the trunk of a tree, consisting ofthe old and matured wood, and usually differing in color from theouter layers. It is technically known as duramen, and distinguishedfrom the softer sapwood or alburnum.
Comrade; boon companion; good fellow; -- a term of familiaraddress and fellowship among sailors. Dickens.
Heated; as, the iron though heat red-hot. [Obs. or Archaic.]Shak.
The state or quality of being heathenish. "The . . .heathenishness and profaneness of most playbooks." Prynne.
To render heathen or heathenish. Firmin.
State of being heathen or like the heathen.

Heath. [Scot.]Gorse and grass And heather, where his footsteps pass, The brighterseem. Longfellow.Heather bell (Bot.), one of the pretty subglobose flowers of twoEuropean kinds of heather (Erica Tetralix, and E. cinerea).
Heathy; abounding in heather; of the nature of heath.
Full of heath; abounding with heath; as, heathy land; heathyhills. Sir W. Scott.

That heats or imparts heat; promoting warmth or heat; excitingaction; stimulating; as, heating medicines or applications. Heatingsurface (Steam Boilers), the aggregate surface exposed to fire or tothe heated products of combustion, esp. of all the plates or sheetsthat are exposed to water on their opposite surfaces; -- called alsofire surface.
In a heating manner; so as to make or become hot or heated.
Destitute of heat; cold. Beau. & Fl.
A horizontal dislocation in a metallic lode, taking place at anintersection with another lode.
An offering or oblation heaved up or elevated before the altar,as the shoulder of the peace offering. See Wave offering. Ex. xxix.27.
To place in happiness or bliss, as if in heaven; to beatify.[R.]We are happy as the bird whose nest Is heavened in the hush of purplehills. G. Massey.
To render like heaven or fit for heaven. [R.] Bp. Hall.
The state or quality of being heavenly. Sir J. Davies.
Having the thoughts and affections placed on, or suitable for,heaven and heavenly objects; devout; godly; pious. Milner.-- Heav"en*ly*mind`ed*ness, n.
A bar used as a lever. Totten.
A disease of horses, characterized by difficult breathing, withheaving of the flank, wheezing, flatulency, and a peculiar cough;broken wind.
subject to much traffic or travel; as, the region's mostheavily traveled highways.Syn. -- heavily traveled.[WordNet 1.5]
The state or quality of being heavy in its various senses;weight; sadness; sluggishness; oppression; thickness.
A lifting or rising; a swell; a panting or deep sighing.Addison. Shak.
Native barium sulphate or barite, -- so called because of itshigh specific gravity as compared with other non-metallic minerals.
Wearing heavy or complete armor; carrying heavy arms.
Dull; stupid. "Gross heavy-headed fellows." Beau. & Fl.
A week; a period of seven days. [R.] Sir T. Browne.
In periods of seven days; weekly. Lowell.
A member of a chapter or convent, whose week it is to officiatein the choir, and perform other services, which, on extraordinaryoccasions, are performed by the superiors.
The goddess of youth, daughter of Jupiter and Juno. She wasbelieved to have the power of restoring youth and beauty to those whohad lost them.
To render obtuse; to dull; to blunt; to stupefy; as, tohebetate the intellectual faculties. Southey
Of or pertaining to the Hebrews, or to the language of theHebrews.
After the manner of the Hebrews or of the Hebrew language.
One versed in the Hebrew language and learning.
Pertaining to, or resembling, the Hebrew language or idiom.
In a Hebraistic sense or form.Which is Hebraistically used in the New Testament. Kitto.
To convert into the Hebrew idiom; to make Hebrew or Hebraistic.J. R. Smith.
Of or pertaining to the Hebrews; as, the Hebrew language orrites.

A sacrifice of a hundred oxen or cattle at the same time;hence, the sacrifice or slaughter of any large number of victims.Slaughtered hecatombs around them bleed. Addison.More than a human hecatomb. Byron.
A name given to the old Parthenon at Athens, because measuring100 Greek feet, probably in the width across the stylobate.

A white, semisolid, spermaceti-like hydrocarbon, C16H34, of theparaffin series, found dissolved as an important ingredient ofkerosene, and so called because each molecule has sixteen atoms ofcarbon; -- called also hexadecane.
An apparatus for separating the threads of warps into sets, asthey are wound upon the reel from the bobbins, in a warping machine.
The European blue titmouse (Parus coeruleus). [Written alsoheckimel, hackeymal, hackmall, hagmall, and hickmall.]
A measure of area, or superficies, containing a hundred ares,or 10,000 square meters, and equivalent to 2.471 acres.
Changed into a hectocotylus; having a hectocotylis.

One of the arms of the male of most kinds of cephalopods, whichis specially modified in various ways to effect the fertilization ofthe eggs. In a special sense, the greatly modified arm of Argonautaand allied genera, which, after receiving the spermatophores, becomesdetached from the male, and attaches itself to the female forreproductive purposes.
A measure of weight, containing a hundred grams, or about 3.527ounces avoirdupois.
A contrivance for multiple copying, by means of a surface ofgelatin softened with glycerin. [Written also hectograph.]
A bully; a blustering, turbulent, insolent, fellow; one whovexes or provokes.
The disposition or the practice of a hector; a bullying. [R.]
Resembling a hector; blustering; insolent; taunting. "Hectorly,ruffianlike swaggering or huffing." Barrow.
A measure of solidity, containing one hundred cubic meters, andequivalent to 3531.66 English or 3531.05 United States cubic feet.
One of the sets of parallel doubled threads which, withmounting, compose the harness employed to guide the warp threads tothe lathe or batten in a loom.
The eye or loop formed in each heddle to receive a warp thread.
The act of drawing the warp threads through the heddle-eyes ofa weaver's harness; the harness itself. Knight.
Of, pertaining to, or resembling, ivy.
Pertaining to, or derived from, the ivy (Hedera); as, hedericacid, an acid of the acetylene series.
Pertaining to, or of, ivy; full of ivy.

A thicket of bushes, usually thorn bushes; especially, such athicket planted as a fence between any two portions of land; and alsoany sort of shrubbery, as evergreens, planted in a line or as afence; particularly, such a thicket planted round a field to fenceit, or in rows to separate the parts of a garden.The roughest berry on the rudest hedge. Shak.Through the verdant maze Of sweetbrier hedges I pursue my walk.Thomson.
Born under a hedge; of low birth. Shak.

A small European insectivore (Erinaceus Europæus), and otherallied species of Asia and Africa, having the hair on the upper partof its body mixed with prickles or spines. It is able to roll itselfinto a ball so as to present the spines outwardly in every direction.It is nocturnal in its habits, feeding chiefly upon insects.
One who makes or mends hedges; also, one who hedges, as, inbetting.
A row of shrubs, or trees, planted for inclosure or separationof fields.By hedgerow elms and hillocks green. Milton.
A hedge bill. See under Hedge.
That branch of moral philosophy which treats of the relation ofduty to pleasure; the science of practical, positive enjoyment orpleasure. J. Grote.
To mind; to regard with care; to take notice of; to attend to;to observe.With pleasure Argus the musician heeds. Dryden.
Full of heed; regarding with care; cautious; circumspect;attentive; vigilant. Shak.-- Heed"ful*ly, adv.-- Heed"ful*ness, n.

Without heed or care; inattentive; careless; thoughtless;unobservant.O, negligent and heedless discipline! Shak.The heedless lover does not know Whose eyes they are that wound himso. Waller.-- Heed"less*ly, adv.-- Heed"less*ness, n.
Heedful. [Obs.] "Heedy shepherds." Spenser.-- Heed"i*ly, adv. [Obs.] -- Heed"i*ness, n. [Obs.] Spenser.
