Preceding as a precursor or harbinger; indicating something tofollow; as, precursory symptoms of a fever.
Of or pertaining to prey; plundering; predatory. [R.] Boyse.
To date anticipation; to affix to (a document) an earlier thanthe actual date; to antedate; as, a predated deed or letter.
The act of pillaging. E. Hall.
Living by preying upon other animals; carnivorous.
To die sooner than. "If children predecease progenitors." Shak.

One who precedes; one who has preceded another in any state,position, office, etc.; one whom another follows or comes after, inany office or position.A prince who was as watchful as his predecessor had been over theinterests of the state. Prescott.
To declare or announce beforehand; to preannounce. Milman.
A dedication made previously or beforehand.

The step, or raised secondary part, of an altar; a superaltar;hence, in Italian painting, a band or frieze of several picturesrunning along the front of a superaltar, or forming a border or frameat the foot of an altarpiece.
To design or purpose beforehand; to predetermine. Mitford.

A term used by Sir William Hamilton to define propositionshaving their quantity indicated by a verbal sign; as, all, none,etc.; -- contrasted with preindesignate, defining propositions ofwhich the quantity is not so indicated.
Of or pertaining to predestination; as, the predestinariancontroversy. Waterland.
The system or doctrine of the predestinarians.
Predestinated; foreordained; fated. "A predestinate scratchedface." Shak.
The purpose of Good from eternity respecting all events;especially, the preordination of men to everlasting happiness ormisery. See Calvinism.
To decree beforehand; to foreordain; to predestinate. Young.
Capable of being determined beforehand. Coleridge.
Determined beforehand; as, the predeterminate counsel of God.
The act of previous determination; a purpose formed beforehand;as, the predetermination of God's will. Hammond.
Preceding the diastole of the heart; as, a prediastolicfriction sound.
The quality or state of being predicable, or affirmable ofsomething, or attributed to something. Reid.
Capable of being predicated or affirmed of something;affirmable; attributable.
Of or pertaining to a predicament. John Hall (1646).
Predicating; affirming; declaring; proclaiming; hence;preaching. "The Roman predicant orders." N. Brit. Rev.
To affirm something of another thing; to make an affirmation.Sir M. Hale.
Expressing affirmation or predication; affirming; predicating,as, a predicative term.-- Pred"i*ca*tive*ly, adv.

A term applied to the pulse wave sometimes seen in a pulsecurve or sphygmogram, between the apex of the curve and the dicroticwave.The predicrotic or tidal wave is best marked in a hard pulse, i. e.,where the blood pressure is high. Landois & Stirling.
To tell or declare beforehand; to foretell; to prophesy; topresage; as, to predict misfortune; to predict the return of a comet.
The act of foretelling; also, that which is foretold; prophecy.The predictions of cold and long winters. Bacon.
To subject (food) to predigestion or artificial digestion.
Artificial digestion of food for use in illness or impaireddigestion.
To elect or choose beforehand. [R.] Walter Harte.
A previous liking; a prepossession of mind in favor ofsomething; predisposition to choose or like; partiality. Burke.
The state of being predisposed; predisposition. [R.]
The superior influence of a planet. Shak.

Having the ascendency over others; superior in strength,influence, or authority; prevailing; as, a predominant color;predominant excellence.Those help . . . were predominant in the king's mind. Bacon.Foul subordination is predominant. Shak.

To be superior in number, strength, influence, or authority; tohave controlling power or influence; to prevail; to rule; to have themastery; as, love predominated in her heart.[Certain] rays may predominate over the rest. Sir. I. Newton.
The act or state of predominating; ascendency; predominance. W.Browne.
Situated in front of the back; immediately in front, or on theventral side the dorsal part of the vertebral column.
Cleared and ready for engagement, as a ship. Smart.

The quality or state of being preëminent; superiority inprominence or in excellence; distinction above others in quality,rank, etc.; rarely, in a bad sense, superiority or notoriety in evil;as, preëminence in honor.The preëminence of Christianity to any other religious scheme.Addison.Painful preëminence! yourself to view Above life's weakness, and itscomforts too. Pope.Beneath the forehead's walled preëminence. Lowell.

Eminent above others; prominent among those who are eminent;superior in excellence; surpassing, or taking precedence of, others;rarely, surpassing others in evil, or in bad qualities; as,preëminent in guilt.In goodness and in power preëminent. Milton.
To employ beforehand. "Preëmployed by him." Shak.
To settle upon (public land) with a right of preemption, asunder the laws of the United States; to take by preëmption.

The act or right of purchasing before others. Specifically:(a) The privilege or prerogative formerly enjoyed by the king ofbuying provisions for his household in preference to others. [Eng.](b) The right of an actual settler upon public lands (particularlythose of the United States) to purchase a certain portion at a fixedprice in preference to all other applicants. Abbott.
One who holds a prior to purchase certain public land. Abbott.
Of or pertaining to preëmption; having power to preëmpt;preëmpting.
One who preëmpts; esp., one who preëmpts public land.
A forked tool used by clothiers in dressing cloth.
To engage by previous contract; to bind or attach previously;to preoccupy.But he was preëngaged by former ties. Dryden.
Prior engagement, obligation, or attachment, as by contract,promise, or affection.My preëngagements to other themes were not unknown to those for whomI was to write. Boyle.
To exist previously; to exist before something else.
Existing previously; preceding existence; as, a preëxistentstate. Pope.
The theory of a preëxistence of souls before their associationwith human bodies. Emerson.
Previous esteem or estimation. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

The prelude or introduction to the canon of the Mass. Addis &Arnold. Proper preface (Ch. of Eng. & Prot. Epis. Ch.), a portion ofthe communion service, preceding the prayer of consecration,appointed for certain seasons.
In a prefatory manner; by way of preface.
Pertaining to, or of the nature of, a preface; introductory toa book, essay, or discourse; as, prefatory remarks.That prefatory addition to the Creed. Dryden.
Of or pertaining to a prefect.
The office or jurisdiction of a prefect.
The office, position, or jurisdiction of a prefect; also, hisofficial residence.
A term collectively applied to the changes or conditionspreceding fecundation, especially to the changes which the ovumundergoes before fecundation.
The quality or state of being preferable; preferableness. J. S.Mill.
Worthy to be preferred or chosen before something else; moredesirable; as, a preferable scheme. Addison.
The quality or state of being preferable.
In preference; by choice.To choose Plautus preferably to Terence. Dennis.
Giving, indicating, or having a preference or precedence; as, apreferential claim; preferential shares.

A system of voting, as at primaries, in which the voters areallowed to indicate on their ballots their preference (usually theirfirst and second choices) between two or more candidates for anoffice, so that if no candidate receives a majority of first choicesthe one receiving the greatest number of first and second choicestogether in nominated or elected.
The quality or state of being prefident. [Obs.] Baxter.
The act of prefiguring, or the state of being prefigured.A variety of prophecies and prefigurations. Norris.
Showing by prefiguration. "The prefigurative atonement." Bp.Horne.
To show, suggest, or announce, by antecedent types andsimilitudes; to foreshadow. "Whom all the various types prefigured."South.
The act of prefiguring; prefiguration; also, that which isprefigured. Carlyle.
Prearranged. [Obs.] " Set and prefinite time." Holland.
That which is prefixed; esp., one or more letters or syllablescombined or united with the beginning of a word to modify itssignification; as, pre- in prefix, con- in conjure.
To form beforehand, or for special ends. "Their natures andpreformed faculties. " Shak.
An old theory of the preëxistence of germs. Cf. Emboîtement.
A formative letter at the beginning of a word. M. Stuart.
Situated in front of the frontal bone, or the frontal region ofthe skull; ectethmoid, as a certain bone in the nasal capsule of manyanimals, and certain scales of reptiles and fishes.-- n.
Prior to the glacial or drift period.
Capable of being entered, taken, or captured; expugnable; as, apregnable fort. [R.] Cotgrave.
In a pregnant manner; fruitfully; significantly.
To bear down; to depress. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.
To descend by gravity; to sink. [R.] Boyle.
Tasting beforehand; having a foretaste. [R.] Ed. Rev.
The act of tasting beforehand; foretaste. [R.] Dr. Walker(1678).
An extra first toe, or rudiment of a toe, on the preaxial sideof the hallux.
To lay hold of; to seize. [Obs.] Middleton.
Adapted to seize or grasp; seizing; grasping; as, theprehensile tail of a monkey.
The act of taking hold, seizing, or grasping, as with the handor other member.
Adapted to seize or grasp; prehensile.
Of or pertaining to a period before written history begins; as,the prehistoric ages; prehistoric man.
A pale green mineral occurring in crystalline aggregates havinga botryoidal or mammillary structure, and rarely in distinctcrystals. It is a hydrous silicate of alumina and lime.

Pertaining to, or designating, a tetrabasic acid of benzeneobtained as a white crystalline substance; -- probably so called fromthe resemblance of the wartlike crystals to the mammillæ on thesurface of prehnite.
Ignition in an internal-combustion engine while the inlet valveis open or before compression is completed.
Having no sign expressive of quantity; indefinite. SeePredesignate.
To instruct previously or beforehand. Dr. H. More.
Previous intimation; a suggestion beforehand. T. Scott.

To judge before hearing, or before full and sufficientexamination; to decide or sentence by anticipation; to condemnbeforehand.The committee of council hath prejudged the whole case, by callingthe united sense of both houses of Parliament" a universal clamor."Swift.
The act of prejudging; decision before sufficient examination.
Of or pertaining to the determination of some matter notpreviously decided; as, a prejudical inquiry or action at law.
Influenced by prejudice; biased. [R.] " With not too hasty andprejudicant ears." Milton.
To determine beforehand, especially to disadvantage; toprejudge.Our dearest friend Prejudicates the business. Shak.
Forming a judgment without due examination; prejudging. Dr. H.More.
A bias on the part of judge, juror, or witness which interfereswith fairness of judgment.
Of or pertaining to printing; typographical. [Obs.] Fuller.
A clergyman of a superior order, as an archbishop or a bishop,having authority over the lower clergy; a dignitary of the church.
The office of a prelate. Harmar.
A woman who is a prelate; the wife of a prelate. Milton.
In a prelatical manner; with reference to prelates. Milton.The last Georgic was a good prelude to the Æneis.
The setting of one above another; preference. [R.] Jer. Taylor.
One who supports of advocates prelacy, or the government of thechurch by prelates; hence, a high-churchman. Hume.I am an Episcopalian, but not a prelatist. T. Scott.
To bring under the influence of prelacy. Palfrey.
To read publicly, as a lecture or discourse.
A lecture or discourse read in public or to a select company."The prelections of Faber." Sir M. Hale.
A reader of lectures or discourses; a lecturer. Sheldon.

Introductory; previous; preceding the main discourse orbusiness; prefatory; as, preliminary observations to a discourse orbook; preliminary articles to a treaty; preliminary measures;preliminary examinations.

An introductory performance, preceding and preparing for theprincipal matter; a preliminary part, movement, strain, etc.;especially (Mus.), a strain introducing the theme or chief subject; amovement introductory to a fugue, yet independent; -- with recentcomposers often synonymous with overture.The last Georgic was a good prelude to the Ænis Addison.The cause is more than the prelude, the effect is more than thesequel, of the fact. Whewell.
One who, or that which, preludes; one who plays a prelude.Mason.
Of or pertaining to a prelude; of the nature of a prelude;introductory. [R.]
Situated immediately in front of the loins;- applied to thedorsal part of the abdomen.
Of the nature of a prelude; introductory; indicating thatsomething of a like kind is to follow. "Prelusive drops." Thomson. --Pre*lu"sive*ly, adv.
The quality or state of being premature; early, or untimely,ripeness; as, the prematurity of genius.

A bone on either side of the middle line between the nose andmouth, forming the anterior part of each half of the upper jawbone;the intermaxilla. In man the premaxillæ become united and form theincisor part of the maxillary bone.
Situated in front of the maxillary bones; pertaining to thepremaxillæ; intermaxillary.-- n.
To think on, and revolve in the mind, beforehand; to contriveand design previously; as, to premeditate robbery.With words premeditated thus he said. Dryden.
The act of meditating or contriving beforehand; previousdeliberation; forethought.
To merit or deserve beforehand. [Obs.] Eikon Basi
The first minister of state; the prime minister.
First; chief; as, a première danseuse. -- n. fem.; pl. -mières(F. pre*myâr").(a) The leading woman of a group, esp. in a theatrical cast.(b) A first performance, as of a play; a first night.
Either of the first two propositions of a syllogism, from whichthe conclusion is drawn.
Situated in front of the molar teeth. --n.
To forewarn; to admonish beforehand. [R.] Herrick.To teach, and to premonish. Bk. of Com. Prayer.
Previous warning or admonition; forewarning. Sir H. Wotton.
Previous warning, notice, or information; forewarning; as, apremonition of danger.
One who, or that which, gives premonition.
Giving previous warning or notice; as, premonitory symptoms ofdisease.-- Pre*mon"i*to*ri*ly, adv.
To show beforehand; to foreshow. [R.] Herbert.
One of a religious order of regular canons founded by St.Norbert at Prémontré, in France, in 1119. The members of the orderare called also White Canons, Norbertines, and Premonstrants.
One who, or that which, premonstrates. [R.]
Terminated abruptly, or as it bitten off. Premorse root orleaves (Bot.), such as have an abrupt, ragged, and irregulartermination, as if bitten off short.
Relating to the time before Moses; as, premosaic history.
Previous motion or excitement to action.
To fortify beforehand; to guard against objection. [Obs.]Fotherby.
The act of fortifying or guarding against objections. [Obs.]
Of or pertaining to a premunire; as, a premunitory process.
Situated in front of the nose, or in front of the nasalchambers.
The power or right of taking a thing before it is offered.Burrill.
Serving as a prefix in a compound name. Sir T. Browne.
The act of prenominating; privilege of being named first. SirT. Browne.
To note or designate beforehand. Foxe.
A notice or notion which precedes something else in time;previous notion or thought; foreknowledge. Bacon.
The act of seizing with violence. [Obs.] Barrow .
An apprentice. [Obs. or Colloq.] Piers Plowman. "My accuser ismy prentice." Shak.
Apprenticehood. [Obs.]This jolly prentice with his master bode Till he was out nigh of hisprenticehood. Chaucer.
Apprenticeship. [Obs. or Colloq.]He served a prenticeship who sets up shop. Pope.
The act of announcing or proclaiming beforehand. [Obs.]
The anterior part of the medulla oblongata. B. G. Wilder.
The act or right of taking possession before another; as, thepreoccupancy of wild land.
Placed just in front of the eyes, as the antennæ of certaininsects.-- n.
To ominate beforehand; to portend. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.
Situated in front of the operculum; pertaining to thepreoperculum.-- n.
The anterior opercular bone in fishes.
Opinion previously formed; prepossession; prejudice. Sir T.Browne.
Situated in front of, or anterior to, the mouth; as, preoralbands.
a. (Anat.) Situated in front or the orbit.
To ordain or appoint beforehand: to predetermine: toforeordain. Milton.
To order to arrange beforehand; to foreordain. Sir W. Hamilton.
The act of foreordaining: previous determination. "Thepreordination of God." Bale.
Capable of being prepared. "Medicine preparable by art." Boyle.

The holding over of a note from one chord into the next chord,where it forms a temporary discord, until resolved in the chord thatfollows; the anticipation of a discordant note in the precedingconcord, so that the ear is prepared for the shock. See Suspension.
Tending to prepare or make ready; having the power ofpreparing, qualifying, or fitting; preparatory.Laborious quest of knowledge preparative to this work. South.
One who prepares beforehand, as subjects for dissection,specimens for preservation in collections, etc. Agassiz.
Preparing the way for anything by previous measures ofadaptation; antecedent and adapted to what follows; introductory;preparative; as, a preparatory school; a preparatory condition.
Made fit or suitable; adapted; ready; as, prepared food;prepared questions.-- Pre*par"ed*ly, adv. Shak.-- Pre*par"ed*ness, n.
One who, or that which, prepares, fits, or makes ready. Wood.
To pay in advance, or beforehand; as, to prepay postage.
Situated in front of, or anterior to, the penis.
To weigh or consider beforehand; to premeditate. [Obs.]Spenser. Sir T. Elyot.
Having superior influence or power; prevailing; predominant.[R.] Boyle.
Preponderating; outweighing; overbalancing; -- used literallyand figuratively; as, a preponderant weight; of preponderantimportance.-- Pre*pon"der*ant*ly, adv.

To exceed in weight; hence, to incline or descend, as the scaleof a balance; figuratively, to exceed in influence, power, etc.;hence; to incline to one side; as, the affirmative sidepreponderated.That is no just balance in which the heaviest side will notpreponderate. Bp. Wilkins.
The act or state of preponderating; preponderance; as, apreponderation of reasons. I. Watts.
To place or set before; to prefix. [Obs.] Fuller.

A word employed to connect a noun or a pronoun, in anadjectival or adverbial sense, with some other word; a particle usedwith a noun or pronoun (in English always in the objective case) tomake a phrase limiting some other word; -- so called because usuallyplaced before the word with which it is phrased; as, a bridge ofiron; he comes from town; it is good for food; he escaped by running.
Of or pertaining to a preposition; of the nature of apreposition. Early.-- Prep`o*si"tion*al*ly, adv.
Put before; prefixed; as, a prepositive particle.-- n.
A scholar appointed to inspect other scholars; a monitor. Todd.
The office or dignity of a provost; a provostship. Lowth.
Tending to invite favor; attracting confidence, favor, esteem,or love; attractive; as, a prepossessing manner.-- Pre`pos*sess"ing*ly, adv.
One who possesses, or occupies, previously. R. Brady.
The capacity, on the part of one of the parents, as comparedwith the other, to transmit more than his or her own share ofcharacteristics to their offspring.
To provide beforehand. "The materials preprovided." Fuller.
Situated in front of, or anterior to, the pubis; pertaining tothe prepubis.
A bone or cartilage, of some animals, situated in the middleline in front of the pubic bones.
Of or pertaining to the prepuce.
Of or pertaining to the style called preraphaelitism; as, apreraphaelite figure; a preraphaelite landscape. Ruskin.
One who reigns before another; a sovereign predecessor. [R.]Warner.
More remote in previous time or prior order.In some cases two more links of causation may be introduced; one ofthem may be termed the preremote cause, the other the postremoteeffect. E. Darwin.
To require beforehand.Some things are prerequired of us. Bp. Hall.
Previously required; necessary as a preliminary to any proposedeffect or end; as, prerequisite conditions of success.
To resolve beforehand; to predetermine. Sir E. Dering.
Endowed with a prerogative, or exclusive privilege. [R.] Shak.
To form or utter a prediction; -- sometimes used with of.Dryden.
Full of presages; ominous.Dark in the glass of some presageful mood. Tennyson.
One who, or that which, presages; a foreteller; a foreboder.Shak.
One who has presbyopia; a farsighted person.
A defect of vision consequent upon advancing age. It is due torigidity of the crystalline lens, which producepresbytia.
Affected by presbyopia; also, remedying presbyopia; farsighted.
One ordained to the second order in the ministry; -- calledalso priest.I rather term the one sort presbyter than priest. Hooker.New presbyter is but old priest writ large. Milton.
Of or pertaining to a presbyter or presbytery; presbyterial.

Of or pertaining to a presbyter, or to ecclesiasticalgovernment by presbyters; relating to those who uphold churchgovernment by presbyters; also, to the doctrine, discipline, andworship of a communion so governed.
That form of church government which invests presbyters withall spiritual power, and admits no prelates over them; also, thefaith and polity of the Presbyterian churches, taken collectively.
The office or station of a presbyter; presbyterate.

A judicatory consisting of all the ministers within a certaindistrict, and one layman, who is a ruling elder, from each parish orchurch, commissioned to represent the church in conjunction with thepastor. This body has a general jurisdiction over the churches underits care, and next below the provincial synod in authority.
The part of the scapula in front of, or above, the spine, ormesoscapula.
(Anat.) Of or pertaining to the prescapula; supraspinous.
Knowledge of events before they take place; foresight.God's certain prescience of the volitions of moral agents. J.Edwards.
Having knowledge of coming events; foreseeing; consciousbeforehand. Pope.Henry . . . had shown himself sensible, and almost prescient, of thisevent. Bacon.
To consider by a separate act of attention or analysis. Sir W.Hamilton.
Foreknowing; having foreknowledge; as, prescious of ills. [R.]Dryden.
To direct, as a remedy to be used by a patient; as, the doctorprescribed quinine.
Directed; prescribed. " A prescript from of words." Jer.Taylor.
, The quality or state of being prescriptible. Story.
Depending on, or derived from, prescription; proper to beprescribed. Grafton.
A direction of a remedy or of remedies for a disease, and themanner of using them; a medical recipe; also, a prescribed remedy.

Consisting in, or acquired by, immemorial or long-continued useand enjoyment; as, a prescriptive right of title; pleading thecontinuance and authority of long custom.The right to be drowsy in protracted toil has become prescriptive. J.M. Mason.
The first of the four pieces composing the dorsal part, ortergum, of a thoracic segment of an insect. It is usually small andinconspicuous.
Priority of place in sitting.[Obs.] Carew.
Previous sensation, notion, or idea. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

Present letters or instrument, as a deed of conveyance, alease, letter of attorney, or other writing; as in the phrase, " Knowall men by these presents," that is, by the writing itself, " per hasliteras praesentes; " -- in this sense, rarely used in the singular.
Ready; quick; immediate in effect; as, presentaneous poison.[Obs.] Harvey.
exhibition; representation; display; appearance; semblance;show.Under the presentation of the shoots his wit. Shak.
Having the right of presentation, or offering a clergyman tothe bishop for institution; as, advowsons are presentative,collative, or donative. Blackstone.
One to whom something is presented; also, one who is presented;specifically (Eccl.), one presented to benefice. Ayliffe.
Implying actual presence; present, immediate. [Obs.]God's mercy is made presential to us. Jer. Taylor.-- Pre*sen"tial*ly, adv. [Obs.]
State of being actually present. [Obs.] South.
Making present. [Obs.] -- Pres`en*tif"ic*ly, adv. [Obs.] Dr. H.More.

Previous sentiment, conception, or opinion; previousapprehension; especially, an antecedent impression or conviction ofsomething unpleasant, distressing, or calamitous, about to happen;anticipation of evil; foreboding.
Of nature of a presentiment; foreboding. [R.] Coleridge.

Bringing a conception or notion directly before the mind;presenting an object to the memory of imagination; -- distinguishedfrom symbolic.How greatly the word "will" is felt to have lost presentive power inthe last three centuries. Earle.-- Pre*sent"ive*ly, adv.-- Pre*sent"ive*ness, n.
The quality or state of being present; presence. [Obs.]"Presentness of mind in danger." Clarendon.
An ornamental tray, dish, or the like, used as a salver.
Capable of being preserved; admitting of preservation.

The act or process of preserving, or keeping safe; the state ofbeing preserved, or kept from injury, destruction, or decay;security; safety; as, preservation of life, fruit, game, etc.; apicture in good preservation.Give us particulars of thy preservation. Shak.
Having the power or quality of preserving; tending to preserve,or to keep from injury, decay, etc.
The office and dignity of president; presidency. Hooker.
a. & n. from Preside. Presiding elder. See under 2d Elder.
A place of defense; a fortress; a garrison; a fortress; agarrison or guardhouse.
The act of signifying or showing beforehand.
To intimate or signify beforehand; to presage.

Situated in front of the sphenoid bone; of or pertaining to theanterior part of the sphenoid bone (i. e., the presphenoid bone).Presphenoid bone (Anat.), the anterior part of the body of thesphenoid bone in front of the basisphenoid. It is usually a separatebone in the young or fetus, but becomes a part of the sphenoid in theadult.
Of or pertaining to the presphenoid bone; presphenoid.
An East Indian insectivore (Tupaia ferruginea). It is arborealin its habits, and has a bushy tail. The fur is soft, and varies fromrusty red to maroon and to brownish black.

A cake of compressed substance, as: in gunpowder manufacture,the cake resulting from compressing the meal powder; in the treatmentof coal tar, the pressed product at various stages of the process;or, in beet-sugar manufacture, the vegetable residue after the sugarjuice has been expressed.
A kind of highly sized rag paper or board, sometimes containinga small admixture of wood pulp; -- so called because used originally,as now, in presses for pressing and finishing knit underwear.

One who, or that which, presses. Presser bar, or Presser wheel(Knitting machine), a bar or wheel which closes the barbs of theneedles to enable the loops of the yarn to pass over them.-- Presser foot, the part of a sewing machine which rests on thecloth and presses it down upon the table of the machine.
Urgent; exacting; importunate; as, a pressing necessity.-- Press"ing*ly, adv.
One of a tribe of wading birds (Pressirostres) including thosewhich have a compressed beak, as the plovers.
Of or pertaining to the pressirosters.
Pressing; urgent; also, oppressive; as, pressive taxation. [R.]Bp. Hall.
One of a press gang, who aids in forcing men into the navalservice; also, one forced into the service.

Causing, or giving rise to, pressure or to an increase ofpressure; as, pressor nerve fibers, stimulation of which excites thevasomotor center, thus causing a stronger contraction of the arteriesand consequently an increase of the arterial blood pressure; --opposed to depressor. Landois & Stirling.
To pack, or prepare for packing, by means of a press.

The action of a force against some obstacle or opposing force;a force in the nature of a thrust, distributed over a surface, oftenestimated with reference to the upon a unit's area. Atmosphericpressure, Center of pressure, etc. See under Atmospheric, Center,etc.-- Back pressure (Steam engine), pressure which resists the motionof the piston, as the pressure of exhaust steam which does not findfree outlet.-- Fluid pressure, pressure like that exerted by a fluid. It is athrust which is normal and equally intense in all directions around apoint. Rankine.-- Pressure gauge, a gauge for indicating fluid pressure; amanometer.
Wires leading from various points of an electric system to acentral station, where a voltmeter indicates the potential of thesystem at those points.
The art of printing from the surface of type, plates, orengravings in relief, by means of a press; the work so done.MacKellar.
A payment of money; a toll or duty; also, the rendering of aservice. Burrill.
One of the veins of the neck when swollen with anger or otherexcitement. [Obs.]
The anterior segment of the sternum; the manubrium.-- Pre*ster"nal, a.
Nimble-fingered; having fingers fit for prestidigitation, orjuggling. [R.] "His prestidigital hand." Charles Reade.
One skilled in legerdemain or sleight of hand; a juggler.
A juggler; prestidigitator. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.
A fund for the support of a priest, without the title of abenefice. The patron in the collator.
Quickly; rapidly; -- a direction for a quick, lively movementor performance; quicker than allegro, or any rate of time exceptprestissimo.
Obstruction, dimness, or defect of sight. [Obs.] Milton.
Such as may be presumed or supposed to be true; that seemsentitled to belief without direct evidence.
In a presumable manner; by, or according to, presumption.
One who presumes; also, an arrogant person. Sir H. Wotton.
By presumption, or supposition grounded or probability;presumably.
The quality or state of being presumptuous.

To suppose beforehand; to imply as antecedent; to take forgranted; to assume; as, creation presupposes a creator.Each [kind of knowledge] presupposes many necessary things learned inother sciences, and known beforehand. Hooker.
Preceding the systole or contraction of the heart; as, thepresystolic friction sound.
Situated in front of the temporal bone.
Making a false appearance; unreal; false; as, pretended friend.-- Pre*tend"ed*ly, adv.
The act of pretending; pretense. [Obs.] Daniel.

The pretender (Eng. Hist.), the son or the grandson of JamesII., the heir of the royal family of Stuart, who laid claim to thethrone of Great Britain, from which the house was excluded by law.It is the shallow, unimproved intellects that are the confidentpretenders to certainty. Glanvill.
The character, right, or claim of a pretender. Swift.
As by right or title; arrogantly; presumptuously. Collier.
Fitted for trial beforehand; experimental. [R.] Sir H. Wotton.
Full of pretension; disposed to lay claim to more than isone's; presuming; assuming.-- Pre*ten"tious*ly, adv.-- Pre*ten"tious*ness, n.
A prefix signifying past, by, beyond, more than; as, preter-mission, a permitting to go by; preternatural, beyond or more than isnatural. [Written also præter.]
Passed through; antecedent; previous; as, preterient states.[R.]
Old name of the tense also called imperfect.
One who believes the prophecies of the Apocalypse to have beenalready fulfilled. Farrar.
Past; -- applied to a tense which expresses an action or stateas past.
A figure by which, in pretending to pass over anything, asummary mention of it is made; as, "I will not say, he is valiant, heis learned, he is just." Called also paraleipsis.
Used only or chiefly in the preterit or past tenses, as certainverbs.
The quality or state of being past. Bentley. Lowell.
To pass by; to omit; to disregard. Bacon.

Beyond of different from what is natural, or according to theregular course of things, but not clearly supernatural or miraculous;strange; inexplicable; extraordinary; uncommon; irregular; abnormal;as, a preternatural appearance; a preternatural stillness; apreternatural presentation (in childbirth) or labor.This vile and preternatural temper of mind. South.
The state of being preternatural; a preternatural condition.
In a preternatural manner or degree. Bacon.
The quality or state of being preternatural.
Old name of the tense also called preterit.
Old name of the tense also called pluperfect.
The act of carrying past or beyond. [R.] Abp. Potter.
To frame; to devise; to disguise or excuse; hence, to pretend;to declare falsely. [Obs.]

Ostensible reason or motive assigned or assumed as a color orcover for the real reason or motive; pretense; disguise.They suck the blood of those they depend on, under a pretext ofservice and kindness. L'Estrange.With how much or how little pretext of reason. Dr. H. More.
Situated in front of the tibia.
A civil officer or magistrate among the ancient Romans.

Of or pertaining to a pretor or magistrate; judicial; exercisedby, or belonging to, a pretor; as, pretorian power or authority.Pretorian bands or guards, or Pretorians (Rom. Hist.), the emperor'sbodyguards, instituted by the Emperor Augustus in nine cohorts of1,000 men each.-- Pretorian gate (Rom. Antiq.), that one of the four gates in acamp which lay next the enemy. Brande & C.
The office or dignity of a pretor. J. Warton
The quality or state of being pretty; -- used sometimes in adisparaging sense.A style . . . without sententious pretension or antitheticalprettiness. Jeffrey.

In some degree; moderately; considerably; rather; almost; --less emphatic than very; as, I am pretty sure of the fact; prettycold weather.Pretty plainly professes himself a sincere Christian. Atterbury.
Affectation of a pretty style, manner, etc. [R.] Ed. Rev.
To prefigure; to exhibit previously in a type. Bp. Pearson.
A kind of German biscuit or cake in the form of a twisted ring,salted on the outside.

The quality or condition of being prevalent; superior strength,force, or influence; general existence, reception, or practice; wideextension; as, the prevalence of virtue, of a fashion, or of adisease; the prevalence of a rumor.The duke better knew what kind of argument were of prevalence withhim. Clarendon.
To collude, as where an informer colludes with the defendant,and makes a sham prosecution.
A sham dealer; one who colludes with a defendant in a shamprosecution.
A going before; anticipation in sequence or order. "The law ofprevenance is simply the well-known law of phenomenal sequence."Ward.
The act of anticipating another's wishes, desires, etc., in theway of favor or courtesy; hence, civility; obligingness. [Obs.]Sterne.
To come before; to anticipate; hence, to hinder; to prevent.[Obs.] Philips.
The act of going before; anticipation. [R.]
Going before; preceding; hence, preventive. "Prevenient gracedescending." Milton.
To come before the usual time. [Obs.]Strawberries . . . will prevent and come early. Bacon.
The quality or state of being preventable.
Capable of being prevented or hindered; as, preventablediseases.
That which prevents; -- incorrectly used instead of preventive.
An auxiliary rope to strengthen a mast. Preventer bolts, orPreventer plates (Naut.), fixtures connected with preventers toreënforce other rigging.-- Preventer stay. (Naut.) Same as Preventer, 3.
So as to prevent or hinder.
That which prevents, hinders, or obstructs; that whichintercepts access; in medicine, something to prevent disease; aprophylactic.
Situated immediately in front, or on the ventral side, of thevertebral column; prespinal.

Going before in time; being or happening before something else;antecedent; prior; as, previous arrangements; a previous illness.The dull sound . . . previous to the storm, Rolls o'er the mutteringearth. Thomson.Previous question. (Parliamentary Practice) See under Question, andcompare Closure.-- Previous to, before; -- often used adverbially for previously."Previous to publication." M. Arnold. "A policy . . . his friends hadadvised previous to 1710." J. H. Newman.
Beforehand; antecedently; as, a plan previously formed.
The quality or state of being previous; priority or antecedencein time.

Anything, as goods, etc., taken or got by violence; anythingtaken by force from an enemy in war; spoil; booty; plunder.And they brought the captives, and the prey, and the spoil, untoMoses, and Eleazar the priest. Num. xxxi. 12.
One who, or that which, preys; a plunderer; a waster; adevourer. Hooker.
A corruption of pair royal. See under Pair, n.
A fine, white, somewhat friable clay; also, the ore containedin a mixture of clay and pebbles. [Written also pryan.]

A species of hexameter verse so constructed as to be divisibleinto two portions of three feet each, having generally a trochee inthe first and the fourth foot, and an amphimacer in the third; --applied also to a regular hexameter verse when so constructed as tobe divisible into two portions of three feet each. Andrews.
More or less permanent erection and rigidity of the penis, withor without sexual desire.
A suborder of Gephyræa, having a cylindrical body with aterminal anal opening, and usually with one or two caudal gills.
Rated in price; valued; as, high-priced goods; low-pricedlabor.
A hydrous borate of lime, from Oregon.
A small roll; as, a prick of spun yarn; a prick of tobacco.
Having erect, pointed ears; -- said of certain dogs.Thou prick-eared cur of Iceland. Shak.
A small marline spike having generally a wooden handle, -- usedin sailmaking. R. H. Dana, Ir.
A buck in his second year. See Note under 3d Buck. Shak.
The first coating of plaster in work of three coats upon laths.Its surface is scratched once to form a better key for the next coat.In the United States called scratch coat. Brande & C.
To prick slightly, as with prickles, or fine, sharp points.Felt a horror over me creep, Prickle skin, and catch my breath.Tennyson.
The quality of being prickly, or of having many prickles.
A tailor; -- so called in contempt. [Old slang] L'Estrange.

Full of sharp points or prickles; armed or covered withprickles; as, a prickly shrub. Prickly ash (Bot.), a prickly shrub(Xanthoxylum Americanum) with yellowish flowers appearing with theleaves. All parts of the plant are pungent and aromatic. The southernspecies is X. Carolinianum. Gray.-- Prickly heat (Med.), a noncontagious cutaneous eruption of redpimples, attended with intense itching and tingling of the partsaffected. It is due to inflammation of the sweat glands, and is oftenbrought on by overheating the skin in hot weather.-- Prickly pear (Bot.), a name given to several plants of thecactaceous genus Opuntia, American plants consisting of fleshy,leafless, usually flattened, and often prickly joints inserted uponeach other. The sessile flowers have many petals and numerousstamens. The edible fruit is a large pear-shaped berry containingmany flattish seeds. The common species of the Northern AtlanticStates is Opuntia vulgaris. In the South and West are many others,and in tropical America more than a hundred more. O. vulgaris, O.Ficus-Indica, and O. Tuna are abundantly introduced in theMediterranean region, and O. Dillenii has become common in India.-- Prickly pole (Bot.), a West Indian palm (Bactris Plumierana), theslender trunk of which bears many rings of long black prickles.-- Prickly withe (Bot.), a West Indian cactaceous plant (Cereustriangularis) having prickly, slender, climbing, triangular stems.-- Prickly rat (Zoöl.), any one of several species of South Americanburrowing rodents belonging to Ctenomys and allied genera. The hairis usually intermingled with sharp spines.
A name given to several species of stonecrop, used asingredients of vermifuge medicines. See Stonecrop.
A pointed steel punch, to prick a mark on metal.
Music written, or noted, with dots or points; -- so called fromthe points or dots with which it is noted down. [Obs.]He fights as you sing pricksong. Shak.
A shrub (Euonymus Europæus); -- so named from the use of itswood for goads, skewers, and shoe pegs. Called also spindle tree.
A small European lamprey (Petromyzon branchialis); -- calledalso prid, and sandpiper.
Full of pride; haughty. Tennyson.-- Pride"ful*ly, adv.-- Pride"ful-ness, n.
Of or pertaining to the day before, or yesterday. [R.]Thackeray.
One who pries; one who inquires narrowly and searches, or isinquisitive.So pragmatical a prier he is into divine secrets. Fuller.

A presbyter elder; a minister; specifically:(a) (R. C. Ch. & Gr. Ch.) One who is authorized to consecrate thehost and to say Mass; but especially, one of the lowest orderpossessing this power. Murdock. (b) (Ch. of Eng. & Prot. Epis. Ch.)
Controlled or oppressed by priests; as, a priest-ridden people.Swift.
A form of redan, so named from its shape; -- called alsoswallowtail.

Priestly policy; the policy of a priesthood; esp., in an illsense, fraud or imposition in religious concerns; management bypriests to gain wealth and power by working upon the religiousmotives or credulity of others.It is better that men should be governed by priestcraft than byviolence. Macaulay.
Priests, collectively; the priesthood; -- so called incontempt. [R.] Milton.
A woman who officiated in sacred rites among pagans. Abp.Potter.
The office of a priest. [Obs.] Milton.
The influence, doctrines, principles, etc., of priests or thepriesthood. [R.]
The quality or state of being priestly. R. Browning.
Of or pertaining to a priest or the priesthood; sacerdotal;befitting or becoming a priest; as, the priestly office; a priestlyfarewell. Shak.
To haggle about the price of a commodity; to bargain hard.[Prov. Eng. & Scot.]
Like a prig; conceited; pragmatical.-- Prig"gish*ly, adv.-- Prig"gish-ness, n.
The first or chief female singer in an opera.
At first view; on the first appearance. Prima facie evidence(of a fact) (Law), evidence which is sufficient to establish the factunless rebutted. Bouvier.

A charge in addition to the freight; originally, a gratuity tothe captain for his particular care of the goods (sometimes calledhat money), but now belonging to the owners or freighters of thevessel, unless by special agreement the whole or part is assigned tothe captain. Homans.
First; primary; original; chief.It hath the primal eldest curse upon it. Shak.The primal duties shine aloft like stars. Wordsworth.
The quality or state of being primal. [Obs.]
In a primary manner; in the first place; in the first place; inthe first intention; originally.
The quality or state of being primary, or first in time, inact, or in intention. Norris.
The highest order of mammals. It includes man, together withthe apes and monkeys. Cf. Pitheci.
The office, dignity, or position of a primate; primacy.
Of or pertaining to a primate. Barrow.
The morning; specifically (R. C. Ch.), the first canonicalhour, succeeding to lauds.Early and late it rung, at evening and at prime. Spenser.
One who, or that which, primes; specifically, an instrument ordevice for priming; esp., a cap, tube, or water containing percussionpowder or other capable for igniting a charge of gunpowder.
A game at cards, now unknown. Shak.
See Primrose. [Obs.] "She was a primerole." Chaucer.
Belonging to the first ages; pristine; original; primitive;primary; as, the primeval innocence of man. "This is the forestprimeval." Longfellow.From chaos, and primeval darkness, came Light. Keats.
In a primeval manner; in or from the earliest times;originally. Darwin.
First born, or first of all; original; primary. SeePrimogenial.
The outermost of the two integuments of an ovule.
The first coating of color, size, or the like, laid on canvas,or on a building, or other surface.
A woman who bears a child for the first time.
Belonging to a first birth; bearing young for the first time.
Of or pertaining to the captain of the vanguard of a Romanarmy. Barrow.
The first fruit; the first year's whole profit of anecclesiastical preferment.The primitias of your parsonage. Spenser.
Being of the first production; primitive; original. [Obs.]Ainsworth.
An original or primary word; a word not derived from another; -- opposed to derivative.
The quality or state of being primitive; conformity toprimitive style or practice.
Quality of being first; primitiveness. [Obs.] Bp. Pearson.
In a prim or precise manner.
The quality or state of being prim; affected formality orniceness; preciseness; stiffness.
First born, made, or generated; original; primary; elemental;as, primogenial light. Glanvill.

The exclusive right of inheritance which belongs to the eldestson. Thus in England the right of inheriting the estate of the fatherbelongs to the eldest son, and in the royal family the eldest son ofthe sovereign is entitled to the throne by primogeniture. Inexceptional cases, among the female children, the crown descends byright of primogeniture to the eldest daughter only and her issue.Blackstone.
The state or privileges of the firstborn. Burke.

Of or pertaining to the lowest beds of the Silurian age,corresponding to the Acadian and Potsdam periods in American geology.It is called also Cambrian, and by many geologists is separated fromthe Silurian.
Devotion to, or persistence in, conditions of the primordialstate. H. Spencer.
At the beginning; under the first order of things; originally.
A name given to several kinds of plums; as, red primordian,amber primordian, etc.
To be formal or affected in dress or manners; -- often with up.[Prov. Eng. & Scot.] Halliwell.
Of or pertaining to the primrose; of the color of a primrose; -- hence, flowery; gay. "The primrose path of dalliance." Shak.

A league of both sexes among the Conservatives, founded in1883. So called because primrose was (erroneously, it is said) takento be the favorite flower of the Conservative statesman BenjaminDisraeli, Earl of Beaconsfield.
The genus of plants including the primrose (Primula vera).
Of or pertaining to an order of herbaceous plants (Primulaceæ),of which the primrose is the type, and the pimpernel, the cyclamen,and the water violet are other examples.

In the Ptolemaic system, the outermost of the revolvingconcentric spheres constituting the universe, the motion of which wassupposed to carry with it all the inclosed spheres with their planetsin a daily revolution from east to west. See Crystalline heavens,under Crystalline.The motions of the greatest persons in a government ought to be, asthe motions of the planets, under primum mobile. Bacon.
One of the bishops of the Episcopal Church of Scotland, whopresides at the meetings of the bishops, and has certain privilegesbut no metropolitan authority. Internat. Cyc.
Being in its prime. [Obs.] "The youth of primy nature." Shak.
The jurisdiction, sovereignty, rank, or estate of a prince.Thrones, princedoms, powers, dominions, I reduce. Milton.
A petty prince; a princeling.The princekins of private life. Thackeray.
The quality of being princely; the state, manner, or dignity ofa prince.
A petty prince; a young prince.
In a princely manner.My appetite was not princely got. Shak.
A term applied to a lady's long, close-fitting dress made withwaist and skirt in one.
The wood of two small tropical American trees (Hameliaventricosa, and Cordia gerascanthoides). It is brownish, veined withlighter color.
Imitative of a prince. [R. & Colloq.] Thackeray.

The first two long feathers of a hawk's wing. Spenser. J. H.Walsh.(f) One of turrets or pinnacles of waxwork and tapers with which theposts and center of a funeral hearse were formerly crowned. Oxf.Gloss.(g) A principal or essential point or rule; a principle. [Obs.]
In a principal manner; primarily; above all; chiefly; mainly.
First principles; fundamental beginnings; elements; as.Newton's Principia.
Relating to principles or beginnings. [R.] Jer. Taylor.
To begin; to initiate. [Obs.] Sir M. Hale.
Analysis into primary or elemental parts. [Archaic] Bacon.

Any original inherent constituent which characterizes asubstance, or gives it its essential properties, and which canusually be separated by analysis; -- applied especially to drugs,plant extracts, etc.Cathartine is the bitter, purgative principle of senna. Gregory.Bitter principle, Principle of contradiction, etc. See under Bitter,Contradiction, etc.
To dress or adjust one's self for show; to prank.

To strike off an impression or impressions of, from type, orfrom stereotype, electrotype, or engraved plates, or the like; in awider sense, to do the typesetting, presswork, etc., of (a book orother publication); as, to print books, newspapers, pictures; toprint an edition of a book.

One who prints; especially, one who prints books, newspapers,engravings, etc., a compositor; a typesetter; a pressman. Printer'sdevil, Printer's gauge. See under Devil, and Gauge.-- Printer's ink. See Printing ink, below.
A place where cloth is printed; print works; also, a printingoffice. [R.]

The act, art, or practice of impressing letters, characters, orfigures on paper, cloth, or other material; the business of aprinter, including typesetting and presswork, with their adjuncts;typography; also, the act of producing photographic prints. Blockprinting. See under Block.-- Printing frame (Photog.), a shallow box, usually having a glassfront, in which prints are made by exposure to light.-- Printing house, a printing office.-- Printing ink, ink used in printing books, newspapers, etc. It iscomposed of lampblack or ivory black mingled with linseed or nut oil,made thick by boiling and burning. Other ingredients are employed forthe finer qualities. Ure.-- Printing office, a place where books, pamphlets, or newspapers,etc., are printed.-- Printing paper, paper used in the printing of books, pamphlets,newspapers, and the like, as distinguished from writing paper,wrapping paper, etc.-- Printing press, a press for printing, books, newspaper,handbills, etc.-- Printing wheel, a wheel with letters or figures on its periphery,used in machines for paging or numbering, or in ticket-printingmachines, typewriters, etc.; a type wheel.

A process by which cloud effects or other features not in theoriginal negative are introduced into a photograph. Portions, such asthe sky, are covered while printing and the blank space thus reservedis filled in by printing from another negative.
A method of printing, in which the image is fully brought outby the direct actinic action of light without subsequent developmentby means of chemicals.
A shop where prints are sold.

Preceding in the order of time; former; antecedent; anterior;previous; as, a prior discovery; prior obligation; -- usedelliptically in cases like the following: he lived alone [in thetime] prior to his marriage.
The dignity, office, or government, of a prior. T. Warton.
A lady superior of a priory of nuns, and next in dignity to anabbess.
The state or office of prior; priorate.
A religious house presided over by a prior or prioress; --sometimes an offshoot of, an subordinate to, an abbey, and calledalso cell, and obedience. See Cell, 2.
A follower of Priscillian, bishop of Avila in Spain, in thefourth century, who mixed various elements of Gnosticism andManicheism with Christianity.
A solid whose bases or ends are any similar, equal, andparallel plane figures, and whose sides are parallelograms.
Glass with one side smooth and the other side formed intosharp-edged ridges so as to reflect the light that passes through,used at windows to throw the light into the interior.
In the form on manner of a prism; by means of a prism.
A body that approaches to the form of a prism.
Having the form of a prismoid; as, prismoidal solids.
Belonging to the earliest period or state; original; primitive;primeval; as, the pristine state of innocence; the pristine mannersof a people; pristine vigor.
A tool employed by blacksmiths for punching or enlarging thenail holes in a horseshoe.
A corruption of pray thee; as, I prithee; generally usedwithout I. Shak.What was that scream for, I prithee L'Estrange.Prithee, tell me, Dimple-chin. E. C. Stedman.
Empty talk; trifling loquacity; prattle; -- used in contempt orridicule. [Colloq.] Abp. Bramhall.
A private friend; a confidential friend; a confidant. [Obs.]Fuller.
In the universities of Germany and some other Europeancountries, a licensed teacher or lecturer having no share in theuniversity government and dependent upon fees for remuneration.
A common soldier; a soldier below the grade of anoncommissioned officer. Macaulay.
An officer or seaman of a privateer.
Implying privation or negation; giving a negative force to aword; as, alpha privative; privative particles; -- applied to suchprefixes and suffixes as a- (Gr. un-, non-, -less.
In a privative manner; by the absence of something; negatively.[R.] Hammond.

An ornamental European shrub (Ligustrum vulgare), much used inhedges; -- called also prim. Egyptian privet. See Lawsonia.-- Evergreen privet, a plant of the genus Rhamnus. See Alatern.-- Mock privet, any one of several evergreen shrubs of the genusPhillyrea. They are from the Mediterranean region, and have been muchcultivated for hedges and for fancifully clipped shrubberies.

See Call, Put, Spread, etc. Breach of privilege. See underBreach.-- Question of privilege (Parliamentary practice), a question whichconcerns the security of a member of a legislative body in hisspecial privileges as such.-- Water privilege, the advantage of having machinery driven by astream, or a place affording such advantage. [ U. S.] -- Writ ofprivilege (Law), a writ to deliver a privileged person from custodywhen arrested in a civil suit. Blackstone.

Invested with a privilege; enjoying a peculiar right,advantage, or immunity. Privileged communication. (Law) (a) Acommunication which can not be disclosed without the consent of theparty making it, -- such as those made by a client to his legaladviser, or by persons to their religious or medical advisers. (b) Acommunication which does not expose the party making it to indictmentfor libel, -- such as those made by persons communicatingconfidentially with a government, persons consulted confidentially asto the character of servants, etc.-- Privileged debts (Law), those to which a preference in payment isgiven out of the estate of a deceased person, or out of the estate ofan insolvent. Wharton. Burrill.-- Privileged witnesses (Law) witnesses who are not obliged totestify as to certain things, as lawyers in relation to theirdealings with their clients, and officers of state as to statesecrets; also, by statute, clergymen and physicans are placed in thesame category, so far as concerns information received by themprofessionally.
In a privy manner; privately; secretly. Chaucer. 2 Pet. ii. 1.

A partaker; a person having an interest in any action or thing;one who has an interest in an estate created by another; a personhaving an interest derived from a contract or conveyance to which heis not himself a party. The term, in its proper sense, isdistinguished from party. Burrill. Wharton.
To move with a lever; to force up or open; to pry. [Writtenalso prise.]
One who estimates or sets the value of a thing; an appraiser.Shak.
The application of a lever to move any weighty body, as a cask,anchor, cannon, car, etc. See Prize, n., 5.

A Latin preposition signifying for, before, forth. Pro confessoEtym: [L.] (Law), taken as confessed. The action of a court of equityon that portion of the pleading in a particular case which thepleading on the other side does not deny.-- Pro rata. Etym: [L. See Prorate.] In proportion; proportion.-- Pro re nata Etym: [L.] (Law), for the existing occasion; asmatters are.
In proportion; proportionately; according to the share,interest, or liability of each.
The investing portion, or spherical envelope, surrounding theeccentric germinal spot of the germinal vesicle.

A prefix signifying before, in front, forth, for, in behalf of,in place of, according to; as, propose, to place before; proceed, togo before or forward; project, to throw forward; prologue, partspoken before (the main piece); propel, prognathous; provide, to lookout for; pronoun, a word instead of a noun; proconsul, a personacting in place of a consul; proportion, arrangement according toparts.

A sailing canoe of the Ladrone Islands and Malay Archipelago,having its lee side flat and its weather side like that of anordinary boat. The ends are alike. The canoe is long and narrow, andis kept from overturning by a cigar-shaped log attached to a frameextending several feet to windward. It has been called the flyingproa, and is the swiftest sailing craft known.
A vertebral rudiment in front of the atlas in some reptiles.
One who holds, in opposition to the probabilists, that a man isbound to do that which is most probably right.
One who maintains that a man may do that which has aprobability of being right, or which is inculcated by teachers ofauthority, although other opinions may seem to him still moreprobable.
Likelihood of the occurrence of any event in the doctrine ofchances, or the ratio of the number of favorable chances to the wholenumber of chances, favorable and unfavorable. See 1st Chance, n., 5.
In a probable manner; in likelihood.Distinguish between what may possibly and what will probably be done.L'Estrange.
A slender elastic rod, as of whalebone, with a sponge on theend, for removing obstructions from the esophagus, etc.

Of or belonging to a probate, or court of probate; as, aprobate record. Probate Court, or Court of Probate, a court for theprobate of wills.-- Probate duty, a government tax on property passing by will.[Eng.]
Of or pertaining to probation; serving for trial.To consider this life . . . as a probationary state. Paley.
The state of being a probationer; novitiate. Locke.
Serving for trial or proof; probationary; as, probativejudgments; probative evidence. South.
One who, when indicted for crime, confessed it, and accusedothers, his accomplices, in order to obtain pardon; a state'sevidence.

An instrument for examining the depth or other circumstances ofa wound, ulcer, or cavity, or the direction of a sinus, of forexploring for bullets, for stones in the bladder, etc. Parr. Probe,or Probe-pointed, scissors (Surg.), scissors used to open wounds, theblade of which, to be thrust into the orifice, has a button at theend. Wiseman.
Having a blunt or button-shaped extremity; -- said of cuttinginstruments.
Tried virtue or integrity; approved moral excellence; honesty;rectitude; uprightness. "Probity of mind." Pope.
Anything which is required to be done; as, in geometry, tobisect a line, to draw a perpendicular; or, in algebra, to find anunknown quantity.
To propose problems. [R.] "Hear him problematize." B. Jonson.

An extensive division of pectinibranchiate gastropods,including those that have a long retractile proboscis, with the mouthat the end, as the cones, whelks, tritons, and cowries. See Illust.of Gastropoda, and of Winkle.
Having the form or uses of a proboscis; as, a proboscidiformmouth.
A hollow organ or tube attached to the head, or connected withthe mouth, of various animals, and generally used in taking food ordrink; a snout; a trunk.
The young tissue of a fibrovascular bundle before its componentcells have begun to be differentiated. Sachs.
The kindling of a disease into action; also, the procatarcticcause. Quincy.
To begin and carry on a legal process.
The course of procedure in the prosecution of an action at law.Blackstone. Proceedings of a society, the published record of itsaction, or of things done at its meetings.
That which comes forth or results; effect; yield; issue;product; sum accruing from a sale, etc.
Consisting of four short syllables; composed of feet of fourshort syllables each.
One of a family of oceanic birds (Procellaridæ) including thepetrels, fulmars, and shearwaters. They are often seen in greatabundance in stormy weather.
Pertaining to, or forming, the front of the head. Procephaliclobe (Zoöl.), that part of the head of an invertebrate animal whichis in front of the mouth.
An order of large birds; the Ratitæ; -- called also Proceri.
The segment next to the flagellum of the antennæ of Crustacea.
An authentic minute of an official act, or statement of facts.
Any marked prominence or projecting part, especially of a bone;anapophysis.
An orderly and ceremonial progress of persons, either from thesacristy to the choir, or from the choir around the church, within orwithout. Shipley.
Of or pertaining to a procession; consisting in a procession.The processional services became more frequent. Milman.
One who goes or marches in a procession. [R.]

Pertaining to a procession; consisting in processions; as,processionary service. Processionary moth (Zoöl.), any moth of thegenus Cnethocampa, especially C. processionea of Europe, whose larvæmake large webs on oak trees, and go out to feed in regular order.They are covered with stinging hairs.
A proceeding prescribed by statute for ascertaining and fixingthe boundaries of land. See 2d Procession. [ Local, U. S.] Bouvier.
Proceeding; advancing.Because it is language, -- ergo, processive. Coleridge.
Next; nearest. Prochein ami or amy ( (Law), the next friend.See under Next.
Situated in front of the notochord; -- applied especially toparts of the cartilaginous rudiments in the base of the skull.
The dating of an event before the time it happened; anantedating; -- opposed to Ant: metachronism.
A state of complete readiness for action. [Obs.] "War inprocinct." Milton.
Leaning forward; -- said of certain monosyllabic words whichare so closely attached to the following word as not to have aseparate accent.
Having a tendency by nature; prone; proclivous. [R.] Mrs.Browning.
Having the incisor teeth directed forward.
A lateral cavity of the prosencephalon; a lateral ventricle ofthe brain. B. G. Wilder.
Concave in front; as, procoelian vertebræ, which have theanterior end of the centra concave and the posterior convex.
An officer who discharged the duties of a consul without beinghimself consul; a governor of, or a military commander in, aprovince. He was usually one who had previously been consul.
The office jurisdiction of a proconsul, or the term of hisoffice.

To put off till to-morrow, or from day to day; to defer; topostpone; to delay; as, to procrastinate repentance. Dr. H. More.Hopeless and helpless Ægeon wend, But to procrastinate his lifelessend. Shak.
The act or habit of procrastinating, or putting off to a futuretime; delay; dilatoriness.Procrastination is the thief of time. Young.
One who procrastinates, or defers the performance of anything.
Of or pertaining to procrastination; dilatory.
Generating; producing; productive; fruitful; assisting inprocreation. [R.] "His pendent bed and procreant cradle." Shak.
To generate and produce; to beget; to engender.
The act of begetting; generation and production of young.South.
Having the power to beget; generative. Sir M. Hale.
One who begets; a father or sire; a generator.
Any species of small moths of the genus Procris. The larvæ ofsome species injure the grapevine by feeding in groups upon theleaves.
Of or pertaining to Procrustes, or the mode of torturepracticed by him; producing conformity by violent means; as, theProcrustean treatment; a Procrustean limit. See Procrustes.
To stretch or contract according to some rule or standard.

A celebrated legendary highwayman of Attica, who tied hisvictims upon an iron bed, and, as the case required, either stretchedor cut of their legs to adapt them to its length; -- whence themetaphorical phrase, the bed of Procrustes.
Inversion and prolapse of the mucous coat of the rectum, fromrelaxation of the sphincter, with more or less swelling; prolapsusani. Dunglison.

One who is employed to manage to affairs of another.Specifically:(a) A person appointed to collect alms for those who could not go outto beg for themselves, as lepers, the bedridden, etc.; hence abeggar. [Obs.] Nares.(b) (Eng. Law) An officer employed in admiralty and ecclesiasticalcauses. He answers to an attorney at common law, or to a solicitor inequity. Wharton.(c) (Ch. of Eng.) A representative of the clergy in convocation.(d) An officer in a university or college whose duty it is to enforceobedience to the laws of the institution.
Management by a proctor, or as by a proctor; hence, control;superintendence; -- in contempt. "The fogging proctorage of money."Milton.
Of or pertaining to a proctor, esp. an academic proctor;magisterial.
The office or dignity of a proctor; also, the term of hisoffice. Clarendon.
An incision into the rectum, as for the division of astricture.
Lying on the ground, but without putting forth roots; trailing;prostrate; as, a procumbent stem.
Capable of being procured; obtainable. Boyle.

A sum of money paid formerly to the bishop or archdeacon, nowto the ecclesiastical commissioners, by an incumbent, as acommutation for entertainment at the time of visitation; -- calledalso proxy. Procuration money (Law), money paid for procuring a loan.Blackstone.
One who manages another's affairs, either generally or in aspecial matter; an agent; a proctor. Chaucer. Shak.
Of or pertaining to a procurator, or proctor; made by aproctor. Ayliffe.
The office or term of a procurator. Bp. Pearson.
a star of the first magnitude in the constellation Canis Minor,or the Little Dog.
To thrust some pointed instrument into; to prick with somethingsharp; as, to prod a soldier with a bayonet; to prod oxen; hence, togoad, to incite, to worry; as, to prod a student. H. Taylor.

Given to extravagant expenditure; expending money or otherthings without necessity; recklessly or viciously profuse; lavish;wasteful; not frugal or economical; as, a prodigal man; the prodigalson; prodigal giving; prodigal expenses.In fighting fields [patriots] were prodigal of blood. Dryden.
Extravagance in expenditure, particularly of money; excessiveliberality; profusion; waste; -- opposed to frugality, economy, andparsimony."The prodigality of his wit." Dryden.
To act as a prodigal; to spend liberally. Sherwood.

In a prodigal manner; with profusion of expense; extravagantly;wasteful; profusely; lavishly; as, an estate prodigally dissipated.Nature not bounteous now, but lavish grows; Our paths with flowersshe prodigally strows. Dryden.
The quality or state of being prodigious; the state of havingqualities that excite wonder or astonishment; enormousness; vastness.
Of or pertaining to prodromes; as, the prodromal stage of adisease.
To extend; -- applied to a line, surface, or solid; as, toproduce a side of a triangle.
A race to be run by the produce of horses named or described atthe time of entry.
One who produces, or offers to notice. [Obs.] Ayliffe.
A furnace for producing combustible gas which is used for fuel.
The quality or state of being producible. Barrow.
Capable of being produced, brought forward, brought forth,generated, made, or extended.-- Pro*du"ci*ble*ness, n.

The number or sum obtained by adding one number or quantity toitself as many times as there are units in another number; the numberresulting from the multiplication of two or more numbers; as, theproduct of the multiplication of 7 by 5 is 35. In general, the resultof any kind of multiplication. See the Note under Multiplication.
The state of being productible; producibility. Ruskin.
Capable of being extended or prolonged; extensible; ductile.
The quality or state of being productive; productiveness.Emerson.Not indeed as the product, but as the producing power, theproductivity. Coleridge.
An extinct genus of brachiopods, very characteristic of theCarboniferous rocks.
Serving to predispose; predisposing; as, a proeguminal cause ofdisease.
Preface; introduction; preliminary observations; prelude.Thus much may serve by way of proem. Swift.
The addition of a day to the lunar calendar. [R.] SeeMetemptosis.
Much good may it do you! -- a familiar salutation or welcome.[Obs.]Master page, good master page, sit. Proface! Shak.
In a profane manner.The character of God profanely impeached. Dr. T. Dwight.
The quality or state of being profane; especially, the use ofprofane language.
One who treats sacred things with irreverence, or defiles whatis holy; one who uses profane language. Hooker.
A setting out; a going forward; advance; progression. [Obs.]Sir T. Browne.
Proceeding from, as from a parent; derived, as from anancestor. [R.]The threefold distinction of profectitious, adventitious, andprofessional was ascertained. Gibbon.
The exhibition or production of a record or paper in opencourt, or an allegation that it is in court.

Openly declared, avowed, acknowledged, or claimed; as, aprofessed foe; a professed tyrant; a professed Christian. Theprofessed (R. C. Ch.) , a certain class among the Jesuits bound by aspecial vow. See the note under Jesuit.
The act of entering, or becoming a member of, a religiousorder.
A person who prosecutes anything professionally, or for alivelihood, and not in the character of an amateur; a professionalworker.
The following of a profession, sport, etc., as an occupation; -- opposed to Ant: amateurism.
In a professional manner or capacity; by profession or calling;in the exercise of one's profession; one employed professionally.
Of or pertaining to a professor; as, the professional chair;professional interest.
The character, manners, or habits of a professor. [R.]
The office or position of a professor, or public teacher.Walton.
Of or pertaining to a professor; professorial. [R.] Bacon.
One who has made considerable advances in any business, art,science, or branch of learning; an expert; an adept; as, proficientin a trade; a proficient in mathematics, music, etc.
A human head represented sidewise, or in a side view; the sideface or half face.
In the construction of fieldworks, the erection at properintervals of wooden profiles, to show to the workmen the sectionalform of the parapets at those points.

To be of service to; to be good to; to help on; to benefit; toadvantage; to avail; to aid; as, truth profits all men.The word preached did not profit them. Heb. iv. 2.It is a great means of profiting yourself, to copy diligentlyexcellent pieces and beautiful designs. Dryden.

Yielding or bringing profit or gain; gainful; lucrative;useful; helpful; advantageous; beneficial; as, a profitable trade;profitable business; a profitable study or profession.What was so profitable to the empire became fatal to the emperor.Arbuthnot.-- Prof"it*a*ble*ness, n.-- Prof"it*a*bly, adv.
Gain; advantage; profit.That thy profiting may appear to all. 1 Tim. iv. 15.
The quality of state of being profligate; a profligate or veryvicious course of life; a state of being abandoned in moral principleand in vice; dissoluteness.
An abandoned person; one openly and shamelessly vicious; adissolute person. "Such a profligate as Antony." Swift.
The quality of being profligate; an abandoned course of life;profligacy.
Quality of being profluent; course. [R.] Sir H. Wotton.
Flowing forward, [R.] "In the profluent stream." Milton.
To cause to sink deeply; to cause to dive or penetrate fardown. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.
In a profound manner.Why sigh you so profoundly Shak.
The quality or state of being profound; profundity; depth.Hooker.
Shining forth; brilliant; effulgent. [Obs.] "Profulgent inpreciousness." Chaucer.
The quality or state of being profound; depth of place,knowledge, feeling, etc. "The vast profundity obscure." Milton.
To pour out; to give or spend liberally; to lavish; tosquander. [Obs.] Chapman.
Extravagance; profusion.Hospitality sometimes degenerates into profuseness. Atterbury.
To beget; to generate; to produce; to procreate; as, toprogenerate a race. [R.] Landor.
An ancestor in the direct line; a forefather.And reverence thee their great progenitor. Milton.
The state of being a progenitor.
Descendants of the human kind, or offspring of other animals;children; offspring; race, lineage. " Issued from the progeny ofkings." Shak.
One of the free, or nearly free, segments of a tapeworm. Itcontains both male and female reproductive organs, and is capable ofa brief independent existence.
A comprehensive group of mankind, including those that haveprognathous jaws.
Projection of the jaws.-- Prog"na*thy, n.
Having the jaws projecting beyond the upper part of the face; -- opposed to orthognathous. See Gnathic index, under Gnathic.Their countenances had the true prognathous character. Kane.
The act or art of foretelling the course and termination of adisease; also, the outlook afforded by this act of judgment; as, theprognosis of hydrophobia is bad.
Indicating something future by signs or symptoms; foreshowing;aiding in prognosis; as, the prognostic symptoms of a disease;prognostic signs.
Capable of being prognosticated or foretold. Sir T. Browne.

To indicate as future; to foretell from signs or symptoms; toprophesy; to foreshow; to predict; as, to prognosticate evil. Burke.I neither will nor can prognosticate To the young gaping heir hisfather's fate. Dryden.
One who prognosticates; a foreknower or foreteller of a futurecourse or event by present signs. Isa. xlvii. 13.
Any law, which, after it had passed the Athenian senate, wasfixed on a tablet for public inspection previously to its beingproposed to the general assembly of the people.

That which is written or printed as a public notice oradvertisement; a scheme; a prospectus; especially, a brief outline orexplanation of the order to be pursued, or the subjects embraced, inany public exercise, performance, or entertainment; a preliminarysketch. Programme music (Mus.), descriptive instrumental music whichrequires an argument or programme to explain the meaning of itsseveral movements.
To make progress in; to pass through. [Obs.] Milton.
Regular or proportional advance in increase or decrease ofnumbers; continued proportion, arithmetical, geometrical, orharmonic.
Of or pertaining to progression; tending to, or capable of,progress.
One who makes, or holds to, progress; a progressionist.

The political party formed, chiefly out of the Republicanparty, by the adherents of Theodore Roosevelt in the presidentialcampaign of 1912. The name Progressive party was chosen at themeeting held on Aug. 7, 1912, when the candidates were nominated andthe platform adopted.  Among the chief articles in the platform arethose demanding direct primaries, preferential primaries forpresidential nominations, direct election of United States senators,women's suffrage, and recall of judicial decisions in certain cases.
One who prohibits or forbids; a forbidder; an interdicter.
That prohibits; prohibitory; as, a tax whose effect isprohibitive.
Tending to prohibit, forbid, or exclude; implying prohibition;forbidding; as, a prohibitory law; a prohibitory price. Prohibitoryindex. (R. C. Ch.) See under Index.
To lop; to trim; to prune; to adorn. [Obs.] Chaucer.The sprigs that did about it grow He proined from the leafy arms.Chapman.

To draw or exhibit, as the form of anything; to delineate; as,to project a sphere, a map, an ellipse, and the like; -- sometimeswith on, upon, into, etc.; as, to project a line or point upon aplane. See Projection, 4.
A part of mechanics which treats of the motion, range, time offlight, etc., of bodies thrown or driven through the air by animpelling force.

The representation of something; delineation; plan; especially,the representation of any object on a perspective plane, or such adelineation as would result were the chief points of the objectthrown forward upon the plane, each in the direction of a line drawnthrough it from a given point of sight, or central point; as, theprojection of a sphere. The several kinds of projection differaccording to the assumed point of sight and plane of projection ineach.
One who projects a scheme or design; hence, one who formsfanciful or chimerical schemes. L'Estrange.
A jutting out beyond a surface.
A plan proposed; a draft of a proposed measure; a project.
The falling down of a part through the orifice with which it isnaturally connected, especially of the uterus or the rectum.Dunglison.

Stretched out; extended; especially, elongated in the directionof a line joining the poles; as, a prolate spheroid; -- opposed tooblate. Prolate cycloid. See the Note under Cycloid.-- Prolate ellipsoid or spheroid (Geom.), a figure generated by therevolution of an ellipse about its major axis. See Ellipsoid ofrevolution, under Ellipsoid.
A mediæval method of determining of the proportionate durationof semibreves and minims. Busby.
A prolate spheroid. See Ellipsoid of revolution, underEllipsoid.

One of the fleshy legs found on the abdominal segments of thelarvæ of Lepidoptera, sawflies, and some other insects. Those ofLepidoptera have a circle of hooks. Called also proped, propleg, andfalseleg.
The deputy or substitute for a legate.
Of the nature of a prolegomenon; preliminary; introductory;prefatory.
A preliminary remark or observation; an introductory discourseprefixed to a book or treatise. D. Stokes (1659). Sir W. Scott.
An error in chronology, consisting in an event being datedbefore the actual time.
The art and science of predicting in medicine. Laycock.
One of the common people; a low person; also, the common peopleas a class or estate in a country.
Of or pertaining to the proletaries; belonging to thecommonalty; hence, mean; vile; vulgar. "Every citizen, if he were nota proletarian animal kept at the public cost." De Quincey.-- n.
The indigent class in the State; the body of proletarians.
The lower classes; beggars. "The Italian proletariate." J. A.Symonds.
A citizen of the lowest class, who served the state, not withproperty, but only by having children; hence, a common person.
The crime of destroying one's offspring, either in the womb orafter birth. Bouvier.
To produce or form cells; especially, to produce cells rapidly.
The continuous development of cells in tissue formation; cellformation. Virchow.
Bearing offspring; -- applied to a flower from within whichanother is produced, or to a branch or frond from which anotherrises, or to a plant which is reproduced by buds or gemmæ.
Producing young or fruit abundantly; fruitful; prolific.-- Pro*lif"ic*al*ly, adv.
To make prolific; to fertilize; to impregnate. Sir T. Browne.
Reproduction by the growth of a plant, or part of a plant,directly from an older one, or by gemmæ.
The quality or state of being prolific; fruitfulness;prolificacy.
Dilatory; tedious; superfluous. [Obs.] "Lay by all nicety, andprolixious blushes." Shak.
The quality or state of being prolix; great length; minutedetail; as, prolixity in discourses and writings. "For fulsomeness ofhis prolixitee." Chaucer.Idly running on with vain prolixity. Drayton.
To search or prowl after; to rob; to plunder. [Obs.] Barrow.
To introduce with a formal preface, or prologue. [R.] Shak.
Capable of being prolonged; as, life is prolongable by care.Each syllable being a prolongable quantity. Rush.
To prolong; to extend in space or in time. [R.]
A rope with a hook and a toggle, sometimes used to drag a guncarriage or to lash it to the limber, and for various other purposes.
One who, or that which, causes an extension in time or space.

A trial before the principal performance; a prelude; hence, anintroductory essay or exercise. "Domestic prolusions." Thackeray.Her presence was in some measure a restraint on the worthy divine,whose prolusion lasted. Sir W. Scott.
The act of flowing forth; emanation; efflux. [Obs.] Dr. H.More.
To walk for pleasure, display, or exercise.

Any one of several species of very brilliant birds belonging toPromerops, Epimarchus, and allied genera, closely related to theparadise birds, and mostly native of New Guinea. They have a longcurved beak and a long graduated tail.
A large American bombycid moth (Callosamia promethea). Itslarva feeds on the sassafras, wild cherry, and other trees, andsuspends its cocoon from a branch by a silken band.

The son of Iapetus (one of the Titans) and Clymene, fabled bythe poets to have surpassed all mankind in knowledge, and to haveformed men of clay to whom he gave life by means of fire stolen fromheaven.
