To cry out with a shrill voice; to utter a sudden, sharpoutcry, or shrill, loud cry, as in fright or extreme pain; to shriek;to screech.I heard the owl scream and the crickets cry. Shak.And scream thyself as none e'er screamed before. Pope.

Any one of three species of South American birds constitutingthe family Anhimidæ, and the suborder Palamedeæ. They have two spineson each wing, and the head is either crested or horned. They areeasily tamed, and then serve as guardians for other poultry. Thecrested screamers, or chajas, belong to the genus Chauna. The hornedscreamer, or kamichi, is Palamedea cornuta.
A pebble; a stone; also, a heap of stones or rocky débris.[Prov. Eng.] Southey.
To utter a harsh, shrill cry; to make a sharp outcry, as interror or acute pain; to scream; to shriek. "The screech owl,screeching loud." Shak.
The picarian birds, as distinguished from the singing birds.
Like a screech; shrill and harsh.
A dwarf wall or partition carried up to a certain height forseparation and protection, as in a church, to separate the aisle fromthe choir, or the like.
The refuse left after screening sand, coal, ashes, etc.

A straight line in space with which a definite linear magnitudetermed the pitch is associated (cf. 5th Pitch, 10 (b)). It is used toexpress the displacement of a rigid body, which may always be made toconsist of a rotation about an axis combined with a translationparallel to that axis.
Adapted for forming a screw by cutting; as, a screw-cuttinglathe.
A tool for turning screws so as to drive them into their place.It has a thin end which enters the nick in the head of the screw.
One who, or that which, screws.
a. & n. from Screw, v. t. Screwing machine. See Screw machine,under Screw.
Capable of being written, or of being written upon. [R.]
Skillful in, or fond of, writing. [Obs.] Barrow.
To card coarsely; to run through the scribling machine.
One who scribles; a literary hack.The scribbler, pinched with hunger, writes to dine. Granville.
The act or process of carding coarsely. Scribbing machine, themachine used for the first carding of wool or other fiber; -- calledalso scribbler.
A writer and doctor of the law; one skilled in the law andtraditions; one who read and explained the law to the people.
A sharp-pointed tool, used by joiners for drawing lines onstuff; a marking awl.
The character and opinions of a Jewish scribe in the time ofChrist. F. W. Robertson.
A screed; a shred; a fragment. [R.]
Thin canvas glued on the inside of panels to prevent shrinking,checking, etc.
The struggle in the rush lines after the ball is put in play.
To make too small or short; to limit or straiten; to put onshort allowance; to scant; to contract; to shorten; as, to scrimp thepattern of a coat.
a. & n. from Scrimp, v. t. Scrimping bar, a device used inconnection with a calico printing machine for stretching the fabricbreadthwise so that it may be smooth for printing. Knight.
A small portion; a pittance; a little bit. [Prov. Eng.]Halliwell.
To ornament, as shells, ivory, etc., by engraving, and(usually) rubbing pigments into the incised lines. [Sailor's cant.U.S.]
A chest, bookcase, or other place, where writings orcuriosities are deposited; a shrine. [Obs.]But laid them up in immortial scrine. Spenser.
A small bag; a wallet; a satchel. [Archaic] Chaucer.And in requital ope his leathern scrip. Milton.
The contents of a scrip, or wallet. [Obs.] Shak.
Type made in imitation of handwriting.

In an abbey or monastery, the room set apart for writing orcopying manuscripts; in general, a room devoted to writing.Writing rooms, or scriptoria, where the chief works of Latinliterature . . . were copied and illuminated. J. R. Green.
Of or pertaining to writing; expressed in writing; used inwriting; as, scriptory wills; a scriptory reed. [R.] Swift.
Contained in the Scriptures; according to the Scriptures, orsacred oracles; biblical; as, a scriptural doctrine.
The quality or state of being scriptural; literal adherence tothe Scriptures.
One who adheres literally to the Scriptures.

One who is strongly attached to, or versed in, the Scriptures,or who endeavors to regulate his life by them.The Puritan was a Scripturist with all his heart, if as yet withimperfect intelligence . . . he cherished the scheme of looking tothe Word of God as his sole and universal directory. Palfrey.
Writing; document; scroll. [Obs.] "Of every scrit and bond."Chaucer.
A screech. [R.]Perhaps it is the owlet's scritch. Coleridge.
One of the smooth areas surrounding the tubercles of a seaurchin.
Pertaining to, or surrounding, scrobiculæ; as, scrobiculartubercles.
Mottled pottery made from scraps of differently colored clays.

A constitutional disease, generally hereditary, especiallymanifested by chronic enlargement and cheesy degeneration of thelymphatic glands, particularly those of the neck, and marked by atendency to the development of chronic intractable inflammations ofthe skin, mucous membrane, bones, joints, and other parts, and by adiminution in the power of resistance to disease or injury and thecapacity for recovery. Scrofula is now generally held to betuberculous in character, and may develop into general or localtuberculosis (consumption).
Any affection of the skin dependent on scrofula.
A stunted shrub, bush, or branch. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.]
Abounding in scrog; also, twisted; stunted. [Prov. Eng. &Scot.] Halliwell.
An ornament formed of undulations giving off spirals or sprays,usually suggestive of plant form. Roman architectural ornament islargely of some scroll pattern.
Formed like a scroll; contained in a scroll; adorned withscrolls; as, scrolled work.
A genus of coarse herbs having small flowers in panicled cymes;figwort.

Of or pertaining to a very large natural order of gamopetalousplants (Scrophulariaceæ, or Scrophularineæ), usually having irregulardidynamous flowers and a two-celled pod. The order includes themullein, foxglove, snapdragon, figwort, painted cup, yellow rattle,and some exotic trees, as the Paulownia.
Of or pertaining to the scrotum; as, scrotal hernia.
A rupture or hernia in the scrotum; scrotal hernia.
The bag or pouch which contains the testicles; the cod.
To crowd; to squeeze. [Prov. Eng. & Colloq. U.S.]
A mean fellow; a wretch. [Obs.] hak.
To rub hard; to wash with rubbing; usually, to rub with a wetbrush, or with something coarse or rough, for the purpose of cleaningor brightening; as, to scrub a floor, a doorplate.
A gas washer. See under Gas.
Of the nature of scrub; small and mean; stunted in growth; as,a scrubby cur. "Dense, scrubby woods." Duke of Argull.
A species of calciferous sandstone. [Prov. Eng.]

To be reluctant or to hesitate, as regards an action, onaccount of considerations of conscience or expedience.We are often over-precise, scrupling to say or do those things whichlawfully we may. Fuller.Men scruple at the lawfulness of a set form of divine worship. South.
To perplex with scruples; to regard with scruples. [Obs.] Bp.Montagu.

The quality or state of being scruppulous; doubt; doubtfulnessrespecting decision or action; caution or tenderness from the far ofdoing wrong or ofending; nice regard to exactness and propierty;precision.The first sacrilege is looked on with horror; but when they have madethe breach, their scrupulosity soon retires. Dr. H. More.Careful, even to scrupulosity, . . . to keep their Sabbath. South.
Discoverable by scrutiny, inquiry, or critical examination.[R.] r. H. More.
One who scrutinizes; a close examiner or inquirer. Ayliffe.

Voting for a group of candidates for the same kind of office onone ticket or ballot, containing a list of them; -- the method, usedin France, as from June, 1885, to Feb., 1889, in elections for theChamber of Deputies, each elector voting for the candidates for thewhole department in which he lived, as disting. from scrutind'arrondissement (da`rôN`des`mäN"), or voting by each elector for thecandidate or candidates for his own arrondissement only.
A scrutinizer; specifically, an examiner of votes, as at anelection.

To examine closely; to inspect or observe with criticalattention; to regard narrowly; as, to scrutinize the measures ofadministration; to scrutinize the conduct or motives of individuals.Whose votes they were obliged to scrutinize. Ayliffe.Thscrutinized his face the closest. G. W. Cable.
Closely examining, or inquiring; careful; sctrict.-- Scru"ti*nous*ly, adv.
An examination of catechumens, in the last week of Lent, whowere to receive baptism on Easter Day.
To squeeze, compress, crush, or bruise. [Obs. or Low] Spenser.
To be driven swiftly, or to run, before a gale, with little orno sail spread.
To run hastily; to hurry; to scuttle.
The back part of the neck; the scruff. [Prov. Eng.] Ld. Lytton.
To sculpture; to carve; to engrave. [Obs. or Humorous.] Sandys.
Formed by carving; graven; as, sculptile images. [Obs.] Sir T.Browne.
Of or pertaining to sculpture. G. Eliot.

To form with the chisel on, in, or from, wood, stone, or metal;to carve; to engrave. Sculptured tortoise (Zoöl.), a common NorthAmerican wood tortoise (Glyptemys insculpta). The shell is markedwith strong grooving and ridges which resemble sculptured figures.
After the manner of sculpture; resembling, or relating to,sculpture.
To form a scum; to become covered with scum. Also usedfiguratively.Life, and the interest of life, have stagnated and scummed over. A.K. H. Boyd.
To void excrement. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Massinger.

To cover lighty, as a painting, or a drawing, with a thin washof opaque color, or with color-crayon dust rubbed on with the stump,or to make any similar additions to the work, so as to produce asoftened effect.
Covered with scum; of the nature of scum. Sir P. Sidney.
To cause to loathe, or feel disgust at. [Scot. & Prov. Eng.]
An opening cut through the waterway and bulwarks of a ship, sothat water falling on deck may flow overboard; -- called also scupperhole.
An American grape, a form of Vitis vulpina, found in theSouthern Atlantic States, and often cultivated.
To move hastily; to scour. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.
Minute membranous scales on the surface of some leaves, as inthe goosefoot. Gray.
Having or producing scurf; covered with scurf; resemblingscurf.

Such as befits a buffoon or vulgar jester; grossly opprobriousor loudly jocose in language; scurrilous; as, scurrile taunts.The wretched affectation of scurrile laughter. Cowley.A scurrile or obscene jest will better advance you at the court ofCharles than father's ancient name. Sir W. Scott.
To hasten away or along; to move rapidly; to hurry; as, therabbit scurried away.
The quality or state of being scurvy; vileness; meanness.

A disease characterized by livid spots, especially about thethighs and legs, due to extravasation of blood, and by spongy gums,and bleeding from almost all the mucous membranes. It is accompaniedby paleness, languor, depression, and general debility. It isoccasioned by confinement, innutritious food, and hard labor, butespecially by lack of fresh vegetable food, or confinement for a longtime to a limited range of food, which is incapable of repairing thewaste of the system. It was formerly prevalent among sailors andsoldiers. Scurvy grass Etym: [Scurvy + grass; or cf. Icel. skarfakalscurvy grass.] (Bot.) A kind of cress (Cochlearia officinalis)growing along the seacoast of Northern Europe and in arctic regions.It is a remedy for the scurvy, and has proved a valuable food toarctic explorers. The name is given also to other allied species ofplants.

The tail of a hare, or of a deer, or other animal whose tail isshort, sp. when carried erect; hence, sometimes, the animal itself."He ran like a scut." Skelton.How the Indian hare came to have a long tail, wheras that part inothers attains no higher than a scut. Sir T. Browne.My doe with the black scut. Shak.
Shield money; commutation of service for a sum of money. SeeEscuage.
Of or pertaining to a shield.A good example of these scutal monstrosities. Cussans.
Protected or covered by bony or horny plates, or large scales.
A kind of pasture grass (Cynodon Dactylon). See Bermuda grass:also Illustration in Appendix.
Emblazoned on or as a shield.Scutcheoned panes in cloisters old. Lowell.
A bony scale of a reptile or fish; a large horny scale on theleg of a bird, or on the belly of a snake.
the entire covering, or mode of arrangement, of scales, as onthe legs and feet of a bird.
Having the form of a scutellum.
Having broad scutella on the front, and small scales on theposterior side, of the tarsus; -- said of certain birds.
A rounded apothecium having an elevated rim formed of theproper thallus, the fructification of certain lichens.
An order of gastropod Mollusca having a heart with two auriclesand one ventricle. The shell may be either spiral or shieldlike.
Having the gills protected by a shieldlike shell; of orpertaining to the Scutibranchiata.-- n.
Any species of chilopod myriapods of the genus Scutigera. Theysometimes enter buildings and prey upon insects.
Having the anterior surface of the tarsus covered withscutella, or transverse scales, in the form of incomplete bandsterminating at a groove on each side; -- said of certain birds.
To run quickly; to scurry; to scuttle. [Prov. Eng.]
To run with affected precipitation; to hurry; to bustle; toscuddle.With the first dawn of day, old Janet was scuttling about the houseto wake the baron. Sir W. Scott.
An oblong shield made of boards or wickerwork covered withleather, with sometimes an iron rim; -- carried chiefly by the heavy-armed infantry.
Arm scye, a cutter's term for the armhole or part of thearmhole of the waist of a garnment. [Cant]
To hide; to secrete; to conceal. [Obs.]

A dangerous rock on the Italian coast opposite the whirpoolCharybdis on the coast of Sicily, -- both personified in classicalliterature as ravenous monsters. The passage between them wasformerly considered perilous; hence, the saying "Between Scylla andCharybdis," signifying a great peril on either hand.
A genus of oceanic nudibranchiate mollusks having the smallbranched gills situated on the upper side of four fleshy laterallobes, and on the median caudal crest.
One of a family (Scyllaridæ) of macruran Crustacea, remarkablefor the depressed form of the body, and the broad, flat antennæ. Alsoused adjectively.
A white crystalline substance of a sweetish taste, resemblinginosite and metameric with dextrose. It is extracted from the kidneyof the dogfish (of the genus Scylium), the shark, and the skate.
The young attached larva of Discophora in the stage when itresembles a hydroid, or actinian.
An order of fishes including the blennioid and gobioid fishes,and other related families.
An order of fresh-water fishes inhabiting tropical Africa. Theyhave rudimentary electrical organs on each side of the tail.
A kind of large drinking cup, -- used by Greeks and Romans,esp. by poor folk.
A scythe-shaped blade attached to ancient war chariots.
Armed scythes, as a chariot.Chariots scythed, On thundering axles rolled. Glover.
One who uses a scythe; a mower. Macaulay.
A stone for sharpening scythes; a whetstone.
Wilson's thrush; -- so called from its note. [Local, U.S.]
Of or pertaining to Scythia (a name given to the northern partof Asia, and Europe adjoining to Asia), or its language orinhabitants. Scythian lamb. (Bot.) See Barometz.
To disdain. [Obs.]But either sdeigns with other to partake. Spenser.
A great brazen laver in the temple at Jerusalem; -- so calledfrom its size.He made a molten sea of ten cubits from brim to brim, round incompass, and five cubits the height thereof. 2 Chron. iv. 2.
Any one of numerous species of soft-bodied Anthozoa, belongingto the order Actrinaria; an actinian.
The fruit of a West Indian palm (Manicaria Plukenetii), oftenfound floating in the sea. A. Grisebach.
A squid of the genus Ommastrephes. See Squid.

((Zoöl.) (a) A large marine food fish (Serranus, orCentropristis, atrarius) which abounds on the Atlantic coast of theUnited States. It is dark bluish, with black bands, and more or lessvaried with small white spots and blotches. Called also, locally,blue bass, black sea bass, blackfish, bluefish, and black perch. (b)A California food fish (Cynoscion nobile); -- called also white seabass, and sea salmon.
Any large marine mammal, as a seal, walrus, or cetacean.
Any swimming bird frequenting the sea; a sea fowl.
A plant (Suæda maritima) of the Goosefoot family, growing insalt marches.
A breaking or overflow of a bank or a dike by the sea.L'Estrange.

Any one of several species of sparoid fishes, especially thecommon European species (Pagellus centrodontus), the Spanish (P.Oweni), and the black sea bream (Cantharus lineatus); -- called alsoold wife.
The captain of a vessel that sails upon the sea.
A chart or map on which the lines of the shore, islands,shoals, harbors, etc., are delineated.
A fleshy plant (Arenaria peploides) growing in large tufts inthe sands of the northern Atlantic seacoast; -- called also seasandwort, and sea purslane.

Any one of the large bivalve mollusks found on the openseacoast, especially those of the family Mactridæ, as the commonAmerican species. (Mactra, or Spisula, solidissima); -- called alsobeach clam, and surf clam.

Coal brought by sea; -- a name by which mineral coal wasformerly designated in the south of England, in distinction fromcharcoal, which was brought by land. Sea-coal facing (Founding),facing consisting of pulverized bituminous coal.

A magnificent palm (Lodoicea Sechellarum) found only in theSeychelles Islands. The fruit is an immense two-lobed nut. It wasfound floating in the Indian Ocean before the tree was known, andcalled sea cocoanut, and double cocoanut.
A large blackfish seaweed (Agarum Turneri), the frond of whichis punctured with many little holes.
The mariner's compass. See under Compass.
A yellow cylindrical mass of egg capsule of certain species ofwhelks (Buccinum), which resembles an ear of maize.
Any crustacean of the genus Palinurus and allied genera, as theEuropean spiny lobster (P. vulgaris), which is much used as anarticle of food. See Lobster.
Any large holothurian, especially one of those belonging to thegenus Pentacta, or Cucumaria, as the common American and Europeanspecies. (P. frondosa).
The little auk, or rotche. See Illust. of Rotche.

Any one of numerous species of ducks which frequent theseacoasts and feed mainly on fishes and mollusks. The scoters,eiders, old squaw, and ruddy duck are examples. They may bedistinguished by the lobate hind toe.

Any one of several species of fish-eating eagles of the genusHaliæetus and allied genera, as the North Pacific sea eagle. (H.pelagicus), which has white shoulders, head, rump, and tail; theEuropean white-tailed eagle (H. albicilla); and the Indian white-tailed sea eagle, or fishing eagle (Polioaëtus ichthyaëtus). The baldeagle and the osprey are also sometimes classed as sea eagles.

A very large seal (Macrorhinus proboscideus) of the Antarcticseas, much hunted for its oil. It sometimes attains a length ofthirty feet, and is remarkable for the prolongation of the nose ofthe adult male into an erectile elastic proboscis, about a foot inlength. Another species of smaller size (M. angustirostris) occurs onthe coast of Lower California, but is now nearly extinct.
Any gorgonian which branches in a fanlike form, especiallyGorgonia flabellum of Florida and the West Indies.
Any gorgonian which branches in a plumelike form.
Any gorgonian which branches like a fern.
An engagement between ships at sea; a naval battle.
A sertularian hydroid, especially Sertularia abietina, whichbranches like a miniature fir tree.
A sea anemone, or any related anthozoan.
Any bird which habitually frequents the sea, as an auk, gannet,gull, tern, or petrel; also, all such birds, collectively.
A hydroid coral of the genus Millepora, especially M.alcicornis, of the West Indies and Florida. So called because itstings the tongue like ginger. See Illust. under Millepore.
A kind of kelp (Laminaria digitata) with palmately cleftfronds; -- called also sea wand, seaware, and tangle.
A marine deity; a fabulous being supposed to live in, or havedominion over, the sea, or some particular sea or part of the sea, asNeptune.
A goddess supposed to live in or reign over the sea, or somepart of the sea.
A gown or frock with short sleeves, formerly worn by mariners.Shak.
The clusters of gelatinous egg capsules of a squid (Loligo).
The green color of sea water.
Any gull living on the seacoast.
Any tectibranchiate mollusk of the genus Aplysia. See Aplysia.
A low perennial plant (Frankenia lævis) resembling heath,growing along the seashore in Europe.
the common guillemot; -- applied also to various other seabirds.
An evergeen seashore plant (Eryngium maritimum). See Eryngium.
One of the leaders among the Norsemen who passed their lives inroving the seas in search of plunder and adventures; a Norse piratechief. See the Note under Viking.
A kind of seaweed (Chorda Filum) having blackish cordlikefronds, often many feet long.
The peculiar language or phraseology of seamen; sailor's cant.
The gray snapper. See under Snapper.
Legs able to maintain their possessor upright in stormy weatherat sea, that is, ability stand or walk steadily on deck when a vesselis rolling or pitching in a rough sea. [Sailor's Cant] Totten.
Any one of several species of nudibranchiate mollusks of thegenus Doris and allied genera, having a smooth, thick, convex yellowbody.
Any one of several species of spotted seals, especiallyOgmorhinus leptonyx, and Leptonychotes Weddelli, of the AntarcticOcean. The North Pacific sea leopard is the harbor seal.
The customary certificate of national character which neutralmerchant vessels are bound to carry in time of war; a passport for avessel and cargo.
The green papery fronds of several seaweeds of the genus Ulva,sometimes used as food.
The level of the surface of the sea; any surface on the samelevel with the sea.

Any one of several large species of seals of the familyOtariidæ native of the Pacific Ocean, especially the southern sealion (Otaria jubata) of the South American coast; the northern sealion (Eumetopias Stelleri) found from California to Japan; and theblack, or California, sea lion (Zalophus Californianus), which iscommon on the rocks near San Francisco.
Any one of numerous species of isopod crustaceans of Cymothoa,Livoneca, and allied genera, mostly parasites on fishes.
Land which borders on the sea; the seashore. Shak.You are near the sea marge of a land teeming with life. J. Burroughs.
Any bryozoan of the genus Flustra or allied genera which formfrondlike corals.
A low, fleshy perennial herb (Glaux maritima) found alongnorthern seashores.
Any branched marine bryozoan resembling moss.
A rich slimy deposit in salt marshes and along the seashore,sometimes used as a manure; -- called also sea ooze.
A large American holothurian (Lophothuria Fabricii) having abright orange convex body covered with finely granulated scales. Itsexpanded tentacles are bright red.

An aquatic carnivore (Enhydris lutris, or marina) found in theNorth Pacific Ocean. Its fur is highly valued, especially by theChinese. It is allied to the common otter, but is larger, with feetmore decidedly webbed. Sea-otter's cabbage (Bot.), a gigantic kelp ofthe Pacific Ocean (Nereocystis Lutkeana). See Nereocystis.
The gilthead (Crenilabrus melops), a fish of the Britishcoasts.
A document carried by neutral merchant vessels in time of war,to show their nationality; a sea letter or passport. See Passport.
A beautiful American ascidian (Cynthia, or Halocynthia,pyriformis) having the size, form, velvety surface, and color of aripe peach.
A pedunculated ascidian of the genus Boltonia.
The oyster catcher, a limicoline bird of the genus Hæmatopus.
A pool of salt water. Spenser.
The horn poppy. See under Horn.
Any fish of the genus Diodon, and allied genera, whose body iscovered with spines. See Illust. under Diodon.
An American compound ascidian (Amoræcium stellatum) which formslarge whitish masses resembling salt pork.
A port on the seashore, or one accessible for seagoing vessels.Also used adjectively; as, a seaport town.
The horny egg case of a skate, and of certain sharks.
The sea-sand reed. See under Reed.
Risk of injury, destruction, or loss by the sea, or while atsea.
See under Robin, and Illustration in Appendix.
Room or space at sea for a vessel to maneuver, drive, or scud,without peril of running ashore or aground. Totten.
One that cruises or roves the sea for plunder; a sea robber; apirate; also, a piratical vessel.
Common salt, obtained from sea water by evaporation.
Any marine saurian; esp. (Paleon.) the large extinct species ofMosasaurus, Icthyosaurus, Plesiosaurus, and related genera.
Any bryozoan which forms rounded or irregular patches of coralon stones, seaweeds, etc.
Any marine snake. See Sea snake.
Any isopod crustacean of the genus Ligia.

Any one of many species of venomous aquatic snakes of thefamily Hydrophidæ, having a flattened tail and living entirely in thesea, especially in the warmer parts of the Indian and Pacific Oceans.They feed upon fishes, and are mostly of moderate size, but somespecies become eight or ten feet long and four inches broad.
An ascidian. See Illust. under Tunicata.
A kind of seaweed; tang; tangle.To their nests of sedge and sea tang. Longfellow.
A term used specifically by seamen; a nautical word or phrase.
A kind of blackish seaweed (Himanthalia lorea) found on thenorthern coasts of the Atlantic. It has a thonglike forking processrising from a top-shaped base.
A great blackish seaweed of the Southern Ocean, having a hollowand expanding stem and a pinnate frond, sometimes twenty feet long.
A breeze, gale, or mist from the sea. Ham. Nav. Encyc.
Any one of numerous species of echinoderms of the orderEchinoidea.
A wall, or embankment, to resist encroachments of the sea.
A gorgonian having a simple stem.
A gorgonian coral with long flexible branches.
(Bot.) A kind of bindweed (Convolvulus Soldanella) growing onthe seacoast of Europe.
A European species of wormwood (Artemisia maritima) growing bythe sea.
Bordering on the sea; situated beside the sea. Drayton.
Built at, in, or by the sea.
Any species of ear-shaped shells of the genus Haliotis. SeeAbalone.
Of a beautiful bluish green color, like sea water on soundings.
Of or pertaining to certain islands along the coast of SouthCarolina and Georgia; as, sea-island cotton, a superior cotton oflong fiber produced on those islands.
, a. Cruising at random on the ocean.
Surrounded, bounded, or protected by the sea, as if by a wall.Shak.
A beach lying along the sea. "The bleak seabeach." Longfellow.
A green seaweed (Cladophora rupestris) growing in dense tufts.
The shore or border of the land adjacent to the sea or ocean.Also used adjectively.
One who follows the sea as a business; a mariner; a sailor.
Following the business of a mariner; as, a seafaring man.
Surrounded by the water of the sea or ocean; as, a seagirtisle. Milton.
Going upon the sea; especially, sailing upon the deep sea; --used in distinction from coasting or river, as applied to vessels.
A Jewish dry measure containing one third of an an ephah.
Soap prepared for use in milling cloth.
Any aquatic carnivorous mammal of the families Phocidæ andOtariidæ.
Of a rich dark brown color, like the fur of the fur seal afterit is dyed.
One who seals; especially, an officer whose duty it is to sealwrits or instruments, to stamp weights and measures, or the like.
A compound of the resinous materials, pigments, etc., used as amaterial for seals, as for letters, documents, etc.
The skin of a seal; the pelt of a seal prepared for use, esp.of the fur seal; also, a garment made of this material.
Grease; tallow; lard. [Obs. or prov. Eng.] Shak. Dryden.
A merman; the male of the mermaid. [R.] "Not to mentionmermaids or seamen." Locke.
Having or showing the skill of a practical seaman.
The skill of a good seaman; the art, or skill in the art, ofworking a ship.
Any elevated object on land which serves as a guide tomariners; a beacon; a landmark visible from the sea, as a hill, atree, a steeple, or the like. Shak.
Out of condition; not in good condition; -- said of a hawk.
The cord or rope at the margin of a seine, to which the meshesof the net are attached. Seaming machine, a machine for uniting theedges of sheet-metal plates by bending them and pinching themtogether.
Without a seam.Christ's seamless coat, all of a piece. Jer. Taylor.
One who sews well, or whose occupation is to sew. [Obs.]
A woman whose occupation is sewing; a needlewoman.
Having a seam; containing seams, or showing them. "Many a seamyscar." Burns.Everything has its fair, as well as its seamy, side. Sir W. Scott.
A session, as of some public body; especially, a meeting ofspiritualists to receive spirit communication, so called.
A bard among the Highlanders of Scotland, who preserved andrepeated the traditions of the tribes; also, a genealogist. [Writtenalso senachy.] [Scot.]
A picture representing a scene at sea; a marine picture.Addison.
The catch in a gunlock by which the hammer is held cocked orhalf cocked. Sear spring, the spring which causes the sear to catchin the notches by which the hammer is held.

To seek; to look for something; to make inquiry, exploration,or examination; to hunt.Once more search with me. Shak.It sufficeth that they have once with care sifted the matter, andsearched into all the particulars. Locke.

One who, or that which, searhes or examines; a seeker; aninquirer; an examiner; a trier. Specifically:(a) Formerly, an officer in London appointed to examine the bodies ofthe dead, and report the cause of death. Graunt.(b) An officer of the customs whose business it is to search ships,merchandise, luggage, etc.(c) An inspector of leather. [Prov. Eng.](d) (Gun.) An instrument for examining the bore of a cannon, todetect cavities.(e) An implement for sampling butter; a butter trier.(j) (Med.) An instrument for feeling after calculi in the bladder,etc.
Exploring thoroughly; scrutinizing; penetrating; trying; as, asearching discourse; a searching eye. "Piercing, searching, biting,cold." Dickens.-- Search"ing*ly, adv.-- Search"ing*ness, n.
Impossible to be searched; inscrutable; impenetrable.
Scorched; cauterized; hence, figuratively, insensible; notsusceptible to moral influences.A seared conscience and a remorseless heart. Macaulay.
The state of being seared or callous; insensibility. Bp. Hall.
A picture representing a scene at sea. [Jocose] Thackeray.
The shell of any marine mollusk.
All the ground between the ordinary highwater and low-watermarks.
The peculiar sickness, characterized by nausea and prostration,which is caused by the pitching or rolling of a vessel.
The land bordering on, or adjacent to, the sea; the seashore.Also used adjectively.

Occurring in good time, in due season, or in proper time forthe purpose; suitable to the season; opportune; timely; as, aseasonable supply of rain.Mercy is seasonable in the time of affliction. Ecclus. xxxv. 20.-- Sea"son*a*ble*ness, n.-- Sea"son*a*bly, adv.

Of or pertaining to the seasons. Seasonal dimorphism (Zoöl.),the condition of having two distinct varieties which appear atdifferent seasons, as certain species of butterflies in which thespring brood differs from the summer or autumnal brood.
One who, or that which, seasons, or gives a relish; aseasoning.
A part or surface on which another part or surface rests; as, avalve seat. Seat worm (Zoöl.), the pinworm.
Directed or situated toward the sea. Donne.Two still clouds . . . sparkled on their seaward edges like a frostedfleece. G. W. Cable.
Seaweed; esp., coarse seaweed. See Ware, and Sea girdles.
Any marine plant of the class Algæ, as kelp, dulse, Fucus,Ulva, etc.
The state or quality of being seaworthy, or able to resist theordinary violence of wind and weather. Kent.
Fit for a voyage; worthy of being trusted to transport a cargowith safety; as, a seaworthy ship.

Pertaining to, or secreting, fat; composed of fat; having theappearance of fat; as, the sebaceous secretions of some plants, orthe sebaceous humor of animals. Sebaceous cyst (Med.), a cyst formedby distention of a sebaceous gland, due to obstruction of itsexcretory duct.-- Sebaceous glands (Anat.), small subcutaneous glands, usuallyconnected with hair follicles. They secrete an oily semifluid matter,composed in great part of fat, which softens and lubricates the hairand skin.

Of or pertaining to fat; derived from, or resembling, fat;specifically, designating an acid (formerly called also sebic, andpyroleic, acid), obtained by the distillation or saponification ofcertain oils (as castor oil) as a white crystalline substance.
The eleventh month of the ancient Hebrew year, approximatelycorresponding with February. W. Smith (Bibl. Dict. ).
The mucilaginous drupaceous fruit of two East Indian trees(Cordia Myxa, and C. latifolia), sometimes used medicinally inpectoral diseases.
A morbidly increased discharge of sebaceous matter upon theskin; stearrhea.
A genus of cereal grasses including rye.
A cutting; an intersection; as, the point of secancy of oneline by another. [R.] Davies & Peck (Math. Dict. ).
Cutting; divivding into two parts; as, a secant line.
Dry. Secco painting, or Painting in secco, painting on dryplaster, as distinguished from fresco painting, which is on wet orfresh plaster.
To withdraw from fellowship, communion, or association; toseparate one's self by a solemn act; to draw off; to retire;especially, to withdraw from a political or religious body.
One of a numerous body of Presbyterians in Scotland who secededfrom the communion of the Established Church, about the year 1733,and formed the Secession Church, so called.
To secrete; as, mucus secerned in the nose. Arbuthnot.
The act or process of secreting.
Retirement; retreat; secession. [Obs.] R. H. More.
The withdrawal of a State from the national Union. SecessionChurch (in Scotland). See Seceder.
The doctrine or policy of secession; the tenets of secession;the tenets of secessionists.
One who holds to the belief that a State has the right toseparate from the Union at its will.

The edible fruit of a West Indian plant (Sechium edule) of theGourd family. It is soft, pear-shaped, and about four inches long,and contains a single large seed. The root of the plant resembles ayam, and is used for food.
Barren; unprofitable. See Rent seck, under Rent.
A small reddish brown sweet and juicy pear. It originated on afarm near Philadelphia, afterwards owned by a Mr. Seckel.

The act of secluding, or the state of being secluded;separation from society or connection; a withdrawing; privacy; as, tolive in seclusion.O blest seclusion from a jarring world, which he, thus occupied,enjoys! Cowper.
Tending to seclude; keeping in seclusion; secluding;sequestering.
An article of merchandise of a grade inferior to the best;esp., a coarse or inferior kind of flour.
Of the rank or degree below the best highest; inferior; second-rate; as, a second-class house; a second-class passage.
Of the second size, rank, quality, or value; as, a second-rateship; second-rate cloth; a second-rate champion. Dryden.

The power of discerning what is not visible to the physicaleye, or of foreseeing future events, esp. such as are of a disastrouskind; the capacity of a seer; prophetic vision.he was seized with a fit of second-sight. Addison.Nor less availed his optic sleight, And Scottish gift of second-sight. Trumbull.
Having the power of second-sight. Addison.
The state of being secondary.Full of a girl's sweet sense of secondariness to the object of herlove. Mrs. Oliphant.
Possessing some quality, or having been subject to someoperation (as substitution), in the second degree; as, a secondarysalt, a secondary amine, etc. Cf. primary.
One who seconds or supports what another attempts, affirms,moves, or proposes; as, the seconder of an enterprise or of a motion.
The second part in a concerted piece.
Secret; secretive; faithful to a secret. [Obs.]To be holden stable and secre. Chaucer.

The parts which modesty and propriety require to be concealed;the genital organs. In secret, in a private place; in privacy orsecrecy; in a state or place not seen; privately.Bread eaten in secret is pleasant. Prov. ix. 17.

The detective service of a government. In the United States, intime of peace the bureau of secret service is under the treasurydepartment, and in time of war it aids the war department in securinginformation concerning the movements of the enemy.
A process in which mercury, or some of its salts, is employedto impart the property of felting to certain kinds of furs. Ure.
Of or pertaining to a secretary; befitting a secretary. [R.]Secretarial, diplomatic, or other official training. Carlyle.

The secretary bird. Secretary Bird. Etym: [So called inallusion to the tufts of feathers at the back of its head, which werefancifully thought to resemble pens stuck behind the ear.] (Zoöl.) Alarge long-legged raptorial bird (Gypogeranus serpentarius), nativeof South Africa, but now naturalized in the West Indies and someother tropical countries. It has a powerful hooked beak, a crest oflong feathers, and a long tail. It feeds upon reptiles of variouskinds, and is much prized on account of its habit of killing anddevouring snakes of all kinds. Called also serpent eater.
The office, or the term of office, of a secretary.

To separate from the blood and elaborate by the process ofsecretion; to elaborate and emit as a secretion. See Secretion.Why one set of cells should secrete bile, another urea, and so on, wedo not known. Carpenter.

The act of secreting; the process by which material isseparated from the blood through the agency of the cells of thevarious glands and elaborated by the cells into new substances so asto form the various secretions, as the saliva, bile, and otherdigestive fluids. The process varies in the different glands, andhence are formed the various secretions.
Parted by animal secretion; as, secretitious humors. Floyer.
Tending to secrete, or to keep secret or private; as, asecretive disposition.
The faculty or propensity which impels to reserve, secrecy, orconcealment.
Causing secretion; -- said of nerves which go to glands andinfluence secretion.
Secreting; performing, or connected with, the office secretion;secernent; as, secretory vessels, nerves.-- n.
One of the portions of space bounded by the three coordinateplanes. Specif. (Crystallog.), one of the parts of a crystal intowhich it is divided by the axial planes.
Pertaining to a sect, or to sects; peculiar to a sect;bigotedly attached to the tenets and interests of a denomination; as,sectarian principles or prejudices.
The quality or character of a sectarian; devotion to theinterests of a party; excess of partisan or denominational zeal;adherence to a separate church organization.
To imbue with sectarian feelings; to subject to the control ofa sect.

A sectarian; a member or adherent of a sect; a follower ordisciple of some particular teacher in philosophy or religion; onewho separates from an established church; a dissenter.I never knew that time in England when men of truest religion werenot counted sectaries. Milton.
A follower; a disciple; an adherent to a sect. [Obs.] Sir W.Raleigh.
Capable of being cut; specifically (Min.), capable of beingsevered by the knife with a smooth cut; -- said of minerals.
The state or quality of being sectile.

The figure made up of all the points common to a superficiesand a solid which meet, or to two superficies which meet, or to twolines which meet. In the first case the section is a superficies, inthe second a line, and in the third a point.
A disproportionate regard for the interests peculiar to asection of the country; local patriotism, as distinguished fromnational. [U. S.]
The state or quality of being sectional; sectionalism.
To divide according to gepgraphical sections or localinterests. [U. S.]The principal results of the struggle were to sectionalize parties.Nicilay & Hay (Life of Lincoln).
One devoted to a sect; a soetary. [R.]
A little or petty sect. [R.] "Some new sect or sectiuncle." J.Martineau.
A part of a circle comprehended between two radii and theincluded arc.
Of or pertaining to a sector; as, a sectoral circle.

Not regular; not bound by monastic vows or rules; not confinedto a monastery, or subject to the rules of a religious community; as,a secular priest.He tried to enforce a stricter discipline and greater regard formorals, both in the religious orders and the secular clergy.Prescett.

One who theoretically rejects every form of religious faith,and every kind of religious worship, and accepts only the facts andinfluences which are derived from the present life; also, one whobelieves that education and other matters of civil policy should bemanaged without the introduction of a religious element.
Supreme attention to the things of the present life;worldliness.A secularity of character which makes Christianity and its principaldoctrines distasteful or unintelligible. I. Taylor.

The act of rendering secular, or the state of being renderedsecular; conversion from regular or monastic to secular; conversionfrom religious to lay or secular possession and uses; as, thesecularization of church property.
In a secular or worldly manner.
The quality or state of being secular; worldliness; worldly-minded-ness.
Arranged on one side only, as flowers or leaves on a stalk.Gray.
The second coat, or integument, of an ovule, lying within theprimine.
A right of inheritance belonging to a second son; a property orpossession so inherited.The kingdom of Naples . . . was constituted a secundo-geniture ofSpain. Bancroft.
In a secure manner; without fear or apprehension; withoutdanger; safely.His daring foe . . . securely him defied. Milton.
The act of securing; protection. [R.]Society condemns the securement in all cases of perpetual protectionby means of perpetual imprisonment. C. A. Ives.
The condition or quality of being secure; exemption from fear;want of vigilance; security.
One who, or that which, secures.
Having the form of an ax hatchet.
One of a family of beetles having the maxillary palpiterminating in a hatchet-shaped joint.
A portable chair or covered vehicle for carrying a singleperson, -- usually borne on poles by two men. Called also sedanchair.

Undisturbed by passion or caprice; calm; tranquil; serene; notpassionate or giddy; composed; staid; as, a sedate soul, mind, ortemper.Disputation carries away the mind from that calm and sedate temperwhich is so necessary to contemplate truth. I. Watts.Whatsoever we feel and know Too sedate for outward show. Wordsworth.
The act of calming, or the state of being calm. [R.] Coles.
Tending to calm, moderate, or tranquilize; specifically (Med.),allaying irritability and irritation; assuaging pain.

Remaining in one place, especially when firmly attached to someobject; as, the oyster is a sedentary mollusk; the barnacles aresedentary crustaceans. Sedentary spider (Zoöl.), one of a tribe ofspiders which rest motionless until their prey is caught in theirweb.

A sitting, as of a court or other body.'T is pity we have not Burn's own account of that long sederunt.Prof. Wilson.Acts of sederunt (Scots Law), ordinances of the Court of Session forthe ordering of processes and expediting of justice. Bell.

Any plant of the genus Carex, perennial, endogenous herbs,often growing in dense tufts in marshy places. They have triangularjointless stems, a spiked inflorescence, and long grasslike leaveswhich are usually rough on the margins and midrib. There are severalhundred species.
Made or composed of sedge.With your sedged crowns and ever-harmless looks. Shak.
Overgrown with sedge.On the gentle Severn''s sedgy bank. Shak.
Seats in the chancel of a church near the altar for theofficiating clergy during intervals of service. Hook.
The material of which sedimentary rocks are formed.
Of or pertaining to sediment; formed by sediment; containingmatter that has subsided. Sedimentary rocks. (Geol.) See Aqueousrocks, under Aqueous.
The act of depositing a sediment; specifically (Geol.), thedeposition of the material of which sedimentary rocks are formed.
An inciter or promoter of sedition. Bp. Hall.

One who, or that which, seduces; specifically, one who prevailsover the chastity of a woman by enticements and persuasions.He whose firm faith no reason could remove, Will melt before thatsoft seducer, love. Dryden.
Seductive. "Thy sweet seducing charms." Cowper.-- Se*du"cing*ly, adv.
Tending to lead astray; apt to mislead by flatteringappearances; tempting; alluring; as, a seductive offer.This may enable us to understand how seductive is the influence ofexample. Sir W. Hamilton.

The quality or state of being sedulous; diligent and assiduousapplication; constant attention; unremitting industry; sedulousness.The industrious bee, by his sedulity in summer, lives in honey allthe winter. Feltham.

Diligent in application or pursuit; constant, steady, andpersevering in business, or in endeavors to effect an object;steadily industrious; assiduous; as, the sedulous bee.What signifies the sound of words in prayer, without the affection ofthe heart, and a sedulous application of the proper means that maynaturally lead us to such an end L'Estrange.
A genus of plants, mostly perennial, having succulent leavesand cymose flowers; orpine; stonecrop. Gray.
The generative fluid of the male; semen; sperm; -- not used inthe plural.
A species of lac. See the Note under Lac.
A sweet cake or cooky containing aromatic seeds, as caraway.Tusser.
One who, or that which, sows or plants seed.

The quality or state of being seedy, shabby, or worn out; astate of wretchedness or exhaustion. [Colloq.] G. Eliot.What is called seedness, after a debauch, is a plain proof thatnature has been outraged. J. S. Blackie.
A plant reared from the seed, as distinguished from onepropagated by layers, buds, or the like.
The season proper for sowing.While the earth remaineth, seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat,and summer and winter, and day and night, shall not cease. Gen. viii.22.

(but originally a present participle). In view of the fact(that); considering; taking into account (that); insmuch as; since;because; -- followed by a dependent clause; as, he did well, seeingthat he was so young.Wherefore come ye to me, seeing ye hate me Gen. xxvi. 27.
A kind of choice winter apple, having a subacid taste; --formerly called go-no-further.
One who contrives to give himself vexation. [Archaic.] Sir P.Sidney.

One of a small heterogeneous sect of the 17th century, in GreatBritain, who professed to be seeking the true church, ministry, andsacraments.A skeptic [is] ever seeking and never finds, like our new upstartsect of Seekers. Bullokar.

To close the eyes of (a hawk or other bird) by drawing throughthe lids threads which were fastened over the head. Bacon.Fools climbs to fall: fond hopes, like seeled doves for want ofbetter light, mount till they end their flight with falling. J.Reading.

To appear, or to appear to be; to have a show or semblance; topresent an appearance; to look; to strike one's apprehension or fancyas being; to be taken as. "It now seemed probable." Macaulay.Thou picture of what thou seem'st. Shak.All seemed well pleased; all seemed, but were not all. Milton.There is a way which seemeth right unto a man; but the end thereofare the ways of death. Prov. xiv. 12.It seems, it appears; it is understood as true; it is said.A prince of Italy, it seems, entertained his misstress on a greatlake. Addison.
One who seems; one who carries or assumes an appearance orsemblance.Hence shall we see, If power change purpose, what our seemers be.Shak.

Having a semblance, whether with or without reality; apparent;specious; befitting; as, seeming friendship; seeming truth.My lord, you have lost a friend indeed; And I dare swear you borrownot that face Of seeming sorrow, it is sure your own. Shak.
In appearance; in show; in semblance; apparently; ostensibly.This the father seemingly complied with. Addison.
Semblance; fair appearance; plausibility. Sir K. Digby.
The quality or state of being seemly: comeliness; propriety.

Suited to the object, occasion, purpose, or character;suitable; fit; becoming; comely; decorous.He had a seemly nose. Chaucer.I am a woman, lacking wit To make a seemly answer to such persons.Shak.Suspense of judgment and exercise of charity were safer and seemlierfor Christian men than the hot pursuit of these controversies.Hooker.
Comely or decent appearance. [Obs.] Rom. of R. Spenser.
A scombroid food fish of Maderia (Cybium Commersonii).
A kind of muslin of a texture between nainsook and mull.
The office or quality of a seer.
A light fabric, originally made in the East Indies, of silk andlinen, usually having alternating stripes, and a slightly craped orpuckered surface; also, a cotton fabric of similar appearance.
To decoct or prepare for food in hot liquid; to boil; as, toseethe flesh. [Written also seeth.]Set on the great pot, and seethe pottage for the sons of theprophets. 2 Kings iv. 38.
A pot for boiling things; a boiler.Like burnished gold the little seether shone. Dryden.
A castrated bull. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.] Halliwell.
A case or holder made of fire clay, in which fine pottery isinclosed while baking in the kin. [Written also saggar, sagger, andsegger.] Ure.

A part cut off from a figure by a line or plane; especially,that part of a circle contained between a chord and an arc of thatcircle, or so much of the circle as is cut off by the chord; as, thesegment acb in the Illustration.

The act or process of dividing into segments; specifically(Biol.), a self-division into segments as a result of growth; cellcleavage; cell multiplication; endogenous cell formation.Segmentation cavity (Biol.), the cavity formed by the arrangement ofthe cells in segmentation or cleavage of the ovum; the cavity of theblastosphere. In the gastrula stage, the segmentation cavity in whichthe mesoblast is formed lies between the entoblast and ectoblast. SeeIllust. of Invagination.-- Segmentation nucleus (Biol.), the body formed by fusion of themale and female pronucleus in an impregnated ovum. See the Note underPronucleus.-- Segmentation of the ovum, or Egg cleavage (Biol.), the process bywhich the embryos of all the higher plants and animals are derivedfrom the germ cell. In the simplest case, that of small ova destituteof food yolk, the ovum or egg divides into two similar halves orsegments (blastomeres), each of these again divides into two, and soon, thus giving rise to a mass of cells (mulberry mass, or morula),all equal and similar, from the growth and development of which thefuture animal is to be formed. This constitutes regular segmentation.Quite frequently, however, the equality and regularity of cleavage isinterfered with by the presence of food yolk, from which resultsunequal segmentation. See Holoblastic, Meroblastic, Alecithal,Centrolecithal, Ectolecithal, and Ovum.-- Segmentation sphere (Biol.), the blastosphere, or morula. SeeMorula.
Divided into segments or joints; articulated.
A sign. See Al segno, and Dal segno.
A liliaceous plant (Calochortus Nuttallii) of Western NorthAmerica, and its edible bulb; -- so called by the Ute Indians and theMormons.
Separated from others of the same kind.
Separation from a mass, and gathering about centers or intocavities at hand through cohesive attraction or the crystallizingprocess.
Local oscillations in level observed in the case of some lakes,as Lake Geneva.
A descendant of Mohammed through his daughter Fatima and nephewAli.

Of or pertaining to Seidlitz, a village in Bohemia. [Writtenalso Sedlitz.] Seidlitz powders, effervescing salts, consisting oftwo separate powders, one of which contains forty grains of sodiumbicarbonate mixed with two drachms of RochellRochelle powders.-- Seidlitz water, a natural water from Seidlitz, containingmagnesium, sodium, calcium, and potassium sulphates, with calciumcarbonate and a little magnesium chloride. It is used as an aperient.
obs. imp. sing. of See. Saw. Chaucer.
Of or pertaining to a seignior; seigneurial. "Kingly orseignioral patronage." Burke.
The territory or authority of a seignior, or lord. Milman.
To lord it over. [Obs.]As proud as he that seigniorizeth hell. Fairfax.

A large net, one edge of which is provided with sinkers, andthe other with floats. It hangs vertically in the water, and when itsends are brought together or drawn ashore incloses the fish. Seineboat, a boat specially constructed to carry and pay out a seine.
One who fishes with a seine.
A girdle. [Obs.] "Girt with a seint of silk." Chaucer.
One of several spores arranged in a chain as in certain algæ ofthe genus Callithamnion.
The trace or record of an earth tremor, made by means of aseismograph.
An apparatus for registering the shocks and undulatory motionsof earthquakes.
Of or pertaining to a seismograph; indicated by a seismograph.
Of or pertaining to seismology.-- Seis`mo*log"ic*al*ly, adv.
An instrument for measuring the direction, duration, and forceof earthquakes and like concussions.
Of or pertaining to seismometry, or seismometer; as,seismometric instruments; seismometric measurements.
The mensuration of such phenomena of earthquakes as can beexpressed in numbers, or by their relation to the coördinates ofspace.
Something peculiar to one's self. [R.] Tatler.
To take possession of by virtue of a warrant or other legalauthority; as, the sheriff seized the debtor's goods.
One who, or that which, seizes.

Possession; possession of an estate of froehold. It may beeither in deed or in law; the former when there is actual possession,the latter when there is a right to such possession by constructionof law. In some of the United States seizin means merely ownership.Burrill.
One who seizes, or takes possession.
Sitting, as a lion or other beast. Sejant rampant, sitting withthe forefeet lifted up. Wright.
The act of disjoining, or the state of being disjoined. [Obs.]Bp. Pearson.
Capable of being disjoined. [Obs.] Bp. Pearson.
A place in a pagan temple in which the images of the deitieswere inclosed.
One of the Selachii. See Illustration in Appendix.
An order of elasmobranchs including the sharks and rays; thePlagiostomi. Called also Selacha, Selache, and Selachoidei.
A division of ganoid fishes which includes the paddlefish, inwhich the mouth is armed with small teeth.
A genus of cryptogamous plants resembling Lycopodia, butproducing two kinds of spores; also, any plant of this genus. Manyspecies are cultivated in conservatories.

A word of doubtful meaning, occuring frequently in the Psalms;by some, supposed to signify silence or a pause in the musicalperformance of the song.Beyond the fact that Selach is a musical term, we know absolutelynothing about it. Dr. W. Smith (Bib. Dict.)
Rarely known; unusual; strange. [Obs.][She] wondered much at his so selcouth case. Spenser.
Rarely; not often; not frequently.Wisdom and youth are seldom joined in one. Hooker.

Taken from a number by preferance; picked out as more valuableor exellent than others; of special value or exellence; nicelychosen; selected; choice.A few select spirits had separated from the crowd, and formed a fitaudience round a far greater teacher. Macaulay.
The act of selecting, or the state of being selected; choice,by preference.
Selecting; tending to select.This selective providence of the Almighty. Bp. Hall.

One of a board of town officers chosen annually in the NewEngland States to transact the general public business of the town,and have a kind of executive authority. The number is usually fromthree to seven in each town.The system of delegated town action was then, perhaps, the same whichwas defined in an "order made in 1635 by the inhabitants ofCharlestown at a full meeting for the government of the town, byselectmen;" the name presently extended throughout New England tomunicipal governors. Palfrey.
The quality or state of being select.
A salt of selenic acid; -- formerly called also seleniate.
Of, pertaining to, or designating, hydrogen selenide, H2Se,regarded as an acid analogous to sulphydric acid.
Of or pertaining to selenium; derived from, or containing,selenium; specifically, designating those compounds in which theelement has a higher valence as contrasted with selenious compounds.
A binary compound of selenium, or a compound regarded asbinary; as, ethyl selenide.
Containing, or impregnated with, selenium; as, seleniferouspyrites.
A combining form (also used adjectively) denoting the presenceof selenium or its compounds; as, selenio-phosphate, a phosphatehaving selenium in place of all, or a part, of the oxygen.
Of, pertaining to, or containing, selenium; specifically,designating those compounds in which the element has a lower valenceas contrasted with selenic compounds.

A nonmetallic element of the sulphur group, and analogous tosulphur in its compounds. It is found in small quantities withsulphur and some sulphur ores, and obtained in the free state as adark reddish powder or crystalline mass, or as a dark metallic-looking substance. It exhibits under the action of light a remarkablevariation in electric conductivity, and is used in certain electricapparatus. Symbol Se. Atomic weight 78.9.
Combined with selenium as in a selenide; as, seleniuretedhydrogen. [Written also seleniuretted.] [Obsoles.]
As seen or estimated from the center of the moon; with the mooncentral.
, n. A picture or delineation of the moon's surface, or of anypart of it.
The science that treats of the physical features of the moon; -- corresponding to physical geography in respect to the earth."Accurate selenography, or description of the moon." Sir T. Browne.
That branch of astronomy which treats of the moon.-- Sel`e*no*log"i*cal, a.
A hypothetical radical of selenium, analogous to sulphonium.[R.]

Same; particular; very; identical. [Obs., except in thecompound selfsame.] "On these self hills." Sir. W. Raleigh.To shoot another arrow that self way Which you did shoot the first.Shak.At that self moment enters Palamon. Dryden.
Humbled by consciousness of inferiority, unworthiness, guilt,or shame.
Accused by one's self or by one's conscience. "Die self-accused." Cowper.

Acting of or by one's self or by itself; -- said especially ofa machine or mechanism which is made to perform of or for itself whatis usually done by human agency; automatic; as, a self-acting feedapparatus; a self-acting mule; a self-acting press.
Action by, or originating in, one's self or itself.
Acting of one's self or of itself; acting without depending onother agents.
The quality or state of being self-active; self-action.

Capable of assuming a desired position or condition withrelation to other parts, under varying circumstances, withoutrequiring to be adjusted by hand; -- said of a piece in machinery.Self-adjusting bearing (Shafting), a bearing which is supported insuch a manner that it may tip to accomodate flexure or displacementof the shaft.
One's own affairs; one's private business. [Obs.] Shak.
Frightened at or by one's self. Shak.
Annihilation by one's own acts; annihilation of one's desires.Addison.
Applying to or by one's self.
Approving one's own action or character by one's own judgment.One self-approving hour whole years outweighs Of stupid starers andof loud huzzas. Pope.
asserting one's self, or one's own rights or claims; hence,putting one's self forward in a confident or assuming manner.
The act of asserting one's self, or one's own rights or claims;the quality of being self-asserting.
Assumed by one's own act, or without authority.
Assured by or of one's self; self-reliant; complacent.
Begotten by one's self, or one's own powers.
A reaping machine containing mechanism for binding the graininto sheaves.
Born or produced by one's self.
The quality or state of being self-centered.
A color not mixed or variegated.
Being of a single color; -- applied to flowers, animals, andtextile fabrics.
Control over one's own feelings, temper, etc.; self-control.
Imparting or communicating by its own powers.
Communion with one's self; thoughts about one's self.
The quality of being self-complacent. J. Foster.
Satisfied with one's own character, capacity, and doings; self-satisfied.
Conceit of one's self; an overweening opinion of one's powersor endowments.
Having an overweening opinion of one's own powers, attainments;vain; conceited.-- Self`-con*ceit"ed*ness, n.
Condemnation of one's self by one's own judgment.
The quality or state of being self-confident; self-reliance.A feeling of self-confidence which supported and sustained him.Beaconsfield.
Confident of one's own strength or powers; relying on one'sjudgment or ability; self-reliant.-- Self`-con"fi*dent*ly, adv.
Having the two things that are conjugate parts of the samefigure; as, self-conjugate triangles.
The quality or state of being self-conscious.
Considering in one's own mind; deliberating. Pope.
The quality or state of being self-consistent.
Consistent with one's self or with itself; not deviation fromthe ordinary standard by which the conduct is guided; logicallyconsistent throughout; having each part consistent with the rest.

Having all the essential working parts connected by a bedplateor framework, or contained in a case, etc., so that mutual relationsof the parts do not depend upon fastening outside of the machineitself. Self-contained steam engine. (a) A steam engine having bothbearings for the crank shaft attached to the frame of the engine. (b)A steam engine and boiler combined and fastened together; a portablesteam engine.

The act of contradicting one's self or itself; repugnancy inconceptions or in terms; a proposition consisting of two members, oneof which contradicts the other; as, to be and not to be at the sametime is a self-contradiction.
Control of one's self; restraint exercised over one's self;self-command.
Convicted by one's own consciousness, knowledge, avowal, oracts.
The act of convicting one's self, or the state of being self-convicted.
Created by one's self; not formed or constituted by another.
Culture, training, or education of one's self by one's ownefforts.
The act of deceiving one's self, or the state of being self-deceived; self-deception.
Deceived or misled respecting one's self by one's own mistakeor error.

The act of defending one's own person, property, or reputation.In self-defense (Law), in protection of self, -- it being permittedin law to a party on whom a grave wrong is attempted to resist thewrong, even at the peril of the life of the assailiant. Wharton.
Defending, or tending to defend, one's own person, property, orreputation.
The act of degrading one's self, or the state of being sodegraded.
The act of deluding one's self, or the state of being thusdeluded.
The denial of one's self; forbearing to gratify one's owndesires; self-sacrifice.
Refusing to gratify one's self; self-sacrificing.-- Self`-de*ny"ing*ly, adv.
Dependent on one's self; self-depending; self-reliant.
Corrupted or depraved by one's self. Milton.
One who destroys himself; a suicide.
The destruction of one's self; self-murder; suicide. Milton.
Destroying, or tending to destroy, one's self or itself;rucidal.
Determination by one's self; or, determination of one's acts orstates without the necessitating force of motives; -- applied to thevoluntary or activity.
Capable of self-determination; as, the self-determining powerof will.
Devoted in person, or by one's own will. Hawthorne.
The act of devoting one's self, or the state of being self-devoted; willingness to sacrifice one's own advantage or happinessfor the sake of others; self-sacrifice.
Devouring one's self or itself. Danham.
Having power to diffuse itself; diffusing itself. Norris.
Correction or government of one's self for the sake ofimprovement.
Want of confidence in one' self; diffidence.
Educated by one's own efforts, without instruction, or withoutpecuniary assistance from others.
Having the right of electing one's self, or, as a body, ofelecting its own members.
The holding a good opinion of one's self; self-complacency.
The act of estimating one's self; self-esteem.
The quality or state of being self-evident. Locke.
Evident without proof or reasoning; producing certainty orconviction upon a bare presentation to the mind; as, a self-evidentproposition or truth.-- Self`-ev"i*dent*ly, adv.
Evolution of one's self; development by inherent quality orpower.
The act of exalting one's self, or the state of being soexalted.
One who examines himself; one given to self-examination.The humiliated self-examinant feels that there is evil in our natureas well as good. Coleridge.
An examination into one's own state, conduct, and motives,particularly in regard to religious feelings and duties.
To energize or excite (the field magnets of a dynamo) byinduction from the residual magnetism of its cores, leading all or apart of the current thus produced through the field-magnet coils.
Inherent existence; existence possessed by virtue of a being'sown nature, and independent of any other being or cause; -- anattribute peculiar to God. Blackmore.
Existing of or by himself,independent of any other being orcause; -- as, God is the only self-existent being.
Explaining itself; capable of being understood withoutexplanation.
The act of exposing one's self; the state of being so exposed.
The fertilization of a flower by pollen from the same flowerand without outer aid; autogamy.
Fertilized by pollen from the same flower.
Springing from vainglory or vanity; vain; boastful. Dryden.

Designating, or pert. to, any of various steels that hardenwhen heated to above a red heat and cooled in air, usually in a blastof cold air with moderate rapidity, without quenching. Such steelsare alloys of iron and carbon with manganese, tungsten and manganese,chromium, molybdenum and manganese, etc. They are chiefly used ashigh-speed steels. -- Self`-hard"en*ed, a.
A blue-flowered labiate plant (Brunella vulgaris); the healall.
Having the power or property of healing itself.
The act of aiding one's self, without depending on the aid ofothers.
The act of killing one's self; suicide. Hakewill.
Ignorance of one's own character, powers, and limitations.
Imparting by one's own, or by its own, powers and will. Norris.
An exaggerated estimate of one's own importance or merit, esp.as manifested by the conduct or manners; self-conceit.
Having or manifesting an exaggerated idea of one's ownimportance or merit.
Voluntarily taken on one's self; as, self-imposed tasks.
Imposture practiced on one's self; self-deceit. South.
Indignation at one's own character or actions. Baxter.

Induction in a circuit due to the action of one portion of acurrent upon an adjacent portion during periods of varying currentstrength. The nature of the induction is such as to oppose the actionwhich produces it.
Indulgence of one's appetites, desires, or inclinations; -- theopposite of self-restraint, and self-denial.
Indulging one's appetites, desires, etc., freely.
Private interest; the interest or advantage of one's self.
Particularly concerned for one's own interest or happiness.
Involution in one's self; hence, abstraction of thought;reverie.
One who excuses or justifies himself. J. M. Mason.
Kindled of itself, or without extraneous aid or power. Dryden.
Knowledge of one's self, or of one's own character, powers,limitations, etc.
Life for one's self; living solely or chiefly for one's ownpleasure or good.
The love of one's self; desire of personal happiness; tendencyto seek one's own benefit or advantage. Shak.Self-love, the spring of motion, acts the soul. Pope.
Possessing in itself the property of emitting light. Sir D.Brewster.
Made by one's self. Self-made man, a man who has risen frompoverty or obscurity by means of his own talentss or energies.
Inborn mettle or courage; one's own temper. [Obs.] Shak.
Motion given by inherent power, without external impulse;spontaneus or voluntary motion.Matter is not induced with self-motion. Cheyne.
Moved by inherent power., without the aid of external impulse.
Moving by inherent power, without the aid of external impulse.
A neglecting of one's self, or of one's own interests.Self-love, my liege, is not so vile a sin As self-neglecting. Shak.
Opinion, especially high opinion, of one's self; an overweeningestimate of one's self or of one's own opinion. Collier.
Having a high opinion of one's self; opinionated; conceited.South.
Beginning wwith, or springing from, one's self.
That partiality to himself by which a man overrates his ownworth when compared with others. Kames.
Perplexed by doubts originating in one's own mind.
Disposed or arranged by an action originating in one's self orin itself.These molecular blocks of salt are self-posited. Tyndall.
The act of disposing or arranging one's self or itself.The self-positing of the molecules. R. Watts.
Composed or tranquill in mind, manner, etc.; undisturbed.
The possession of one's powers; calmness; self-command;presence of mind; composure.
The preservation of one's self from destruction or injury.
Propagating by one's self or by itself.

Registering itself; -- said of any instrument so contrived asto record its own indications of phenomena, whether continuously orat stated times, as at the maxima and minima of variations; as, aself-registering anemometer or barometer.
Regulated by one's self or by itself.
Tending or serving to regulate one's self or itself. Whewell.
Reliance on one's own powers or judgment; self-trust.
Reliant upon one's self; trusting to one's own powers orjudgment.
The act of renouncing, or setting aside, one's own wishes,claims, etc.; self-sacrifice.
The quality or state of being self-repelling.
Made up of parts, as molecules or atoms, which mutually repeleach other; as, gases are self-repelling.
Repetition of one's self or of one's acts; the saying or doingwhat one has already said or done.
The act of reproaching one's self; censure by one's ownconscience.
Reproached by one's own conscience or judgment.
The act of reproving one's self; censure of one's conduct byone's own judgment.
Reproved by one's own conscience or one's own sense of guilt.
Reproving one's self; reproving by consciousness of guilt.
Respect for one's self; regard for one's character; laudableself-esteem.
Restrained by one's self or itself; restrained by one's ownpower or will.
Restraint over one's self; self-control; self-command.
A reverent respect for one's self. Tennyson.
Righteous in one's own esteem; pharisaic.
The quality or state of being self-righteous; pharisaism.
The act of sacrificing one's self, or one's interest, forothers; self-devotion.
Yielding up one's own interest, ffeelings, etc; sacrificingone's self.
The quality or state of being self-satisfied.
Satisfied with one's self or one's actions; self-complacent.
One who seeks only his own interest, advantage, or pleasure.
Seeking one's own interest or happiness; selfish. Arbuthnot.

A mechanism (usually one operated by electricity, compressedair, a spring, or an explosive gas), attached to an internal-combustion engine, as on an automobile, and used as a means ofstarting the engine without cranking it by hand.
The quality or state of being self-sufficient.
Sufficing for one's self or for itself, without needingexternal aid; self-sufficient.-- Self`-suf*fi"cing*ness, n. J. C. Shairp.
Suspended by one's self or by itself; balanced. Southey.
Suspicious or distrustful of one's self. Baxter.
The act of inflicting pain on one's self; pain inflicted onone's self.
One with itself; separate from others. [Obs.] Sylvester.
A view if one's self; specifically, carefulness or regard forone's own interests
One's own will, esp. when opposed to that of others; obstinacy.
Governed by one's own will; not yielding to the wishes ofothers; obstinate.
The idolizing of one's self; immoderate self-conceit.
Wrong done by a person himself. Shak.
Existence as a separate self, or independent person; consciouspersonality; individuality. Bib. Sacra.
Believing or teaching that the chief motives of human actionare derived from love of self.Hobbes and the selfish school of philosophers. Fleming.
In a selfish manner; with regard to private interest only orchiefly.

The quality or state of being selfish; exclusive regard toone's own interest or happiness; that supreme self-love or self-preference which leads a person to direct his purposes to theadvancement of his own interest, power, or happiness, withoutregarding those of others.Selfishness,- a vice utterly at variance with the happiness of himwho harbors it, and, as such, condemned by self-love. Sir J.Mackintosh.
Concentration of one's interests on one's self; self-love;selfishness. Emerson.
Having no regard to self; unselfish.Lo now, what hearts have men! they never mount As high as woman inher selfless mood. Tennyson.
Quality or state of being selfless.
Precisely the same; the very same; identical.His servant was healed in the selfsame hour. Matt. viii. 13.
A short piece of land in arable ridges and furrows, ofuncertain quantity; also, a ridge of land lying between two furrows.[Obs. or Prov. Eng.]

Of or pertaining to Seljuk, a Tartar chief who embracedMohammedanism, and began the subjection of Western Asia to that faithand rule; of or pertaining to the dynasty founded by him, or theempire maintained by his descendants from the 10th to the 13thcentury. J. H. Newman.
A mineral water from Sellers, in the district of Nassan,Germany, containing much free carbonic acid.
A skein or hank of rope yarns wound round with yarns ormarline, -- used for stoppers, straps, etc.
A division of Discophora having large free mouth lobes. Itincludes Aurelia, and Pelagia. Called also Semeostoma. See Illustr.under Discophora, and Medusa.
A signal telegraph; an apparatus for giving signals by thedisposition of lanterns, flags, oscillating arms, etc.
One who manages or operates a semaphore.
The science of meanings or sense development (of words); theexplanation of the development and changes of the meanings of words.--Se*ma`si*o*log"ic*al (#), a.
Significant; ominous; serving as a warning of danger; --appliedesp. to the warning colors or forms of certain animals.
The doctrine of signs as the expression of thought orreasoning; the science of indicating thought by signs. Smart.
An instrument for signaling by reflecting the rays of the sunin different directions. Knight.
Resembling. [Obs.]And all is semblative a woman's part. Shak.

It seems; -- chiefly used impersonally in reports and judgmentsto express an opinion in reference to the law on some point notnecessary to be decided, and not intended to be definitely settled inthe cause.
The practice of attracting the males of Lepidoptera or otherinsects by exposing the female confined in a cage.
Sprinkled or sown; -- said of field, or a charge, when strewedor covered with small charges.
A daughter of Cadmus, and by Zeus mother of Bacchus.
A period of six months; especially, a term in a college oruneversity which divides the year into two terms.
The young of an insect in a stage between the larva and pupa.
A prefix signifying half, and sometimes partly or imperfectly;as, semiannual, half yearly; semitransparent, imperfectlytransparent.

A member of a branch of the Arians which did not acknowledgethe Son to be consubstantial with the Father, that is, of the samesubstance, but admitted him to be of a like substance with theFather, not by nature, but by a peculiar privilege.
The doctrines or tenets of the Semi-Arians.

Designating an internal-combustion engine of a type resemblingthe Diesel engine in using as fuel heavy oil which is injected in aspray just before the end of the compression stroke and is firedwithout electrical ignition. The fuel is sprayed into an iron box(called a hot bulb or hot pot) opening into the combustion chamber,and heated for ignition by a blast-lamp until the engine is running,when it is, ordinarily, kept red hot by the heat of combustion.

A follower of John Cassianus, a French monk (died about 448),who modified the doctrines of Pelagius, by denying human merit, andmaintaining the necessity of the Spirit's influence, while, on theother hand, he rejected the Augustinian doctrines of election, theinability of man to do good, and the certain perseverance of thesaints.
The doctrines or tenets of the Semi-Pelagians.
Half Saxon; -- specifically applied to the languageintermediate between Saxon and English, belonging to the period 1150-1250.
Partially amplexicaul; embracing the stem half round, as aleaf.
The half of a given, or measuring, angle.
Having the figure of a half circle; forming a semicircle. Grew.
One half of the axis of an
Half barbarous or uncivilized; as, semibarbaric display.
The quality or state of being half barbarous or uncivilized.
A note of half the time or duration of the breve; -- nowusually called a whole note. It is the longest note in general use.
A bull issued by a pope in the period between his election andcoronation.
Half or partially calcareous; as, a semicalcareous plant.
To deprive of one testicle.-- Sem`i*cas*tra"tion,n.
Of or pertaining to half of a century, or a period of fiftyyears; as, a semicentennial commemoration.
A half chorus; a passage to be sung by a selected portion ofthe voices, as the female voices only, in contrast with the fullchoir.
Having the form of half of a circle. Addison. Semicircularcanals (Anat.), certain canals of the inner ear. See under Ear.
A semicircular hollow or opening among trees or hills.Wordsworth.
The punctuation mark [;] indicating a separation between partsor members of a sentence more distinct than that marked by a comma.
A half column; a column bisected longitudinally, or along itsaxis.
Like a semicolumn; flat on one side and round on the other;imperfectly columnar.
Half conscious; imperfectly conscious. De Quincey.
A short cope, or an inferier kind of cope. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Half crystalline; -- said of certain cruptive rocks composedpartly of crystalline, partly of amorphous matter.
Of or pertaining to the square root of the cube of a quantity.Semicubical parabola, a curve in which the ordinates are proportionalto the square roots of the cubes of the abscissas.
Half deisticsl; bordering on deism. S. Miller.
Half detached; partly distinct or separate. Semidetached house,one of two tenements under a single roof, but separated by a partywall. [Eng.]
Half of a diameter; a right line, or the length of a rightline, drawn from the center of a circle, a sphere, or other curvedfigure, to its circumference or periphery; a radius.
An imperfect or diminished fifth. Busby.
Half or imperfect transparency; translucency. [R.] Boyle.
Half or imperfectly transparent; translucent. Woodward.
A lesser third, having its terms as 6 to 5; a hemiditone. [R.]
A roof or ceiling covering a semicircular room or recess, orone of nearly that shape, as the apse of a church, a niche, or thelike. It is approximately the quarter of a hollow sphere.
An office or feast celebrated with less solemnity than thedouble ones. See Double, n., 8.
That which is part fable and part truth; a mixture of truth andfable. De Quincey.
A floscule, or florest, with its corolla prolonged into astrap-shaped petal; -- called also semifloret.
Having all the florets ligulate, as in the dandelion.
A half form; an imperfect form.
Half formed; imperfectly formed; as, semiformed crystals.

A peptonelike body, insoluble in alcohol, formed by boilingcollagen or gelatin for a long time in water. Hemicollin, a likebody, is also formed at the same time, and differs from semiglutin bybeing partly soluble in alcohol.
Half or party historical. Sir G. C. Lewis.
The half of a lens divided along a plane passing through itsaxis.
Half lenticular or convex; imperfectly resembling a lens.Kirwan.
Half or partially ligneous, as a stem partly woody and partlyherbaceous.
The quality or state of being semiliquid; partial liquidity.
