A word employed in the phrase, To ride Skimmington; that is toride on a horse with a woman, but behind her, facing backward,carrying a distaff, and accompanied by a procession of jeeringneighbors making mock music; a cavalcade in ridicule of a henpeckedman. The custom was in vogue in parts of England.
To save; to be parsimonious or niggardly. [Prov. Eng. & Colloq.U.S.]
The external membranous integument of an animal.
Not deeper than the skin; hence, superficial. Lowell.
Having the skin adhering closely and rigidly to the flesh;hidebound. Skinbound disease. (Med.) See Sclerema neonatorum, underSclerema.
To give scant measure; to squeeze or pinch in order to effect asaving. [Prev. Eng. & Colloq. U.S.]
A penurious person; a miser; a niggard. Sir W. Scott.
As much as a skin can hold.
Any one of numerous species of regularly scaled harmlesslizards of the family Scincidæ, common in the warmer parts of all thecontinents.
One who serves liquor; a tapster.
Having no skin, or a very thin skin; as, skinless fruit.
Consisting, or chiefly consisting, of skin; wanting flesh. "Herskinny lips." Shak.He holds him with a skinny hand. Coleridge.
An iron bucket, which slides between guides, for hoistingmineral and rock.
An elater; a snap bug, or snapping beetle.
In a skipping manner; by skips, or light leaps.
To utter in a shrill tone; to scream. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.]
The missel thrush; -- so called from its harsh alarm note.[Prev. Eng.]
A shrill cry or sound; a crying shrilly; a skirl. [Prov. Eng. &Scot.] Sir W. Scott.When the skirling of the pipes cleft the air his cold eyes softened.Mrs. J. H. Ewing.
To fight slightly or in small parties; to engage in a skirmishor skirmishes; to act as skirmishers.
To ramble over in order to clear; to scour. [Archaic] Shak.
An umbelliferous plant (Sium, or Pimpinella, Sisarum). It is anative of Asia, but has been long cultivated in Europe for its edibleclustered tuberous roots, which are very sweet.
To be on the border; to live near the border, or extremity.Savages . . . who skirt along our western frontiers. S. S. Smith.
To cast reflections on; to asperse. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.] Crose.
To move or pass (something) over a surface quickly so that ittouches only at intervals; to skip.

Pertaining to the game of skittles. Skittle alley, an alley orcourt in which the game of skittles is played.-- Skittle ball, a disk or flattish ball of wood for throwing at thepins in the game of skittles.
An English game resembling ninepins, but played by throwingwooden disks, instead of rolling balls, at the pins.
A rail; as, the water rail (called also skitty cock, and skittycoot); the spotted crake (Porzana maruetta), and the moor hen. [Prov.Eng.]
The iron lap used by diamond polishers in finishing the facetsof the gem.
Any jager gull; especially, the Megalestris skua; -- calledalso boatswain.

To hide, or get out of the way, in a sneaking manner; to lieclose, or to move in a furtive way; to lurk. "Want skulks in holesand crevices." W. C. Bryant.Discovered and defeated of your prey, You skulked behind the fence,and sneaked away. Dryden.
A school, company, or shoal. [Obs.]A knavish skull of boys and girls did pelt at him. Warner.These fishes enter in great flotes and skulls. Holland.
Any plant of the labiate genus Scutellaria, the calyx of whoseflower appears, when inverted, like a helmet with the visor raised.
A whaler's name for a whale more than two years old.

Any one of several species of American musteline carnivores ofthe genus Mephitis and allied genera. They have two glands near theanus, secreting an extremely fetid liquid, which the animal ejects atpleasure as a means of defense.
Like the skunk, especially in odor.
A boat; a small vessel. [Obs.] Sir R. Williams.
A mineral of a bright metallic luster and tin-white to palelead-gray color. It consist of arsenic and cobalt.
A person licensed as a pilot. [Slang]
Having the blue color of the sky; azure; as, a sky-blue stone.Wordsworth.
Surrounded by sky. [Poetic & R.] "The skyed mountain." Thomson.
Like the sky; ethereal; being in the sky. "Skyey regions."Thackeray.Sublime on the towers of my skyey bowers, Lightning, my pilot, sits.Shelley.
Like the sky, or approaching the sky; lofty; ethereal. [R.]Shak.

A lark that mounts and sings as it files, especially the commonspecies (Alauda arvensis) found in Europe and in some parts of Asia,and celebrated for its melodious song; -- called also sky laverock.See under Lark.
The act of running about the rigging of a vessel in sport;hence, frolicking; scuffing; sporting; carousing. [Colloq.]
A window placed in the roof of a building, in the ceiling of aroom, or in the deck of a ship, for the admission of light fromabove.
A rocket that ascends high and burns as it flies; a species offireworks.
The sail set next above the royal. See Illust. under Sail.
A name for the one of the fancy sails alleged to have beensometimes set above the skysail. [Obs.](b) A very tall building.(c) Hence, anything usually large, high, or excessive. [Slang orColloq.]
Having flat sides; hence, tall, or long and lank. [Colloq. U.S.]
To let saliva or some liquid fall from the mouth carelessly,like a child or an idiot; to drivel; to drool. [Written also slaver,and slobber.]
One who slabbers, or drools; hence, an idiot.
Like, or covered with, slabber or slab; slippery; sloppy.
Adapted for forming slabs, or for dressing flat surfaces.Slabbing machine, a milling machine.
Small coal; also, coal dust; culm. Raymond.
A spongy, semivitrifled substance which miners or smelters mixwith the ores of metals to prevent their fusion. [Written alsoslakin.]
The quality or state of being slack.
Of or pertaining to slag; resembling slag; as, slaggy cobalt.
To come or swing against something, or to shut, with suddenforce so as to produce a shock and noise; as, a door or shutterslams.
With great violence; with a slamming or banging noise.[Colloq.]

Formerly, defamation generally, whether oral or written; inmodern usage, defamation by words spoken; utterance of false,malicious, and defamatory words, tending to the damage and derogationof another; calumny. See the Note under Defamation. Burril.
One who slanders; a defamer; a calumniator. Jer. Taylor.
One who uses abusive slang; a ranting partisan. [Colloq. orHumorous] W. Irving.
Of or pertaining to slang; of the nature of slang; disposed touse slang. [Written also slangey.]
To be turned or inclined from a right line or level; to lieobliquely; to slope.On the side of younder slanting hill. Dodsley.
A blow, esp. one given with the open hand, or with somethingbroad.
To apply, or apply something to, in a hasty, careless, or roughmanner; to roughcast; as, to slapdash mortar or paint on a wall, orto slapdash a wall. [Colloq.] Halliwell.
Slippery; smooth; crafty; hypocritical. [Prov. Eng.] Slape ale,plain ale, as opposed to medicated or mixed ale. [Prov. Eng.]
A soft-spoken, crafty hypocrite. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.
A flat batter cake cooked on a griddle; a flapjack; agriddlecake. [Local, U.S.]
To strike violently and at random, esp. with an edgedinstrument; to lay about one indiscriminately with blows; to cuthastily and carelessly.Hewing and slashing at their idle shades. Spenser.
A kind of pine tree (Pinus Cubensis) found in Southern Floridaand the West Indies; -- so called because it grows in "slashes."
Divided into many narrow parts or segments by sharp incisions;laciniate.
A machine for applying size to warp yarns.
A thin, narrow strip or bar of wood or metal; as, the slats ofa window blind.
An argillaceous rock which readily splits into thin plates;argillite; argillaceous schist.
Of a dark gray, like slate.
One who lays slates, or whose occupation is to slate buildings.
A slab of stone used as a veneer for coarse masonry. Knight.
To be careless, negligent, or aswkward, esp. with regard todress and neatness; to be wasteful. Ray.
A woman who is negligent of her dress or house; one who is notneat and nice.
The quality or state of being slatternly; slovenliness;untidiness.
Resembling a slattern; sluttish; negligent; dirty.-- adv.
A dance or game played by boys, requiring active exercise.[Obs.] Gayton.

Resembling slate; having the nature, appearance, or properties,of slate; composed of thin parallel plates, capable of beingseparated by splitting; as, a slaty color or texture. Slaty cleavage(Min.), cleavage, as of rocks, into thin leaves or plates, like thoseof slate; -- applied especially to those cases in which the planes ofcleavage are not parallel to the planes of stratification. It is nowbelieved to be caused by the compression which the strata haveundergone.-- Slaty gneiss (Min.), a variety of gneiss in which the scales ofmica or crystals of hornblende, which are usually minute, form thinlaminæ, rendering the rock easily cleavable.
The act of killing. Specifically:(a) The extensive, violent, bloody, or wanton destruction of life;carnage.On war and mutual slaughter bent. Milton.
A house where beasts are butchered for the market.
Destructive; murderous. Shak. M. Arnold.-- Slaugh"ter*ous*ly, adv.

One of a race of people occupying a large part of Eastern andNorthern Europe, including the Russians, Bulgarians, Roumanians,Servo-Croats, Slovenes, Poles, Czechs, Wends or Sorbs, Slovaks, etc.[Written also Slave, and Sclav.]
To smear with saliva issuing from the mouth; to defile withdrivel; to slabber.
Drooling; defiling with saliva.-- Slav"er*ing*ly, adv.
Of or pertaining to slaves; such as becomes or befits a slave;servile; excessively laborious; as, a slavish life; a slavishdependance on the great.-- Slav"ish*ly, adv.-- Slav"ish*ness, n.
The common feeling and interest of the Slavonic race.
The persons or interest formerly representing slaverypolitically, or wielding political power for the preservation oradvancement of slavery. [U. S.]
A native or inhabitant of Slavonia; ethnologically, a Slav.
Sliced cabbage served as a salad, cooked or uncooked.

To put to death with a weapon, or by violence; hence, to kill;to put an end to; to destroy.With this sword then will I slay you both. Chaucer.I will slay the last of them with the sword. Amos ix. 1.I'll slay more gazers than the basilisk. Shak.
One who slays; a killer; a murderer; a destrroyer of life.
To separate, as threads; to divide, as a collection of threads;to sley; -- a weaver's term.
Raw; not spun or wrought; as, sleaved thread or silk.Holinshed.
Wanting firmness of texture or substance; thin; flimsy; as,sleazy silk or muslin. [Spelt also slazy.]
To convey or transport on a sled; as, to sled wood or timber.
To travel or convey in a sledge or sledges. Howitt.
The quality or state of being sleek; smoothness and glossinessof surface.
A plant (Tragopogon pratensis) which closes its flowers atmidday; a kind of goat's beard. Dr. Prior.
An animal that hibernates, as the bear.
Strongly inclined to sleep; very sleepy.-- Sleep"ful*ness, n.
The quality or state of being sleepy.

from Sleep. Sleeping car, a railway car or carrriage, arrangedwith apartments and berths for sleeping.-- Sleeping partner (Com.), a dormant partner. See under Dormant.-- Sleeping table (Mining), a stationary inclined platform on whichpulverized ore is washed; a kind of buddle.
Disposed to sleep; sleepy; drowsy.Your sleepish, and more than sleepish, security. Ford.
On in a state of magnetic or mesmeric sleep.
The state of one mesmerized, or in a partial and morbid sleep.
One who walks in his sleep; a somnambulist.
The part of a mortar extending from the chamber to thetrunnions.
Mud or slime, such as that at the bottom of rivers. [Scot.]
Of or pertaining to sleet; characterized by sleet; as, a sleetystorm; sleety weather.
Having sleeves; furnished with sleeves; -- often incomposition; as, long-sleeved.
The part of a sleeve nearest the hand; a cuff or wristband.[Obs.] Shak.
To sley, or prepare for use in the weaver's sley, or slaie.Shak.
Uttered with a thin tone; -- the opposite of broad; as, theslender vowels long e and i.-- Slen"der*ly, adv.-- Slen"der*ness, n.
A burrowing rodent (Spalax typhlus), native of Russia and AsiaMinor. It has the general appearance of a mole, and is destitute ofeyes. Called also mole rat.
The track of man or beast as followed by the scent. [Scot.]Halliwell.
A hound that tracks animals by the scent; specifically, abloodhound. [Spelt variously slouthhound, sluthhound, etc.]
To separate or part the threads of, and arrange them in a reed;-- a term used by weavers. See Sleave, and Sleid.
One who, or that which, slices; specifically, the circular sawof the lapidary.
Sleek; smooth. "Both slick and dainty." Chapman.
The pulverized matter from a quartz mill, or the lighter soilof hydraulic mines. [Local, U. S.]
That which makes smooth or sleek. Specifically:(a) A kind of burnisher for leather.(b) (Founding) A curved tool for smoothing the surfaces of a moldafter the withdrawal of the pattern.
The state or quality of being slick; smoothness; sleekness.
To pass from one note to another with no perceptible cassationof sound.
A way along which something slides.
An instrument for indicating and recording shocks to railwaycars occasioned by sudden stopping.
The quality or state of being slight; slenderness; feebleness;superficiality; also, formerly, negligence; indifference; disregard.
Bitumen. [Archaic]Slime had they for mortar. Gen. xi. 3.
The quality or state of being slimy.
In a state of slimness; in a slim manner; slenderly.
The quality or state of being slim.

Of or pertaining to slime; resembling slime; of the nature ofslime; viscous; glutinous; also, covered or daubed with slime;yielding, or abounding in, slime.Slimy things did crawl with legs Upon the slimy sea. Coleridge.
To pass a rope round, as a cask, gun, etc., preparatory toattaching a hoisting or lowering tackle.
One who slings, or uses a sling.
To cast prematurely; -- said of female beasts; as, a cow thatslinks her calf.
A portion of the columns of a newspaper or other work struckoff by itself; a proof from a column of type when set up and in thegalley.
A kind of overcoat worn upon the shoulders in the manner of acloak. [Scot.]
A rich variety of new cheese, resembling butter, but white.Halliwell.
Sledge runners on which a skip is dragged in a mine.
knot which slips along the rope or line around which it ismade.
The act of slipping; also, the amount of slipping.

A piece, usually a plate, applied to a sliding piece, toreceive wear and afford a means of adjustment; -- also called shoe,and gib. Slipper animalcule (Zoöl.), a ciliated infusorian of thegenus Paramecium.-- Slipper flower.(Bot.) Slipperwort.-- Slipper limpet, or Slipper shell (Zoöl.), a boat shell.
Slipperiness. [R.] "The slippiness of the way." Sir W. Scott.
Weak, poor, or flat liquor; weak, profitless discourse orwriting.
One who has shaken off restraint; a prodigal. [Obs.] Cotgrave.
A cut; as, slish and slash. [Colloq.] Shak.
3d. pers. sing. pres. of Slide. Chaucer.

Any species of Pleurotomaria, a genus of beautiful, pearly,spiral gastropod shells having a deep slit in the outer lip. Manyfossil species are known, and a few living ones are found in deepwater in tropical seas.
One who, or that which, slits.

from Slit. Slitting file. See Illust. (i) of File.-- Slitting mill. (a) A mill where iron bars or plates are slit intonarrow strips, as nail rods, and the like. (b) A machine used bylapidaries for slicing stones, usually by means of a revolving disk,called a slicer, supplied with diamond powder.-- Slitting roller, one of a pair of rollers furnished with ribsentering between similar ribs in the other roller, and cutting likeshears, -- used in slitting metals.
To cut or divide into long, thin pieces, or into very smallpieces; to cut or rend lengthwise; to slit; as, to sliver wood. Shak.They 'll sliver thee like a turnip. Sir W. Scott.
A species of seaweed. [Spelled also slowcawn.] See 3d Laver.
A layer of earth between coal seams.
A narrow piece of timber which holds together large pieces; aslat; as, the sloats of a cart.
from Slock. Slocking stone, a rich piece of ore displayed inorder to tempt persons to embark in a mining enterprise.
A small, bitter, wild European plum, the fruit of theblackthorn (Prunus spinosa); also, the tree itself.
To hit hard, esp. with little attention to aim or the like, asin cricket or boxing; to slug. [Cant or Slang]
The war cry, or gathering word, of a Highland clan in Scotland;hence, any rallying cry. Sir W. Scott.
A hard hitter; a slugger. [Cant or Slang]  T. Hughes.
Sluggish. [Obs.]Somnolence that is sloggy slumbering Chaucer.

A vessel having one mast and fore-and-aft rig, consisting of aboom-and-gaff mainsail, jibs, staysail, and gaff topsail. The typicalsloop has a fixed bowsprit, topmast, and standing rigging, whilethose of a cutter are capable of being readily shifted. The sloopusually carries a centerboard, and depends for stability upon breadthof beam rather than depth of keel. The two types have rapidlyapproximated since 1880. One radical distinction is that a slop maycarry a centerboard. See Cutter, and Illustration in Appendix. Sloopof war, formerly, a vessel of war rigged either as a ship, brig, orschooner, and mounting from ten to thirty-two guns; now, any warvessel larger than a gunboat, and carrying guns on one deck only.

Dirty water; water in which anything has been washed or rinsed;water from wash-bowls, etc. Slop basin, or Slop bowl, a basin or bowlfor holding slops, especially for receiving the rinsings of tea orcoffee cups at the table.-- Slop molding (Brickmaking), a process of manufacture in which thebrick is carried to the drying ground in a wet mold instead of on apallet.
Sloping. "Down the slope hills." Milton.A bank not steep, but gently slope. Bacon.
State of being slope. Sir H. Wotton.
Inclining or inclined from the plane of the horizon, or from ahorizontal or other right line; oblique; declivous; slanting.-- Slop"ing*ly, adv.The sloping land recedes into the clouds. Cowper.
The quality or state of being sloppy; muddiness.
Wet, so as to spatter easily; wet, as with something sloppedover; muddy; plashy; as, a sloppy place, walk, road.
One who sells slops, or ready-made clothes. See 4th Slop, 3.
A shop where slops. or ready-made clothes, are sold.
The manufacture of slops, or cheap ready-made clothing; also,such clothing; hence, hasty, slovenly work of any kind.No slopwork ever dropped from his [Carlyle's] pen. Froude.
To shut with violence; to slam; as, to slot a door. [Obs. orProv. Eng.]
A machine the operation of which is started by dropping a coininto a slot, for delivering small articles of merchandise, showingone's weight, exhibiting pictures, throwing dice, etc.

Any one of several species of arboreal edentates constitutingthe family Bradypodidæ, and the suborder Tardigrada. They have longexserted limbs and long prehensile claws. Both jaws are furnishedwith teeth (see Illust. of Edentata), and the ears and tail arerudimentary. They inhabit South and Central America and Mexico.
Addicted to sloth; inactive; sluggish; lazy; indolent; idle.He also that is slothful in his work is brother to him that is agreat waster. Prov. xviii. 9.-- Sloth"ful*ly, adv.-- Sloth"ful*ness, n.
The act or process of making slots, or mortises.
To cause to hang down; to depress at the side; as, to slouththe hat.
Hanging down at the side; limp; drooping; without firmness orshapeliness; moving in an ungainly manner.
The act of casting off the skin or shell, as do insects andcrustaceans; ecdysis.
A man or boy habitually negligent of neathess and order; -- thecorrelative term to slattern, or slut. Pope.He became a confirmed sloven. Macaulay.
The quality or state of being slovenly.
imp. of Slee, to slay. Slew. Chaucer.
Dull of apprehension; not possessing quick intelligence.
A lubber; an idle fellow; a loiterer. [Old Slang] Dr. Favour.
In a slow manner; moderately; not rapidly; not early; notrashly; not readly; tardly.
The quality or state of being slow.

Lit., skilled mechanical work, such as that required in woodcarving; trade work; hence, a system (usually called the sloydsystem) of manual training in the practical use of the tools andmaterials used in the trades, and of instruction in the making anduse of the plans and specifications connected with trade work. Thesloyd system derives its name from the fact that it was adopted orlargely developed from a similar Swedish system, in which woodcarving was a chief feature. Its purpose is not only to affordpractical skill in some trade, but also to develop the pupilsmentally and physically.
A roll of wool slightly twisted; a rove; -- called alsoslubbing.
In a slovenly, or hurried and imperfect, manner. [Low] Drayton.
from Slub. Slubbing billy, or Slubbing machine, the machine bywhich slubs are formed.
See Slime, 4. Sludge hole, the hand-hole, or manhole, in asteam boiler, by means of which sediment can be removed.
Impure dark-colored sulphuric acid that has been used in therefining of petroleum.
A bucket for removing mud from a bored hole; a sand pump.
To turn about a fixed point, usually the center or axis, as aspar or piece of timber; to turn; -- used also of any heavy body.

Any one of numerous species of terrestrial pulmonate mollusksbelonging to Limax and several related genera, in which the shell iseither small and concealed in the mantle, or altogether wanting. Theyare closely allied to the land snails.
An erroneous form of the Scotch word slughorne, or sloggorne,meaning slogan.
One who indulges in lying abed; a sluggard. [R.] "Fie, youslugabed!" Shak.
A person habitually lazy, idle, and inactive; a drone.Go to the ant, thou sluggard; considered her ways, and be wise. Prov.vi. 6.
The state of being a sluggard; sluggishness; sloth. Gower.Idleness is rotten sluggardy. Chaucer.
One who strikes heavy blows; hence, a boxer; a prize fighter.[Cant or Slang]
Any caterpillar which has the general appearance of a slug, asdo those of certain moths belonging to Limacodes and allied genera,and those of certain sawflies.
A long box or trough through which water flows, -- used forwashing auriferous earth. Sluice gate, the sliding gate of a sluice.

An artificial channel into which water is let by a sluice;specifically, a trough constructed over the bed of a stream, so thatlogs, lumber, or rubbish can be floated down to some convenient placeof delivery.
Falling copiously or in streams, as from a sluice.And oft whole sheets descend of sluicy rain. Dryden.

Sleep; especially, light sleep; sleep that is not deep orsound; repose.He at last fell into a slumber, and thence into a fast sleep, whichdetained him in that place until it was almost night. Bunyan.Fast asleep It is no matter; Enjoy the honey-heavy dew of slumber.Shak.Rest to my soul, and slumber to my eyes. Dryden.
The impure residue, consisting of cocoons, propolis, etc.,remaining after the wax is extracted from honeycombs.
The gross amount; the mass; the lump. [Scot.]
Easily broken through; boggy; marshy; swampy. [Prov. Eng. &Colloq. U.S.] Bartlett.
imp. & p. p. of Sling. Slung shot, a metal ball of small size,with a string attached, used by ruffians for striking.
To sing or perform in a smooth, gliding style; to connectsmoothly in performing, as several notes or tones. Busby.
Marked with a slur; performed in a smooth, gliding style, likenotes marked with a slur.
A mixture of white lead and lime, with which the bright partsof machines, such as the connecting rods of steamboats, are paintedto be preserved from oxidation.
Abounding in slush; characterized by soft mud or half-meltedsnow; as, the streets are slushy; the snow is slushy. "A dark,drizzling, slushy day." Blackw. Mag.
The qualities and practices of a slut; sluttishness;slatternlines. Drayton.

Like a slut; untidy; indecently negligent of cleanliness;disorderly; as, a sluttish woman.Why is thy lord so slutish, I thee pray. Chaucer.An air of liberal, though sluttish, plenty, indicated the wealthyfarmer. Sir W. Scott.-- Slut"tish*ly, adv.-- Slut"tish*ness, n.
A humerous appellation for a sly, cunning, or waggish person.Slyboots was cursedly cunning to hide 'em. Goldsmith.
In a sly manner; shrewdly; craftily.Honestly and slyly he it spent. Chaucer.
The quality or state of being sly.
A narrow passage between two buildings, as between the transeptand chapter house of a monastery. [Eng.]
A small sailing vessel, commonly rigged as a sloop, usedchiefly in the coasting and fishing trade.
A sharp, quick noise; a smack.Like the faint smacking of an after kiss. Dryden.
A biennial umbelliferous plant (Apium graveolens) native of theseacoats of Europe and Asia. When deprived of its acrid and evenpoisonous properties by cultivation, it becomes celery.
A man's garment for the hips and thighs; breeches. SeeBreeches.
The quality or state of being small.

A contagious, constitutional, febrile disease characterized bya peculiar eruption; variola. The cutaneous eruption is at first acollection of papules which become vesicles (first flat, subsequentlyumbilicated) and then pustules, and finally thick crusts which sloughafter a certain time, often leaving a pit, or scar.
A light sword used for thrusting only; especially, the swordworn by civilians of rank in the eighteenth century.
In a small quantity or degree; with minuteness. [R.] Ascham.
A deep blue pigment or coloring material used in various arts.It is a vitreous substance made of cobalt, potash, and calcinedquartz fused, and reduced to a powder.
Of or pertaining to emerald; resembling emerald; of an emeraldgreen.
A green foliated kind of amphibole, observed in eclogite andsome varietis of gabbro.
To cause a smart in. "A goad that . . . smarts the flesh." T.Adams.
To make smart or spruce; -- usually with up. [Colloq.]She had to go and smarten herself up somewhat. W. Black.
The quality or state of being smart.
An acrid plant of the genus Polygonum (P. Hydropiper), whichproduces smarting if applied where the skin is tender.
To break in pieces by violence; to dash to pieces; to crush.Here everything is broken and smashed to pieces. Burke.
Taste; tincture; smack. [Obs.]Thy life hath had some smatch of honor in it. Shak.
One who has only a slight, superficial knowledge; a sciolist.
A slight, superficial knowledge of something; sciolism.I had a great desire, not able to attain to a superficial skill inany, to have some smattering in all. Burton.
Having the color mark ings ill defined, as if rubbed; as, thesmeared dagger moth (Apatela oblinita).
Tending to smear or soil; adhesive; viscous. Rowe.
A hydrous silicate of alumina, of a greenish color, which, incertain states of humidity, appears transparent and almostgelatinous.
To smoke; to blacken with smoke; to rub with soot. [Obs.]

The matter secreted by any of the sebaceous glands.Specifically:(a) The soapy substance covering the skin of newborn infants.(b) The cheesy, sebaceous matter which collects between the glanspenis and the foreskin.
Being of the nature of soap; soapy; cleansing; detersive.
A salt glaze on pottery, made by adding common salt to anearthenware glaze.
Destitute of smell; having no odor.Daisies smell-less, yet most quaint. Beau & Fl.
An aromatic preparation of carbonate of ammonia and, often,some scent, to avoid or relieve faintness, headache, or the like.
One who, or that which, smelts.
A house or place for smelting.
a. & n. from Smelt. Smelting furnace (Metal.), a furnace inwhich ores are smelted or reduced.
To look amorously or wantonly; to smirk.
Amorous glance or inclination. [Obs.] "A smickering to ouryoung lady." Dryden.
A woman's under-garment; a smock. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Johnson.
A match for firing a charge of powder, as in blasting; a fuse.
A little smile. [R.]Those happy smilets That played on her ripe lip. Shak.
Quality or state of being smiling.And made despair a smilingness assume. Byron.
An extinct genus of saber-toothed tigers. See Mach.
Any one of numerous small species of springtails, of the familySminthurid, -- usually found on flowers. See Illust. underCollembola.
To smear with something which stains, or makes dirty; tosmutch; to begrime; to soil; to sully.I'll . . . with a kind of umber smirch my face. Shak.
To smile in an affected or conceited manner; to smile withaffected complaisance; to simper.
imp. & p. p. of Smite. Spenser.Smit with the beauty of so fair a scene. Cowper.
To strike; to collide; to beat. [Archaic]The heart meleth, and the knees smite together. Nah. ii. 10.
One who smites.I give my back to the smiters. Isa. l. 6.
To beat into shape; to fprge. [Obs.] Chaucer.What smith that any [weapon] smitheth. Piers Plowman.
The art or occupation of a smith; smithing. [R.] Sir W.Raleigh.
Fragments; atoms; finders. [Prov. Eng.]Smash the bottle to smithers. Tennyson.
The act or art of working or forging metals, as iron, into anydesired shape. Moxon.
Of or pertaining to the Englishman J.L.M. Smithson, or to thenational institution of learning which he endowed at Washington,D.C.; as, the Smithsonian Institution; Smithsonian Reports.-- n.
Native zinc carbonate. It generally occurs in stalactitic,reniform, or botryoidal shapes, of a white to gray, green, or browncolor. See Note under Calamine.
The workshop of a smith, esp. a blacksmith; a smithery; astithy. [Written also smiddy.]Under a spreading chestnut tree The village smithy stands. Lonfellow.
Fine clay or ocher made up into balls, used for marking sheep.[Eng.] Woodsward.

Of or pertaining to a smock; resembling a smock; hence, of orpertaining to a woman. Smock mill, a windmill of which only the capturns round to meet the wind, in distinction from a post mill, whosewhole building turns on a post.-- Smock race, a race run by women for the prize of a smock. [Prov.Eng.]
A coarse frock, or shirt, worn over the other dress, as by farmlaborers. Macaulay.
Having a feminine countenance or complexion; smooth-faced;girlish. Fenton.
Capable of being smoked; suitable or ready to be smoked; as,smokable tobacco.
To dry by or in smoke.
A building where meat or fish is cured by subjecting it to adense smoke.
A contrivance for turning a spit by means of a fly or wheelmoved by the current of ascending air in a chimney.
Making or having no smoke. "Smokeless towers." Pope.
A high-explosive gunpowder whose explosion produces little, ifany, smoke.
A chimney; esp., a pipe serving as a chimney, as the pipe whichcarries off the smoke of a locomotive, the funnel of a steam vessel,etc.
The quality or state of being smoky.

from Smoke. Smoking bean (Bot.), the long pod of the catalpa,or Indian-bean tree, often smoked by boys as a substitute for cigars.-- Smoking car, a railway car carriage reserved for the use ofpassengers who smoke tobacco.
To smother; to suffocate; to choke. [Obs.] Holinshed.Palsgrave.
A young salmon two or three years old, when it has acquired itssilvery color.
To suffocate or smother. [Written also smore.] [Obs. or Prov.Eng. & Scot.] Sir T. More. Burns.
Causing no resistance to a body sliding along its surface;frictionless.
Having a smooth chin; beardless. Drayton.
Having a smooth tongue; plausible; flattering.
Having a bore of perfectly smooth surface; -- distinguishedfrom rifled.-- n.
One who, or that which, smooths.
fr. Smooth, v. Smoothing iron, an iron instrument with apolished face, for smoothing clothes; a sadiron; a flatiron.-- Smoothing plane, a short, finely set plane, for smoothing andfinishing work.
Quality or state of being smooth.
To smother. See Smoor. [Obs.]Some dying vomit blood, and some were smored. Du Bartas.
imp. (and rare p. p.) of Smite.
Checkmate given when movement of the king is completelyobstructed by his own men.
The quality or state of being smothery.
The quality or state of being smudged, soiled, or blurred. C.A. Young.

Studiously neat or nice, especially in dress; spruce;affectedly precise; smooth and prim.They be so smug and smooth. Robynson (More's Utopia).The smug and scanty draperies of his style. De Quincey.A young, smug, handsome holiness has no fellow. Beau & Fl.
To import or export in violation of the customs laws.
The quality or state of being smug.
Bad, soft coal, containing much earthy matter, found in theimmediate locality of faults.
A stain; a dirty spot. B. Jonson.
Of or pertaining to Smyrna.-- n.
A pipefish of the genus Syngnathus. See Pipefish.
A kind of bridle bit, having a joint in the part to be placedin the mouth, and rings and cheek pieces at the ends, but having nocurb; -- called also snaffle bit.

One of the secondary branches of an antler. Snag boat, asteamboat fitted with apparatus for removing snags and otherobstructions in navigable streams. [U.S.] -- Snag tooth. Same asSnag, 2.How thy snag teeth stand orderly, Like stakes which strut by thewater side. J. Cotgrave.
A spiral cam, or a flat piece of metal of spirally curvedoutline, used for giving motion to, or changing the position of,another part, as the hammer tail of a striking clock.
Like or suiting a snail; as, snail-like progress.
Slow-moving, like a snail.Bid the snail-paced Ajax arm for shame. Shak.
Any species of the order Ophidia; an ophidian; a serpent,whether harmless or venomous. See Ophidia, and Serpent.
Any one of several plants of different genera and species, mostof which are (or were formerly) reputed to be efficacious as remediesfor the bites of serpents; also, the roots of any of these.
An ammonite; -- so called from its form, which resembles thatof a coiled snake.
Having the qualities or characteristics of a snake; snaky.
To bevel the end of a timber to fit against an inclinedsurface.
A hemispherical or rounded head to a rivet or bolt; also, aswaging tool with a cavity in its face for forming such a roundedhead.
Any one of several species of large sparoid food fishes of thegenus Lutjanus, abundant on the southern coasts of the United Statesand on both coasts of tropical America.

a. & n. from Snap, v. Snapping beetle. (Zoöl.) See Snap beetle,under Snap.-- Snapping turtle. (Zoöl.) (a) A large and voracious aquatic turtle(Chelydra serpentina) common in the fresh waters of the UnitedStates; -- so called from its habit of seizing its prey by a snap ofits jaws. Called also mud turtle. (b) See Alligator snapper, underAlligator.

An instrument, consisting usually of a wireloop or noose, forremoving tumors, etc., by avulsion. Snare drum, the smaller commonmilitary drum, as distinguished from the bass drum; -- so calledbecause (in order to render it more resonant) it has stretched acrossits lower head a catgut string or strings.
One who lays snares, or entraps.
To form raised work upon the outer surface of (thin metal ware)by the repercussion of a snarling iron upon the inner surface.
One who snarls; a surly, growling animal; a grumbling,quarrelsome fellow.

from Snarl, v. Snarling iron, a tool with a long beak, used inthe process of snarling. When one end is held in a vise, and theshank is struck with a hammer, the repercussion of the other end, orbeak, within the article worked upon gives the requisite blow forproducing raised work. See 1st Snarl.
Resembling, or consisting of, snares; entangling; insidious.Spiders in the vault their snary webs have spread. Dryden.
The snuff, or burnt wick, of a candle. [Obs.] Bacon.
To attempt to seize something suddenly; to catch; -- often withat; as, to snatch at a rope.
a kind of block with an opening in one side to receive thebight of a rope.
One who snatches, or takes abruptly.
The handle of a scythe; a snead. [Variously written in Englandsnead, sneed, sneath, sneeth, snathe, etc.; in Scotland writtensned.]
A chip; a alice. [Prov. Eng.] Gayton.
To hide, esp. in a mean or cowardly manner. [Obs.] "[Slander]sneaks its head." Wake.
A current which, though too feeble to blow the usual fuse or toinjure at once telegraph or telephone instruments, will in time burnthem out.
One who sneaks from his cups; one who balks his glass. [Obs.]Shak.
Marked by cowardly concealment; deficient in openness andcourage; underhand; mean; crouching.-- Sneak"ing*ly, adv.-- Sneak"ing*ness, n.
A paltry fellow; a sneak. [Obs.] "Such a bashful sneaksby."Barrow.
A reprimand; a rebuke. [Obs.]My lord, I will not undergo this sneap without reply. Shak.
To reprimand; to sneap. [Obs.] "Scold and sneb the good oak."Spenser.
To fasten by a hatch; to latch, as a door. [Scot. & Prov. Eng.]Sneck up, be silent; shut up; hold your peace. Shak.
A door latch, or sneck. [Prov. Eng.]

To emit air, chiefly through the nose, audibly and violently,by a kind of involuntary convulsive force, occasioned by irritationof the inner membrane of the nose. Not to be sneezed at, not to bedespised or contemned; not to be treated lightly. [Colloq.] "He hadto do with old women who were not to be sneezed at." Prof. Wilson.
A yellow-flowered composite plant (Helenium autumnale) the odorof which is said to cause sneezing.
The wood of a South African tree. See Neishout.
A European herbaceous plant (Achillea Ptarmica) allied to theyarrow, having a strong, pungent smell.
The act of violently forcing air out through the nasal passageswhile the cavity of the mouth is shut off from the pharynx by theapproximation of the soft palate and the base of the tongue.
Active; brisk; nimble; quick; sharp. [Archaic or Prov. Eng. &Scot.]That horny-handed, snell, peremptory little man. Dr. J. Brown.
The fat of a deer. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.]
To snow; to abound. [Obs.]It snewed in his house of meat and drink. Chaucer.
To check; to sneap; to sneb. [Obs.]Him would he snib sharply for the nones. Chaucer.
A slight hit or tip of the ball, often unintentional.
A half suppressed, broken laugh. [Written also snigger.]
Tricky; deceptive; contemptible; as, a snide lawyer; snidegoods. [Slang]
To draw air audibly up the nose; to snuff; -- sometimes done asa gesture of suspicion, offense, or contempt.So ye grow squeamish, gods, and sniff at heaven. M. Arnold.
A rapid inspiratory act, in which the mouth is kept shut andthe air drawn in through the nose.
To snuffle, as one does with a catarrh. [Prov. Eng.]

from Snift. Snifting valve, a small valve opening into theatmosphere from the cylinder or condenser of a steam engine, to allowthe escape of air when the piston makes a stroke; -- so called fromthe noise made by its action.
To chop off; to cut. [Prov. Eng.]
To fish for eels by thrusting the baited hook into their holesor hiding places. Walton.

To cut off the nip or neb of, or to cut off at once with shearsor scissors; to clip off suddenly; to nip; hence, to break off; tosnatch away.Curbed and snipped in my younger years by fear of my parents fromthose vicious excrescences to which that age was subject. Fuller.The captain seldom ordered anything out of the ship's stores . . .but I snipped some of it for my own share. De Foe.
A tart dialogue with quick replies. [R.] Pope.
Any one of numerous species of limicoline game birds of thefamily Scolopacidæ, having a long, slender, nearly straight beak.
A small part or piece.To be cut into snippets and shreds. F. Harrison.
Ridiculously small; petty. "Snippety facts." London Spectator.
One who snivels, esp. one who snivels habitually.
Running at the nose; sniveling pitiful; whining.
The quality of being snobbish; snobbishness.
Of or pertaining to a snob; characteristic of, or befitting, asnob; vulgarly pretentious.-- Snob"bish*ly, adv.
Vulgar affectation or ostentation; mean admiration of meanthings; conduct or manners of a snob.
A fillet; a headband; a snood. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.]
A short candle end used for igniting a fuse. Raymond.
To bind or braid up, as the hair, with a snood. [Scot.]
Wearing or having a snood. "The snooded daughter." Whittier.
To lurk; to lie in ambush. [Obs.]
To breathe with a rough, hoarse, nasal voice in sleep.

The act of respiring through the open mouth so that thecurrents of inspired and expired air cause a vibration of the uvulaand soft palate, thus giving rise to a sound more or less harsh. Itis usually unvoluntary, but may be produced voluntarily.
The act of snorting; the sound produced in snorting.
The wheather; -- so called from its cry. [Prov. Eng.]
To blow, wipe, or clear, as the nose.
To snivel; to cry or whine. [Prov. Eng.] Grose.
Filth; abomination. [Obs.]To purge the snottery of our slimy time. Marston.
Foul with snot; hence, mean; dirty.-- Snort"ti*ly, adb.-- Snot"ti*ness, n.
To furnish with a nozzle or point.
Resembling a beast's snout.The nose was ugly, long, and big, Broad and snouty like a pig. Otway.
A square-rigged vessel, differing from a brig only in that shehas a trysail mast close abaft the mainmast, on which a large trysailis hoisted.
A bannerlike stream of snow blown into the air from a mountainpeak, often having a pinkish color and extending horizontally forseveral miles across the sky.
Affected with blindness by the brilliancy of snow.-- Snow"-blind`ness, n.
Enveloped in, or confined by, snow. Whittier.
Snow and water mixed, or snow just melted; very cold liquor.Shak.
Having the top capped or covered with snow; as, snow-cappedmountains.
White as snow; very white. "Snow-white and rose-red" Chaucer.
The Guelder-rose. Snowball tree (Bot.), the Guelder-rose.

A name of several shrubs with white berries; as, theSymphoricarpus racemosus of the Northern United States, and theChiococca racemosa of Florida and tropical America. Creepingsnowberry. (Bot.) See under Creeping.
A very small humming bird (Microchæra albocoronata) native ofNew Grenada.

A bulbous plant (Galanthus nivalis) bearing white flowers,which often appear while the snow is on the ground. It is cultivatedin gardens for its beauty. Snowdrop tree. See Silver-bell tree, underSilver, a.
A shelter to protect from snow, esp. a long roof over anexposed part of a railroad.

A slight frame of wood three or four feet long and about onethird as wide, with thongs or cords stretched across it, and having asupport and holder for the foot; -- used by persons for walking onsoft snow.
One who travels on snowshoes; an expert in using snowshoes. W.G. Beers.
A large mass or avalanche of snow which slips down the side ofa mountain, etc.
Having a short, flat nose, slightly turned up; as, the snub-nosed eel. Snub-nosed cachalot (Zoöl.), the pygmy sperm whale.
To lie snug or quiet. [Obs.] Herbert.
The part of a candle wick charred by the flame, whether burningor not.If the burning snuff happens to get out of the snuffers, you have achance that it may fall into a dish of soup. Swift.
A small box for carrying snuff about the person.
An instrument for cropping and holding the snuff of a candle.

To speak through the nose; to breathe through the nose when itis obstructed, so as to make a broken sound.One clad in purple Eats, and recites some lamentable rhyme . . .Snuffling at nose, and croaking in his throat. Dryden.
One who snuffles; one who uses cant.
To move one way and the other so as to get a close place; tolie close for comfort; to cuddle; to nestle.
In a snug manner; closely; safely.
The quality or state of being snug.
An upward bend in a piece of timber; the sheer of a vessel.
A curved plank, placed edgewise, to work in the bows of avessel. R. H. Dana, Jr.

Provided that; on condition that; in case that; if.Though all the winds of doctrine were let loose play upon the earth,so truth be in the field, we do injuriously, by licensing andprohibiting, to misdoubt her strength. Milton.
So named; called by such a name (but perhaps called thus withdoubtful propriety).

Neither very good nor very bad; middling; passable; tolerable;indifferent.In some Irish houses, where things are so-so, One gammon of baconhangs up for a show. Goldsmith.He [Burns] certainly wrote some so-so verses to the Tree of Liberty.Prof. Wilson.
The act of soaking, or the state of being soaked; also, thequantity that enters or issues by soaking.
Wetting thoroughly; drenching; as, a soaking rain.-- Soak"ing*ly, adv.
A chain by which a leading horse draws a plow. Knight.

A substance which dissolves in water, thus forming a lather,and is used as a cleansing agent. Soap is produced by combining fatsor oils with alkalies or alkaline earths, usually by boiling, andconsists of salts of sodium, potassium, etc., with the fatty acids(oleic, stearic, palmitic, etc.). See the Note below, and cf.Saponification. By extension, any compound of similar composition orproperties, whether used as a cleaning agent or not.
Any tree of the genus Sapindus, esp. Sapindus saponaria, thefleshy part of whose fruit is used instead of soap in washing linen;-- also called soap tree.
Any serranoid fish of the genus Rhypticus; -- so called fromthe soapy feeling of its skin.
Quality or state of being soapy.
A perennial herb (Gypsophila Struthium) the root of which isused in Spain as a substitute for soap.
A common plant (Saponaria officinalis) of the Pink family; --so called because its bruised leaves, when agitated in water, producea lather like that from soap. Called also Bouncing Bet.
The act of soaring; upward flight.This apparent soar of the hooded falcon. Coleridge.
A series of short, convulsive inspirations, the glottis beingsuddenly closed so that little or no air enters into the lungs.
To make sober.There shallow draughts intoxicate the brain, And drinking largelysobers us again. Pope.
Having a disposition or temper habitually sober.-- So"ber-mind`ed*ness, n.
In a sober manner; temperately; cooly; calmly; gravely;seriously.
The quality or state of being sober.
Producing soboles. See Illust. of Houseleek.
The unicameral national assembly of Bulgaria, elected for aterm of five years by universal suffrage of adult males.
An assumed name; a fanciful epithet or appellation; a nickname.[Sometimes less correctly written soubriquet.]

A tenure of lands and tenements by a certain or determinateservice; a tenure distinct from chivalry or knight's service, inwhich the obligations were uncertain. The service must be certain, inorder to be denominated socage, as to hold by fealty and twentyshillings rent. [Written also soccage.]
A tennant by socage; a socman.
The quality of being sociable; sociableness.
Naturally growing in groups or masses; -- said of manyindividual plants of the same species.

A theory or system of social reform which contemplates acomplete reconstruction of society, with a more just and equitabledistribution of property and labor. In popular usage, the term isoften employed to indicate any lawless, revolutionary social scheme.See Communism, Fourierism, Saint-Simonianism, forms of socialism.[Socialism] was first applied in England to Owen's theory of socialreconstruction, and in France to those also of St. Simon and Fourier. . . The word, however, is used with a great variety of meaning, . .. even by economists and learned critics. The general tendency is toregard as socialistic any interference undertaken by society onbehalf of the poor, . . . radical social reform which disturbs thepresent system of private property . . . The tendency of the presentsocialism is more and more to ally itself with the most advanceddemocracy. Encyc. Brit.We certainly want a true history of socialism, meaning by that ahistory of every systematic attempt to provide a new social existencefor the mass of the workers. F. Harrison.
One who advocates or practices the doctrines of socialism.
The quality of being social; socialness.
The quality or state of being social.
Of or pertaining to society; social.The all-sweeping besom of societarian reformation. Lamb.
Of or pertaining to Socinus, or the Socinians.

The tenets or doctrines of Faustus Socinus, an Italiantheologian of the sixteenth century, who denied the Trinity, thedeity of Christ, the personality of the Devil, the native and totaldepravity of man, the vicarious atonement, and the eternity of futurepunishment. His theory was, that Christ was a man divinelycommissioned, who had no existence before he was conceived by theVirgin Mary; that human sin was the imitation of Adam's sin, and thathuman salvation was the imitation and adoption of Christ's virtue;that the Bible was to be interpreted by human reason; and that itslanguage was metaphorical, and not to be taken literally.
To cause to conform to Socinianism; to regulate by, or imbuewith, the principles of Socinianism.
One who treats of, or devotes himself to, the study ofsociology. J. S. Mill.
That branch of philosophy which treats of the constitution,phenomena, and development of human society; social science. H.Spencer.
A combination of two hooks which close upon each other, bymeans of a spring, as soon as the fish bites. [U. S.]
Destitute of socks or shoes. B. & Fl.
One who holds lands or tenements by socage; a socager. Cowell.
A custom of tenants to grind corn at the lord's mill. Cowell.
Of or pertaining to Socotra, an island in the Indian Ocean, onthe east coast of Africa.-- n.
The philosophy or the method of Socrates.
A disciple or follower of Socrates.
Pertaining to, or containing, soda. "Sodaic powder." Ure.
A mineral of a white to blue or gray color, occuring commonlyin dodecahedrons, also massive. It is a silicate of alumina and sodawith some chlorine.
Specifically, a lay association for devotion or for charitablepurposes.
A greenish or reddish crystalline substance, NaNH2, obtained bypassing ammonia over heated sodium.
Boiled; seethed; also, soaked; heavy with moisture; saturated;as, sodden beef; sodden bread; sodden fields.
Consisting of sod; covered with sod; turfy. Cotgrave.
Of or pertaining to sodium; containing sodium.
A combining form (also used adjectively) denoting the presenceof sodium or one of its compounds.

A common metallic element of the alkali group, in nature alwaysoccuring combined, as in common salt, in albite, etc. It is isolatedas a soft, waxy, white, unstable metal, so readily oxidized that itcombines violently with water, and to be preserved must be kept underpetroleum or some similar liquid. Sodium is used combined in manysalts, in the free state as a reducer, and as a means of obtainingother metals (as magnesium and aluminium) is an important commercialproduct. Symbol Na (Natrium). Atomic weight 23. Specific gravity0.97. Sodium amalgam, an alloy of sodium and mercury, usuallyproduced as a gray metallic crystalline substance, which is used as areducing agent, and otherwise.-- Sodium bicarbonate, a white crystalline substance, HNaCO3, with aslight alkaline taste resembling that of sodium carbonate. It isfound in many mineral springs and also produced artificially,. It isused in cookery, in baking powders, and as a source of carbonic acidgas (carbon dioxide) for soda water. Called also cooking soda,saleratus, and technically, acid sodium carbonate, primary sodiumcarbonate, sodium dicarbonate, etc.-- Sodium carbonate, a white crystalline substance, Na2CO3.10H2O,having a cooling alkaline taste, found in the ashes of many plants,and produced artifically in large quantities from common salt. It isused in making soap, glass, paper, etc., and as alkaline agent inmany chemical industries. Called also sal soda, washing soda, orsoda. Cf. Sodium bicarbonate, above and Trona. Sodium chloride,common, or table, salt, NaCl.-- Sodium hydroxide, a white opaque brittle solid, NaOH, having afibrous structure, produced by the action of quicklime, or of calciumhydrate (milk of lime), on sodium carbonate. It is a strong alkali,and is used in the manufacture of soap, in making wood pulp forpaper, etc. Called also sodium hydrate, and caustic soda. Byextension, a solution of sodium hydroxide.
A salt well known as a catharic under the name of Glauber'ssalt, which term is properly applied to the hydrate, Na2SO4.10H2O.
Pertaining to, or of the nature of, sodomy.-- Sod`om*it"ic*al*ly, adv.
Carnal copulation in a manner against nature; buggery. Gen.xix. 5.
A large wooden vessel for holding water; a cowl. [Obs. or Prov.Eng.] Dr. H. More.

A word compounded of so and ever, used in composition with who,what, where, when, how, etc., and indicating any out of all possibleor supposable persons, things, places, times, ways, etc. It issometimes used separate from the pronoun or adverb.For unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required.Luke xii. 48.What great thing soever a man proposed to do in his life, he shouldthink of achieving it by fifty. Sir W. Temple.

A long seat, usually with a cushioned bottom, back, and ends; -- much used as a comfortable piece of furniture.Let fall the curtains, wheel the sofa round. Cowper.Sofa bed, a sofa so contrived that it may be extended to form a bed;-- called also sofa bedstead.
The under side of the subordinate parts and members ofbuildings, such as staircases, entablatures, archways, cornices, orthe like. See Illust. of Lintel.
A soft or foolish person; an idiot. [Colloq.] G. Eliot.
Steel low in carbon; mild steel; ingot iron.
Having the fin rays cartilaginous or flexible; without spines;-- said of certain fishes.
Having softness or tenderness of heart; susceptible of pity orother kindly affection; gentle; meek.-- Soft"-heart`ed*ness, n.
Speaking softly; having a mild or gentle voice; hence, mild;affable.
Any one attached to a Mohammedan mosque, esp. a student of thehigher branches of theology in a mosque school. [Written alsosophta.]
To make soft or more soft. Specifically: --(a) To render less hard; -- said of matter.Their arrow's point they soften in the flame. Gay.
One who, or that which, softens. [Written also, less properly,softner.]

from Soften, v. Softening of the brain, or Cerebral softening(Med.), a localized softening of the brain substance, due tohemorrhage or inflammation. Three varieties, distinguished by theircolor and representing different stages of the morbid process, areknown respectively as red, yellow, and white, softening.
A soft, effeminate person; a voluptuary. [R.] Bp. Woolton. .
The quality or state of being soft; -- opposed to Ant:hardness, and used in the various specific senses of the adjective.
Var. of Soldier. [Dial. or Slang]  R. H. Dana, Jr.
The quality or state of being soggy; soddenness; wetness.
Filled with water; soft with moisture; sodden; soaked; wet; as,soggy land or timber.
Ho; -- a word used in calling from a distant place; asportsman's halloo. Shak.

To feed, as cattle or horses, in the barn or an inclosure, withfresh grass or green food cut for them, instead of sending them outto pasture; hence (such food having the effect of purging them), topurge by feeding on green food; as, to soil a horse.
A pipe or drain for carrying off night soil.
Stain; pollution. Shak.Then fearing rust or soilure, fashioned for it A case of silk.Tennyson.
An evening party; -- distinguished from levee, and matinée.
An Asiatic leguminous herb (Glycine Soja) the seeds of whichare used in preparing the sauce called soy.

To dwell for a time; to dwell or live in a place as a temporaryresident or as a stranger, not considering the place as a permanenthabitation; to delay; to tarry.Abram went down into Egypt to sojourn there. Gen. xii. 30.Home he goeth, he might not longer sojourn. Chaucer.The soldiers first assembled at Newcastle, and there sojourned threedays. Hayward.
One who sojourns.We are strangers before thee, and sojourners. 1. Chron. xxix. 15.
The act or state of one who sojourns.
Temporary residence, as that of a stranger or a traveler. [R.]
An African anthropoid ape, supposed to be a variety of thechimpanzee.
Gold; -- so called from its brilliancy, color, and value.Chaucer.
To sing the notes of the gamut, ascending or descending; as, door ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la, si, do, or the same in reverse order.Yet can I neither solfe ne sing. Piers Plowman.
To take comfort; to be cheered. Shak.
The act of solacing, or the state of being solaced; also, thatwhich solaces. [R.]
Affording solace; as, a solacious voice. [Obs.] Bale.
Of or pertaining to plants of the natural order Solanaceæ, ofwhich the nightshade (Solanum) is the type. The order includes alsothe tobacco, ground cherry, tomato, eggplant, red pepper, and manymore.
An alkaloid produced by the action of hydrochloric acid onsolanidine, as a tasteless yellow crystalline substance.
An alkaloid produced by the decomposition of solanine, as awhite crystalline substance having a harsh bitter taste.

A poisonous alkaloid glucoside extracted from the berries ofcommon nightshade (Solanum nigrum), and of bittersweet, and frompotato sprouts, as a white crystalline substance having an acrid,burning taste; -- called also solonia, and solanina.
A hot, oppressive wind which sometimes blows in theMediterranean, particularly on the eastern coast of Spain.
Resembling a potato; -- said of a kind of cancer.
A genus of plants comprehending the potato (S. tuberosum), theeggplant (S. melongena, and several hundred other species;nightshade.
A loft or upper chamber; a garret room. [Obs.] [Written alsosoler, solere, sollar.] Oxf. Gloss.
A myth which essentially consists of allegory based upon ideasas to the sun's course, motion, influence, or the like.
The parallax of the sun, that is, the angle subtended at thesun by the semidiameter of the earth. It is 8."80, and is thefundamental datum.

Any one of several species of handsome marine spiral shells ofthe genus Solarium and allied genera. The shell is conical, andusually has a large, deep umbilicus exposing the upper whorls. Calledalso perspective shell.
Injury of a photographic picture caused by exposing it for toolong a time to the sun's light in the camera; burning; excessiveinsolation.
To injure by too long exposure to the light of the sun in thecamera; to burn.
Anything which alleviates or compensates for suffering or loss;a compensation; esp., an additional allowance, as for injuredfeelings.
A plant of the genus Soldanella, low Alpine herbs of thePrimrose family.
The country ruled by a soldan, or sultan. [Poet.] Sir W. Scott.

A metal or metallic alloy used when melted for uniting adjacentmetallic edges or surfaces; a metallic coment. Hence, anything whichunites or cements. Hard solder, a solder which fuses only at a redheat, as one composed of zinc and copper, or silver and copper, etc.-- Soft solder, a solder fusible at comparatively low temperatures;as, plumbers' solder, consisting of two parts lead and one part tin,is a soft solder.
from Solder, v. t. Soldering iron, Soldering tool, aninstrument for soldering, consisting of a bit or bolt of copperhaving a pointed or wedge-shaped end, and furnished with a handle.
The red or cuckoo gurnard (Trigla pini.) [Prov. Eng.]
Like or becoming a real soldier; brave; martial; heroic;honorable; soldierlike. "Soldierly discipline." Sir P. Sidney.
Military qualities or state; martial skill; behavior becoming asoldier. [R.] Shak.
A showy leguminous plant (Calliandra purpurea) of the WestIndies. The flowers have long tassels of purple stamens.
A small Italian coin worth a sou or a cent; the twentieth partof a lira.

The bottom of the body of a plow; -- called also slade; also,the bottom of a furrow.(b) (Far.) The horny substance under a horse's foot, which protectsthe more tender parts.(c) (Fort.) The bottom of an embrasure.(d) (Naut.) A piece of timber attached to the lower part of therudder, to make it even with the false keel. Totten.(e) (Mining) The seat or bottom of a mine; -- applied to horizontalveins or lodes. Sole leather, thick, strong, used for making thesoles of boots and shoes, and for other purposes.
One who commits a solecism. Blackwall.
Pertaining to, or involving, a solecism; incorrect. "He thoughtit made the language solecistical and absurd." Blackwall.
To commit a solecism. [R.] Dr. H. More.
Singly; alone; only; without another; as, to rest a causesolely one argument; to rely solelyn one's own strength.
Made in form; ceremonious; as, solemn war; conforming with alllegal requirements; as, probate in solemn form. Burrill. Jarman.Greenleaf. Solemn League and Covenant. See Covenant, 2.
Solemnness.Some think he wanted solemnes. Sir H. Wotton.
A solemn or formal observance; proceeding according to dueform; the formality which is necessary to render a thing done valid.
To solemnize; as, to solemnizate matrimony. [R.] Bp. Burnet.
The act of solemnizing; celebration; as, the solemnization of amarriage.
Solemnization. [R.]Though spoused, yet wanting wedlock's solemnize. Spenser.
In a solemn manner; with gravity; seriously; formally.There in deaf murmurs solemnly are wise. Dryden.I do solemnly assure the reader. Swift.
The state or quality of being solemn; solemnity;impressiveness; gravity; as, the solemnness of public worship.[Written also solemness.]
Solemn; grand; stately; splendid; magnificent. [Obs.] Chaucer.
A cradle, as for a broken limb. See Cradle, 6.
Any species of marine bivalve shells belonging to the familySolenidæ.
Of or pertaining to the solens or family Solenidæ.
The state of being sole, or alone; singleness. [R.]Chesterfield.

Either one of two species of singular West Indian insectivores,allied to the tenrec. One species (Solendon paradoxus), native of St.Domingo, is called also agouta; the other (S. Cubanus), found inCuba, is called almique.
An order of lowly organized Mollusca belonging to theIsopleura. A narrow groove takes the place of the foot of othergastropods.
Pertaining to the Selenoglypha. See Ophidia.-- n.
A suborder of serpents including those which have tubularerectile fangs, as the viper and rattlesnake. See Fang.

An electrodynamic spiral having the conjuctive wire turned backalong its axis, so as to neutralize that component of the effect ofthe current which is due to the length of the spiral, and reduce thewhole effect to that of a series of equal and parallel circularcurrents. When traversed by a current the solenoid exhibits polarityand attraction or repulsion, like a magnet.
A tribe of lophobranch fishes having a tubular snout. Thefemale carries the eggs in a ventral pouch.
A loft or garret. See Solar, n. Sir W. Scott.
The quality or state of being solert. [Obs.] Bp. Hacket.
The state of being sole, or alone; soleness. [R.] Sir E.Dering.
A volcanic area or vent which yields only sulphur vapors,steam, and the like. It represents the stages of the volcanicactivity.
To sol-fa. See Sol-fa, v. i.
The system of arranging the scale by the names do, re, mi, fa,sol, la, si, by which singing is taught; a singing exercise uponthese syllables.
A brilliant deep pink color with a purplish tinge, one of thedyes derived from aniline; -- so called from Solferino in Italy,where a battle was fought about the time of its discovery.

The second law officer in the government of Great Britain;also, a similar officer under the United States government, who isassociated with the attorney-general; also, the chief law officer ofsome of the States.

Disposed to solicit; eager to obtain something desirable, or toavoid anything evil; concerned; anxious; careful. "Solicitous of myreputation." Dryden. "He was solicitous for his advice." Calerendon.Enjoy the present, whatsoever it be, and be not solicitous about thefuture. Jer. Taylor.The colonel had been intent upon other things, and not enoughsolicitous to finish the fortifications. Clarendon.-- So*lic"it*ous*ly, adv.-- So*lic"it*ous*ness, n.

The state of being solicitous; uneasiness of mind occasioned byfear of evil or desire good; anxiety.The many cares and great labors of worldly men, their solicitude andoutward shows. Sir W. Raleigh.The mother looked at her with fond solicitude. G. W. Cable.
Having all the geometrical dimensions; cubic; as, a solid footcontains 1,728 solid inches.

Drawn out from a heated solid bar, as by a process of spiralrolling which first hollows the bar and then expands the cavity byforcing the bar over a pointed mandrel fixed in front of the rolls; -- said of a weldless tube.
A genus of yellow-flowered composite perennial herbs; golden-rod.
A small piece of money. [Obs.] Shak.

An entire union or consolidation of interests andresponsibilities; fellowship; community.Solidarity [a word which we owe to the French Communists], signifiesa fellowship in gain and loss, in honor and dishonor, in victory anddefeat, a being, so to speak, all in the same boat. Trench.The solidarity . . . of Breton and Welsh poetry. M. Arnold.
Having community of interests and responsibilities.Men are solidary, or copartners; and not isolated. M. Arnold.
To make solid or firm. [Obs.] Cowley.
Act of solidifying, or state of being solidified.
To make solid or compact.Every machine is a solidified mechanical theorem. H. Spencer.

The doctrine that refers all diseases to morbid changes of thesolid parts of the body. It rests on the view that the solids aloneare endowed with vital properties, and can receive the impression ofagents tending to produce disease.
An advocate of, or believer in, solidism. Dunglison.
The solid contents of a body; volume; amount of inclosed space.
In a solid manner; densely; compactly; firmly; truly.
A tribe of ungulates which includes the horse, ass, and relatedspecies, constituting the family Equidæ.
One who maintains that faith alone, without works, issufficient for justification; -- opposed to nullifidian. Hammond.
Like the sun in form, appearance, or nature; resembling thesun. [R.] "Soliform things." Cudworth.
A division of arachnids having large, powerful fangs and asegmented abdomen; -- called also Solpugidea, and Solpugides.
To utter a soliloquy; to talk to one's self.

A mammal having a single hoof on each foot, as the horses andasses; a solidungulate. [Written also solipede.]The solipeds, or firm-hoofed animals, as horses, asses, and mules,etc., -- they are, also, in mighty number. Sir T. Browne.
Following the course of the sun; as, solisequious plants. [R.]Sir T. Browne.
A hermit; a solitary. [Obs.] Sir R. Twisden.
The state of being solitary; solitariness. [Obs.] Cudworth.
In a solitary manner; in solitude; alone. Mic. vii. 14.

Not associated with others of the same kind. Solitary ant(Zoöl.), any solitary hymenopterous insect of the family Mutillidæ.The female of these insects is destitute of wings and has a powerfulsting. The male is winged and resembles a wasp. Called also spiderant.-- Solitary bee (Zoöl.), any species of bee which does not formcommunities.-- Solitary sandpiper (Zoöl.), an American tattler (Totanussolitarius).-- Solitary snipe (Zoöl.), the great snipe. [Prov. Eng.] -- Solitarythrush (Zoöl.) the starling. [Prov. Eng.]
A platform in a shaft, especially one of those between theseries of ladders in a shaft.
A flexible steel shoe (or one of the plates forming such ashoe), worn with mediæval armor.
The act of sol-faing. [Written also solmisation.]
A tune, air, strain, or a whole piece, played by a singleperson on an instrument, or sung by a single voice.
A card game played with the full pack ranking as at whist, eachplayer declaring for which of seven different points he proposes toplay.
One who sings or plays a solo.

One of the kings of Israel, noted for his superior wisdom andmagnificent reign; hence, a very wise man.-- Sol`o*mon"ic, a. Solomon's seal (Bot.), a perennial liliaceousplant of the genus Polygonatum, having simple erect or curving stemsrising from thick and knotted rootstocks, and with white or greenishnodding flowers. The commonest European species is Polygonatummultiflorum. P. biflorum and P. giganteum are common in the EasternUnited States. See Illust. of Rootstock. False Solomon's seal (Bot.),any plant of the liliaceous genus Smilacina having small whitishflowers in terminal racemes or panicles.
A celebrated Athenian lawmaker, born about 638 b. c.; hence, alegislator; a publicist; -- often used ironically.
Of or pertaining to the Solifugæ.-- n.
The tendency to separate readily into parts by spuriousarticulations, as the pods of tick trefoil.
Quality or state of being soluble.
Not adhering; loose; -- opposed to adnate; as, a solutestipule.

The act or process by which a body (whether solid, liquid, orgaseous) is absorbed into a liquid, and, remaining or becoming fluid,is diffused throughout the solvent; also, the product reulting fromsuch absorption.
Tending to dissolve; loosening; laxative. Bacon.

To explain; to resolve; to unfold; to clear up out to a resultor conclusion; as, to solve a doubt; to solve difficulties; to solvea problem.True piety would effectually solve such scruples. South.God shall solve the dark decrees of fate. Tickell.
The quality or state of being solvent.

A substance (usually liquid) suitable for, or employed in,solution, or in dissolving something; as, water is the appropriatesolvent of most salts, alcohol of resins, ether of fats, and mercuryor acids of metal, etc.
One who, or that which, solves.
The whole axial portion of an animal, including the head, neck,trunk, and tail. B. G. Wilder.
The science which treats of the general properties of matter;somatology.
One who admits the existence of material beings only; amaterialist. Glanvill.
A cavity in the primary nectocalyx of certain Siphonophora. SeeIllust. under Nectocalyx.

The outer, or parietal, one of the two lamellæ into which thevertebrate blastoderm divides on either side of the notochord, andfrom which the walls of the body and the amnion are developed. SeeSplanchopleure.
of or pertaining to the somatopleure.
A directive influence exercised by a mass of matter upongrowing organs. Encyc. Brit.
A kind of broad-brimmed hat, worn in Spain and in SpanishAmerica. Marryat.
Gloomy; somber. "Tall and sombrous pines." Longfellow.-- Som"brous*ly, adv.-- Som"brous*ness, n.
In some degree; somewhat. [Written also sumdel, sumdeale, andsumdele.] [Obs.] "She was somedeal deaf." Chaucer.Thou lackest somedeal their delight. Spenser.

In one way or another; in some way not yet known or designated;by some means; as, the thing must be done somehow; he lives somehow.By their action upon one another they may be swelled somehow, so asto shorten the length. Cheyne.

, adv. In some degree; somewhat; to some exrent; at somedistance. Shak.I something fear my father's wrath. Shak.We have something fairer play than a reasoner could have expectedformerly. Burke.My sense of touch is something coarse. Tennyson.It must be done to-night, And something from the palace. Shak.
Having been formerly; former; late; whilom.Our sometime sister, now our queen. Shak.Ion, our sometime darling, whom we prized. Talfourd.
Former; sometime. [Obs.]Thy sometimes brother's wife. Shak.
In some degree or measure; a little.His giantship is gone, somewhat crestfallen. Milton.Somewhat back from the village street. Longfellow.
In some place unknown or not specified; in one place oranother. "Somewhere nigh at hand." Milton.
Once; for a time.Though, under color of shepherds, somewhile There crept in wolves,full of fraund and guile. Spenser.
To some indeterminate place; to some place or other.Driven by the winds of temptation somewhither. Barrow.
One of the actual or ideal serial segments of which an animal,esp. an articulate or vertebrate, is composed; somatome; metamere.-- So*mit`ic, a.
Of or pertaining to somnambulism; somnambulistic. Mrs.Browning.
The act of walking in sleep.

A condition of the nervous system in which an individual duringsleep performs actions approppriate to the waking state; a state ofsleep in which some of the senses and voluntary powers are partiallyawake; noctambulism.
A person who is subject to somnambulism; one who walks in hissleep; a sleepwalker; a noctambulist.

Of or pertaining to a somnambulist or somnambulism; affected bysomnambulism; appropriate to the state of a somnambulist.Whether this was an intentional and waking departure, or asomnambulistic leave-taking and waking in her sleep, may remain asubject of contention. Dickens.
A summoner; esp., one who summons to an ecclesiastical court.[Obs.] Piers Plowman.
Of or pertaining to sleep or dreams.The somnial magic superinducted on, without suspending, the activepowers of the mind. Coleridge.
Pertaining to sleep or dreams; somnial. [Obs. or R.] Urquhart.
Causing or inducing sleep; soporific; dormitive; as, asomniferous potion. Walton.
The act of talking in one's sleep; somniloquism.
The act or habit of talking in one's sleep; somniloquy.Coleridge.
One who talks in his sleep.
A talking in sleep; the talking of one in a state ofsomnipathy. [R.] Coleridge.
A person in a state of somniapathy.
Sleep from sympathy, or produced by mesmerism or the like.[Written also somnopathy.]
Sleepy; drowsy; inclined to sleep.-- Som"no*lent*ly, adv.He had no eye for such phenomens, because he had a somnolent want ofinterest in them. De Quincey.
The somnolent state induced by animal magnetism. Thomas (Med.Dict.).
A summoner; an apparitor; a sompnour. [Obs.] Piers Plowman.

Jesus Christ, the Savior; -- called the Son of God, and the Sonof man.We . . . do testify that the Father sent the Son to be the Savior ofthe world. 1 John iv. 14.Who gave His Son sure all has given. Keble.
The husband of one's daughter; a man in his relationship to hiswife's parents.To take me as for thy son in lawe. Chaucer.

Uttered, as an element of speech, with tone or proper vocalsound, as distinguished from mere breath sound; intonated; voiced;tonic; the opposite of nonvocal, or surd; -- sid of the vowels,semivowels, liquids, and nasals, and particularly of the consonantsb, d, g hard, v, etc., as compared with their cognates p, t, k, f,etc., which are called nonvocal, surd, or aspirate.-- n.
An extended composition for one or two instruments, consistingusually of three or four movements; as, Beethoven's sonatas for thepiano, for the violin and piano, etc.
The musk shrew. See under Musk.

A special class of small yachts developed in Germany under thepatronage of Emperor William and Prince Henry of Prussia, and socalled because these yachts do not conform to the restrictions forthe regular classes established by the rules of the InternationalYacht Racing Union. In yachts of the sonderclass, as prescribed forthe season of 1911, the  aggregate of the length on water line,extreme beam, and extreme draft must be not more than 32 feet; theweight, not less than 4,035 pounds (without crew); the sail area, notmore than 550 square yards; and the cost of construction (forAmerican boats) not more than $2400. The crew must be amateurs andcitizens of the country in which the yacht was built.
The art of making songs or verse; metrical composition;versification.A half-effected inscription. Written with little skill of songcraft.Longfellow.
Disposed to sing; full of song.
Destitute of the power of song; without song; as, songlessbirds; songless woods.
A woman who sings; a female singing bird. Thomson.
A kind of ear trumpet for the deaf, or the partially deaf.
The act of producing sound, as the stridulation of insects.
Being without a son. Marston.As no baron who was sonless could give a husband to his daughter,save with his lord's consent. J. R. Green.
To compose sonnets. "Strains that come almost to sonneting."Milton.
A composer of sonnets, or small poems; a small poet; -- usuallyin contempt.What woful stuff this madrigal would be In some starved hackneysonneteer or me! Pope.
A sonneter, or sonneteer. Bp. Hall.
Like the sun; sunny; golden. [Obs.] "Her sonnish hairs."Chaucer.

An instrument for exhibiting the transverse vibrations ofcords, and ascertaining the relations between musical notes. Itconsists of a cord stretched by weight along a box, and divided intodifferent lengths at pleasure by a bridge, the place of which isdetermined by a scale on the face of the box.

Pertaining to or designating the arid division of the Australzone, including the warmer parts of the western United States andcentral Mexico. It is divided into the Upper Sonoran, which lies nextto the Transition zone, and the Lower Sonoran, next to the Tropical.
Producing sound; as, the sonorific quality of a body. [R.] I.Watts.
The quality or state of being sonorous; sonorousness.

Sonant; vibrant; hence, of sounds produced in a cavity, deep-toned; as, sonorous rhonchi. Sonorous figures (Physics), figuresformed by the vibrations of a substance capable of emitting a musicaltone, as when the bow of a violin is drawn along the edge of a pieceof glass or metal on which sand is strewed, and the sand arrangesitself in figures according to the musical tone. Called also acousticfigures.-- Sonorous tumor (Med.), a tumor which emits a clear, resonantsound on percussion.-- So*no"rous*ly, adv.-- So*no"rous*ness, n.
The state of being a son, or of bearing the relation of a son;filiation. Dr. H. More.
A knitted worsted jacket, worn over the waist of a woman'sdress.
Probably from "saintes" saints, or from sanctities; -- used asan oath. [Obs.] Shak.

In the western United States, one who settles on governmentland before it is legally open to settlement in order to gain theprior claim that the law gives to the first settler when the land isopened to settlement; hence, any one who does a thing prematurely oranticipates another in acting in order to gain an unfair advantage.
A preparation of antimony with which Mohammedan men anointtheir eyelids.
A kind of dolphin (Platanista Gangeticus) native of the riverGanges; the Gangetic dolphin. It has a long, slender, somewhatspatulate beak. [Written also susu.]

A black substance formed by combustion, or disengaged from fuelin the process of combustion, which rises in fine particles, andadheres to the sides of the chimney or pipe conveying the smoke;strictly, the fine powder, consisting chiefly of carbon, which colorssmoke, and which is the result of imperfect combustion. See Smoke.

A kind of false birth, fabled to be produced by Dutch womenfrom sitting over their stoves; also, an abortion, in a figurativesense; an abortive scheme.Fruits of dull heat, and sooterkins of wit. Pope.
One who, or that which, soothes.

Firmly fixed in, or founded upon, the thruth; true; genuine;real; also, truthful; faithful. [Archaic] -- Sooth"fast`ness, n.[Archaic] "In very soothfastness." Chaucer.Why do not you . . . bear leal and soothfast evidence in her behalf,as ye may with a clear conscience! Sir W. Scott.
In truth; truly; really; verily. [Obs.] "Soothly for to say."Chaucer.
To foretell; to predict. "You can not soothsay." Shak. "Oldsoothsaying Glaucus' spell." Milton.
The quality or state of being sooty; fuliginousness. Johnson.
To black or foul with soot. [R.]Sootied with noisome smoke. Chapman.
To steep or dip in any liquid.
Sophism. [Obs.]I trow ye study aboute some sophime. Chaucer.

The doctrine or mode of reasoning practiced by a sophist;hence, any fallacy designed to deceive.When a false argument puts on the appearance of a true one, then itis properly called a sophism, or "fallacy". I. Watts.Let us first rid ourselves of sophisms, those of depraved men, andthose of heartless philosophers. I. Taylor.
A student who is advanced beyond the first year of hisresidence.

To render worthless by admixture; to adulterate; to damage; topervert; as, to sophisticate wine. Howell.To sophisticate the understanding. Southey.Yet Butler professes to stick to plain facts, not to sophisticate,not to refine. M. Arnold.They purchase but sophisticated ware. Dryden.
The act of sophisticating; adulteration; as, the sophisticationof drugs. Boyle.
One belonging to the second of the four classes in an Americancollege, or one next above a freshman. [Formerly written alsosophimore.]
To lay asleep; to put to sleep; to quiet. [Obs.]The king's declaration for the sopiting of all Arminian heresies.Fuller.
The act of putting to sleep, or the state of being put tosleep; sleep. [Obs.]Dementation and sopition of reason. Sir T. Browne.
Profound sleep from which a person can be roused only withdifficulty.
To lay or put to sleep; to stupefy. [Obs.] Cudworth.
Causing sleep; somniferous; soporific. "Soporiferous medicine."Swift. --- Sop`o*rif"er*ous*ly, adv.-- Sop`o*rif"er*ous*ness, n.
Causing sleep; tending to cause sleep; soporiferous; as, thesoporific virtues of opium.
more recent version of soppy. Used esp. in phrase sopping wet.
Soaked or saturated with liquid or moisture; very wet orsloppy.It [Yarmouth] looked rather spongy and soppy. Dickens.
See Sops of wine, under Sop.

A North American rail (Porzana Carolina) common in the EasternUnited States.
